5.name: Current Below Normal Or Open Circuit
5.description_tr: Akım normalin altında veya açık devre (Kablo Kopuk / Temassız)
5.diagnostic_action: Aktüatör/solenoid bobin direncini ölçün ve soket kilit tırnaklarını kontrol edin.

6.name: Current Above Normal Or Grounded Circuit
6.description_tr: Akım normalin üzerinde veya devre şasiye aşırı yüklenmiş
6.diagnostic_action: Bobin sargısında dahili izolasyon delinmesi veya aktüatör mekanik sıkışması kontrolü yapın.

7.name: Mechanical System Not Responding Or Out Of Adjustment
7.description_tr: Mekanik sistem yanıt vermiyor veya kalibrasyon dışı (Mekanik Sıkışma)

8.name: Abnormal Frequency Or Pulse Width Or Period
8.description_tr: Anormal frekans, darbe genişliği (PWM) veya periyot

9.name: Abnormal Update Rate
9.description_tr: Anormal veri güncelleme hızı (CAN Zaman Aşımı)
9.diagnostic_action: Sensör veya kaynak modülün CAN-Bus hattına bağlı olduğunu ve adres aldığını (Address Claim) doğrulayın.

10.name: Abnormal Rate Of Change
10.description_tr: Anormal değişim hızı (Fiziksel Olarak İmkansız Sıçrama)
10.diagnostic_action: Sensör içindeki elemanın gevşediğini veya soket pini korozyonunu inceleyin.

11.name: Root Cause Not Known

16.name: Data Valid But Above Normal - Moderate Severity

16.diagnostic_action: Motor tork sınırlandırması (Derate) başlamadan önce ilgili devreyi temizleyin.

17.name: Data Valid But Below Normal - Least Severe Level

dd_procedures.title: Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 1 – Engine Oil Pressure Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 1 – Engine Oil Pressure Low
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 1 indicates that engine oil pressure has dropped below safe operating levels. This condition may trigger immediate engine protection derate.
Symptoms
Oil pressure warning light
Audible engine noise
Reduced engine power
Check engine light illuminated
Possible shutdown warning
Cause
This fault may be caused by low oil level, worn oil pump, clogged oil filter, internal engine wear, or faulty oil pressure sensor.
Can You Keep Driving?
Driving is not recommended. Low oil pressure can result in severe engine damage if not addressed immediately.
Recommended Action
Safely stop the vehicle and check oil level. Inspect for leaks. Do not continue driving if oil pressure remains low. Seek professional diagnostics immediately.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 1 mean?
 
SPN 100 FMI 1 indicates that engine oil pressure has dropped below safe operating limits and may trigger engine protection.
 
 
What causes SPN 100 FMI 1?
 
Common causes include low oil level, clogged oil filter, failing oil pump, internal engine wear, or a faulty oil pressure sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 100 FMI 1?
 
Driving is not recommended. Low oil pressure can cause severe engine damage if the vehicle continues operating.
 
 
Will SPN 100 FMI 1 cause a shutdown?
 
Yes. If oil pressure remains low, the engine control module may reduce power or initiate shutdown to protect internal components.
 
 
How do I fix SPN 100 FMI 1?
 
Stop the vehicle safely, check oil level immediately, inspect for leaks, and seek professional diagnostics before restarting the engine.

procedures_full.overview: On Kenworth, SPN 100 FMI 0 is a Engine Oil Pressure fault (Data Valid But Above Normal Operating Range - Most Severe Level). Prove wiring/live data first; do not parts-cannon the component. This guide covers symptoms, root causes, live-data checks, and misdiagnoses for Kenworth platforms.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie or Diesel Laptops and record SPN 100 FMI 0 with freeze-frame load/temp.
Inspect harness and connector at the engine oil pressure for chafe, corrosion, and bent pins.
Verify 5V reference / ground / signal integrity with a multimeter where applicable.
Compare PID to mechanical gauge at idle and rated
Repair the proven fault, clear only after repair, and verify under the same conditions as freeze-frame.

Soft power, unstable idle, or poor response when engine oil pressure data is irrational.
procedures_full.source_title: Kenworth SPN 100 FMI 0: Engine Oil Pressure Diagnosis

procedures_full.overview: FMI 1 on engine oil pressure indicates the sensor reports below the minimum acceptable pressure for current speed and temperature conditions. Low oil level, wrong viscosity, worn pump or bearings, restricted pickup, sensor bias, and overheated oil are the primary causes. False low from a failed sender is a common cause that triggers unnecessary engine teardown. True low pressure from oil dilution events — fuel or coolant in oil — is a documented pattern that requires oil condition evaluation before any internal engine work. A mechanical gauge is mandatory before any internal engine conclusions.
causes: Low oil level — insufficient oil volume
Wrong viscosity — oil too thin for conditions
Worn pump or bearings — internal engine wear
Restricted pickup — screen plugged with debris
Sensor bias — failed sender reading low
Overheated oil — viscosity breakdown from thermal stress
Oil dilution — fuel or coolant contamination reducing viscosity
steps: Single Action Gate — Oil Level and Condition Check

Check oil level and condition immediately. Low oil level is the most common cause of true low oil pressure. Inspect oil for fuel dilution (thin, fuel smell), coolant contamination (milky appearance), or overheating (dark, burned smell).
Binary Decision Gate — Mechanical Gauge Verification

Install a mechanical gauge and verify actual oil pressure at idle and at operating speed. This is mandatory before any internal engine conclusions. A mechanical gauge reading normal with a low ECM reading confirms sender failure.
Override Manager — Oil Dilution Assessment

If oil condition shows dilution, identify the source before any engine work. Fuel dilution from injector faults or failed injection seals and coolant contamination from head gasket or cooler leaks both reduce oil viscosity and pressure.
Safety Interceptor — Sender Circuit Check
If mechanical gauge confirms true low pressure, verify sender circuit before internal engine work. A short-to-ground signal fault can cause false low readings that trigger protection events.
Resume Point — Pickup Screen Inspection
If true low pressure is confirmed with good oil level and condition, inspect the oil pickup screen. A plugged pickup screen from sludge or debris restricts oil flow to the pump.
Verification Loop — Post-Service Pressure Confirmation

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 1 on a Detroit Diesel engine is a critical, confirmed-valid oil pressure fault that triggers immediate engine protection shutdown on DD13, DD15, and DD16 platforms. The ECM has confirmed pressure is below the minimum survivable level and cut fuel to prevent bearing damage. This is a tow-truck situation unless a mechanical gauge immediately confirms normal pressure.
causes: Worn or failed oil pump (mechanical)
High

The gear-type oil pump on DD13/DD15 engines wears through normal service life. Above 750,000 miles, rotor-to-housing and gear-mesh clearances commonly exceed the maximum allowable value, producing internal bypass severe enough to drop oil pressure below the FMI 1 threshold at hot idle.
Spun or severely worn main/rod bearings (mechanical)
Medium–High

Worn or seized bearings dramatically increase the lube circuit's internal flow path, allowing oil to escape faster than the pump can maintain pressure. This is the worst-case finding—metallic debris in the oil filter element or magnetic drain plug is the tell.
Oil pressure sensor internal short-to-ground (electrical/sensor)
Medium

The sender's sensing element can develop an internal short to the sensor body, pulling the ECM signal line to near 0V regardless of actual lube circuit pressure. Only a mechanical gauge test can distinguish a shorted sensor from genuine mechanical low pressure.
Oil filter module O-ring bypass (mechanical)
Medium

The main seal O-ring on the DD15 integrated filter/cooler module is a known wear point. A damaged or incorrectly seated O-ring routes pressurized oil from supply to return without passing through the lube galleries, producing a real measured pressure drop.
Internal oil gallery plug failure (mechanical)
Low

A dislodged or blown gallery plug can dump pressurized oil internally faster than the pump can sustain circuit pressure, causing sudden FMI 1 onset with no prior FMI 18 history. Look for this on engines that recently had a head or block repair.
steps: 1. Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) or Diesel Laptops and pull the full fault history. Check whether SPN 100 FMI 18 preceded this FMI 1 event—gradual onset vs. sudden onset changes the diagnostic direction.
2. Check oil level with the dipstick before anything else. On a DD15, being a full quart low is enough to trigger FMI 18 at idle; two quarts low will reach FMI 1.

3. Install a calibrated mechanical gauge at the primary pressure tap on the DD13/DD15 block (main gallery port near the oil filter module). Crank the engine—if pressure does not build above 15 psi within 5 seconds of cranking, stop and investigate immediately.
4. Note cold-start cranking pressure: healthy DD15 reaches 30+ psi within 3 seconds. Full warm idle spec: 15 psi minimum. Normal operating range at speed: 40–65 psi.

5. If mechanical pressure is confirmed critically low, shut down immediately. Inspect the oil filter module O-ring (DD15 known wear point) for bypass, check for external oil leaks, and inspect the filter element for metallic debris.

6. If mechanical gauge reads normal while DDDL shows low, the sensor is the suspect. Disconnect the connector and measure reference supply voltage (should be 5V ± 0.25V) and signal pin voltage with a multimeter. An internal short-to-ground pulls the signal to 0V.
7. Replace sensor only after confirming mechanical pressure is in spec. Reset fault in DDDL, monitor live data at operating temperature for 20+ minutes before releasing.
symptoms: Red stop engine lamp (SEL) with immediate fuel cutoff on DD13/DD15/DD16
Engine shuts down within seconds of fault activation—no 30-second window
Mechanical oil pressure gauge confirms below 5 psi at idle
SPN 100 FMI 18 (moderate precursor) often found in recent fault history
Possible audible rod knock if the engine was run through an early pressure-decline event

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 1 on a Volvo is a critical low oil pressure fault. Always verify actual oil pressure with a mechanical gauge before restarting — a failed sensor is common, but true low pressure causes catastrophic engine damage within seconds.
causes: Failed or out-of-calibration oil pressure sensor
The electronic oil pressure sensor on Volvo D13/D11 engines is a wear item that can fail to report correct pressure after extended service, triggering a false FMI 1 fault despite normal lubrication.
Low engine oil level
Insufficient oil volume allows the oil pump to ingest air under certain operating conditions (cornering, heavy grade, hard braking), causing momentary real pressure drops.
Clogged oil filter or restricted oil passage
An overdue oil filter or debris in a main oil gallery restricts oil flow, reducing delivery pressure below the minimum threshold.
Oil pump wear or relief valve failure
A worn oil pump gear set or a stuck-open relief valve allows oil to bypass internally, reducing system pressure — a serious condition requiring immediate engine removal for inspection.
steps: Do not continue operating the engine if the red stop lamp is illuminated. Pull over safely and shut down. Connect a Texa or Jaltest diagnostic tool to confirm SPN 100 FMI 1 is the active fault and identify any companion codes.

Check the engine oil level using the dipstick. If oil level is low, add the correct specification oil and restart to see if pressure returns. A low oil level causing real low pressure will always produce knocking noise — do not restart if knocking is audible.

Install a mechanical oil pressure gauge in the sending unit port to verify the actual oil pressure independently of the electronic sensor. If mechanical pressure is normal (typically 25–80 PSI at operating temperature and idle), the issue is the sensor or wiring, not a lubrication failure.

Test the oil pressure sensor circuit with a digital multimeter. With the ignition ON and engine OFF, measure sensor supply voltage and signal output. A signal voltage stuck at 0 V with normal supply voltage indicates a failed sensor.

If mechanical oil pressure is confirmed low, inspect the engine oil filter for restriction, the oil pump relief valve for sticking open, and any recent engine work that may have left an oil passage blocked.
symptoms: Red stop lamp illuminated with immediate derate or engine shutdown.
Oil pressure gauge reading below minimum operating band.
Engine knocking or bearing noise in true low-pressure scenarios.
SPN 100 FMI 1 stored as active fault — may be accompanied by a driver alert to stop immediately.
Loss of power followed by automatic engine shutdown in severe cases.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 2 means Detroit ECM oil pressure readings are erratic or intermittent, not steadily low. The fault can cause unexpected derates or shutdowns. Confirm real pressure with a mechanical gauge and inspect wiring before replacing the sensor assembly. Erratic oil pressure codes frustrate drivers because the truck runs fine until it does not. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats Detroit SPN 100 FMI 2 as a signal-integrity problem first and a mechanical problem second, because the FMI tells you the data itself is unstable.

Vibration and heat cycling break conductors inside the harness, producing dropouts that match FMI 2.
Failing oil pressure sensor with internal intermittent element

steps: Log the fault in Detroit DDDL8 with timestamp, RPM, and oil temperature freeze-frame data before clearing anything.

Inspect the sensor ground path to the cylinder head stud. Clean star washers and torque to spec; poor ground is a top cause of erratic FMI 2 readings.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 3 indicates the oil pressure sensor signal is above the expected voltage range. On 5V ratiometric sensors, an open circuit causes the signal to float toward the reference voltage, producing a high-voltage reading. A failed sender can trigger false engine protection events — shutdown or derate — without any actual oil pressure problem. Connector corrosion near oil filters and coolers is a documented cause. Confirming true oil pressure with a mechanical gauge is mandatory for safety before any engine operation decisions.
causes: Open signal circuit — signal floating toward reference voltage
Failed sensor — internal open circuit
Connector corrosion — near oil filters and coolers
Harness damage — pigtail damage near filters or coolers
steps: Single Action Gate — Mechanical Gauge Safety Check

Install a mechanical gauge and verify actual oil pressure immediately. This is a safety-critical step — a failed sender can trigger false engine protection events. Confirm true oil pressure is adequate before any other diagnostic work.
Binary Decision Gate — Sender Circuit Check

With true pressure confirmed safe, check sender circuit. Verify 5V reference and ground at the sender connector. Measure signal voltage — a signal near reference voltage with the sender connected indicates an open signal circuit or failed sender.
Override Manager — Sender Disconnect Test

Disconnect the sender and re-evaluate the circuit. If signal drops with sender disconnected, the sender has an internal open. If signal remains high with sender disconnected, the fault is in the harness or ECM.
Safety Interceptor — Connector and Harness Inspection
Inspect sender pigtail for damage near oil filters and coolers. Connector corrosion from oil contamination near the sender is a documented cause of FMI 3 on oil pressure circuits.
Resume Point — Continuity Test
Perform continuity test on signal wire from sender connector to ECM connector. An open wire confirms harness fault rather than sender failure.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Confirmation
After repair, verify signal voltage is within OEM specification. Confirm mechanical gauge pressure matches ECM sender reading.
Repair Ledger Output — Sender or Harness Decision
Replace sender if internal open is confirmed by disconnect test. Repair harness if open wire is found. Always confirm with mechanical gauge after repair.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1. Install mechanical gauge to confirm true oil pressure before any repair.
2. Repair any open signal wire or harness damage found.
3. Repair connector corrosion near oil filters or coolers.
4. Replace oil pressure sender if internal open is confirmed.
5. Verify mechanical gauge matches ECM reading after repair.
Verification Steps
Confirm mechanical gauge pressure matches ECM sender reading after repair.
Verify signal voltage is within OEM specification after repair.
Confirm SPN 100 FMI 3 does not return after repair.
Monitor for false protection events after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect oil pressure sender pigtail at every oil change.
✓ Protect sender connector from oil contamination.
✓ Address oil leaks near the sender connector promptly.
✓ Inspect sender circuit at every major service.

Medium electrically; treat as High until true pressure is confirmed safe with a mechanical gauge. A failed sender can trigger false engine protection events. Never operate without confirming true oil pressure.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 3 means the oil pressure sensor circuit is shorted high or open, not that oil pressure is actually too high. It's High severity because the ECM treats any oil pressure signal fault cautiously. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com never skips the mechanical gauge cross-check on this fault, since missing a real low-pressure condition can be catastrophic.
causes: Failed oil pressure sensor
Electrical fault - internal sensor failure sends an implausible high-voltage signal.
Chafed harness wire shorted to a power source
Electrical fault - a wire rubbing against a powered circuit near the filter housing injects voltage onto the signal line.
Corroded sensor connector
Electrical fault - a compromised connection produces an erratic high-voltage signal.
Genuine oil pump or regulator failure
A true mechanical failure - only relevant if a mechanical gauge check confirms an actual abnormal pressure reading.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) or Jaltest and confirm the fault is active, comparing the reported value against a mechanical test gauge.
Unplug the oil pressure sensor connector and check for a short to power or an open ground on the signal wire.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 3 means the oil pressure sensor circuit is shorted high or open, not that oil pressure is actually too high. It's High severity because the ECM treats any oil pressure signal problem cautiously, even though this is typically just an electrical fault. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always verifies real oil pressure with a mechanical gauge on this fault before touching any wiring, since the consequences of missing a genuine low-pressure condition are severe.

Electrical fault - internal sensor failure sends an out-of-range high signal to the ECM.
Chafed harness wire shorted to a power source
Electrical fault - a wire rubbing against a powered circuit near the turbo or filter housing injects voltage onto the signal line.
Corroded sensor connector
Electrical fault - a compromised connection can produce an erratic high-voltage reading.
Genuine oil pump or pressure regulator failure
A true mechanical failure - only relevant if a mechanical gauge check confirms an actual abnormal pressure reading rather than a sensor circuit fault.
steps: Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and confirm whether the fault is active, then compare the reported oil pressure value against a mechanical test gauge for cross-reference.
Unplug the oil pressure sensor connector and check for battery voltage or a short to power on the signal wire with the sensor disconnected.

Inspect the connector and harness for corrosion or chafing near the oil filter housing and turbocharger, where heat exposure is highest.
Install a mechanical oil pressure gauge directly on the engine block as a cross-check before condemning the sensor, especially if the truck has any history of oil pressure complaints.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 17 on Detroit DD13/DD15 engines means oil pressure is reading below normal at the least severe level. Despite the mild FMI rating, treat any oil pressure fault as high-severity - it's an early warning worth chasing down immediately rather than dismissing. Oil pressure codes deserve more respect than their FMI severity level sometimes suggests. SPN 100 FMI 17 is technically the least severe stage of a low oil pressure reading, but ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats every oil pressure fault the same way - as a warning that protects the most expensive parts of the engine from irreversible damage. The good news is the most common cause is also the simplest to check: oil level.
causes: Low engine oil level
Oil consumption, a slow leak, or a missed top-off between service intervals can drop the level enough to reduce pump pickup efficiency and pressure.
Incorrect oil viscosity or degraded oil condition
Fuel dilution or using the wrong viscosity for ambient conditions can reduce pressure, particularly noticeable at idle.
Faulty oil pressure sensor or corroded connector
A sensor reading falsely low can trigger the fault without an actual pressure problem, but this should only be assumed after confirming with a mechanical gauge.
Worn oil pump or restricted pickup screen
Mechanical wear in the oil pump or a partially blocked pickup screen reduces actual pressure and requires professional evaluation to confirm and repair.
steps: Pull the fault with DDDL and confirm SPN 100 FMI 17 is active; check the reported oil pressure value at idle and at a moderate RPM against the engine's known-good specification.
Check the oil level on the dipstick first - low oil level is the single most common and easiest-to-fix cause of a low pressure reading.
Inspect the oil pressure sensor and its wiring for corrosion or a loose connector that could produce a falsely low reading.
If oil level is correct and the sensor checks out electrically, install a mechanical oil pressure gauge at the test port to confirm whether the low reading reflects a real condition.
If mechanical pressure is genuinely low, check oil viscosity and condition - the wrong viscosity oil or an overdue oil change with excessive dilution can reduce pressure, especially at idle.
If pressure remains low after ruling out level, sensor, and oil condition, escalate to a professional inspection of the oil pump and pickup screen before continuing operation.
symptoms: Slightly lower-than-normal oil pressure reading on the dash gauge or scan tool
Amber Check Engine lamp
No obvious performance symptom in the earliest stages
Possible ticking or knocking noise if the condition has been present for a while without being caught
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 17: Diagnosing Low Engine Oil Pressure

procedures_full.overview: FMI 18 on engine oil pressure indicates the oil pressure is below the moderate calibrated threshold for the current speed and temperature conditions. Low level, wrong viscosity, hot idle pressure drop from wear, restricted pickup screen, weak pump, sensor bias low, and fuel dilution are the primary causes. False lows from failed senders and true lows after dilution from injector leak-down are documented patterns. Mechanical gauge verification is mandatory before internal engine conclusions — a sensor that reads low while the engine has adequate pressure is a sensor fault, not an engine fault.
causes: Low level — oil level below specification reducing pump supply
Wrong viscosity — incorrect oil viscosity for conditions
Hot idle pressure drop from wear — bearing wear producing low hot idle pressure
Restricted pickup screen — pickup screen restriction reducing pump supply
Weak pump — oil pump wear reducing output pressure
Sensor bias low — oil pressure sensor bias producing false low reading
Fuel dilution — fuel dilution reducing oil viscosity and pressure
steps: Single Action Gate — Level and Condition Check

Check oil level and condition before any pressure diagnosis. Low oil level reduces pump supply and produces low pressure. Contaminated or fuel-diluted oil has reduced viscosity and produces low pressure. Confirm oil level is correct and oil condition is acceptable — check for fuel smell and low viscosity on the dipstick.
Binary Decision Gate — Mechanical Gauge Verification

Install a mechanical gauge and verify oil pressure. Mechanical gauge verification is mandatory before internal engine conclusions. A mechanical gauge reading that is normal while the ECM reports low pressure confirms a sensor fault. A mechanical gauge reading that confirms low pressure requires further diagnosis.
Override Manager — Check for Fuel Dilution

Check for fuel dilution if oil condition is suspect. Fuel dilution from injector leak-down reduces oil viscosity and produces low pressure. Check for fuel smell on the dipstick and low viscosity. Identify the source of fuel dilution before any engine repair.
Safety Interceptor — Evaluate Hot Idle vs High-RPM Pressure

Evaluate hot idle pressure versus high-RPM pressure. A pressure that is low at hot idle but acceptable at higher RPM suggests bearing wear or pump wear. A pressure that is low at all speeds suggests a more severe fault. Compare hot idle and high-RPM pressure to OEM specifications.
Resume Point — Mechanical Diagnosis Only With Gauge Proof

Perform mechanical diagnosis only with gauge proof of low pressure. A mechanical gauge that confirms low pressure at hot idle or all speeds justifies further mechanical diagnosis. Do not perform engine teardown based on sensor readings alone.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Pressure Confirmation

After repair, verify oil pressure meets specification at hot idle and high RPM with a mechanical gauge. Confirm SPN 100 FMI 18 does not return. Monitor for return of low oil pressure events over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Oil Service, Sensor, Pickup, Pump, or Engine Decision

Service oil and filter if oil condition is confirmed degraded or diluted. Replace sensor if sensor bias is confirmed by mechanical gauge comparison. Service pickup screen if restriction is confirmed. Replace oil pump if pump wear is confirmed. Perform deeper engine repair only if bearing wear is confirmed by gauge-proven low pressure.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1. Service oil and filter if oil condition is confirmed degraded or diluted.
2. Replace sensor if sensor bias is confirmed by mechanical gauge comparison.
3. Service pickup screen if restriction is confirmed.
4. Replace oil pump if pump wear is confirmed.
5. Perform deeper engine repair only if bearing wear is confirmed by gauge-proven low pressure.
Verification Steps
Confirm oil pressure meets specification at hot idle and high RPM with a mechanical gauge after repair.
Verify SPN 100 FMI 18 does not return after repair.
Confirm no protection derates after repair.
Monitor for return of low oil pressure events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Check oil level and condition at every service interval.
✓ Use OEM-specified oil viscosity for the operating temperature range.
✓ Service oil and filter at OEM-specified intervals to prevent degradation.
✓ Monitor oil pressure PID trend over time to identify wear before it becomes severe.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High if confirmed low Severity
High if confirmed low. Shut down to protect the engine when gauge-proven. The FSM gauge gate protects against unnecessary teardown.

Oil pressure below normal
Engine protection oil pressure derate
Hot idle low oil pressure
Oil pressure warning light diesel

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 18 is an early, moderately severe low oil pressure warning. It's a High severity fault worth addressing promptly since it can escalate to a shutdown-level fault if the underlying cause isn't found. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this code as an opportunity, not just a warning - catching an oil pressure trend here is a lot cheaper than dealing with the same problem once it's severe enough to derate the truck.
causes: Slightly low oil level or wrong viscosity for the season
A basic maintenance issue rather than an electrical or mechanical failure - correcting level and viscosity often resolves this warning entirely.
Early-stage oil pressure sensor drift
An electrical/sensor fault where the sensor's accuracy has degraded slightly, reporting pressure lower than actual.
Partially restricted oil filter
A mechanical restriction that reduces flow and pressure slightly without yet causing a critical shortfall.
Early oil pump wear
A genuine mechanical wear issue that, if ignored, will progress toward a more severe pressure fault over time.
steps: Check oil level on the dipstick with the truck on level ground and the engine warm but off.
Verify the correct oil viscosity is in use for the season and climate - the wrong viscosity can produce chronically low pressure readings at idle.
Connect Mack Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and log oil pressure against RPM; pressure should climb steadily as RPM increases from idle.
Tee in a mechanical oil pressure gauge to confirm the ECM's reading matches reality before assuming a sensor fault.
If the mechanical gauge confirms genuinely low pressure, inspect the oil filter for restriction and check pump output before considering more invasive engine work.
symptoms: Amber oil pressure warning lamp
Oil pressure gauge reading on the low side of normal, especially at idle
No immediate derate, but the warning persists across drive cycles
Possible slight engine tapping noise if pressure has been marginal for a while

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 18 on a Cummins engine is a confirmed-valid but moderately low oil pressure reading. The ECM responds with a yellow MIL and a power derate; an immediate shutdown countdown follows if pressure continues to drop. Always verify with a calibrated mechanical gauge before condemning the sensor or the lube circuit.
causes: Worn oil pump with reduced output (mechanical)
High

On ISX15 engines above 700,000 miles, gear-type oil pump rotor-to-housing clearance commonly reaches the 0.006 in. wear limit, allowing internal bypass that prevents the pump from maintaining minimum idle pressure at hot operating temperature.
Oil pressure regulator valve stuck open (mechanical)
Medium

The spring-loaded relief valve inside the oil pump housing bleeds off excess pressure. Varnish buildup or a fatigued spring can hold the valve partially open even at low circuit pressures, consistently pulling the reading below the FMI 18 threshold despite normal pump output.
Drifted or failed oil pressure sensor (electrical/sensor)
Medium

The 3-wire pressure transducer can develop internal diaphragm fatigue or connector pin corrosion over time, producing a signal voltage that reads lower than actual pressure. This is a false-positive fault—mechanical pressure is normal but the ECM sees a below-threshold signal.
Oil filter bypass or clogged pickup strainer (mechanical)
Low–Medium

A damaged oil filter adapter O-ring can route return oil into the supply circuit, dropping circuit pressure. A partially blocked pickup strainer—most common after extended oil intervals or metallic debris from a prior failure—starves the pump inlet, reducing output at idle.
Incorrect oil viscosity or severely degraded oil (mechanical)
Low

Operating with 10W-30 in an ISX15 spec'd for 15W-40, or oil with critically low TBN and degraded viscosity additives, can legitimately drop idle pressure below the 10 psi threshold on a fully warm engine—especially at elevated ambient temperatures.
steps: 1. Connect Cummins INSITE, capture the fault freeze-frame—note engine hours, RPM, oil temperature, and reported pressure at fault activation.
2. Check oil level on the dipstick with the engine cold. A level below the ADD mark is the first thing to correct before proceeding.

3. Install a calibrated mechanical oil pressure gauge at the main pressure tap on the block (behind the oil filter housing on ISX15). Idle the engine to full operating temperature (195°F+ coolant). ISX15 minimum hot-idle spec: 10 psi. Comfortable lower limit: 15 psi. Road-load spec at governed RPM: 30–50 psi.
4. If the mechanical gauge also reads low (< 10 psi hot idle), the fault is mechanical—proceed to inspect the oil pump, relief valve, and bearing clearances. Do not continue running.

5. If mechanical gauge reads normal and ECM still shows low, the sensor is the suspect. Measure the 5V reference supply at the sensor connector pin A (pin numbers per ISX15 wiring diagram) with a multimeter. Signal voltage should track pressure per the sensor curve in Cummins Quickserve.
6. Verify the oil filter is not plugged and the filter bypass valve is not stuck open—a bypassing filter drops circuit pressure without any external leak.

7. Clear the fault in Cummins INSITE and road-test for 20+ minutes monitoring the oil pressure parameter. Pressure must hold above 15 psi at hot idle and above 40 psi under load before releasing the vehicle.
symptoms: Yellow check engine lamp active with SPN 100 FMI 18 logged
25–35% engine power derate on ISX15/X15 calibrations
30-second shutdown countdown if fault stays active at idle
Oil pressure parameter below 10 psi in Cummins INSITE live data at hot idle
Fault may go inactive at high RPM (pump flow increases) but returns at idle
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 100 FMI 18 – Engine Oil Pressure Below Normal (Moderate)

procedures_full.overview: SPN 100 FMI 18 on an International engine is a valid confirmed oil pressure reading that falls below the acceptable lower limit. The ECM derates the engine and begins a shutdown countdown. Verify actual mechanical pressure with a calibrated gauge—the International A26's gerotor oil pump has a specific wear pattern that shows up as hot-idle pressure collapse.
causes: Worn gerotor oil pump with increased thermal clearance (mechanical)
High

The A26 uses a gerotor pump driven off the crankshaft front. As the gerotor rotor and housing wear over high mileage, internal clearance increases. At hot operating temperature, thermal expansion of the aluminum housing further opens this clearance, creating a hot-idle pressure collapse that doesn't appear at cold start or at operating RPM—the pump can sustain higher RPM but can't hold minimum pressure at idle.
Oil pressure sensor drift or connector corrosion (electrical/sensor)
Medium

The 3-wire pressure transducer on the A26 block can develop resistance drift or intermittent contact due to connector corrosion in the engine bay environment. A partially corroded connector produces a signal that reads low-normal at ambient temperature but drifts below threshold at heat-soak temperatures—mimicking the same thermal-decline pattern as gerotor wear.
Oil filter bypass valve stuck open (mechanical)
Medium

The bypass valve on the A26 oil filter base opens under extreme filter restriction. If the valve sticks open due to debris or spring failure, oil bypasses the filter and recirculates through a shorter path, reducing effective circuit pressure especially at idle where pump flow is lowest.
Low oil level or incorrect viscosity (mechanical)
Medium

Operating below the full mark on the dipstick or using a thinner viscosity grade than specified allows the gerotor pump to cavitate at hot idle, especially on inclines. The A26 spec calls for CK-4 15W-40 in most applications; using 5W-30 without manufacturer approval reduces idle pressure by 5–8 psi on a warm engine.
steps: 1. Connect Navistar Diamond Logic or ServiceMaxx and pull active and inactive faults with freeze-frame data. Record engine hours, RPM, coolant temperature, and oil temperature at fault activation.
2. Check oil level on the dipstick. Even a half-quart low on an A26 can cause marginal idle pressure.

3. Install a calibrated mechanical oil pressure gauge at the main oil pressure tap on the A26 block (driver-side, near the oil filter base). Idle the engine to full operating temperature. A26 minimum hot-idle spec: 12 psi. Normal operating range at speed: 35–55 psi.

4. If mechanical gauge confirms low pressure (< 12 psi hot idle), shut the engine down immediately. Begin mechanical diagnosis: inspect the oil filter for bypass, check the filter bypass valve on the block, and inspect the oil pump drive gear.

5. If mechanical pressure is normal but ServiceMaxx reports low, inspect the oil pressure sensor connector for corrosion, water intrusion, or a backed-out terminal. Measure 5V reference supply at the sensor connector with a multimeter.

6. Perform a Texa or Jaltest component test on the oil pressure sensor if the platform supports it—these tools can command the ECM to read the raw sensor signal without performing a functional test, useful for distinguishing sensor drift from wiring issues.

7. Clear fault, verify mechanical pressure is in spec, then road-test with ServiceMaxx logging oil pressure. Confirm pressure holds above 15 psi at hot idle and above 35 psi at governed speed for 20+ minutes before releasing the vehicle.
symptoms: Yellow check engine lamp with SPN 100 FMI 18 logged in ServiceMaxx
Engine derate active (25–30% torque reduction typical on A26 platform)
30-second shutdown countdown initiated if fault remains active at idle
Oil pressure parameter reading below 10 psi in ServiceMaxx live data at hot idle
Oil pressure may recover at highway speed but drops again at idle—classic low-flow pump behavior

troubleshooting_faq.question: Does SPN 110 FMI 0 mean the coolant temperature sensor has failed?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: FMI 0 means the measured temperature value is genuinely high, not that the sensor circuit has failed electrically. A sensor that shorts to voltage or opens would typically set FMI 3 or FMI 4. If the dash gauge and Insite both confirm high temperature, the sensor is likely accurate and the cooling system needs physical attention.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can a low coolant level trigger this code before the engine shows signs of overheating?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: Yes. If the coolant level drops enough that the sensor tip is no longer submerged in liquid coolant, the sensor reads the temperature of the surrounding steam pocket or metal �?which can be significantly higher than normal coolant temperature. Low coolant level is therefore treated as urgent even before the engine shows obvious distress.

troubleshooting_faq.question: After the cooling system is repaired, does anything in Insite need to be reset?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The active fault typically clears once coolant temperature returns to the normal range. Stored codes can be cleared in Insite after the repair is confirmed. If engine protection events were recorded, a Cummins dealer can review the protection history to assess whether any heat-related damage occurred during the overtemperature event.

troubleshooting_faq.question: How do I know if SPN 110 FMI 0 is from a real overtemperature or a failed sensor on a Detroit?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: FMI 0 means the temperature value is valid and genuinely high �?not that the sensor circuit has failed. A failed sensor typically sets FMI 3 (voltage high, reading maximum temperature) or FMI 4 (voltage low or open). If the dash gauge and DiagnosticLink both show high temperature, the sensor is almost certainly reading accurately and the cooling system has a real problem.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can the Detroit fan clutch be verified without special tools?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: A basic check: confirm the fan engages and stays engaged when the engine is at operating temperature with the A/C on. DiagnosticLink can also command the fan clutch on and off to verify it responds to ECM commands. If the fan does not engage when commanded, the likely causes are a failed fan clutch solenoid, a wiring fault, or the clutch assembly itself.

troubleshooting_faq.question: After the cooling system is repaired, does anything need to be reset in DiagnosticLink?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The active fault should clear once coolant temperature returns to the normal range. Stored fault codes can be cleared in DiagnosticLink after confirming the repair. If protection events were recorded, a Detroit service facility can review the protection history to assess whether heat exposure was severe enough to warrant additional inspection.

procedures_full.overview: Engine coolant temperature is above the high limit. Sustained overheating warps heads and damages the engine, so the ECM warns and will derate; treat it as stop-now once confirmed on the gauge.
procedures_full.severity_action: Stop as soon as it's safe
causes: Low coolant level or a leak (hose, radiator, water pump, EGR cooler)
Stuck thermostat or failed water pump
Plugged radiator/CAC fins, debris, or a failed cooling fan/clutch
Coolant-temp sensor fault reading high (verify before assuming)
first_moves: Reduce load and get to a safe stop; idling briefly can help, but don't keep climbing a grade hot.
Once cooled, check coolant level (NEVER open a hot pressurized cap) and look for leaks/steam.
Inspect the fan engagement and the radiator/CAC face for bugs, mud, or debris blocking airflow.
Compare gauge to actual — a sensor fault can read high, but confirm before continuing.
common_misdiagnoses: Adding coolant and driving on without finding the leak or stuck thermostat.
Blaming the sensor while the fan clutch isn't engaging.
Overlooking a packed radiator/charge-air-cooler face as the airflow restriction.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 0 means coolant temperature has reached a critically high level on a Kenworth with a PACCAR MX engine. It's a Critical fault with active shutdown risk - stop and let it cool before diagnosing further.
causes: Coolant leak from a hose, water pump, or radiator core
A straightforward mechanical failure - lost coolant volume reduces the system's capacity to absorb and reject engine heat.
Failed fan clutch or restricted radiator airflow
A mechanical cooling system failure where airflow across the radiator drops even with adequate coolant, causing heat to build under load.
Internal coolant leak from a cracked head or blown gasket
A serious mechanical engine failure where combustion gases or oil contaminate the cooling system, reducing its effectiveness.
Failed coolant temperature sensor
An electrical/sensor fault where the reading itself is wrong despite normal cooling system operation - always confirm with an independent check.
steps: Pull over safely and shut the engine down before the ECM forces a shutdown on its own.
Let the engine cool completely before opening the coolant system - never remove a cap on a hot, pressurized system.
Check coolant level in the surge tank once cool, and inspect for leaks at hoses, the water pump, and radiator core.
Connect PACCAR Davie4 and verify the coolant temperature sensor reading matches an independent infrared thermometer check at the thermostat housing.
If coolant level and sensor readings check out, inspect fan clutch engagement and radiator airflow for a mechanical cooling system failure.
symptoms: Red Stop Engine lamp with an audible overheat alarm
Coolant temperature gauge pinned in the red zone
Steam or a strong coolant smell from under the hood
Sudden power derate or automatic engine shutdown

procedures_full.overview: The ECT sensor (SPN 110) monitors coolant temperature for engine protection. FMI 0 (most severe) triggers when temperature exceeds the highest protection threshold. True overheat can cause head gasket failure, liner distortion, and catastrophic engine damage. However, a failed ECT sensor or air pocket after service can mimic overheat without actual thermal damage. Separate true overheat from sensor fault before any teardown.
causes: Low coolant level — leak or consumption
Failed thermostat — stuck closed
Weak water pump — insufficient flow
Clogged radiator or CAC package — debris or scale
Fan clutch failure — not engaging at temperature
Fan modulator/control fault
ECT sensor bias — false high reading
Air pocket after service — false overheat reading
steps: Single Action Gate — Sensor vs True Thermal Separation
Compare ECT gauge reading to an infrared temperature measurement at the sender location. A large discrepancy suggests sensor bias rather than true overheat.
Binary Decision Gate — Coolant Level & Pressure Test
Check coolant level and perform a pressure cap test. Low level or failed cap is the most common cause of true overheat.
Override Manager — Combustion Gas Check
If coolant loss is unexplained, test for combustion gases in the coolant (block test or combustion leak test). Positive result indicates head gasket or liner issue.
Safety Interceptor — Fan Command & Operation
Verify fan is being commanded on at temperature and is actually engaging. Fan clutch failure or modulator fault is a common cause of overheat at low speed.
Resume Point — Thermostat Differential Test
Measure temperature differential across the thermostat. A stuck-closed thermostat will show a large temperature difference between inlet and outlet.
Verification Loop — Airflow Package Inspection
Inspect radiator, CAC, and condenser for debris packing, bent fins, or scale buildup. Restricted airflow causes overheat at high ambient or load.
Repair Ledger Output — Major Engine Work Decision
Avoid head gasket or major engine work without positive combustion leak test or physical evidence of failure. Document all findings.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair coolant leaks and restore proper level.
2 . Replace failed thermostat if stuck closed.
3 . Replace fan clutch or repair fan modulator if fan is not engaging.
4 . Clean or replace radiator/CAC if airflow is restricted.
5 . Replace water pump if flow is insufficient.
6 . Replace ECT sensor if bias is confirmed.
7 . Perform head gasket or major engine repair only with positive combustion leak test evidence.
Verification Steps
Confirm coolant temperature stays within normal range under load after repair.
Verify fan engages at correct temperature.
Confirm no coolant loss after repair.
Monitor for return of SPN 110 FMI 0 over 50+ miles.
Verify combustion leak test is negative after any head work.
Preventative Measures
✓ Maintain coolant level and condition per OEM service intervals.
✓ Replace thermostat at high mileage or at every major service.
✓ Inspect fan clutch operation at every service.
✓ Clean radiator and CAC package annually or as needed.
✓ Use OEM-specified coolant and inhibitor concentration.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity
High severity. Stop the vehicle if temperature is in the severe range. Continued operation risks catastrophic engine damage. Verify true overheat versus sensor fault before any teardown.
symptoms: Engine overheat warning on dash
Coolant temperature gauge in red zone
Derate or engine protection shutdown
Fan running continuously or not engaging
Steam from coolant system
Coolant loss

procedures_full.overview: On Kenworth, SPN 110 FMI 2 is a Engine Coolant Temperature fault (Data Erratic, Intermittent, or Incorrect). Prove wiring/live data first; do not parts-cannon the component. This guide covers symptoms, root causes, live-data checks, and misdiagnoses for Kenworth platforms.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie or Diesel Laptops and record SPN 110 FMI 2 with freeze-frame load/temp.
Inspect harness and connector at the engine coolant temperature for chafe, corrosion, and bent pins.
Verify 5V reference / ground / signal integrity with a multimeter where applicable.
Compare ECT to infrared at thermostat housing
Repair the proven fault, clear only after repair, and verify under the same conditions as freeze-frame.
symptoms: Check-engine / amber warning lamp illuminated.
Soft power, unstable idle, or poor response when engine coolant temperature data is irrational.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 3 on engine coolant temperature indicates the ECM detected a signal voltage above the valid maximum on the ECT circuit. Open signal wire, failed thermistor, unplugged connector, corroded terminals, and poor 5V or ground reference are the primary causes. False extreme cold readings after service when the connector is left loose and open circuit causing incorrect fueling and fan strategy are documented patterns. Thermistor sensors typically show high voltage when the circuit is open — the ECM reads the signal as an extreme cold temperature when the circuit is open.
causes: Open signal wire — open circuit in ECT signal wire producing high voltage
Failed thermistor — thermistor failure producing open circuit
Unplugged connector — ECT connector not plugged in
Corroded terminals — terminal corrosion producing open circuit
Poor 5V or ground reference — reference circuit fault producing incorrect signal voltage
steps: Single Action Gate — Visual Connector Check

Inspect the ECT sensor connector at the housing or thermostat area. Inspect for chafe near brackets and coolant intrusion into the connector body. A connector that is not fully seated or has coolant intrusion produces an open circuit that reads as high voltage. Confirm the connector is fully seated and the terminals are clean and undamaged.
Binary Decision Gate — Ref/Ground/Signal Checks

Verify reference voltage, ground, and signal voltage at the ECT connector. Confirm the reference voltage is present and within specification. Confirm the ground is intact. A signal voltage that is at or near the reference voltage with a good reference and ground confirms an open signal circuit or failed sensor.
Override Manager — Resistance Check

Perform a resistance check on the ECT sensor. Thermistor sensors show resistance that decreases as temperature increases. An OL or very high resistance reading confirms an open thermistor. Compare the measured resistance to the OEM resistance-versus-temperature chart when available.
Safety Interceptor — IR Correlation

Compare the scan tool ECT reading to an IR thermometer reading at the sender location. An extreme cold reading on the scan tool with a normal temperature reading on the IR thermometer confirms a false reading from an open circuit or failed sensor. A scan tool reading that matches the IR reading confirms the sensor is reading correctly.
Resume Point — Circuit Proof Before Sensor Replacement

Complete circuit proof before sensor replacement. Confirm the reference, ground, and signal circuit integrity before replacing the sensor. A sensor replaced without circuit proof may be replaced into a circuit fault that will fail the new sensor.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair ECT Reading Confirmation
After repair, verify the ECT reading matches the actual coolant temperature. Confirm SPN 110 FMI 3 does not return. Confirm fan engagement and fueling strategy return to normal after repair.
Repair Ledger Output — Connector, Harness, or Sensor Decision

Repair connector or harness if open circuit is confirmed in the circuit path. Replace ECT sensor if thermistor failure is confirmed after circuit proof. Do not replace the thermostat or fan for an open ECT circuit.

Repair Steps
1 . Repair connector or harness if open circuit is confirmed in the circuit path.
2 . Replace ECT sensor if thermistor failure is confirmed after circuit proof.
3 . Clean and reseat connector if coolant intrusion is found.
4 . Do not replace thermostat or fan for an open ECT circuit.
Verification Steps

Verify SPN 110 FMI 3 does not return after repair.
Confirm fan engagement and fueling strategy return to normal after repair.
Monitor for return of false cold readings over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect ECT connector for coolant intrusion at every major service.
✓ Verify ECT connector seating after any cooling system service.
✓ Inspect ECT harness for chafe near brackets at every major service.

Medium Severity
Medium. Incorrect temp sensing can delay fan engagement or skew fueling. ECT high-voltage codes are electrical open diagnostics until proven otherwise.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 3 means the coolant temperature sensor circuit is shorted high or open, not that the engine is actually overheating. It's Medium severity - an electrical fault that pushes the ECM into a conservative fan and fueling strategy until repaired. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always confirms this is a wiring/sensor fault with a resistance check before letting a driver panic about overheating - the two conditions look identical on the dash but have very different fixes.
causes: Open or failed coolant temperature sensor
Electrical fault - an internal open circuit in the thermistor produces a signal the ECM reads as impossibly high voltage.
Corroded or disconnected sensor connector
Electrical fault - a poor connection has the same effect as a fully open sensor circuit.
Chafed harness wire shorted to a power source
Electrical fault - a signal wire rubbing against a powered circuit near the valve cover can inject voltage directly onto the sensor line.
Genuine coolant system issue causing extreme overheating
A true mechanical failure - only relevant if actual coolant temperature is confirmed abnormally high by an independent thermometer, not just the dash gauge.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) and confirm the fault is active, then check the reported coolant temp value - a reading pegged at the sensor's max scale confirms an open/shorted-high circuit rather than real overheating.

Unplug the coolant temp sensor connector and measure resistance across the sensor pins - a typical thermistor should read roughly 2,000-3,000 ohms at 68°F, dropping as temperature rises. An open reading (infinite resistance) confirms a bad sensor or open circuit.
With the sensor unplugged, check for battery voltage or a short to power on the signal wire back at the ECM connector.
Inspect the harness routing near the thermostat housing and valve cover for heat damage or chafing against brackets.
Clean and inspect the sensor connector pins for corrosion before reconnecting - a loose pin can present as an open circuit intermittently.
symptoms: Coolant temp gauge pegged at maximum or showing an implausible reading
Cooling fan runs constantly regardless of actual engine temperature
Amber check engine light
Possible slight fuel economy drop from conservative fueling maps
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 110 FMI 3: Coolant Temp Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 3 on Cummins means the coolant temp sensor circuit voltage is above normal, making the ECM read an artificially cold engine. This masks true overheating and can delay a protective derate or shutdown, risking severe engine damage if coolant is actually hot. Always diagnose with Cummins INSITE live data before assuming sensor failure. Cummins SPN 110 FMI 3 indicates the Engine Coolant Temperature sensor is delivering a voltage-above-normal signal to the ECM on ISX, X15, ISB, and ISL platforms. FMI 3 corresponds to an open or high-resistance circuit: the ECM receives more than ~4.75 V on the 5 V reference signal line, typically because the sensor or its wiring has failed open. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees this fault commonly after wiring harness chafing near the front engine cover or after coolant leaks corrode the sensor connector. The danger is not the fault code itself but what it hides: a genuinely overheating engine may not trigger normal high-temp protection while this code is active. Address this code the same day it sets.
causes: Failed ECT sensor (open internal thermistor)

The NTC thermistor element breaks open, removing the pull-down load on the 5 V reference line and causing the ECM to see maximum voltage. Infinite resistance across the sensor terminals confirms this failure.
Open or corroded signal wire and connector pin

Chafing against the engine block or heat shields cuts the signal wire, and corrosion on connector pins increases resistance until the ECM reads above 4.75 V. Continuity testing quickly isolates this cause.
Low coolant level exposing sensor tip to air

When coolant drops and the sensor tip is no longer submerged, it reads ambient air temperature (high resistance, high voltage). Refilling coolant and retesting confirms this cause without any part replacement needed.
steps: With engine off and key on, connect Cummins INSITE with a Diesel Laptops USB-Link 2 adapter. Navigate to Live Data and observe ECT sensor voltage. FMI 3 (voltage above normal) reads above 4.75 V; a healthy sensor at 70 F ambient reads roughly 2.0-2.5 V on the 5 V reference circuit.

Inspect the ECT sensor connector in the water inlet housing near the front of the cylinder head. Look for backed-out terminals, spread pins, or corrosion creating an open circuit. A loose pin causes the ECM to see maximum reference voltage and log FMI 3.

Unplug the connector and measure resistance across the two ECT sensor terminals. At 70 F (21 C) a Cummins NTC thermistor reads approximately 2,200-2,500 ohms; at 200 F (93 C) it drops to 200-270 ohms. Infinite resistance confirms a failed sensor element.

Inspect the signal wire (Pin A) from the sensor connector back to ECM connector C1 or C2 for chafing against the block or a heat shield. Measure pin-to-pin continuity; an open circuit confirms wiring damage requiring harness repair before any sensor is ordered.
Install replacement sensor (torque 25-30 ft-lb with thread sealant), clear faults with Cummins INSITE, perform a key cycle, and confirm live ECT voltage returns to 2.0-2.5 V at ambient temperature.
symptoms: Amber Check Engine light illuminated with possible yellow warning lamp active on cluster.
Coolant temperature gauge reads abnormally low or pegged at cold end of scale even after full warm-up.
Engine runs extended cold-start enrichment because the ECM thinks coolant remains cold.
Reduced fuel economy during prolonged operation as cold-start fueling tables stay active.
Occasional amber derate if ECM detects sensor implausibility versus other thermal inputs.
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 110 FMI 3: Engine Coolant Temperature Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 3 on Freightliner trucks means the coolant temperature sensor circuit voltage is above normal, typically a short to 5V or power. The ECM may use default temp values affecting fan and emissions logic. Unplug the sensor and test signal voltage before cooling system repairs. A pegged-hot coolant gauge on a cold engine is a wiring problem until proven otherwise. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com walks Freightliner operators through pin-level checks on SPN 110 FMI 3 before they start throwing thermostats and water pumps at an electrical fault.
causes: ECT signal wire shorted to 5V or battery positive
Rubbed harness near exhaust or battery cables pulls signal voltage high regardless of actual coolant temperature.
Failed coolant temperature sensor internal short
Age and coolant contamination short the NTC element, sending a high voltage signal to the ECM.
Connector pin corrosion bridging supply and signal
Moisture and glycol create conductive paths between pins at the sensor Deutsch connector.
steps: Connect Noregon JPRO and read ECT voltage on SPN 110; above 4.8V at cold soak confirms FMI 3.
Unplug the ECT sensor at the thermostat housing. Key on, measure signal pin voltage; above 0.5V unplugged indicates a harness short to power.
Verify 5.0V +/- 0.25V on the reference/supply pin with sensor disconnected.
Inspect harness along the firewall and near exhaust routing for melted insulation shorting signal to battery positive.
Replace sensor or repair harness; NTC sensors typically read 2-4k ohms at 77F pin-to-pin. Clear code and confirm temp tracks ambient after cold soak.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with SPN 110 FMI 3 active in JPRO or OEM software
Coolant temp gauge pegged hot or reading implausibly high at cold start
Radiator fan may run continuously or not at all depending on default strategy
DEF regen or DPF events may be inhibited with incorrect temp data
Fault may be present key-on with engine cold

procedures_full.overview: FMI 4 on engine coolant temperature indicates the ECM detected a signal voltage below the valid minimum on the ECT circuit. Signal short to ground, failed sensor, damaged insulation, and water-intruded connector bridging are the primary causes. False overheat warnings from shorted ECT circuits are a documented pattern — the ECM reads the signal as an extreme hot temperature when the circuit is shorted to ground. Treat as High until true temperature is confirmed safe — a false overheat reading can trigger protection derates that are not warranted.
causes: Signal short to ground — ECT signal wire shorted to ground producing low voltage
Failed sensor — sensor failure producing low voltage output
Damaged insulation — insulation damage producing short to ground
Water-intruded connector bridging — water intrusion bridging signal to ground in connector
steps: Single Action Gate — Disconnect Sensor and Recheck Harness

Disconnect the ECT sensor and recheck the harness for a residual short to ground. A short that clears when the sensor is disconnected confirms the sensor is the source. A short that remains with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness fault. Inspect for rubbed wires near sharp brackets and clamps at the front engine dress.
Binary Decision Gate — Harness Short Test

Perform a harness short test with the sensor disconnected. Measure signal wire voltage and resistance to ground with the sensor disconnected. A signal wire that reads near zero volts or shows low resistance to ground with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness short to ground.
Override Manager — Ref/Ground Verification

Verify reference voltage and ground integrity at the ECT connector. A reference voltage that is shorted to ground produces a false low reading. Confirm the reference and ground circuits are intact and not cross-connected.
Safety Interceptor — IR vs Scan Correlation

Compare the scan tool ECT reading to an IR thermometer reading at the sender location. A false hot reading on the scan tool with a normal temperature reading on the IR thermometer confirms a false reading from a shorted circuit or failed sensor. A scan tool reading that matches the IR reading confirms the sensor is reading correctly — treat as a true overheat event and protect the engine.
Resume Point — True Overheat vs False Sensor Split

Split true overheat from false sensor before major cooling work. A confirmed false reading from a shorted circuit requires electrical repair, not cooling system work. A confirmed true overheat requires cooling system diagnosis — do not dismiss a true overheat as a sensor fault without IR confirmation.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair ECT Reading Confirmation
After repair, verify the ECT reading matches the actual coolant temperature. Confirm SPN 110 FMI 4 does not return. Confirm protection derates clear and fan strategy returns to normal after repair.
Repair Ledger Output — Harness, Sensor, or Cooling System Decision

Repair harness if short to ground is confirmed in the harness path. Replace ECT sensor if sensor failure is confirmed after harness integrity is confirmed. Perform cooling system diagnosis only if true overheat is confirmed by IR correlation. Do not perform head gasket or cooling system work for a shorted ECT circuit.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness if short to ground is confirmed in the harness path.
2 . Replace ECT sensor if sensor failure is confirmed after harness integrity is confirmed.
3 . Perform cooling system diagnosis only if true overheat is confirmed by IR correlation.
4 . Do not perform head gasket or cooling system work for a shorted ECT circuit.
Verification Steps
Confirm ECT reading matches actual coolant temperature after repair.
Verify SPN 110 FMI 4 does not return after repair.
Confirm protection derates clear and fan strategy returns to normal after repair.
Monitor for return of false hot readings over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect ECT connector for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect ECT harness for rub-through near sharp brackets at every major service.
✓ Compare ECT scan reading to IR thermometer at every major service on high-mileage engines.
✓ Verify ECT connector seating after any cooling system service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium electrically; treat as High until true temperature is confirmed safe Severity

Medium electrically; treat as High until true temperature is confirmed safe. False overheat readings can trigger protection derates. True overheat vs false sensor split is required before major cooling work.

ECT shorted
False hot reading on coolant temp
Derate from false overheat
Fan always on from false hot reading

procedures_full.overview: Caterpillar SPN 110 FMI 16 indicates the ECM is reading a valid but moderately elevated coolant temperature. The engine will derate to reduce heat rejection, and a more severe shutdown-level fault will follow if the temperature continues to climb. Check the cooling system mechanically before assuming the sensor is wrong. Caterpillar SPN 110 FMI 16 is the ECM's early warning that coolant temperature has crossed the upper threshold for normal operation—valid reading, real heat. On C13 and C15 ACERT platforms this code typically appears between 205°F and 215°F coolant temperature and activates a protective derate before the engine reaches the FMI 0 threshold where shutdown is imminent. The causes range from a simple thermostat, a slipping fan clutch, or a blocked radiator core all the way to coolant pump wear or head gasket failure. A systematic cooling system inspection using Cat ET live data and basic mechanical checks—documented step by step on ProfessionalDieselRepair.com—separates a sensor reading from a real thermal event before any parts are touched.
causes: Thermostat stuck closed or slow to open (mechanical)
High

A wax-element thermostat that fails in the closed or partially-open position restricts coolant flow to the radiator, causing a progressive temperature rise that typically begins 5–10 minutes after a cold start once the thermostat should have opened. Temperature climbs continuously rather than stabilizing around 190–195°F.
Radiator core blockage or collapsed hose (mechanical)
Medium–High

A radiator core with compressed fins or external debris reduces heat rejection capacity. A partially collapsed upper or lower radiator hose restricts coolant flow—most visibly under load when suction increases. Either condition causes a temperature spike under load that may not appear at idle.
Slipping or failed fan clutch (mechanical)
Medium

A viscous fan clutch that slips at high temperature (when it should be fully engaged) fails to provide adequate airflow through the radiator at low road speeds or high idle. The result is load-dependent temperature spikes that resolve at highway speed when ram air compensates.
Drifted engine coolant temperature sensor (electrical/sensor)
Medium

The ECT sensor's NTC thermistor can drift toward lower resistance over time, causing the signal voltage to indicate a higher temperature than actual coolant temperature. The signal is technically 'valid' in terms of FMI logic, but the number is inflated—compare against a contact thermometer to identify sensor drift.
Low coolant level with aeration (mechanical/aftertreatment-adjacent)
Medium

Air pockets in the cooling system create localized hot spots around the temperature sensor—the coolant in the block can be 20–30°F hotter than the average temperature in the radiator. This is common after any coolant work that wasn't bled properly or after a small head gasket seep.
steps: 1. Connect Cat ET and pull the active fault with freeze-frame data—record coolant temperature, engine load, ambient temperature, and RPM at fault activation.
2. Check coolant level in the surge/deaeration tank with the engine cold. A low level introduces air pockets that cause hot spots and inaccurate temperature sensor readings.

3. With the engine fully warm, compare the Cat ET coolant temperature reading against a known-accurate contact thermometer or infrared gun at the thermostat housing outlet. If the ECM value is 15°F+ higher than the physical measurement, suspect the sensor.
4. Inspect the radiator core face for debris blockage (bugs, chaff, compressed fins). A 25% blocked radiator face can raise coolant temperature 20–30°F under load on a hot day.

5. Check thermostat function: after a cold start, coolant should remain below 170°F until the thermostat opens, then stabilize around 185–195°F. If temperature climbs continuously without stabilizing, the thermostat is stuck closed.
6. Inspect the fan clutch engagement under load—a slipping fan clutch on a C15 ACERT can allow coolant temperature to climb 20–30°F above normal during low-speed, high-load operation.

7. If mechanical cooling system checks out, measure the ECT sensor's resistance using a multimeter: disconnect the 2-pin connector and compare resistance at known coolant temperature against the Caterpillar spec chart in Cat ET or SIS. Replace the sensor if resistance is out of range.
symptoms: Yellow check engine lamp with SPN 110 FMI 16 in Cat ET fault log
Engine coolant temperature parameter above 210°F (99°C) in Cat ET live data
25–35% power derate active to reduce engine heat load
Temperature gauge in cab showing elevated but not yet critical reading
Increased cooling fan speed or continuous fan lockup noted by driver

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 16 means coolant temperature is above the safe range but below critical shutdown. Check coolant level, external leaks, and fan clutch operation first. This code is the ECM's early warning before a full overheat shutdown. Catching it here - rather than waiting for the more severe FMI 0 version - usually means the fix is simple and cheap if addressed right away.
causes: Low coolant level from a slow leak
Even a small external leak reduces the system's heat capacity enough to push temps up under load.
Fan clutch not engaging properly
A weak or failed clutch can't pull enough air through the radiator at low road speed or idle.
Radiator externally clogged with debris
Mud, insects, and road grime packed into the fins block airflow even with a perfectly good fan and coolant level.
Failing thermostat stuck partially closed
Restricts coolant flow to the radiator, causing heat to build even with adequate coolant volume.
steps: Check coolant level in the surge tank once safely cooled - low coolant is the single most common cause of an overheat code.
Inspect for external leaks at hoses, the water pump, and radiator seams while the system is cool.
Verify the fan clutch is engaging under heat load - a clutch that free-wheels won't pull enough air through the radiator.
Check radiator fins for mud, bugs, or debris packed in from the outside, which chokes airflow.
Pressure test the cooling system once cool to confirm it's holding pressure and not pushing coolant out through a weak spot.
symptoms: Dash coolant temp gauge reading noticeably higher than normal, often approaching or past the red zone
Noticeable power reduction as the ECM derates to cut heat load
Steam or coolant smell if the condition has progressed
Fan clutch running constantly, trying to compensate

procedures_full.overview: SPN 110 FMI 16 means the ECM has confirmed a genuine moderate overheating condition. It's High severity - address it promptly to prevent escalation to a critical shutdown-level fault. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com starts with the radiator fins and fan clutch on this fault, since airflow restriction is a common and inexpensive cause.
causes: Radiator fins restricted by debris or road grime
Mechanical fault - reduced airflow through the radiator directly reduces cooling capacity under load.
Failing fan clutch or electric fan not engaging properly
Mechanical/electrical fault - insufficient fan speed at the correct temperature threshold allows heat to build.
Partially stuck thermostat not opening fully
Mechanical fault - restricted coolant flow through the radiator raises engine temperature even with everything else functioning.
Moderately low coolant level
Reduces the system's overall heat capacity without necessarily triggering a separate low-coolant-level fault.
steps: Connect Mercedes-Benz Xentry or Diesel Laptops and confirm the fault is active, checking freeze-frame temperature and the conditions (load, ambient temp) when it occurred.
Check coolant level once safely cooled - a moderately low level can cause elevated temperatures without triggering the more severe low-coolant fault directly.
Inspect the radiator fins for debris, bugs, or road grime restricting airflow, especially on trucks running in dusty or agricultural environments.
Verify the cooling fan clutch or electric fan engages properly at the correct temperature threshold using live data or a manual override test.
Pressure-test the cooling system to rule out a developing leak or a partially failed thermostat not opening fully.
symptoms: Coolant temperature gauge reading noticeably elevated but not yet at maximum
Amber warning lamp
Possible reduced power as the ECM manages heat load
Cooling fan running more aggressively than normal

procedures_full.overview: This condition is typically coolant temperature out of range (drifted low/high).‪
causes: This condition is typically coolant temperature out of range (drifted low/high).‪
steps: Note: When diagnosing rationality erratic data faults (FMI 14) always refer to SILs or SIBs for any known issues first.
Rationality Check for Temperature Drift
Check cooling system integrity (lack of heat complaints).
Connect DDDL 7.0 and monitor the engine oil temperature and the engine coolant temperature.
With the engine running at idle and the engine oil temperature above 160°, is the coolant temperature within X degrees of the oil temperature?
If yes, go to step 4.

If no, disconnect the ECT Sensor and the MCM connector. Bridge pins X and X of the sensor, measure the resistance at the MCM between pins X and X. If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, repair the harness. If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the sensor. Refer to "29.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".
With the engine running at 1500 rpm and oil temperature above 160°, check the coolant temperature. Is it within X degrees of the oil temperature?
If yes, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center (313–592–5800).

If no, disconnect the ECT Sensor and the MCM connector. Bridge pins X and X of the sensor and measure resistance at the MCM between pins X and X. If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω repair the harness. If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the sensor. Refer to "29.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

field_evidence.title: Kenworth T700 2012 Cummins ISX Engine Speed Sensor Code SPN-723 FMI 2
field_evidence.excerpt: The Kenworth T700 2012 model equipped with the Cummins ISX engine can experience fault code SPN-723 FMI 2, which relates to an engine speed sensor 2 issue. This problem commonly causes the check engine light to activate intermittently. This engine speed sensor fault can stem from wiring or connector issues, such as damage or corrosion in the sensor’s wiring harness and connectors. These faults can disrupt sensor signals or resistance readings, leading to detection of a malfunction by the engine control module (ECM). To address the SPN-723 FMI 2 code, inspect the engine speed sensor’s wiring harness and connector closely for any visible damage or corrosion. dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 171: Engine Speed
dd_procedures.overview: The Transmission Control Module (TCM)) receives the vehicle’s Engine Speed message over the Primary Data Link and Engine Speed Sensor #2 message over the Secondary Data Link. The TCM uses the Engine Speed as the primary engine speed message during normal transmission operation. If Engine Speed becomes unavailable, the Engine Speed Sensor #2 message allows the transmission to operate in a degraded mode.

procedures_full.overview: The Transmission Control Module (TCM) receives the vehicle's Engine Speed message from a vehicle Electronic Control Unit (ECU) over the Primary Data Link (J1939A). This information is used to determine transmission operation. The TCM also receives the Engine Speed message over the Secondary Data Link (J1939B). The Secondary Data Link is used in the event that the Primary Data Link is inoperative and allows the transmission to operate in a degraded mode. The Primary Data Link (J1939A) is connected to the TCM at the 20-Way TCM Vehicle Harness Connector. The Secondary Data Link (J1939B) is connected to the TCM at the 20-Way TCM Body Harness Connector.
procedures_full.detection: The TCM monitors Engine Speed messages on the Primary Data Link (J1939A). If messages are not received or are invalid, the fault is set Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 9 - Abnormal Update Rate: Engine Speed message not received for 5 seconds. FMI 13 – Out Of Calibration: Engine Speed message not available for 5 seconds. FMI 19 – Received Network Data In Error: Engine Speed messages invalid for 5 seconds.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: FMI 9, 13, 19: Engine Speed messages received and valid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: FMI 9, 13, 19: Amber warning lamp on Coast Mode and Neutral Coast prohibited Urge to Move and Creep Mode prohibited Inertia Brake activation prohibited Upshifts prohibited Clutch engagements prohibited Non-Neutral modes prohibited PTO mode prohibited Hill Start Aid prohibited If vehicle is moving: Red stop lamp on Note: Vehicle may have additional fallback modes. Refer to OEM. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive FMI 9, 13, 19: Engine Speed messages received and valid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.possible_causes: FMI 9, 13, 19: Vehicle Components Engine Speed message not enabled on Primary Data Link (J1939A) Other vehicle ECU(s) faulted Vehicle Harness - Primary Data Link (J1939A) Wiring shorted to power, shorted to ground or open Terminals bent, spread, corroded, or loose Note: Refer to OEM for troubleshooting a failed system.
