procedures_full.overview: SPN 175 FMI 3 on Freightliner is an oil temperature sensor high-voltage electrical fault. Unplug the sensor and check harness signal voltage before buying a new sensor — this is almost always a wiring or sensor short, not real overheating. An oil temperature sensor reading off the top of the chart on a Freightliner does not automatically mean the engine is about to cook — FMI 3 tells you the signal voltage is too high, which is an electrical symptom. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always unplugs the sensor first and puts a meter on the harness before the parts truck shows up. Nine times out of ten, it is a wiring issue that takes 30 minutes to fix.
causes: Signal wire chafed against battery positive or alternator output wiring (electrical)
Very Common

The oil temperature sensor signal wire routed near the engine wiring loom can wear through insulation against a voltage source, producing a constant above-normal voltage at the ECM input and triggering FMI 3.
Internally failed oil temperature sensor shorted to its own reference supply (electrical)
A sensor that has failed with an internal short between the signal pin and the 5V reference or power supply pin reports maximum-range voltage to the ECM.
ECM connector pin-to-pin contact with an adjacent power circuit (electrical)
Less Common
A bent or spread terminal at the ECM connector causing contact between the oil temperature signal pin and a neighboring power circuit pin creates an above-normal signal reading.
steps: 1. Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) or Texa and confirm SPN 175 FMI 3, and check whether SPN 175 FMI 0 (actual confirmed high temp) is also active — if not, this is likely a circuit fault rather than a real overtemp.

2. Unplug the oil temperature sensor connector with the key on. Measure voltage on the signal wire in the harness connector. FMI 3 means you should see near supply voltage (approximately 12-5V) rather than the normal 0.5-4.5V range signal.

3. With the sensor disconnected, check if the high voltage is still present — if yes, the harness has a short to power upstream of the connector. If voltage drops to 0 or the ECM reading changes to FMI 4, the sensor itself is internally shorted high.

4. Walk the signal harness from the sensor connector back toward the ECM, looking for areas where it routes near power supply wires, battery cables, or ignition circuits — even a pinhole in the insulation contacting a 12V wire pulls the signal to FMI 3.

5. Test the sensor body resistance with a multimeter across the signal terminals at known ambient temperature — a sensor that measures far outside the expected temperature-resistance curve has failed internally.
6. Check the ECM connector terminal at the oil temperature signal pin for bent or backed-out pins that could be making contact with an adjacent power circuit pin.
symptoms: Oil temperature gauge reading at maximum or stuck in the red zone
Oil temperature warning lamp active despite no other signs of overheating
Possible precautionary derate from the ECM loss of a reliable oil temp input
No physical signs of overheating if the fault is purely electrical in nature
procedures_full.source_title: Freightliner SPN 175 FMI 3: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 175 FMI 3 on Mercedes-Benz heavy-duty engines means the oil temperature sensor circuit is reading voltage above normal, consistent with a short to a high source. It's a medium-severity fault that mainly affects cooling fan logic and oil condition monitoring accuracy. Oil temperature might not seem as critical as coolant temperature, but it plays into cooling fan activation and long-term oil life monitoring on Mercedes-Benz heavy-duty engines. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats SPN 175 FMI 3 as a fault worth chasing down promptly, since an inaccurate high reading can cause the fan to run more than necessary, adding unwanted wear, while also potentially masking a genuine cooling issue that a correctly functioning sensor would have caught.
causes: Chafed wiring shorting the signal to a power circuit
The oil temperature sensor harness routes near the engine block and can rub against brackets or other wiring over time, developing a short.
Corroded sensor connector
Oil seepage and heat cycling at the connector location can accelerate corrosion, creating an unintended electrical path.
Failed sensor element
Internal failure of the sensor itself can produce an out-of-range high voltage reading independent of the wiring.
steps: Pull the code with Mercedes-Benz Xentry or a Jaltest interface and confirm SPN 175 FMI 3 is active; check the reported oil temperature value against a known-good baseline for the current engine state.
Locate the oil temperature sensor, typically threaded into the oil pan or block near the oil filter housing, and inspect the connector for corrosion or a pinched wire nearby.
Disconnect the sensor and check the signal wire for a short to a nearby power source with the harness isolated from the ECM.
Test the sensor's resistance at a known oil temperature (engine cold, ambient temperature) and compare to the manufacturer's resistance chart.
Repair any chafed wiring found, or replace the sensor if it fails the resistance test, then clear the code.
Confirm the reported oil temperature climbs realistically as the engine warms up during a test run before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Cooling fan running more than expected, even when the engine isn't actually hot
Amber Check Engine lamp
Inaccurate oil temperature reading on the dash or scan tool display
No direct power loss in most cases - primarily an accuracy and monitoring issue
procedures_full.source_title: Mercedes-Benz SPN 175 FMI 3: Diagnosing an Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Fault

procedures_full.overview: SPN 175 FMI 3 on Peterbilt is an oil temperature sensor high-voltage electrical fault. The ECM is reading above normal signal voltage — check the harness for a short to power before replacing the sensor. FMI 3 on any temperature sensor means the signal circuit is reading too high — either a shorted harness or a failed sensor is pulling the voltage toward battery level instead of the normal midrange temperature signal. SPN 175 FMI 3 on a Peterbilt is almost never actual oil overheating. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com starts with the wiring, not the sensor, and gets it right the first time.
causes: Signal harness chafed against a voltage source (electrical)
Very Common
The oil temp sensor signal wire running near battery cables, alternator wiring, or the valve cover can wear through insulation and pick up supply voltage, driving the ECM reading above normal.
Failed oil temperature sensor internally shorted high (electrical)
A sensor that has failed with an internal short to its own supply circuit reports maximum-range voltage at the signal pin.
Loose or corroded connector introducing a high-impedance path (electrical)
A connector that is intermittently floating can allow the ECM's internal pull-up to dominate the reading, potentially registering above normal.
steps: 1. Connect PACCAR Davie4 or Jaltest and confirm SPN 175 FMI 3 is set, then note if any other sensor supply or temperature codes are present alongside it.

2. With the engine cold and the sensor connector unplugged, measure voltage at the signal wire in the harness connector. FMI 3 means voltage is high — expect to see near supply voltage rather than a low midrange signal voltage.

3. With the sensor still disconnected, ground the signal wire through a 10k ohm resistor and check if the ECM reading drops to a plausible temperature — this isolates whether the high voltage is coming from the harness or ECM side.

4. Inspect the sensor harness for contact with the voltage supply wire or chafing against battery positive cabling — a rubbed-through insulation spot can pull the signal line to battery voltage and set exactly this FMI 3.
5. If the harness is clean, test the sensor itself with a multimeter: resistance should drop predictably as temperature rises. A sensor shorted internally can also pull the signal high.
6. Verify connector terminal condition and pin tension at both the sensor and ECM ends before ordering a new sensor.
symptoms: Oil temperature gauge pegged at maximum or reading erratically
Possible oil temperature warning light illuminated
ECM may apply a precautionary derate if oil temp defaults to max
No physical signs of overheating if the fault is purely electrical
procedures_full.source_title: Peterbilt SPN 175 FMI 3: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically engine oil temperature circuit failed high.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically engine oil temperature circuit failed high.‪
steps: Open Circuit/Short to Power Check

Check for multiple codes.

If no voltage is present on pin 1 of the SFT Sensor, repair the open between pin 55 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor, the Engine Oil Temperature Sensor and the Supply Fuel Temperature Sensor. Refer to "35.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If the resistance is greater than 4 kΩ, replace the sensor. Refer to "35.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

procedures_full.overview: SPN 175 FMI 16 on a Mack means engine oil temperature is above the normal operating range. Check coolant level and condition, inspect the oil cooler for restriction, and verify the sensor reading with an infrared thermometer before replacing parts. Mack SPN 175 FMI 16 is a high oil temperature warning indicating the engine oil has risen above its normal operating band — a FMI 16 (moderately above normal) condition that precedes the more severe FMI 0 shutdown threshold. SPN 175 is Engine Oil Temperature 1. On Mack MP8 and MP7 platforms, oil temperature is managed through the internal oil cooler that uses engine coolant as its heat-exchange medium. When the cooler is fouled, coolant flow is restricted, or ambient conditions are extreme, oil temperature rises faster than the cooling system can manage. FMI 16 gives the driver and technician an early warning window to diagnose and repair before the engine enters protection mode. Technicians at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com emphasize that this warning-level fault should never be deferred — the progression from FMI 16 to a derate can happen quickly under sustained load.
causes: Fouled or scaled internal oil cooler core
Silicate gel precipitation from degraded coolant or improper SCA concentration coats the oil cooler passages, reducing heat transfer and allowing oil temperature to rise above normal.
Low coolant level or flow restriction
Insufficient coolant volume or a partially blocked coolant circuit reduces the oil cooler's ability to shed heat, causing oil temperature to rise under load.
Failed or drifted oil temperature sensor
An out-of-calibration sensor reports a temperature above actual, triggering FMI 16 without any true thermal event — most common on high-mileage engines.
steps: Connect a Texa or Jaltest diagnostic tool to the Mack diagnostic port and read active fault codes. Confirm SPN 175 FMI 16 and note any simultaneous coolant temperature faults (SPN 110) — co-occurrence points to a shared cooling system problem such as a blocked radiator or insufficient coolant flow.

Check the engine coolant level in the overflow reservoir and radiator. Low coolant reduces the heat exchange capacity of the oil cooler and allows oil temperature to rise above normal before coolant temperature peaks.
Inspect the external oil cooler, if equipped, for fin blockage from road debris, insects, or mud. Clean with low-pressure water or compressed air directed against the airflow direction.

With the engine at operating temperature, use a calibrated infrared thermometer to measure oil temperature at the drain plug area and compare to the ECM reading from Texa or Jaltest live data. A significant difference between measured and reported temperature helps confirm sensor calibration drift.

If oil and coolant temperatures are both elevated, the internal engine oil cooler core (integrated with the block on MP8) may be fouled with scale or silicate gel from degraded coolant. A coolant flush and oil cooler cleaning may be required.
symptoms: Amber warning lamp illuminated on Mack GuardDog Connect or instrument cluster.
Oil temperature gauge reading near or above the normal operating band.
Engine entering a mild derate in sustained high-temperature conditions.
Possible elevated coolant temperature reading if the oil cooler is blocked.
SPN 175 FMI 16 logged as active with driver advisory to reduce load or idle.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 183 FMI 9 means the International ECM is receiving fuel rate data too slowly or inconsistently to trust during operation. Hesitation or a mild derate can follow until CAN communication and fuel metering inputs update at the expected rate. Abnormal update rate faults frustrate fleets because the engine may run mostly fine at cruise, but ProfessionalDieselRepair.com finds intermittent grounds and sensor dropouts are the usual root cause rather than a failed injection pump.
causes: Intermittent ECM power or ground
Voltage dips cause the fuel rate calculation loop to miss cycles, setting FMI 9 even when injectors physically deliver fuel.
Faulty fuel rail pressure sensor signal
Fuel rate is derived partly from rail pressure data; a lagging sensor stalls update timing.
J1939 backbone noise or terminator issues
CAN errors delay shared parameter broadcasts the ECM uses for fuel rate modeling.
steps: Log SPN 183 fuel rate update frequency in ServiceMaxx at idle and 1500 RPM; updates should occur multiple times per second, not stall for longer than 1 second.
Check ECM main power and ground at the battery box; voltage drop from battery positive to ECM supply should stay under 0.3V cranking.
Inspect the fuel rail pressure sensor connector and high-pressure pump wiring for intermittent pins causing calculated rate gaps.
Wiggle-test the ECM 70-pin harness while monitoring fuel rate — a frozen value confirms a communication break.
Update ECM software if bulletin exists for fuel rate calculation patches, then clear codes and repeat a loaded snap throttle test.
symptoms: MIL active with SPN 183 FMI 9 in ServiceMaxx or Noregon JPRO

Fuel economy display freezes or jumps erratically

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3242 FMI 16 – DPF Inlet Temperature High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 16 – DPF Inlet Temperature High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 16 indicates that the temperature at the DPF inlet has exceeded the acceptable operating threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and like the outlet temperature fault is a serious condition that can damage the DPF substrate and exhaust components. The inlet sensor is located before the DPF and high readings here often point to combustion or regen system issues upstream of the filter.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF warning light illuminated Active engine derate condition 
Excessive exhaust temperatures 
Possible burning smell from exhaust system 
Regeneration may be active or stuck 
May appear alongside DPF outlet temperature codes
Cause
This code triggers when the DPF inlet temperature sensor detects temperatures above the maximum threshold before the exhaust enters the filter. Common causes include:
Engine running excessively rich causing high exhaust temperatures 
Uncontrolled regeneration or over fueling during regen cycle 
Faulty HC dosing injector delivering too much fuel 
Turbocharger issues affecting exhaust temperature management 
Failed DPF inlet temperature sensor giving false readings 
Exhaust brake or restriction causing heat buildup 
Faulty regen control system unable to regulate inlet temperatures
Can You Keep Driving?
No. High DPF inlet temperatures can rapidly damage the filter substrate and exhaust components. Stop the vehicle safely away from flammable materials and allow the exhaust system to cool before any further diagnosis or operation.
Recommended Action
Stop the vehicle and allow the exhaust to cool completely. Do not initiate a regeneration with this fault active. Have the HC dosing injector, engine fueling system, turbocharger, and regen control system inspected by a qualified diesel technician. Check for signs of DPF substrate damage before returning to service.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the temperature entering the DPF has exceeded the maximum acceptable threshold, indicating a serious condition upstream of the filter that requires immediate attention.
 
 
What causes SPN 3242 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are engine over fueling, an uncontrolled regeneration, a faulty HC dosing injector, turbocharger issues, or a failed DPF inlet temperature sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3242 FMI 16?
 
No. Continued operation with high DPF inlet temperatures risks permanent damage to the filter and exhaust system components. Stop safely and allow the system to cool.
 
 
Will SPN 3242 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. The ECM will trigger an immediate derate to protect the DPF and exhaust system from damage caused by excessive inlet temperatures.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3242 FMI 16?
 
The root cause must be diagnosed and repaired. Have the HC dosing injector, engine fueling, and regen control system inspected. Do not attempt regeneration until the cause of the high inlet temperature has been identified and resolved.

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3242 FMI 1 – DPF Inlet Temperature Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 1 – DPF Inlet Temperature Low
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 1 indicates that the temperature at the DPF inlet is below the minimum threshold required for proper aftertreatment operation. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and means the exhaust is not reaching the temperatures needed to support passive or active regeneration, which will allow soot to accumulate in the DPF over time.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF or regen warning light illuminated 
Passive regeneration unable to occur 
DPF soot load gradually increasing 
Reduced aftertreatment system efficiency 
May appear during cold weather or extended idling operation
Cause
This code triggers when the DPF inlet temperature sensor detects exhaust temperatures below the minimum required threshold. Common causes include:
Extended idling preventing exhaust from reaching operating temperatures 
Frequent short trip operation not allowing engine to fully warm up 
Faulty or stuck open thermostat causing low coolant and exhaust temperatures Failed 
DPF inlet temperature sensor giving false low readings 
Exhaust system heat loss from damaged insulation or wrapping 
Engine running lean or misfiring reducing exhaust temperatures 
Cold weather operation combined with light load duty cycles
Can You Keep Driving?
Driving is possible but low DPF inlet temperatures prevent passive regeneration from occurring. Over time soot will accumulate requiring active or parked regeneration. If the underlying cause is a faulty thermostat or sensor it should be addressed to prevent ongoing aftertreatment issues.
Recommended Action
Check engine operating temperature and thermostat function first. Review the vehicle duty cycle — extended idling and short trips are common causes. If operating temperatures are normal inspect the DPF inlet temperature sensor and wiring for faults. Ensure exhaust system insulation is intact to prevent excessive heat loss.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 1 mean?
 
It means the DPF inlet temperature is below the minimum required threshold, preventing passive regeneration from occurring and allowing soot to gradually accumulate in the filter.
 
 
What causes SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
The most common causes are extended idling, frequent short trips, a faulty thermostat causing low engine temperatures, or a failed DPF inlet temperature sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
Driving is possible but the inability to passively regenerate will cause soot to accumulate over time leading to more severe DPF faults if not addressed.
 
 
Will SPN 3242 FMI 1 cause a derate?
 
Not immediately but ongoing soot accumulation from lack of passive regeneration will eventually trigger DPF soot load codes and derate conditions.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
Address the root cause of low exhaust temperatures — check the thermostat, review duty cycle, and inspect the temperature sensor. Once DPF inlet temperatures return to normal operating range the code should clear.

DPF or regen warning light illuminated 
Passive regeneration unable to occur 
DPF soot load gradually increasing 
Reduced aftertreatment system efficiency 
May appear during cold weather or extended idling operation
Cause
This code triggers when the DPF inlet temperature sensor detects exhaust temperatures below the minimum required threshold. Common causes include:
Extended idling preventing exhaust from reaching operating temperatures 
Frequent short trip operation not allowing engine to fully warm up 
Faulty or stuck open thermostat causing low coolant and exhaust temperatures Failed 
DPF inlet temperature sensor giving false low readings 
Exhaust system heat loss from damaged insulation or wrapping 
Engine running lean or misfiring reducing exhaust temperatures 
Cold weather operation combined with light load duty cycles
Can You Keep Driving?
Driving is possible but low DPF inlet temperatures prevent passive regeneration from occurring. Over time soot will accumulate requiring active or parked regeneration. If the underlying cause is a faulty thermostat or sensor it should be addressed to prevent ongoing aftertreatment issues.
Recommended Action
Check engine operating temperature and thermostat function first. Review the vehicle duty cycle — extended idling and short trips are common causes. If operating temperatures are normal inspect the DPF inlet temperature sensor and wiring for faults. Ensure exhaust system insulation is intact to prevent excessive heat loss.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 1 mean?
 
It means the DPF inlet temperature is below the minimum required threshold, preventing passive regeneration from occurring and allowing soot to gradually accumulate in the filter.
 
 
What causes SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
The most common causes are extended idling, frequent short trips, a faulty thermostat causing low engine temperatures, or a failed DPF inlet temperature sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
Driving is possible but the inability to passively regenerate will cause soot to accumulate over time leading to more severe DPF faults if not addressed.
 
 
Will SPN 3242 FMI 1 cause a derate?
 
Not immediately but ongoing soot accumulation from lack of passive regeneration will eventually trigger DPF soot load codes and derate conditions.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3242 FMI 1?
 
Address the root cause of low exhaust temperatures — check the thermostat, review duty cycle, and inspect the temperature sensor. Once DPF inlet temperatures return to normal operating range the code should clear.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 0 on DOC temperature indicates the aftertreatment system has detected temperatures above the calibrated severe threshold. True causes include excessive regen fueling, abnormal combustion events, and exhaust restriction effects. Sensor bias high — a failed EGT sensor reading extreme values — is a common cause that produces the fault without any actual thermal event. Comparing multiple aftertreatment temperature sensors for plausibility is the most efficient first gate before any major fueling component replacement.
causes: Failed EGT sensor — reading extreme values without true overtemp
Excessive regen fueling — uncontrolled hydrocarbon injection
Abnormal combustion events — raw fuel reaching DOC
Exhaust restriction effects — backpressure affecting temperature distribution
Uncontrolled regen fueling issues — injector or dosing control fault
steps: Single Action Gate — Multi-Sensor Temperature Correlation

Compare DOC inlet, DOC outlet, and DPF inlet temperatures for plausibility. A single sensor reading extreme values while others are normal supports sensor failure. Correlated high temperatures across multiple sensors support a true thermal event.
Binary Decision Gate — EGT Sensor Circuit Check

Verify EGT sensor circuit integrity. EGT sensors are thermocouple or RTD style depending on OEM. An open circuit or failed sensor can produce extreme high readings. Check sensor resistance and circuit continuity.
Override Manager — Regen Fueling Strategy Evaluation

Evaluate regen fueling control. If a true thermal event is confirmed by multiple sensors, investigate regen fueling strategy. Check for uncontrolled hydrocarbon injection from a stuck-open dosing injector or abnormal post-injection fueling.
Safety Interceptor — Exhaust Restriction Check
Inspect for exhaust restriction that could affect temperature distribution. A severely restricted DPF can cause abnormal temperature gradients during regen.
Resume Point — Combustion Abnormality Evaluation
Evaluate for combustion abnormalities contributing to raw fuel reaching the DOC. Misfiring cylinders or injector faults can deliver unburned fuel to the aftertreatment system.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Temperature Confirmation
After repair, monitor DOC temperature during a regen cycle. Confirm temperatures remain within OEM specification throughout the regen event.
Repair Ledger Output — Component Decision
Replace EGT sensor if circuit failure is confirmed. Address regen fueling components only after true thermal event is confirmed by multi-sensor correlation.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace EGT sensor if circuit failure or extreme bias is confirmed.
2 . Address regen fueling control components if uncontrolled fueling is confirmed.
3 . Repair any combustion faults contributing to raw fuel in the exhaust.
4 . Address exhaust restriction if found.
5 . Do not attempt regen until root cause is identified and repaired.
Verification Steps
Confirm DOC temperature remains within OEM specification during regen after repair.
Verify multi-sensor temperature correlation is plausible after repair.
Confirm SPN 3242 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Monitor regen completion without overtemp abort.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGT sensor circuits at every major aftertreatment service.
✓ Address injector faults promptly to prevent raw fuel in exhaust.
✓ Maintain DPF soot load within normal range to prevent extreme regen temperatures.
✓ Inspect regen fueling components per OEM service intervals.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity

High if true overtemp. Stop regen attempts until root cause is verified safe. A failed sensor producing a false overtemp is less dangerous than an uncontrolled regen event — treat as High until multi-sensor correlation confirms sensor failure.
symptoms: DOC overtemp fault active
Aftertreatment temperature high
Regen temperature excessive
Regen abort from overtemp
Aftertreatment protection strategy active

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 1 means the DPF intake gas temperature sensor on Detroit Diesel engines reads below the ECM normal range, often during regeneration. Failed regen cycles allow soot to accumulate, leading to progressive derate and possible five-MPH limp mode. Verify probe placement and exhaust integrity before replacing the sensor. The DPF intake gas temperature probe tells the Detroit aftertreatment module whether exhaust entering the filter is hot enough for safe regeneration. When SPN 3242 FMI 1 sets, regen may abort and soot load climbs until the truck derates. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com finds probe seating and upstream exhaust leaks cause this code more often than a failed probe element on DD15 OneBox systems.
causes: DPF intake temperature probe pulled out of exhaust stream
Vibration loosens the probe in its bore, so the tip sits in ambient air instead of hot exhaust, reading 200-400°F during active regen.
Upstream exhaust leak cooling the probe tip
Leaking flex pipe or V-clamp joints upstream of the probe draw in ambient air, lowering measured temperature despite normal combustion.
Failed temperature probe (open circuit)
Internal probe element failure produces maximum resistance, which the ECM reads as extremely low exhaust temperature.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) and monitor SPN 3242 (DPF intake temp) and SPN 3246 (DPF outlet temp) during a forced parked regen — intake should reach 900-1,100°F within 20 minutes; readings stuck below 300°F indicate sensor or upstream heat loss.
Inspect the DPF intake temperature probe at the DOC/DPF inlet flange; verify the probe tip is fully seated in the exhaust stream and the 4-pin connector is tight with no soot staining at the seal.
Measure probe resistance at room temperature — Detroit probes typically read 200-300 ohms at 77°F; an open circuit above 5,000 ohms confirms probe failure.
Check for exhaust leaks upstream of the probe (flex pipe, V-clamps, EGR cooler gasket) that allow ambient air to cool the sensor tip and produce a falsely low reading.
Verify the 5V reference on the sensor circuit reads 4.8-5.2V with key on — low reference voltage can bias temperature readings across multiple aftertreatment sensors.
Replace the probe or repair leaks, perform a forced regen, and confirm SPN 3242 exceeds 900°F and tracks within 150°F of SPN 3246 during active regen.
symptoms: DPF regen attempts start then abort within 5-10 minutes
SPN 3242 intake gas temperature reads below 200°F during active regen when outlet temp is rising
Amber check lamp with increasing soot load percentage on DDDL
Reduced fuel economy as passive regen efficiency drops
Eventual torque derate as soot load exceeds 80-100% threshold
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 1: Low DPF Intake Gas Temperature

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 3 means the DPF intake gas temperature sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage, an electrical fault rather than a genuine overtemp event. It's a medium-severity code with no derate - check the harness before replacing the sensor. This is a straightforward circuit fault that mostly affects regen scheduling accuracy rather than posing an immediate risk. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always confirms the fault is electrical, not thermal, before touching any parts.
causes: Chafed or heat-damaged signal wire near the DPF canister
Prolonged heat exposure degrades wire insulation over time, letting the signal wire short against a powered or grounded surface.
Corroded connector pin
Moisture intrusion at the connector can corrode pins, producing an intermittent high-voltage reading.
Internally failed sensor element
A cracked thermocouple inside the sensor can present as an open circuit, mimicking the same electrical fault signature.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on Mack Premium Tech Tool to confirm the reading is pinned at an unrealistic high value.
Locate the DPF intake temperature sensor ahead of the filter and unplug the connector.
Back-probe signal and ground with a multimeter, key on engine off - a reading near 5V with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness-side fault.
Inspect the signal wire for chafing or heat damage along its routing near the DPF canister and exhaust piping.
Test sensor resistance at the connector against the OEM temperature/resistance chart to rule out an internally open sensor.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor as needed, then clear the code and confirm a plausible reading returns.
symptoms: Check engine lamp illuminated, typically no derate
Possible irregular or delayed regeneration cycles
No major drivability complaint in most cases
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 3242 FMI 3: DPF Intake Temperature Circuit Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 3 means the DPF intake gas temperature sensor circuit is reading voltage above normal, usually an open sensor or broken wire. It is Medium severity and typically halts DPF regeneration until repaired, though it does not shut the engine down. The DPF intake temperature sensor sits right at the entrance to the diesel particulate filter and gives the ECM its first read on exhaust temperature entering the aftertreatment system. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees SPN 3242 FMI 3 most often on trucks that have recently had DPF or exhaust work done, since the sensor connector is easy to bump loose or leave partially seated during reassembly. Because the ECM uses this reading as a safety input before allowing regeneration, the fault effectively stops the truck from cleaning its own filter until it's addressed, which makes prompt repair worthwhile even though the engine keeps running normally otherwise.
causes: Loose or corroded DPF intake sensor connector
Exhaust heat cycling degrades connector seals over time, and a connector left partially seated after service work reads as an open circuit.
Broken sensor signal wire from heat damage
The wiring near the DPF canister is exposed to high exhaust temperatures, and insulation can crack and break the conductor over time.
Failed internal sensor element
Thermocouple-style temperature sensors can fail internally from thermal fatigue after extended high-heat cycling near the DPF.
Cracked or damaged DPF canister causing exhaust leaks near the sensor bung
A cracked canister can affect sensor readings indirectly by changing local exhaust flow and temperature around the sensor mount.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) and confirm SPN 3242 FMI 3, then check current DPF soot load percentage to gauge urgency.
Locate the DPF intake temperature sensor at the front of the DPF canister and inspect the connector for corrosion or a disconnected pin.
With the connector unplugged, verify the sensor circuit isn't open by checking for the expected 5-volt reference and ground at the harness side connector.
Check sensor resistance with a multimeter against Detroit Diesel spec at ambient temperature - an open sensor will read infinite resistance (OL), consistent with the voltage-above-normal fault.
Replace the sensor if it reads open, or repair the harness if voltage checks point to a broken wire, then clear codes and monitor for successful regeneration on the next drive cycle.
symptoms: Amber MIL illuminated
DPF regeneration inhibited or failing to complete
Rising soot load percentage over time without successful regen
Possible reduced power warning if soot load climbs too high
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 3: DPF Intake Temp Sensor High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 3 on Peterbilt means the DPF inlet temperature sensor signal is shorted to a high source or above normal voltage range. This is an electrical fault, not a real overtemperature event. Check the sensor element and harness before replacing any aftertreatment hardware. A high-voltage fault on a temperature sensor is almost always a broken wire or a dead sensor, not a real fire in the DPF. SPN 3242 FMI 3 on Peterbilt trucks tells you the signal circuit is electrically faulted — the ACM is reading the equivalent of a disconnected sensor pegged at maximum scale. Tracing that circuit to the DPF inlet sensor and its harness is a straightforward task that can be done with basic tools.
causes: Signal wire shorted to power supply (electrical)

If the sensor signal wire insulation chafes against a 12V supply wire or body ground near the DPF housing, it can create a short-to-power condition that forces the signal voltage to the rail, registering as a full-scale high temperature reading at the ACM.
Open circuit in sensor element or wiring (electrical)

A broken wire or failed internal sensor element presents as infinite resistance on the signal circuit. On some ACM designs, an open circuit pulls the signal line to supply voltage, triggering FMI 3 rather than FMI 5 (open circuit) depending on the internal pull-up resistor configuration.
Internal sensor failure from heat cycling (aftertreatment)
Moderate

The DPF inlet temperature sensor operates in extreme thermal cycles, from cold start to regeneration temperatures above 600°C. Repeated thermal stress fatigues the internal element connections, causing the sensor to fail open or intermittently.
Damaged connector body or terminal corrosion (electrical)
Moderate

The connector positioned at the DPF inlet is exposed to condensation, road spray, and heat cycles that corrode terminals and crack the connector body, creating intermittent or sustained signal faults without any obvious wire damage.
steps: 1. Connect PACCAR Davie4 and read live SPN 3242 temperature. FMI 3 typically shows the sensor pegged at maximum scale (often >950°C or full-range analog value) rather than a realistic exhaust temperature. Confirm the fault is active and not stored-only.

2. With the key ON and engine OFF, measure the signal circuit voltage at the sensor connector with a multimeter. Normal resting signal voltage on PACCAR temperature circuits is typically 0.5-1.0 V (corresponding to ambient). A reading of 4.5-5 V or above confirms the signal wire is shorted to supply voltage.

3. Disconnect the sensor and measure resistance across the sensor element pins. A thermocouple element that has failed open will show infinite resistance; a thermistor-type sensor should show resistance within the range specified in the PACCAR service manual for the ambient temperature.

4. Inspect the harness from the DPF inlet sensor back toward the ACM for chafing against the DPF canister, exhaust flex, or firewall grommet. Heat damage to insulation at the DPF mounting region is a common failure point — the harness runs in a high-temperature zone.

5. Substitute a known-good DPF inlet temperature sensor and clear the fault with Diesel Laptops or Davie4. If the live temperature reads a plausible exhaust value and the fault does not return, the original sensor has failed internally.
symptoms: Moderate derate or regen-inhibit lamp on dash
Active regen disabled or prevented by ACM
DPF intake temperature reads implausibly high (maxed out) or erratic in Davie4
No other aftertreatment faults if the sensor or harness is the isolated failure
procedures_full.source_title: Peterbilt SPN 3242 FMI 3: DPF Intake Gas Temperature Sensor Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 16 means DPF intake gas temperature is running above the moderately severe threshold, usually during a regeneration event. This is a high-severity aftertreatment code - address it before repeated hot regens crack the DPF substrate. Overtemp regen events are one of the more expensive mistakes a shop can miss. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this code as a call to check doser and fueling behavior immediately, since letting the ECM keep running hot regens on a truck with an underlying fueling problem is how a sensor-level warning turns into a substrate-replacement bill.
causes: Stuck-open or over-fueling HC doser injector
Excess raw fuel dumped into the exhaust during active regen drives DPF intake temperature well past the target range.
Excessive post-injection fueling from a compensating ECM strategy
The ECM may over-fuel during regen to compensate for a separate fault elsewhere in the aftertreatment system, indirectly overheating the DPF.
Drifting or failed DPF intake temperature sensor
A sensor reading falsely high can trigger the code without a genuine overtemp condition, but this should only be assumed after cross-checking against the DOC outlet sensor.
steps: Pull freeze-frame data on DDDL and compare DPF intake gas temperature against the DOC outlet and DPF outlet temps to see where the excess heat originates.
Check the fuel injector spray pattern and HC doser (if equipped) for a stuck-open condition dumping excess fuel into the exhaust stream during regen.
Inspect the DPF intake temperature sensor wiring for damage, since a drifting sensor can also produce a falsely high reading.
Verify turbo and EGR operation are not forcing the ECM to compensate with more aggressive regen fueling.
Run a forced parked regeneration on DDDL while monitoring temperature rise rate against OEM specification to confirm the fault is a genuine overtemp event.
If temperatures are confirmed abnormally high, do not clear the code and return to service without addressing the root cause - repeated overtemp regens can crack the DPF substrate.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with possible active regen indicator staying lit longer than normal
Strong exhaust heat smell or shimmer visible near the DPF during regen
Elevated EGT readings on the dash gauge if equipped
Possible power derate if temperature climbs further
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3242 FMI 16: DPF Intake Temperature Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 16 on PACCAR means DPF intake temperature is above the moderately severe high threshold. The ACM has suspended regen and may derate the engine. Check HC doser function and engine oil consumption before concluding the sensor is faulty. High DPF inlet temperature on a PACCAR MX is not always a sensor problem — it can represent a genuinely dangerous thermal event if the HC doser is stuck open or oil is feeding an uncontrolled exotherm in the DOC. SPN 3242 FMI 16 demands that you figure out whether the temperature reading is real before deciding how to fix it. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always cross-checks the inlet temp against adjacent sensors in Davie4 first — an isolated spike on SPN 3242 alone is a sensor story; widespread elevated temperatures across the aftertreatment system is a doser or combustion story.
causes: HC doser injector stuck open or leaking check valve (aftertreatment)

The hydrocarbon dosing injector that provides fuel to the DOC for active regen can stick in the open position or develop a leaking check valve. Uncontrolled fuel delivery to the DOC creates an exothermic reaction that produces extreme temperatures at the DPF inlet.
Engine oil entering the exhaust stream (mechanical)
Moderate

Oil bypassing into the exhaust via worn valve stem seals, piston rings, or a degraded crankcase breather/separator provides hydrocarbons to the DOC that oxidize and spike aftertreatment temperatures above expected regen levels.
DPF inlet temperature sensor reading falsely high (electrical)
Moderate

The sensor element or its signal circuit can fail in a high-reading direction, producing an FMI 16 fault without any actual overtemperature event in the aftertreatment system. Confirmed by comparing SPN 3242 to adjacent temperature sensors.
Active regen thermal runaway (aftertreatment)
Less Common

Under certain conditions — high altitude, maximum load, or accumulated excess soot — an active regen can generate more exothermic heat than expected, pushing DPF inlet temperature above the FMI 16 threshold. This is a real temperature event, not a sensor fault.
steps: 1. Connect PACCAR Davie4 and pull the freeze-frame data from when SPN 3242 FMI 16 set. Note the DPF inlet temperature value, engine RPM, load, active regen status, and HC doser commanded state at the moment of fault set. This establishes whether the overtemperature occurred during regen or under normal driving conditions.

2. Check the HC (hydrocarbon) doser injector via Davie4. If the fault set during an active regen, verify HC doser rail pressure and commanded dosing rate were within spec. An HC doser injector stuck open floods the DOC with fuel, causing an uncontrolled exothermic reaction that spikes DPF inlet temperature.

3. Verify DPF inlet temperature against adjacent sensors. In Davie4, compare SPN 3242 (DPF inlet temp) against exhaust temperature sensors upstream (before DOC, if available). If SPN 3242 reads 200°C above the upstream exhaust gas temperature without a regen active, the sensor is reading falsely high.

4. Check for engine oil consumption — inspect the air intake for oil mist, check crankcase breather/separator function, and review oil consumption rate at the last few oil changes. Oil bypassing into the exhaust provides uncontrolled hydrocarbon to the DOC that oxidizes and raises DPF inlet temperature beyond regen conditions.

5. Inspect the HC doser check valve. A failed check valve allows fuel to seep passively into the exhaust stream between commanded doses. Use Jaltest or Davie4 to monitor DPF inlet temperature at idle with regens disabled — a persistently elevated temperature without active dosing indicates passive fuel seep from the doser circuit.
symptoms: High-temperature or aftertreatment warning lamp on dash
Power derate or regen inhibit condition in Davie4
SPN 3242 reading above approximately 700-800°C during regen or above 500°C at highway cruise
Possible smell of burning oil or visible smoke if oil is entering the exhaust
Active regen suspended or terminated early by ACM
procedures_full.source_title: PACCAR SPN 3242 FMI 16: DPF Intake Gas Temperature Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3242 FMI 18 means the DPF inlet temperature is valid but too low for expected regen or load conditions. Verify thermocouple wiring, HC doser operation, and exhaust leaks before replacing sensors. DPF inlet temperature tells the ECM whether active regeneration can safely oxidize soot. On Kenworth trucks, SPN 3242 FMI 18 often appears when regens abort for lack of heat or when a thermocouple reads ambient instead of exhaust gas. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com traces heat input first — the sensor is usually reporting accurately about a cold exhaust stream.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 or Noregon JPRO and log SPN 3242 with DOC outlet (SPN 4766) and DPF outlet (SPN 3246) during a stationary regen.
Verify DPF inlet thermocouple connector pins and harness continuity — open circuits often read ambient temperature.
Inspect for exhaust leaks between the turbo and DPF that bleed heat before the sensor location.
Review HC doser or 7th injector operation on Cummins platforms — no dosing means no regen heat.
Compare sensor reading to an infrared pyrometer at the thermocouple boss before replacing the probe.
symptoms: Amber check-engine or aftertreatment lamp
DPF inlet temperature stuck low during commanded regen attempts
Regen aborts with insufficient temperature logged
DPF soot load climbing because regens cannot reach target heat
Possible white exhaust smoke if HC dosing occurs without adequate temperature rise

field_evidence.excerpt: Kenworth trucks can experience recurring engine derate warnings accompanied by diagnostic trouble codes SPN-5298 FMI 18 and SPN-3246 FMI 25 during their warranty periods. These codes indicate specific issues that may contribute to the engine derate, a protective measure to prevent component damage. The SPN-5298 FMI 18 code points to a fuel system issue, while SPN-3246 FMI 25 relates to problems within the aftertreatment system. Both conditions can trigger engine derate to safeguard the truck’s engine and emission components. Common causes for these codes include faults in fuel filters, pressure sensors, blockages in the diesel particulate filter (DPF), or sensor failures within the selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system. To address this fault, examine the sensor wiring and connectors for any damage or poor contact that may affect signal integrity. Additionally, inspect the fuel pressure sensor itself, ensuring it is free from contamination or signs of failure. procedures_full.overview: FMI 1 on DPF outlet temperature indicates the sensor reports below-normal temperatures during conditions where higher temperatures are expected — typically during active regen. Failed EGT sensor, exhaust leaks before the sensor, insufficient regen fueling, DOC inefficiency, and low-load conditions are the primary causes. An open EGT circuit after harness service is a documented cause — the harness runs near hot exhaust components where damage is common. Replacing the DOC or DPF without proving EGT sensor integrity is the most expensive misdiagnosis on this fault.
causes: Failed EGT sensor — dead-low fixed reading from open circuit
Exhaust leak before sensor — diluting temperature reading with ambient air
Insufficient regen fueling — not enough heat for light-off
DOC inefficiency — catalyst not generating expected exotherm
Open EGT circuit after harness service — documented post-service cause
Low-load conditions — insufficient exhaust temperature for regen
steps: Single Action Gate — EGT Sensor Correlation

Compare DPF outlet temperature to DOC inlet and DOC outlet temperatures. A dead-low fixed reading on the outlet sensor while other sensors show normal temperatures confirms sensor or circuit failure. An open EGT circuit typically reads near ambient or at a fixed low value.
Binary Decision Gate — EGT Circuit Continuity

Check EGT sensor circuit continuity. EGT sensors are thermocouple or RTD style — an open circuit produces a fixed low reading. Inspect harness for damage near exhaust components, especially after any recent aftertreatment service.
Override Manager — Exhaust Leak Inspection

Inspect exhaust connections before the DPF outlet sensor for leaks. An exhaust leak allows ambient air to dilute the temperature reading, producing a false low value. Inspect gaskets, clamps, and sensor boss seating.
Safety Interceptor — Regen Fueling Evaluation

Evaluate regen fueling enable conditions and fueling quantity. If sensor and exhaust integrity are confirmed, insufficient regen fueling from a dosing injector fault or control issue prevents light-off.
Resume Point — DOC Health Assessment

Assess DOC health if regen fueling is confirmed correct but outlet temperatures remain low. A degraded DOC catalyst does not generate the expected exotherm, preventing DPF outlet temperatures from reaching regen levels.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Temperature Confirmation
After repair, monitor DPF outlet temperature during a regen cycle. Confirm temperatures reach OEM regen threshold and regen completes successfully.
Repair Ledger Output — Component Decision
Replace EGT sensor if circuit failure is confirmed. Address regen fueling or DOC only after sensor and exhaust integrity are proven.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace EGT sensor or repair harness if open circuit is confirmed.
2 . Repair exhaust leaks before the DPF outlet sensor.
3 . Address regen fueling faults if fueling is confirmed insufficient.
4 . Replace DOC only after sensor, exhaust, and fueling are proven good.
5 . Seal harness routing against future heat damage near exhaust components.
Verification Steps
Confirm DPF outlet temperature reaches regen threshold after repair.
Verify regen completes successfully after repair.
Confirm SPN 3246 FMI 1 does not return after repair.
Monitor soot load returns to normal range after successful regens.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGT harness routing after any aftertreatment service.
✓ Verify exhaust connections near EGT sensors at every major service.
✓ Maintain DOC health per OEM service intervals.
✓ Address regen fueling faults promptly to prevent soot accumulation.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High when regens cannot complete. Soot load increases with each failed regen. Address before soot load reaches critical levels requiring forced regen or DPF service.
symptoms: DPF outlet temp low fault active
Regen will not light off
Failed regen temperature
Incomplete regen from low outlet temp
High soot load from failed regens

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3246 FMI 3 means the Cat DPF outlet gas temperature sensor circuit is reading voltage above normal, typically from an open sensor or broken wire. It is Medium severity and will usually inhibit DPF regeneration, though the engine keeps running normally. The DPF outlet temperature sensor measures exhaust temperature as it leaves the particulate filter, giving the Cat ECM the second half of the temperature picture it needs to safely manage active regeneration. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com regularly sees SPN 3246 FMI 3 alongside its upstream counterpart, SPN 3242, since both sensors sit in the same harsh thermal environment and share similar failure patterns. The key thing to understand is that this fault stops the truck from regenerating its own filter rather than causing any immediate drivability problem, so it's worth fixing quickly before soot load builds to a level that forces a more involved cleaning or forced regen.
causes: Heat-damaged sensor wiring near the DPF canister
Extended exposure to high exhaust temperatures cracks wire insulation over time, eventually breaking the conductor and opening the circuit.
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Vibration and thermal cycling loosen connector locks over time, and moisture intrusion corrodes the pin contacts.
Failed internal sensor element
The thermocouple element inside the sensor can fail from repeated extreme heat cycling during active regeneration events.
Physical damage from a DPF canister repair or replacement
Sensor bungs or wiring can be accidentally damaged during aftertreatment component service if care isn't taken during reassembly.
steps: Connect Cat ET and confirm SPN 3246 FMI 3 is active, then check current DPF soot load and regeneration status.
Locate the outlet temperature sensor at the rear of the DPF canister and inspect the connector for corrosion or heat damage to the wiring.
Unplug the sensor and check for the expected reference voltage at the harness connector, then verify sensor resistance with a multimeter against Cat spec.
Inspect the wiring route from the sensor to the ECM for chafing or heat-damaged insulation near the exhaust piping.
Replace the sensor or repair the harness as needed, clear codes with Cat ET, and confirm normal regeneration behavior on the next duty cycle.
symptoms: Amber diagnostic lamp illuminated
DPF regeneration inhibited or repeatedly interrupted
Rising soot load percentage on scan tool over successive drive cycles
No noticeable change in drivability initially

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3246 FMI 3 on a Freightliner is a DPF outlet gas temperature sensor voltage-high fault—the signal circuit is shorted to a power source. This is an electrical wiring fault, not a temperature or aftertreatment mechanical failure. Perform a sensor unplug test with the key on to isolate the short before ordering a sensor. Freightliner SPN 3246 FMI 3 is an aftertreatment instrumentation fault: the DPF outlet exhaust gas temperature sensor signal voltage is above the valid range, indicating a short to a high-voltage source somewhere in the signal circuit. On Cascadia trucks with DD13 or DD15 engines, the EGT sensors are critical feedback for active DPF regeneration—without an accurate outlet temperature, the ACM cannot confirm a regen is reaching target temperature (typically 500–600°C DOC outlet) and will halt regeneration. The sensor itself is rarely the problem with FMI 3; the wiring harness near the aftertreatment system heat shield is the most common failure point. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com documents the Cascadia aftertreatment harness routing and common chafe locations.
causes: Sensor harness chafed against exhaust heat shield, shorted to 5V reference (electrical/sensor)
High

The DPF outlet sensor harness runs along the aftertreatment canister where it is exposed to high heat and vibration. Insulation breakdown at metal edge contact points allows the signal wire to short to the adjacent 5V reference wire or sensor supply wire, pulling the signal above the valid range and triggering FMI 3.
Moisture or contamination in the sensor connector causing cross-pin short (electrical/sensor)
Medium

Water intrusion or road grime contamination in the EGT sensor connector can create a conductive path between the 5V reference pin and the signal pin. This is most common on Cascadia trucks operating in heavy rain or high-pressure wash environments where the connector seal has degraded.
Wiring harness short to battery positive from adjacent circuit damage (electrical/sensor)
Medium

Harness bundles that include both EGT signal wires and 12V or 24V power wires can short together if the harness protective sleeve deteriorates at a common routing clip. This type of short produces full battery voltage on the signal wire—far above the 5V valid range—and often damages the sensor's internal circuit if left unresolved.
Failed DPF outlet temperature sensor with internal short to supply (electrical/sensor)
Low

In a minority of cases the sensor's internal sensing element shorts to the 5V supply pin within the sensor body. This produces FMI 3 even with the harness in perfect condition. The connector unplug test distinguishes this from a harness fault—if FMI 3 persists with the sensor unplugged, the fault is external; if it changes to FMI 5 (open), the sensor was the source.
symptoms: Yellow check engine lamp with SPN 3246 FMI 3 active in DDDL
Active DPF regeneration may be inhibited or produce no temperature feedback
Additional aftertreatment-related codes may follow if regeneration is blocked for extended period (high DPF soot load)
Sensor reads maximum or out-of-range value in DDDL live data (typically full-scale voltage indicating a short to power)
No performance derate in most calibrations—this is an instrumentation fault, not a derate trigger

procedures_full.overview: Mack SPN 3246 FMI 16 means the DPF outlet gas temperature is reading above the normal operating range, indicating a regen runaway, incomplete regen, or failed outlet temperature sensor reading too high. This High-severity fault risks DPF substrate damage and engine derate if the root cause is not identified with Texa or Jaltest live data before any parts are replaced. Mack SPN 3246 FMI 16 is a High-severity aftertreatment fault on MP7 and MP8 engines indicating the DPF outlet gas temperature has exceeded the normal operating range for the current conditions. Unlike a sensor circuit fault (FMI 3 or FMI 4), FMI 16 means the data is valid - the outlet is genuinely reading high, or the sensor has drifted high while still producing a plausible-range signal. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees two primary causes: runaway or incomplete regens from short-haul duty cycles, and HC doser over-dosing that drives exothermic reactions beyond normal regen temperatures. Systematic use of Texa or Jaltest to review regen history and live outlet temp trends separates these causes without unnecessary hardware replacement.
causes: Incomplete or runaway DPF regeneration cycle

Short-haul duty cycles that repeatedly abort regens before completion cause soot accumulation. When a full regen finally attempts, the high soot load generates an exothermic reaction that drives outlet temps above normal range, setting FMI 16.
HC doser stuck open or over-dosing

A failed-open diesel oxidation catalyst hydrocarbon doser injects excess fuel into the exhaust, creating a runaway exothermic oxidation reaction. DPF outlet temps can exceed 900 C (1650 F) in severe cases, causing substrate damage.
Drifted DPF outlet temperature sensor reading high

The thermocouple or NTC sensor element drifts high over time from thermal fatigue. The temperature reading exceeds FMI 16 threshold even under normal regen conditions. Comparing SPN 3246 to SPN 3242 (DPF inlet temp) during idle reveals an implausible differential.
steps: Connect Texa Navigator TXTs or Jaltest diagnostic software and navigate to Aftertreatment. Read SPN 3246 live data alongside SPN 3242 (DPF inlet gas temp) and SPN 1209 (exhaust gas pressure). Normal DPF outlet temp during active regen is 500-700 C (930-1290 F); FMI 16 sets when values exceed the upper normal operating range for the conditions.

Check whether an active or recently commanded regen is in progress. If a regen is actively running, allow it to complete and monitor outlet temp trend. If temp continues to rise above 750 C (1382 F) without stabilizing, stop the regen via Texa or Jaltest service function to prevent DPF substrate melting.

Inspect the DPF outlet temperature sensor (located downstream of the DPF canister) for wiring integrity. Unplug the connector and measure signal voltage at key-on engine-off: normal range is 0.5-4.5 V. A reading above 4.75 V indicates an FMI 3 open circuit on the sensor itself; an above-normal reading with the sensor plugged in and measured in live data confirms actual high temperature.

Check fuel dosing to the diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC) or DPF for evidence of over-dosing. A HC doser stuck open injects excess hydrocarbons into the exhaust stream, creating a runaway exothermic reaction in the DOC and DPF that drives outlet temps well above normal. Check SPN 3480 (HC doser fuel pressure) for anomalies.

If sensor and regen control check out, inspect the DPF canister for cracking or substrate damage from a prior overtemp event. Use Texa or Jaltest to verify differential pressure (SPN 3609) is within normal range; high backpressure combined with high outlet temp confirms DPF restriction as the primary cause.
symptoms: Amber aftertreatment warning lamp active; possible derate if outlet temp continues to rise.
Regen cycle appears to be running longer than normal or failing to complete within expected time.
Exhaust outlet noticeably hotter than usual; potential for heat damage to nearby chassis components.
DPF backpressure (SPN 1209) may also be elevated if a restriction is forcing incomplete regen.
Fault may recur rapidly after clearing if a regen runaway condition is present.
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 3246 FMI 16: DPF Outlet Gas Temperature Above Normal Operating Range

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3246 FMI 16 means the DPF outlet gas temperature on Caterpillar engines exceeds the ECM safe maximum, often above 1,150-1,250°F during regeneration. Runaway regen or a damaged DPF substrate can trigger immediate derate and engine shutdown. Check HC doser fuel pressure and probe integrity before clearing the code.
causes: HC doser over-fueling during active regeneration
A stuck-open doser or fuel pressure above 90 psi dumps excess diesel into the exhaust, spiking outlet temperature beyond 1,250°F.
Melted or collapsed DPF substrate restricting flow
A previously overheated DPF creates localized hot spots that read as high outlet temperature even when intake temperature appears normal.
Failed outlet temperature probe reading high
Probe drift or shorted signal can report temperatures 200°F above actual, though this is less common than genuine thermal events.
steps: Connect Caterpillar ET and log SPN 3246 (DPF outlet temp), SPN 3242 (DPF intake temp), and SPN 4094 (soot load) during the fault event — outlet exceeding intake by more than 400°F with soot above 80% suggests runaway regen.
Inspect the DPF outlet temperature probe at the filter exit flange; confirm the probe is properly seated and the connector shows no melted insulation or soot blow-by at the fitting.
Check the 7th injector (hydrocarbon doser) spray pattern and fuel line pressure — HC doser supply should read 70-90 psi on Cat engines; over-dosing raises outlet temperature above safe limits.
Verify the exhaust brake and variable geometry turbo actuator function — a stuck-closed exhaust brake traps heat in the DPF during regen.
If outlet temp exceeded 1,300°F, inspect the DPF for substrate melt signs (collapsed can, bulged shell, restricted flow) using backpressure test — target below 4.5 kPa at 1,800 RPM.
Replace the probe if resistance is out of spec (200-300 ohms at 77°F), service the HC doser, and perform a controlled parked regen monitoring outlet temp — it must stay below 1,150°F.
symptoms: DPF outlet temperature exceeds 1,250°F on Cat ET during regen — normal peak is 1,000-1,150°F
Amber or red aftertreatment lamp with rapid torque derate
Visible white or blue exhaust smoke during forced regen
Acrid exhaust odor and possible glowing exhaust pipe visible at night
Regen may be forcibly terminated by the ECM with a shutdown countdown
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 3246 FMI 16: High DPF Outlet Gas Temperature

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3246 FMI 18 means DPF outlet gas temperature is valid but below expected range. Compare inlet and outlet readings during regen and inspect exhaust leaks before replacing the thermocouple. The DPF outlet thermocouple confirms soot burn-off is generating enough downstream heat for the SCR and confirms regen progress. Peterbilt trucks throwing SPN 3246 FMI 18 usually have a regen that never warmed the outlet — or a sensor circuit reading ambient. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com validates the temperature gradient across the DPF before any parts swap.
causes: Failed or incomplete regen with insufficient heat at DPF outlet
Regens that abort early leave outlet temperature below the calibrated minimum.
Open DPF outlet thermocouple circuit or corroded connector
Wiring faults pull the reading toward ambient even when exhaust is hot.
Exhaust leak at DPF outlet flange or flex section
Heat escapes before the sensor location, dropping measured outlet temperature.
Heat sink effect from damaged or missing exhaust insulation
Excessive heat loss on cold-weather short trips can keep outlet below threshold.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 or Cummins INSITE depending on engine and log SPN 3246 with SPN 3242 inlet and SPN 4766 DOC outlet.
During stationary regen, verify outlet temperature rises within expected delta of inlet — large gap suggests heat loss or sensor fault.
Inspect outlet thermocouple connector and harness for corrosion, chafing, or broken shield ground.
Check for exhaust leaks at the DPF outlet clamp, flex pipe, or SCR inlet connection bleeding heat.
Cross-check outlet probe with an infrared pyrometer before ordering a replacement thermocouple.
symptoms: Aftertreatment warning lamp with SPN 3246 active
DPF outlet temperature lagging inlet temperature during regen
Regen abort for insufficient outlet temperature rise
Soot load climbing on companion SPN 4094 codes
Cool exhaust at the stack during commanded regen attempts

procedures_full.overview: Diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) tank level is low. Early on this is just a warning, but if you run the tank dry the truck will stage warnings and ultimately a speed-limiting inducement derate. Easy to fix if you catch it in time.
procedures_full.severity_action: Usually OK to continue — monitor closely
causes: DEF tank genuinely low — needs a refill
Faulty DEF level/quality sensor reading low
DEF header/sender wiring or connector fault
Frozen DEF in cold weather reading as low/empty
first_moves: Add DEF — refilling is the first and usually the only step needed for a true low-level warning.
Use fresh, in-spec DEF (don't dilute with water or use contaminated fluid).
If the tank is actually full but it still reads low, suspect the level sensor/wiring.
In freezing temps, allow the DEF heater to thaw the system before condemning the sensor.
common_misdiagnoses: Replacing the level sensor when the tank was simply low.
Topping off with water or off-spec fluid, which then triggers a DEF-quality fault.
Ignoring the warning until it escalates into a speed-limiting inducement derate.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 1 on DEF tank level indicates the level sensor reports below the minimum threshold. The most common cause is actual low fluid — operators ignoring the DEF low warning until the fault sets. A failed level sensor stuck after contamination and harness issues are secondary causes. Performing electrical diagnosis before confirming physical DEF level is the most common wasted-time pattern on this fault. The physical level gate must come first every time.
causes: Actual low fluid — operator ignored DEF low warning
Failed level sensor — stuck after contamination
Harness fault — open or short in level sensor circuit
Tank contamination affecting float or quality header
Sensor stuck after DEF quality event
steps: Single Action Gate — Physical Level Verification

Visually inspect or physically measure DEF tank level before any electrical diagnosis. This is the mandatory first gate — performing electrical diagnosis before confirming physical DEF level wastes time on the most common cause of this fault.
Binary Decision Gate — Refill with Quality DEF

If DEF level is confirmed low, refill with ISO 22241-compliant DEF from a verified source. Test DEF concentration with a refractometer before refilling if quality is suspect. Re-evaluate the fault after refill.
Override Manager — Level Sensor Evaluation
If physical level is confirmed adequate but fault persists after refill, evaluate the level sensor. Level sensor diagnostics are OEM-specific — follow OEM procedure for the specific platform.
Safety Interceptor — Harness and Connector Check
Inspect the DEF tank header connector and ground integrity. A corroded connector or open ground can cause false low level readings regardless of actual DEF volume.
Resume Point — Contamination Assessment
If level sensor is stuck after a DEF quality event, assess tank contamination. Contaminated DEF can affect float operation and quality header function.
Verification Loop — Post-Refill Level Confirmation
After refill, confirm level sensor reads correctly and fault clears. Monitor for return of low level fault over the next operating cycle.
Repair Ledger Output — Header or Sensor Service
Service or replace DEF tank header or level sensor only after physical level is confirmed adequate and electrical diagnosis confirms sensor failure.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Refill DEF tank with ISO 22241-compliant DEF if level is confirmed low.
2 . Test DEF quality with refractometer if contamination is suspected.
3 . Repair connector corrosion or harness faults if found.
4 . Replace level sensor or tank header if sensor failure is confirmed after physical level is adequate.
5 . Drain and flush tank if contamination is found.
Verification Steps
Confirm level sensor reads correctly after refill.
Verify SPN 1761 FMI 1 clears after refill.
Monitor for return of low level fault over the next operating cycle.
Confirm inducement condition does not trigger after refill.
Preventative Measures
✓ Train operators to respond to DEF low warning before the fault sets.
✓ Establish DEF refill intervals based on consumption rate.
✓ Use only ISO 22241-compliant DEF to prevent sensor contamination.
✓ Inspect DEF tank header connector at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High. Running empty risks inducement derate. Physical level verification and refill is the fastest resolution — do not delay for electrical diagnosis when the tank may simply be empty.
symptoms: DEF level low fault active
Empty DEF tank indication
DEF lamp illuminated
Inducement risk from low DEF
SCR dosing reduction from low level

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1761 FMI 1 means the DEF tank level has fallen below the critical threshold and an engine power reduction is imminent. It's Critical severity, but the fix is usually as simple as refilling with certified DEF.
causes: DEF tank genuinely run low or empty
Not a fault at all - the ECM is doing exactly what it's designed to do when fluid runs low. Refilling resolves it immediately.
Corroded DEF tank sender connector
Electrical fault - DEF's corrosive nature attacks the sender's pins over time, producing a false low reading on a full tank.
Failed ultrasonic level sender unit
A genuine sensor hardware failure - confirmed by comparing physical tank level to the sensor's reported percentage in INSITE.
Contaminated or diluted DEF
Fluid quality issue rather than an electrical fault - the wrong concentration can confuse the level/quality sensor's readings.
steps: Visually check the actual DEF level at the tank - this fault is a genuinely low fluid condition most of the time, not a sensor failure.
If the tank is visibly full but the gauge reads empty, connect Cummins INSITE and compare the sensor's reported percentage to the physical level.
Inspect the DEF tank sender wiring harness at the tank header for corrosion - DEF is corrosive and attacks connector pins over time.
If refilling the tank doesn't clear the fault within a normal drive cycle, check the sender unit resistance against Cummins spec using INSITE's live data screen.
Refill with API-certified DEF only - contaminated or diluted DEF can also cause the tank quality sensor to misreport level.
symptoms: DEF gauge reading empty or near-empty
Amber warning light with countdown message on the dash display
Gradual engine power reduction if DEF isn't added
Eventual 5mph speed limit if the tank runs completely dry

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1761 FMI 2 indicates DEF level reading unstable or implausible. Failing level sensor, contaminated header, intermittent wiring, tank slosh with failed damping logic, and connector crystals are the primary causes. False empty warnings with a visually full tank due to header faults is a documented pattern. Replacing the level sensor before proving fluid volume and connector integrity is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Failing level sensor — failing level sensor producing unstable readings
Contaminated header — contaminated DEF tank header producing unstable level signal
Intermittent wiring — intermittent wiring producing unstable level signal
Tank slosh with failed damping logic — tank slosh with failed damping logic producing erratic level reading
Connector crystals — urea crystal contamination at header connector producing intermittent signal
steps: Step 1 — Visual Level Proof

Confirm the actual DEF level visually. False empty warnings with a visually full tank due to header faults is a documented pattern. Confirm the actual DEF volume before any sensor assessment. A visually full tank with a false empty warning confirms a sensor or header fault.
Step 2 — Connector Service

Service the header connector. Urea crystal contamination at the header connector producing intermittent signal is a documented cause. Inspect the header connector for urea crystal contamination, corrosion, and pin tension. Clean or replace the connector if contamination is confirmed.
Step 3 — PID Stability Checks Parked vs Driving

Check PID stability parked versus driving. Monitor the DEF level PID parked and during driving. A PID that is stable parked but erratic during driving confirms a tank slosh or wiring intermittent. A PID that is erratic parked confirms a sensor or connector fault.
Step 4 — Sensor Diagnostics Only After Fluid Volume Is Confirmed

Perform sensor diagnostics only after fluid volume is confirmed. Electrical opens and shorts are only valid after fluid volume is confirmed. Inspect the level sensor and header wiring for electrical faults after fluid volume and connector integrity are confirmed.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Clean or replace header connector if urea crystal contamination is confirmed.
2 . Repair wiring if intermittent is confirmed.
3 . Replace level sensor or header assembly if failure is confirmed after fluid and connector proof.
4 . Refill DEF if level is actually low.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF level reading is stable after repair.
Verify SPN 1761 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Confirm no false empty warnings after repair.
Monitor for return of erratic DEF level events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect header connector for urea crystal contamination at every major service.
✓ Inspect DEF level sensor wiring at every major service.
✓ Use OEM-specification DEF to minimize crystal formation.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium. Can create unnecessary inducement risk if false empty is trusted. Severity
Medium. Can create unnecessary inducement risk if false empty is trusted. Erratic DEF level is volume proof plus header and sensor integrity.

Level sensor intermittent
DEF level erratic
False empty DEF
False empty warning with visually full tank

It's Medium severity and usually resolved with a simple DEF top-off. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this exactly like a low-fuel light - a routine reminder, not a repair concern.
