procedures_full.overview: FMI 18 on DEF tank level indicates the level is below the progressive low threshold, triggering warning escalation toward inducement. True low volume, level sensor stuck, wiring issues, and incorrect refill detection are the primary causes. Operators continuing to drive into inducement on low DEF warnings is a documented operational pattern — refill before dispatch when possible. Physical level proof first prevents sensor diagnosis for a tank that simply needs to be refilled.
causes: True low volume — DEF tank genuinely low from consumption
Level sensor stuck — level sensor stuck at low reading
Wiring issues — wiring fault producing false low reading
Incorrect refill detection — refill not detected by level sensor
steps: Single Action Gate — Verify Physical DEF Level

Verify the physical DEF level by direct inspection or dipstick where accessible. Physical level proof first prevents sensor diagnosis for a tank that simply needs to be refilled. Operators continuing to drive into inducement on low DEF warnings is a documented operational pattern.
Binary Decision Gate — Refill with Verified DEF

Refill the DEF tank with verified ISO 22241-compliant DEF if the physical level is confirmed low. Use a verified DEF source. Confirm the DEF meets specification with a refractometer if quality is in question.
Override Manager — Recheck Status After Refill

Recheck DEF level status after refill. A level that returns to normal after refill confirms the fault was a true low volume condition. A level that remains low after confirmed refill confirms a level sensor or wiring fault.
Safety Interceptor — Diagnose Sensor If Mismatch Remains

Diagnose the level sensor and wiring if the level reading does not match the confirmed physical level after refill. Inspect the tank header connector for corrosion. Perform level sensor circuit tests per OEM procedure.
Resume Point — Refill Before Dispatch When Possible

Refill DEF before dispatch when the progressive low warning is active. The progressive low warning escalates toward inducement as the level continues to drop. Refilling before dispatch prevents inducement during operation.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Level Confirmation
After repair, verify DEF level reads correctly after refill. Confirm SPN 1761 FMI 18 does not return after refill. Monitor for return of false low level readings over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Refill, Sensor, or Wiring Decision
Refill DEF tank if true low volume is confirmed. Repair header connector corrosion if found. Replace level sensor if stuck reading is confirmed after refill and circuit integrity is proven.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Refill DEF tank with verified ISO 22241-compliant DEF.
2 . Repair header connector corrosion if found.
3 . Replace level sensor if stuck reading is confirmed after refill and circuit integrity is proven.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF level reads correctly after refill.
Verify SPN 1761 FMI 18 does not return after refill.
Confirm no inducement warning after refill.
Monitor for return of false low level readings over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Monitor DEF level before every dispatch.

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3031 FMI 1 – DEF Tank Temperature Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 1 – DEF Tank Temperature Low (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 1 indicates that the Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) tank temperature has dropped below the acceptable operating range. This code is most commonly seen on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines during cold weather operation and can affect DEF flow and SCR system performance.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF system warning light illuminated 
Reduced SCR system performance 
Possible engine derate in severe cases
Cause
DEF freezes at 12°F (-11°C). This code triggers when the DEF tank temperature sensor detects fluid that is too cold to flow properly through the dosing system. Common causes include:
Extreme cold weather operation 
Faulty DEF tank heater 
Failed DEF temperature sensor 
Broken or disconnected heater wiring
Can You Keep Driving?
Short distances may be possible but if the DEF system cannot supply fluid to the SCR system due to frozen or cold DEF, a derate condition can follow. In very cold conditions address this before operating the vehicle.
Recommended Action
Allow the vehicle to warm up so the DEF tank heater can bring fluid to operating temperature. If the code persists in normal temperatures, inspect the DEF tank heater, temperature sensor, and associated wiring for faults.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 1 mean?
 
It means the DEF tank temperature has dropped below the minimum operating threshold, which can prevent proper DEF flow to the SCR system.
 
 
What causes SPN 3031 FMI 1?
 
Most commonly cold weather causing DEF to freeze or become too cold to flow. It can also be caused by a failed DEF tank heater or a faulty temperature sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3031 FMI 1?
 
Limited driving may be possible but if the DEF system cannot function properly due to temperature, a derate condition may follow.
 
 
Will SPN 3031 FMI 1 cause a derate?
 
It can if the SCR system is unable to dose DEF properly as a result of the low temperature condition.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3031 FMI 1?
 
Allow the vehicle to warm up fully. If the code clears once the DEF reaches operating temperature, no further action is needed. If it persists, inspect the DEF heater system and temperature sensor.
 
 
Related codes

SPN 3364 FMI 2 
SPN 520372 FMI 16

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3031 FMI 16 - DEF Tank Temperature High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 16 – DEF Tank Temperature High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 16 indicates that the DEF tank temperature has risen above the acceptable operating range. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and is important to address promptly as excessive heat can degrade DEF fluid quality, damage the DEF tank and components, and affect SCR system performance.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF or SCR warning light illuminated 
DEF fluid may degrade faster than normal 
SCR system performance may be affected 
Engine derate possible if DEF quality is compromised
Cause
This code triggers when the DEF tank temperature sensor detects fluid above the maximum acceptable threshold. Common causes include:
Faulty DEF tank cooling system 
DEF tank heater stuck in the on position 
Excessive heat exposure from nearby exhaust components 
Faulty DEF temperature sensor giving false high readings 
Operating in extremely high ambient temperatures 
Blocked or restricted DEF tank cooling lines
Can You Keep Driving?
Short distances may be possible but prolonged exposure to high temperatures will degrade DEF fluid quality and can damage the tank and dosing components. If DEF quality becomes compromised a derate condition will follow. Address this fault promptly.
Recommended Action
Check the DEF tank heater to ensure it is not stuck in the on position. Inspect the DEF tank cooling system and lines for blockages or failures. If the temperature reading seems inconsistent with conditions, have the DEF temperature sensor tested. Allow the system to cool and recheck before continuing operation.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3031 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the DEF tank temperature has risen above the acceptable operating range, which can degrade DEF fluid quality and affect SCR system performance.
 
 
What causes SPN 3031 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are a DEF tank heater stuck on, a failed cooling system for the DEF tank, excessive heat from nearby exhaust components, or a faulty DEF temperature sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3031 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but continued operation with high DEF tank temperature risks degrading the fluid and damaging dosing components, which can lead to further faults and derate.
 
 
Will SPN 3031 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
It can if the high temperature condition degrades DEF quality to the point where the SCR system can no longer meet emissions thresholds.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3031 FMI 16?
 
Identify and fix the heat source — check the DEF tank heater, cooling lines, and temperature sensor. Once the tank temperature returns to the acceptable range and the sensor confirms normal readings the code should clear.

SPN 3509 FMI 16 
SPN 3364 FMI 2 
SPN 3936 FMI 1

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3031 FMI 0 indicates soot load above the highest calibrated threshold. Repeated incomplete regens, underboost soot overproduction, EGR and fueling contributors, short-trip duty cycle, and sensor bias affecting the model are the primary causes. Endless forced regens without correcting abort causes or upstream soot sources is a documented pattern. Replacing the DPF without correcting upstream soot producers is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Repeated incomplete regens — repeated incomplete regens allowing soot to accumulate above highest threshold
Underboost soot overproduction — underboost producing excessive soot overloading the DPF
EGR and fueling contributors — EGR and fueling deviations producing excessive soot
Short-trip duty cycle — short-trip duty cycle preventing regen completion
Sensor bias affecting model — DP or EGT sensor bias producing incorrect soot model inputs
steps: Step 1 — Validate Sensors

Validate DP and EGT sensors before major DPF conclusions. Correlate soot percentage with delta-P and regen history. A conflict between soot model and delta-P requires sensing path service before DPF condemnation. Sensor bias affecting the soot model is a documented cause.
Step 2 — Decode Regen Aborts

Decode regen abort reasons. Endless forced regens without correcting abort causes is a documented pattern. Retrieve the abort reason using OEM abort reason PIDs. Identify the specific abort cause before any regen re-attempt.
Step 3 — Fix Upstream Soot Producers

Fix upstream soot producers before any regen attempt. Underboost producing excessive soot overloading the DPF is a documented cause. Evaluate boost system operation, EGR system operation, and fueling. Address upstream soot contributors before any regen attempt.
Step 4 — Perform Proper Regen

Perform a proper regen after abort cause and upstream soot producers are repaired. Confirm abort cause is repaired and enable sensors are verified before re-running the regen. Monitor EGT trajectory during the regen. A successful regen produces the expected EGT rise and completion.
Step 5 — Clean or Replace DPF When Physical Restriction or Ash Is Proven

Clean or replace the DPF only when physical restriction or ash is proven. A DPF that does not respond to a successful regen confirms physical restriction requiring DPF service. DPF replacement cost is $2,500–$7,000+. Confirm physical restriction before any DPF service.

procedures_full.overview: The ECM models DPF soot load using exhaust temperature, delta-P, and engine operating data. FMI 0 (highest threshold) is set when the model indicates maximum soot accumulation. Repeatedly forcing regens without correcting the root cause — regen aborts, underboost, EGR faults, or fueling issues — will result in immediate return of the fault and potential DPF damage.
causes: Repeated incomplete regens — operator aborts or inhibit conditions
Underboost — excess soot production from insufficient combustion air
EGR faults — abnormal soot production from EGR malfunction
Fueling issues — over-fueling increasing particulate output
Short-trip duty cycle — insufficient time/temperature for regen completion
Sensor bias — bad exhaust temp or delta-P sensors affecting soot model
steps: Single Action Gate — Soot vs Delta-P Agreement
Compare soot load % to delta-P reading. If soot model is high but delta-P is low, suspect sensor bias in the soot model. If both are high, restriction is real.
Binary Decision Gate — Regen Abort History Review
Review regen abort history and inhibit conditions. Identify why regens are not completing — operator aborts, inhibit switches, temperature faults, or system faults.
Override Manager — Exhaust Temp Sensor Verification
Verify exhaust temperature sensor plausibility. Bad temp sensors cause poor regen control and can prevent regens from reaching the required temperature.
Safety Interceptor — Upstream Soot Contributor Check
Check boost levels, EGR operation, and fueling for abnormal soot production. Underboost and EGR faults accelerate DPF loading and must be corrected before regen.
Resume Point — Regen Inhibit Correction
Correct all regen inhibit conditions before attempting a parked regen. A regen attempted with inhibit conditions active will abort again.
Verification Loop — Parked Regen Execution
Perform a parked regen after all upstream corrections. Monitor regen progress and completion. Verify soot load decreases after successful regen.
Repair Ledger Output — DPF Service Decision
If soot load remains high after successful regen, evaluate DPF for ash loading or physical damage. Service or replace as needed.

Repair Steps
1 . Correct all regen inhibit conditions (operator settings, inhibit switches, system faults).
2 . Repair upstream soot contributors (boost leaks, EGR faults, fueling issues).
3 . Verify exhaust temp sensors are plausible.
4 . Perform a successful parked regen after upstream corrections.
5 . Clean DPF if ash loading is confirmed ($400–$1,200).
6 . Replace DPF if cleaning fails or substrate is damaged ($2,500–$7,000+).
Verification Steps
Confirm soot load decreases after successful parked regen.
Verify no regen abort codes return during test drive.
Confirm upstream soot contributors are corrected.
Monitor for return of SPN 3031 FMI 0 over 50+ miles.
Preventative Measures
✓ Follow OEM DPF cleaning intervals.
✓ Train operators not to abort parked regens unless safety requires it.
✓ Address boost and EGR faults promptly.
✓ Avoid excessive short-trip or idle-heavy duty cycles.

High Severity

High severity at highest threshold. Minimize driving until service strategy is completed. Do not continue forcing regens without identifying and correcting the root cause — it will not resolve the fault.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3031 FMI 2 indicates DPF soot load value unstable or conflicting with related sensors. Delta-P sensor and hose issues, EGT instability, software model conflicts, and intermittent sensor supplies are the primary causes. Plugged DP hoses creating unstable calculated restriction and soot behavior is a documented pattern. Replacing the DPF for an unstable soot load reading that is actually a DP hose or sensor input fault is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Delta-P sensor and hose issues — DP sensor or hose fault producing unstable soot model input
EGT instability — EGT sensor instability producing unstable soot model input
Software model conflict — software model conflict producing unstable soot calculation
Intermittent sensor supplies — intermittent sensor supply producing unstable sensor readings
steps: Step 1 — Inspect DP Hoses and Ports

Inspect the differential pressure hoses and ports. Plugged DP hoses creating unstable calculated restriction and soot behavior is a documented pattern. Inspect the DP hoses for plugging, moisture, and damage. Inspect the DP ports on the DPF for plugging and debris. Clean or replace hoses and clear ports if plugging is found.
Step 2 — Validate DP Sensor Electrical

Validate the DP sensor electrical circuit. Verify reference voltage, ground, and signal circuit integrity at the sensor connector. An intermittent sensor supply producing unstable readings requires circuit repair.
Step 3 — Check EGT Stability

Check EGT sensor stability. Wild soot swings with stable pressures suggest model or sensor input faults. Correlate soot percentage with delta-P and EGT. An EGT sensor producing unstable readings requires EGT sensor diagnosis.
Step 4 — Review DPF Service and Reset Status

Review recent DPF service and reset status. A DPF that was serviced without a proper reset may produce unstable soot model behavior. Verify the DPF reset was performed correctly after any recent DPF service.
Step 5 — Address Input Faults Before DPF Decision
Address all input faults before any DPF replacement decision. A DPF replaced for an unstable soot model that is actually a DP hose or sensor input fault will not resolve the unstable soot model.
Step 6 — Verify After Repair
Verify soot load readings are stable after repair. Confirm SPN 3031 FMI 2 does not return. Monitor for return of erratic soot load events over extended operation.

Repair Steps
1 . Clean or replace DP hoses if plugging is found.
2 . Clear DP ports if plugging is found.
3 . Repair DP sensor circuit if intermittent is confirmed.
4 . Repair EGT sensor circuit if instability is confirmed.
5 . Perform DPF reset per OEM procedure after any DPF service.
Verification Steps
Confirm soot load readings are stable after repair.
Verify SPN 3031 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Confirm regen strategy is stable after repair.
Monitor for return of erratic soot load events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect DP hoses for plugging and moisture at every major service.
✓ Inspect DP ports for plugging at every major service.
✓ Verify DPF reset after any DPF service.
✓ Inspect EGT sensor connectors at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. Unstable strategy can delay needed service or overuse regen. Erratic soot load is an input-correlation problem first.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3031 FMI 10 means Cummins EGR valve is not reaching commanded position. Clean carbon deposits and test actuator drive before replacing the valve. The EGR valve recirculates exhaust gas to lower combustion temperatures. When the valve cannot move at the expected rate, Cummins sets SPN 3031 FMI 10 and emissions performance suffers.
causes: Carbon buildup restricting EGR valve movement
Soot and oil vapors pack the valve seat and pintle, causing slow or stuck operation.
Failed EGR actuator motor or vacuum diaphragm
Actuator cannot generate enough force to overcome carbon or binding linkage.
Faulty EGR position sensor feedback
Erratic position signal makes a good valve appear stuck to the ECM.
steps: Command EGR valve open and closed in Cummins INSITE — position should track command within 5% in under 3 seconds.
Remove EGR valve and inspect for carbon packing — clean carbon with walnut blast or OEM-approved cleaner.
Test EGR actuator vacuum supply at 18–22 in-Hg on pneumatic units, or 12.5 V supply on electric actuators.
Check EGR position sensor signal: 0.5–4.5 V sweep across full travel on most units.
Inspect EGR cooler for internal clogging if valve tests good but flow codes persist.
symptoms: Rough idle and combustion knock at low RPM
Excessive black smoke on acceleration
EGR position does not match commanded value in live data
Amber MIL with EGR or emissions message
Failed regen attempts due to high exhaust temperatures

procedures_full.overview: Scania SPN 3031 FMI 10 indicates high resistance in the EGR valve control circuit. This can lead to increased NOx emissions and potential engine derate. Prompt diagnosis and repair are crucial. The Scania SPN 3031 FMI 10 fault code is a critical alert indicating high resistance in the EGR valve control circuit. This issue is significant because it can lead to increased nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and potentially cause the engine to derate as a protective measure. Understanding and addressing this fault code is essential for maintaining engine performance and compliance with emissions standards. Ignoring it can result in reduced engine efficiency and possible legal repercussions due to non-compliance with emissions regulations. Regular diagnostics and proactive maintenance can prevent such issues from escalating.
causes: Corroded connectors

Corrosion at the connectors can increase resistance in the circuit, disrupting the EGR valve's operation. Regular inspection and cleaning can prevent this issue. Corrosion typically occurs due to exposure to moisture and contaminants, which can be mitigated by using dielectric grease and proper sealing techniques.
Damaged wiring harness

Physical damage or wear to the wiring harness can lead to high resistance. This often occurs due to vibration or exposure to harsh conditions. Inspecting the harness for chafing, breaks, or pinched wires can help identify and rectify these issues before they cause significant problems.
Faulty EGR valve

A malfunctioning EGR valve can itself be a source of resistance. This may be due to internal electrical faults or mechanical failure. Testing the valve's electrical components and ensuring its mechanical parts move freely can help determine if the valve is the root cause of the issue.
steps: Inspect the EGR valve wiring harness for visible signs of damage or corrosion. Repair or replace any compromised sections. Ensure that no wires are frayed or exposed, as this can lead to increased resistance.

Use a multimeter to measure the resistance in the EGR control circuit. Compare readings against manufacturer specifications. A higher than normal resistance reading indicates a problem that needs addressing.
Check the EGR valve for proper operation and cleanliness. Remove carbon deposits if necessary, ensuring that the valve moves freely and is not obstructed by soot or debris.
Examine the connectors for any corrosion or loose connections. Clean and tighten as needed. Use a contact cleaner to remove any oxidation that might impede electrical flow.
Clear the fault code with an OBD-II scanner after repairs to verify resolution. Ensure that the code does not reappear after a test drive, indicating that the issue has been successfully resolved.
symptoms: Engine knocking due to improper exhaust gas recirculation.
Poor emissions test results indicating high NOx levels.
Reduced engine performance and efficiency.
Warning lights on the dashboard, indicating an emissions issue.
Potential engine derate to prevent further emissions violations.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 18 on DPF soot load indicates the soot model reports below the expected minimum for conditions, or the model conflicts with other indicators. Faulty delta-P inputs, bad temperature sensors affecting the model, software model drift, recent DPF service without required reset or adaptation, and sensor replacement without calibration process are the primary causes. DPF replaced or cleaned without proper service resets leading to model confusion is a documented pattern on some platforms. An implausible 'always low soot' reading with high delta-P is a conflict that requires investigation — not a confirmation that the filter is clean.
causes: Faulty delta-P inputs — delta-P sensor or hose fault affecting soot model
Bad temperature sensors — EGT sensor fault affecting soot estimation
Software model drift — model calibration drift over time
DPF service without reset — DPF replaced or cleaned without required service reset
Sensor replacement without calibration — sensor replaced without required adaptation process
steps: Single Action Gate — Compare Soot Percentage to Delta-P

Compare the soot load percentage to the delta-P reading. An implausible "always low soot" reading with high delta-P is a conflict — the model is not tracking the actual filter condition. A soot reading that correlates with delta-P and regen frequency confirms the model is tracking correctly.
Binary Decision Gate — Verify Delta-P Sensor and Hoses

Verify delta-P sensor and hose integrity. Faulty delta-P inputs are the most common cause of soot model conflicts. Inspect hoses for contamination and blockage. Verify sensor baseline at KOEO is near zero differential pressure.
Override Manager — Verify EGT Sensor Integrity

Verify EGT sensor integrity. Bad temperature sensors affecting the soot model can produce below-normal soot readings without any actual filter condition change. Compare EGT readings to expected values for operating conditions.
Safety Interceptor — Check Service Reset Status

Check service reset status after any recent DPF service. DPF replaced or cleaned without proper service resets leads to model confusion on some platforms. Follow OEM model relearn procedures if a service reset was not performed after DPF service.
Resume Point — OEM Model Relearn Procedures

Follow OEM model relearn procedures if model drift or post-service confusion is confirmed. Some platforms require specific adaptation procedures after DPF service to re-establish the soot model baseline.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Model Correlation Confirmation

After repair, verify soot load percentage correlates with delta-P and regen frequency. Confirm the model is tracking actual filter condition. Monitor for return of model conflict over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Sensor, Reset, or Model Relearn Decision

Repair or replace delta-P sensor or hoses if faulty inputs are confirmed. Repair or replace EGT sensor if temperature sensor fault is confirmed. Perform OEM model relearn if post-service model confusion is confirmed. Address actual restriction if present after model correction.

2 . Repair or replace EGT sensor if temperature sensor fault is confirmed.

4 . Address actual restriction if present after model correction.
Verification Steps

procedures_full.overview: Electronic injector control circuits are monitored by the ECM for current feedback. FMI 5 (current below normal / open circuit) is set when the ECM cannot drive sufficient current through the injector circuit. This causes a cylinder misfire, rough idle, and power loss. Extended misfire can damage the DPF with unburned fuel. Harness opens and oil-contaminated connectors are more common than injector failure.
causes: Open connector — backed-out or corroded pin under valve cover
Broken injector wire — flex point open at harness loom
Failed injector coil or piezo circuit — internal open
Oil intrusion in valve cover connector — corrosion causing open
ECM driver failure — rare, last resort
steps: Single Action Gate — Connector Inspection
Remove valve cover and inspect injector connector for oil intrusion, corrosion, or backed-out pins. Oil-soaked connectors are the most common cause of FMI 5 on many platforms.
Binary Decision Gate — Injector Resistance Check
Measure injector coil resistance versus OEM specification. An open reading (infinite resistance) confirms internal injector failure. Within spec means the injector is electrically good.
Override Manager — Harness Continuity Test
With injector disconnected, measure continuity from injector connector to ECM connector. Any open in the harness confirms wiring fault before injector replacement.
Safety Interceptor — Short Checks
Verify no short to ground or power on the injector circuit. Shorts can damage ECM drivers and must be found before reconnecting.
Resume Point — Controlled Swap Test
If OEM procedure allows, swap injector to another cylinder and verify fault follows the injector. Only perform if swap is safe and documented per OEM procedure.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Circuit Confirmation
After repair, verify injector circuit resistance and continuity are within spec before starting engine.
Repair Ledger Output — Injector Replacement
Replace injector only after circuit is proven good. Note: some platforms require injector coding or trim file programming after replacement.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 5 means cylinder 1's injector circuit is open or has insufficient current. It's a High severity fault causing a rough idle and power loss - check the wiring before assuming the injector itself is bad. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com finds that a large share of single-cylinder injector codes like this one come down to a broken harness wire, not the injector, especially on trucks that have been through a few valve cover gasket services.
causes: Broken or chafed wire at the injector harness connector
An electrical/wiring fault, not an injector failure - the injector itself may be perfectly healthy while a broken wire prevents it from firing.
Corroded injector connector pins
Another wiring-side issue where poor contact at the connector prevents adequate current flow to the solenoid.
Failed injector solenoid coil
A genuine internal injector failure where the solenoid coil itself has gone open, requiring injector replacement.
ECM driver circuit failure
A control module fault rather than a harness or injector issue, confirmed only if the fault follows neither the harness nor a swapped injector.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) and run the injector solenoid test for cylinder 1 specifically to confirm the open circuit.
Backprobe the cylinder 1 injector connector and check for continuity through the solenoid coil - a healthy injector solenoid typically reads a few ohms of resistance depending on design.
Inspect the injector harness for chafing or a broken wire at the connector, which is a common failure point on high-mileage trucks.
Swap the suspect injector's connector pigtail with a known-good cylinder temporarily to see if the fault follows the wiring rather than the injector.
If the injector itself tests open internally rather than the harness, replace the injector rather than continuing to chase wiring.
symptoms: Rough idle with a felt miss, especially noticeable at low RPM
Check engine light, often with a companion multi-cylinder misfire code
Reduced power and increased fuel consumption
Possible unburned fuel smell from the exhaust
procedures_full.source_title: Freightliner SPN 651 FMI 5: Cylinder 1 Injector Open Circuit

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 5 means the ECM sees an open circuit in the cylinder #1 injector solenoid driver and cannot fire that injector. It is a High severity fault that causes a rough-running miss and MIL, not an automatic shutdown. SPN 651 FMI 5 is one of the most common single-cylinder fault codes techs see on Cummins ISX and ISL engines running the CM2350 or CM2250 ECM. As covered in ProfessionalDieselRepair.com's injector diagnostic guides, the number after SPN simply tells you which cylinder is affected (651 is cylinder 1, 652 is cylinder 2, and so on up through 674), while FMI 5 specifically means current below normal, which almost always points to an open circuit rather than a short. The truck will keep running because the ECM shuts fuel off to the dead cylinder and lets the others carry the load, but that means you are driving on fewer cylinders with reduced power and a rough idle until it is fixed. This code is a good example of a fault that is often blamed on the injector when the real problem is sitting in the harness.
causes: Chafed or broken injector harness wire
The valve cover harness runs tight against the rocker housing and vibrates against sharp edges over time, wearing through insulation and eventually breaking the conductor completely.
Corroded or backed-out harness connector pin
Moisture intrusion at the injector connector corrodes the pin contact surface, raising resistance until the ECM reads it as an open circuit.
Failed injector solenoid winding
The internal solenoid coil inside the injector can open from heat cycling and vibration fatigue, especially past 300,000 miles.
ECM injector driver output failure
An internal ECM driver stage failure will show the same fault, but only after the injector and full harness have already tested good.
steps: Pull the code with Cummins INSITE and confirm SPN 651 FMI 5 is active, then run a cylinder cutout test to verify cylinder #1 contributes nothing to RPM.
Shut the engine off, unplug the injector #1 harness connector at the valve cover, and inspect the pins for corrosion, melted plastic, or backed-out sockets.

With the connector unplugged, measure resistance across the two injector solenoid terminals with a multimeter - most Cummins ISX/ISL CM2350 injector solenoids read between 0.5 and 3 ohms. Infinite (OL) resistance confirms an open winding inside the injector.

If the injector reads good, check the harness itself for continuity from the injector connector back to the ECM injector driver pin, and inspect the valve cover grommet for chafing where the harness passes through.
Clear the code with INSITE, restart, and re-run the cutout test to confirm cylinder #1 is back online before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Rough idle and a noticeable single-cylinder miss under load
Amber MIL illuminated, sometimes flashing during acceleration
Loss of power and reduced fuel economy
Cylinder #1 shows zero contribution on a cylinder cutout test

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 5 means the cylinder #1 injector solenoid circuit is open, causing a misfire on that cylinder. This is a high-severity code with noticeable power loss and rough running - check the valve cover harness before replacing the injector. A single dead cylinder shows up fast in the way a truck runs, and this code points the finger right at it. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always checks the valve cover harness pass-through first, since that's a well-known chafe point on MaxxForce engines that produces the exact same fault as a failed injector.
causes: Chafed or broken wire at the valve cover harness grommet
The harness pass-through point at the valve cover is a known wear spot where insulation rubs through over time, breaking the injector circuit.
Failed injector solenoid
Internal solenoid winding failure directly opens the circuit and requires injector replacement.
Corroded or damaged injector connector
Moisture intrusion at the connector can corrode pins enough to open the circuit intermittently or permanently.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on Navistar's diagnostic software or a comparable Jaltest connection to confirm cylinder #1 is the affected injector.
Inspect the injector #1 connector for corrosion, looseness, or heat damage at the valve cover harness.
Back-probe the injector solenoid circuit with a multimeter, key on engine off, to check for continuity through the driver circuit.
Measure injector solenoid resistance at the connector and compare against OEM specification, typically in the low single-digit ohm range.
Trace the wiring from the injector connector back to the ECM valve cover harness for chafing or a broken conductor.
Replace the injector only after confirming the solenoid itself is open, since a harness break produces the identical fault code.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp with active misfire on cylinder #1
Rough idle and noticeable engine shake at low RPM
Noticeable power loss and possible white smoke from unburned fuel
Increased fuel consumption from the cylinder not firing correctly

procedures_full.overview: FMI 6 on the injector circuit indicates the ECM driver is seeing above-normal current, which is the short or low-resistance class. A shorted injector coil or piezo path, harness short to power, oil-intruded connector bridging pins, and damaged pass-through connectors are the primary causes. Valve-cover connector oil migration causing intermittent shorts is a documented pattern on multiple platforms. Replacing the injector without isolating the short first risks damaging the ECM driver if the short is in the harness rather than the injector. Do not repeatedly command a shorted driver.
causes: Shorted injector coil or piezo path — internal injector failure
Harness short to power — insulation damage or chafe
Oil-intruded connector bridging pins — valve-cover connector oil migration
Damaged pass-through connector — pin-to-pin short
Pinched loom at bracket — insulation damage from installation
steps: Single Action Gate — Disconnect Injector and Remeasure Circuit

Disconnect the cylinder 1 injector and remeasure the circuit. If the high-current condition clears with the injector disconnected, the fault is in the injector. If the high-current condition persists with the injector disconnected, the fault is in the harness. This is the mandatory first isolation step — do not repeatedly command a shorted driver.
Binary Decision Gate — Resistance Check

Measure resistance across the injector terminals. Resistance below OEM minimum specification supports an internal short. Compare to OEM injector resistance specification for the specific injector type (solenoid vs piezo values differ significantly).
Override Manager — Short-to-Power and Short-to-Ground Tests
Test for short to battery voltage and short to ground on the injector circuit harness. Inspect under-cover injector connectors for oil contamination, pinched looms, and rubbed insulation at brackets.
Safety Interceptor — Harness Isolation

Inspect valve-cover connector for oil migration. Oil migrating through the valve-cover connector can bridge pins and create intermittent shorts that appear to be injector failures. Inspect the full harness run from pass-through to injector connector.
Resume Point — Pass-Through Connector Inspection
Inspect the injector harness pass-through connector for pin-to-pin shorts. Damaged pass-through connectors are a documented cause of injector circuit shorts that affect multiple cylinders.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Circuit Confirmation
After repair, verify circuit resistance is within OEM specification. Confirm no short-to-power or short-to-ground conditions remain. Verify cylinder 1 contribution returns to normal after repair.
Repair Ledger Output — Injector or Harness Decision
Replace injector after circuit isolation confirms internal short. Repair harness if short is in the wiring. Replace injector with coding or trim where required by OEM procedure.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness short if found in wiring.
2 . Clean or replace valve-cover connector if oil migration is found.
3 . Repair pass-through connector if pin-to-pin short is found.
4 . Replace injector after circuit isolation confirms internal short.
5 . Code or trim replacement injector per OEM procedure where required.
Verification Steps
Confirm circuit resistance is within OEM specification after repair.
Verify no short-to-power or short-to-ground conditions remain.
Confirm cylinder 1 contribution returns to normal.
Confirm SPN 651 FMI 6 does not return after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect valve-cover connector for oil migration at every valve cover service.
✓ Inspect injector harness for chafe at every major service.
✓ Address valve cover oil leaks promptly to prevent connector contamination.
✓ Inspect pass-through connector at every injector service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity

High if active misfire. Extended misfire can damage aftertreatment from unburned fuel. Do not repeatedly command a shorted driver — ECM driver damage risk. Isolate the short before any injector replacement.
symptoms: Injector cylinder 1 circuit high current fault active
Cylinder 1 misfire
Rough idle from cylinder 1 contribution loss
Rail pressure instability from injector fault
Possible ECM driver damage if short is not isolated

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 6 on Mercedes-Benz heavy-duty engines means cylinder #1's injector circuit is reading current above normal, consistent with a short to ground. It's a high-severity fault that shuts down that injector's driver and causes a real misfire until repaired. A grounded injector circuit is more urgent than a simple open circuit because it risks damaging the ECM's driver stage if left unresolved. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats SPN 651 FMI 6 as a fault to diagnose thoroughly and quickly - checking for melted insulation or a pinched wire near the valve cover before it has a chance to cause secondary damage to the control module itself.
causes: Chafed or pinched harness wire shorting to a grounded surface
Vibration and heat cycling near the valve cover can wear through wire insulation, allowing the conductor to contact grounded engine components.
Melted or damaged connector at the injector
Heat exposure near the injector can degrade connector plastic, creating an unintended path to ground at the terminal level.
Internal injector solenoid short
The injector's internal winding can fail and short internally to the injector body, which is grounded to the engine.
Water or coolant intrusion into the connector
A compromised seal allowing fluid into the connector can create a temporary or permanent short-to-ground condition.
steps: Pull the fault with Mercedes-Benz Xentry and confirm SPN 651 FMI 6 is active; check for signs of a repeat fault, since a short-to-ground condition can sometimes blow a driver circuit fuse if present long enough.
Inspect the cylinder #1 injector connector and surrounding harness closely for melted insulation, a burnt connector, or a wire pinched against the valve cover or cylinder head.
Disconnect the connector and check resistance from each injector terminal to engine ground - any continuity confirms a short, whereas a healthy circuit should show no continuity to ground.
If the short is found within the injector itself (isolated from the harness), replace that injector using the correct Mercedes-Benz procedure and calibration data entry.
If the short is in the harness, repair or replace the damaged section with appropriate heat-resistant wire and loom, then reseal any disturbed grommets.
Clear the code and verify cylinder #1 is firing correctly using a cylinder cutout or contribution test before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Noticeable rough idle and a distinct miss under load
Check Engine lamp illuminated
Possible burnt smell or visible damage near the injector connector if the short has been present for a while
Reduced power and fuel economy from the ECM compensating with the remaining cylinders
procedures_full.source_title: Mercedes-Benz SPN 651 FMI 6: Diagnosing a Shorted Cylinder #1 Injector Circuit

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 6 on Volvo means the cylinder 1 injector circuit is drawing current above normal — typically a short. Ohm test the injector and inspect the valve cover harness before replacing parts. SPN 651 identifies the cylinder 1 injector circuit on Volvo heavy-duty engines. FMI 6 means current above normal, pointing to a shorted injector winding or chafed harness rather than an open circuit (FMI 5). ProfessionalDieselRepair.com stresses immediate connector disconnection on FMI 6 to protect the ECM injector driver from permanent damage.
causes: Injector solenoid internal short to ground
Very Common
Heat and fuel pressure cycling degrade the solenoid coil insulation, dropping resistance below 0.3 ohms and drawing excess current.
Chafed valve cover harness short to ground
The injector harness rubs against the rocker housing through the valve cover grommet, wearing insulation and shorting the driver circuit.
Moisture intrusion at injector connector causing conductive path
Moderate
Fuel vapor and condensation at the valve cover connector create a conductive film that shorts injector terminals to ground.
steps: Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) or Jaltest and confirm SPN 651 FMI 6. Run cylinder cutout test — cylinder 1 should show abnormal contribution compared to cylinders 2-6.

Shut engine off, disconnect injector 1 connector at the valve cover. Measure resistance across the two solenoid terminals — Volvo D13 unit injectors typically read 0.5-2.5 ohms. Below 0.3 ohms indicates internal short; above 10 ohms indicates open winding.

With connector unplugged, measure harness-side resistance to ground and to battery positive. Any reading below 10 kΩ indicates a harness short that will damage the ECM driver if the injector is reconnected.
Inspect the valve cover harness grommet where the loom passes through the cover — Volvo D13 harnesses chafe at the rocker stand contact point, causing short-to-ground on injector circuits.

After repair, clear codes in PTT, restart, and re-run cutout test. Cylinder 1 RPM drop should match other cylinders within 15%. Monitor injector driver current in live data — normal peak is 15-25A per firing event on D13.
symptoms: Rough idle with noticeable single-cylinder miss
Amber MIL illuminated, possible flashing under acceleration
Cylinder 1 shows zero or erratic contribution on Premium Tech Tool cutout test
Possible fuel dilution smell if injector is stuck partially open
ECM may set additional cylinder 1 misfire codes alongside SPN 651

procedures_full.overview: SPN 651 FMI 7 means cylinder 1 injector mechanical response is out of adjustment. Verify fuel supply, harness, and contribution tests in Davie4 before replacing the injector. PACCAR MX common-rail injectors are precisely controlled, and FMI 7 tells you the ECM sees a mechanical mismatch on cylinder 1 specifically. That can be a stuck needle, but it can also be starved fuel or a connector full of engine oil. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com isolates cylinder 1 with contribution testing — not guesswork at the parts counter.
causes: Stuck or worn cylinder 1 injector needle and nozzle
Internal mechanical wear prevents commanded fuel quantity from delivering in the cylinder.
Low common-rail pressure from supply restriction
Starved rail pressure affects all injectors but may set on cylinder 1 first depending on calibration.
Cylinder 1 injector harness or connector fault
Oil wicking into the connector causes intermittent solenoid response misread as mechanical failure.
Contaminated fuel damaging injector internals
Water or metal debris in fuel causes erratic needle lift on the first cylinder to show symptoms.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 and run cylinder cutout or contribution test on cylinder 1.
Log rail pressure commanded vs actual during cranking and idle on MX-13 common-rail systems.
Inspect cylinder 1 injector connector and harness for oil intrusion or bent pins.
Compare cylinder 1 correction values to other cylinders — isolated high correction suggests mechanical injector fault.
Perform leak-back or return flow test per PACCAR procedure before authorizing injector replacement.
symptoms: Rough idle or misfire on cylinder 1
Check-engine lamp with SPN 651 FMI 7
White or black smoke from cylinder 1 imbalance
Reduced power under load with audible knock on cold start
Possible companion rail pressure or cylinder balance codes

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically an open circuit, short to ground or short to power.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically an open circuit, short to ground or short to power.‪

Disconnect injector #1.
Measure the resistance between pin 10 and pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and pin 1 of the injector #1 harness connector.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "59.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 16.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and pin 2 of the injector #1 harness connector.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 17.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "59.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the resistance between pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "59.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

Measure the resistance between pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground. If using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #1 pin 1 and ground.

Disconnect the injector #1 connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground. If using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #1 pin 1 and ground.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "59.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace injector #1. Refer to "59.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

procedures_full.overview: FMI 5 on the cylinder 2 injector circuit indicates the ECM driver is seeing below-expected current, which is the open-circuit class. An open wire, unseated connector, failed injector winding, and broken pin at the pass-through connector are the primary causes. Oil contamination and vibration-related opens are documented patterns across platforms. Cylinder-specific circuit mapping reduces the shotgun injector replacement pattern — the open is in the cylinder 2 branch, but shared pass-through connectors must also be inspected for terminal backout affecting multiple cylinders.
causes: Open wire — broken conductor in cylinder 2 branch
Unseated connector — terminal backout at injector or pass-through
Failed injector winding — internal open circuit
Broken pin at pass-through — vibration or corrosion damage
Oil contamination — connector corrosion from oil migration
steps: Single Action Gate — Connector Inspection

Inspect the cylinder 2 injector connector for terminal backout, corrosion, and oil contamination. Inspect the shared pass-through connector for terminal backout affecting the cylinder 2 branch. Terminal backout at the pass-through is a documented cause of open-circuit faults that appear cylinder-specific.
Binary Decision Gate — Resistance Test

Measure resistance across the cylinder 2 injector terminals. Infinite or very high resistance confirms an open circuit — either in the injector winding or in the harness. Compare to OEM injector resistance specification.
Override Manager — Continuity Test
Perform continuity test on the cylinder 2 injector circuit from ECM connector to injector connector. An open wire in the cylinder 2 branch confirms a harness fault rather than injector failure.
Safety Interceptor — Safe Cylinder Comparison

Compare cylinder 2 circuit resistance to an adjacent cylinder as a sanity check. A significantly different reading on cylinder 2 versus adjacent cylinders with the same injector type confirms a cylinder 2 specific fault.
Resume Point — Harness Repair Verification
After any harness repair, verify continuity and resistance are within OEM specification before reinstalling the injector. Confirm the repair is secure against vibration and oil exposure.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Contribution Confirmation
After repair, verify cylinder 2 contribution returns to normal. Confirm no misfire or power balance fault remains on cylinder 2.
Repair Ledger Output — Injector or Harness Decision
Replace injector only after circuit continuity is confirmed good and injector internal open is proven by resistance test. Repair harness if open wire or terminal backout is found.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair terminal backout at injector or pass-through connector.
2 . Repair open wire in cylinder 2 branch.
3 . Clean or replace connector if oil contamination is found.
4 . Replace injector after circuit proof confirms internal open winding.
5 . Code or trim replacement injector per OEM procedure where required.
Verification Steps
Confirm circuit continuity and resistance are within OEM specification after repair.
Verify cylinder 2 contribution returns to normal.
Confirm SPN 652 FMI 5 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of misfire or power balance fault on cylinder 2.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect injector harness pass-through connector at every injector service.
✓ Inspect cylinder 2 injector connector for oil contamination at every valve cover service.
✓ Secure harness against vibration at every major service.
✓ Address oil leaks near injector connectors promptly.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High with active misfire. Avoid high load until corrected. Cylinder-specific circuit proof takes less time than injector replacement and prevents unnecessary parts cost.
symptoms: Injector cylinder 2 circuit open fault active
Cylinder 2 misfire
Rough idle from cylinder 2 contribution loss
Power balance fault on cylinder 2
Possible rail pressure instability from cylinder 2 disable

procedures_full.overview: SPN 652 FMI 5 on Mack means the cylinder 2 injector circuit is open — no current flow. Ohm test the injector solenoid and inspect the valve cover harness before replacing the injector. SPN 652 targets the cylinder 2 injector circuit on Mack MP7, MP8, and MP10 engines. FMI 5 means current below normal, almost always an open circuit rather than a mechanical injector failure. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com guides Mack techs to test the valve cover harness first — chafe at the rocker housing is the leading cause on high-mileage MP8 trucks.
causes: Chafed or broken valve cover injector harness wire
Very Common
The harness vibrates against the rocker shaft through the valve cover grommet, eventually breaking the conductor and creating an open circuit.
Corroded or backed-out connector pin at injector 2
Moisture and heat cycles at the valve cover connector corrode pin contacts until resistance exceeds the ECM detection threshold.
Failed injector solenoid open winding
Internal coil fatigue from heat and vibration opens the solenoid winding, typically past 400,000 miles on MP8 engines.
steps: Connect Mack Diagnostic Protocol (MDP) via Jaltest or Texa and confirm SPN 652 FMI 5. Run cylinder cutout test — cylinder 2 should show no RPM drop when disabled, confirming the injector is not firing.
Shut engine off, unplug injector 2 connector at the valve cover. Inspect pins for corrosion, backed-out sockets, or melted plastic from arcing.
Measure resistance across the two injector solenoid terminals — Mack MP8 unit injectors typically read 0.5-3.0 ohms. Infinite (OL) resistance confirms open winding inside the injector.

If injector ohms good, check harness continuity from the connector to the ECM injector driver pin using a wiring diagram. Mack MP8 valve cover harnesses fail at the grommet where the loom crosses the rocker shaft.

Clear codes in Jaltest after repair, restart, and re-run cutout test. Cylinder 2 RPM drop should match other cylinders within 20 RPM. Wiggle-test the harness during live monitoring to confirm no intermittent open.
symptoms: Rough idle and noticeable miss under acceleration
Amber MIL illuminated on Mack dash
Cylinder 2 shows zero contribution on MDP diagnostic cutout test
Possible slight increase in exhaust smoke if unburned fuel enters the dead cylinder
Fuel economy drop of 5%-8% from running on one fewer cylinder

procedures_full.overview: SPN 652 FMI 5 on Scania engines means cylinder #2's injector circuit is reading current below normal, consistent with an open circuit. It's a high-severity fault causing a real misfire on that cylinder, often traced to a connector issue rather than a failed injector. An open injector circuit takes a cylinder completely out of the firing sequence, and on Scania engines SPN 652 pinpoints that failure directly to cylinder #2. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com approaches this fault the same way as any single-cylinder injector code - verify the connector and harness integrity before condemning the injector itself, since a corroded pin produces an identical open-circuit reading without any actual injector failure.
causes: Corroded or backed-out harness connector pin
A pin that isn't making solid contact at the injector connector reads as an open circuit even though the injector itself may be perfectly healthy.
Broken wire within the injector harness
Repeated flexing at a harness routing point can eventually fracture a wire internally, creating an open circuit without visible external damage.
Failed injector solenoid winding
The injector's internal coil can fail open after extended service life, requiring injector replacement rather than a wiring repair.
ECM driver circuit fault for that cylinder
An internal ECM issue isolated to one injector driver circuit is uncommon but worth considering if harness and injector both test normal.
steps: Pull the fault with Scania SDP3 and confirm SPN 652 FMI 5 is active; check whether any adjacent cylinder codes are present, which could point to a shared harness section rather than an isolated connector issue.
Locate the cylinder #2 injector connector and inspect it for corrosion, a bent or backed-out pin, or a connector that isn't fully seated.
Disconnect the connector and measure resistance across the injector solenoid winding, comparing to spec and to a known-good cylinder on the same engine.
If resistance reads open, trace the harness from the connector back toward the ECM, checking for a break at any point where it flexes or routes near a hot component.
If the injector itself tests open internally at its own terminals, replace the injector following Scania's proper procedure, including any required calibration data entry.
Clear the code and use SDP3's cylinder contribution test to confirm cylinder #2 is now firing evenly with the rest before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Rough idle with a distinct, feelable miss
Reduced power and torque, especially under load
Check Engine lamp illuminated
Increased fuel consumption from the ECM compensating on remaining cylinders

procedures_full.overview: SPN 652 FMI 6 means the ECM measured below-normal actuator current on cylinder 2 injector circuit. Misfire, rough idle, and possible injector shutdown derate can follow until resistance and wiring are verified against OEM specs. Cylinder-specific injector current faults are common on PACCAR and Cummins-powered Kenworth trucks, and ProfessionalDieselRepair.com isolates harness versus injector failures with swap tests before recommending a full set replacement.
causes: Failed cylinder 2 injector solenoid coil
High internal resistance drops current below ECM thresholds and weakens injection events.
Valve-cover harness oil intrusion
Oil degrades connector pins and increases circuit resistance at the injector branch.
ECM injector driver degradation
A weak driver channel on the ECM cannot supply rated current even with a good injector.
steps: Run cylinder cutout test in JPRO; cylinder 2 change in RPM should be minimal compared to healthy cylinders.
Measure injector connector resistance on cylinder 2 — many common-rail solenoids read 0.5-2.0 ohms at 68°F; above 3 ohms indicates failing coil.
Backprobe ECM injector driver output during cranking; compare peak current on cyl 2 versus cyl 1 — below 10A peak suggests driver or wiring loss.
Inspect valve-cover harness pigtail for oil soak and cracked insulation at the cylinder 2 branch.
Swap cylinder 2 injector connector with cylinder 4 temporarily; if the fault follows the connector, repair harness — if it stays on cyl 2, replace injector.
symptoms: Rough idle and cylinder 2 misfire logged in Noregon JPRO or OEM tool
White or gray smoke at idle that clears at higher RPM
Engine vibration noticeable at low speed in gear
Fuel trim or balance rates show cylinder 2 contributing low
Fault may appear after harness repair near valve cover

procedures_full.overview: SPN 652 FMI 6 means the cylinder #2 injector driver circuit on a Detroit Diesel engine is shorted to ground or drawing excessive current. It is High severity, does not shut the engine down, but should be repaired quickly to avoid damaging the ECM injector driver stage. Detroit Diesel DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines use individual injector cylinder codes just like Cummins, with SPN 652 covering cylinder #2 specifically. The FMI 6 designation means current above normal, which is the electrical opposite of an open circuit - this is a short, not a break. As ProfessionalDieselRepair.com explains to shops handling these engines, a shorted injector circuit deserves faster attention than an open one because repeated key cycles with an active short can overheat and damage the injector driver transistor built into the ECM, turning a simple harness repair into an expensive control module replacement.
causes: Chafed injector harness shorting to the cylinder head or valve cover
The tight routing of the valve cover harness against metal surfaces on DD platforms makes this the single most frequent cause of a shorted injector circuit.
Water intrusion at the injector connector
A failed connector seal lets coolant or wash water into the injector plug, creating a conductive path to ground.
Internally shorted injector solenoid
Heat and vibration fatigue can break down the internal winding insulation of the solenoid, shorting it to the injector body.
Damaged ECM injector driver stage
If the short has been present for an extended period, the ECM's own driver circuit for that cylinder can be damaged and require ECM replacement or repair.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) and confirm SPN 652 FMI 6 is active, then check for any accompanying injector or harness fault codes.
Shut down and unplug the cylinder #2 injector connector, inspecting for melted plastic, burnt pins, or visible arcing which would confirm a hard short.
Measure resistance from each injector terminal to chassis ground with a multimeter - any reading other than infinite (OL) confirms a short to ground either in the injector or the harness.
If the injector itself reads shorted internally, replace it; if it reads clean, trace the harness from the connector back toward the ECM for a chafe point against the valve cover or head.
After repair, clear codes with DDDL and verify no injector driver damage occurred by checking injector balance rates in live data before returning to service.
symptoms: Rough idle with a noticeable miss traceable to cylinder #2
Amber MIL illuminated
Possible burnt smell or visible damage near the injector connector
Reduced power and fuel economy

steps: Open Circuit, Short to Ground or Short to Power Check
Check for multiple codes.
If fault code 168/1 is active in addition to other codes, service 168/1 first. Refer to "32.2 SPN 168/FMI 1".
If fault 651/14 and 653/14 are active in addition to 652/14, go to step 2.
If only fault code 652/14 is active, go to step 10.
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector.
Inspect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector for bent or spread pins, inspect the connector seal for damage (signs of water or oil intrusion).
If water or oil intrusion, bent or spread pins are found, repair as necessary. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If connector shows no signs of damage, go to step 5.
Measure the resistance between pins 10 and 1 on the valve cover side of the Front Injector Harness. If using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #2 pins 1 and 2.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness.Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 6.
Disconnect the MCM 120–pin connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 11of the MCM 120–pin connector and pin 10 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector. See Figure
"120–pin MCM Connector".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 8.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, repair the open between pin 11 of the MCM 120–pin connector and pin 10 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the negative battery cable.
Measure the resistance between the positive battery post and pin 11of the MCM 120–pin connector.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800 for MCM replacement authorization.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, repair the short to power between battery positive and pin 11of the MCM 120–pin connector. See Figure
"120–pin MCM Connector"
. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Figure 1. 120–pin MCM Connector
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 10 and pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, go to step 13.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 18.
Remove the upper valve cover.
Disconnect injector #2.
Measure the resistance between pin 10 and pin 1 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and pin 1 of the injector #2 harness connector.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 16.
Measure the resistance between pin 3 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and pin 2 of the injector #2 harness connector.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 17.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the resistance between pin 3 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace injector #2. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the resistance between pin 3 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground. If using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #2 pin 1 and ground.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 19.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, go to step 22.
Remove the upper valve cover.
Disconnect the injector #2 connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 3 on the valve cover side of the injector harness and ground. If using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #2 pin 1 and ground.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover injector harness. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace injector #2. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the MCM.
Measure the resistance between pin 3 on the MCM side of the injector harness connector and pin 22 of the 120–pin MCM connector.

If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, repair the open circuit between pin 3 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and pin 22 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 3 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and pin 22 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "60.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 5 on the cylinder 3 injector indicates the ECM driver monitored current rise during injection events and found an open-circuit condition. The ECM monitors current through the injector circuit during each commanded injection event — if current does not rise as expected, FMI 5 sets. True causes include open connectors, broken conductors, failed injector winding, and pass-through terminal exits. Detroit oil-intruded under-cover connectors, Cummins broken injector pigtails, PACCAR harness chafe at head clamps, and Volvo/Mack connector backout after valve-cover service are documented platform patterns. Replacing the injector without circuit proof wastes the injector cost when the fault is a backed-out connector pin.
causes: Open connector — backed-out pin or unseated connector at cylinder 3
Broken conductor — harness break at flex point or clamp
Failed injector winding — internal open in injector coil or piezo path
Pass-through terminal exit — open at valve-cover pass-through connector
Oil-intruded connector — oil contamination bridging or corroding terminals (Detroit pattern)
Harness chafe — insulation worn through at head clamps (PACCAR pattern)
steps: Single Action Gate — Visual Connector and Oil Check

Inspect the cylinder 3 injector connector first. Check for backed-out pins, incomplete latch, and oil contamination. Detroit under-cover connectors are prone to oil intrusion. Volvo/Mack connectors are prone to backout after valve-cover service. Inspect shared pass-through connectors for backed-out pins.
Binary Decision Gate — Resistance Test

Measure injector circuit resistance versus OEM specification. Infinite resistance or OL indicates an open circuit. A reading within specification supports a connector intermittent rather than a true open. Compare to adjacent cylinder injector resistance for reference.
Override Manager — Continuity to ECM

Confirm continuity from the ECM connector to the injector connector. An open between the ECM and the injector connector confirms a harness fault. An open only at the injector connector confirms a connector or injector fault.
Safety Interceptor — Short-to-Ground and Short-to-Power Checks
Verify no short-to-ground or short-to-power on the cylinder 3 circuit. A circuit that is open at the injector but shorted elsewhere requires harness repair before injector replacement.
Resume Point — Injector Internal Open Proof

If circuit integrity from ECM to injector connector is confirmed and resistance at the injector connector is OL, the injector itself is internally open. This is the only condition that justifies injector replacement for FMI 5.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Contribution Confirmation
After repair, verify cylinder 3 contribution returns to normal. Confirm rough idle and misfire do not persist. Monitor for return of FMI 5 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Connector, Harness, or Injector Decision

Repair connector or harness if open is found in the circuit. Replace injector only after internal open is proven by circuit integrity confirmation. Code or trim replacement injector per OEM procedure where required.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair backed-out pin or unseated connector at cylinder 3.
2 . Repair harness break at flex point or clamp.
3 . Repair oil-intruded connector terminals.
4 . Replace injector only after internal open is proven by circuit integrity confirmation.
5 . Code or trim replacement injector per OEM procedure where required.
Verification Steps
Confirm cylinder 3 contribution returns to normal after repair.
Verify rough idle and misfire do not persist after repair.
Confirm SPN 653 FMI 5 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of misfire under load after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Verify injector connector latch after every valve-cover service.
✓ Inspect cylinder 3 harness for chafe at head clamps at every major service.
✓ Address oil leaks near injector connectors to prevent oil intrusion.
✓ Inspect pass-through connectors for backed-out pins at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High. Misfire under load can overwork aftertreatment. Avoid prolonged high-load operation with an active cylinder 3 open fault.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 653 FMI 5 means the Volvo ECM sees an open circuit in the cylinder #3 injector driver and cannot fire that injector. It's a High severity fault causing a rough idle and reduced power, but it does not shut the engine down. Volvo D11, D13, and D16 engines number their injector cylinder codes just like other J1939 platforms, with SPN 653 covering cylinder #3 specifically. FMI 5 means current below normal, the electrical signature of an open circuit rather than a short. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com covers this fault often because Volvo's tight valve cover harness routing on the D13 platform makes chafing a genuinely common cause, and separating a wiring problem from an actual dead injector saves significant unnecessary parts expense.
causes: Chafed valve cover harness wire
The D13's harness runs close to rocker arm hardware, and vibration over time can wear through insulation until the wire breaks completely.
Corroded or partially disengaged injector connector
Moisture intrusion or an improperly locked connector creates a high-resistance or open contact that the ECM reads as a dead circuit.
Failed injector solenoid winding
The internal solenoid coil can open from heat and vibration fatigue over extended service life.
ECM injector driver stage failure
An internal ECM fault on that specific driver channel would produce the same code, but only after the injector and harness both test clean.
steps: Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and confirm SPN 653 FMI 5 is active, then run a cylinder cutout test to verify cylinder #3 contributes nothing.
Shut down and unplug the cylinder #3 injector connector, checking for corrosion, bent pins, or a partially disengaged locking tab.
Measure resistance across the injector solenoid terminals with a multimeter - compare the reading to Volvo spec, typically in the low single-digit ohm range for common rail solenoid injectors.
If the injector reads good, trace the harness back toward the ECM for chafing near the valve cover or rocker arm assembly.
Repair or replace the faulty component, clear the code with PTT, and re-run the cutout test to confirm cylinder #3 is firing normally before road testing.
symptoms: Rough idle with a miss traceable to cylinder #3
Amber warning lamp illuminated
Reduced power output and fuel economy
Possible white smoke from unburned fuel washing past the dead cylinder
