procedures_full.overview: EGR flow is calculated by the ECM using inputs from MAP, MAF, delta-P sensors (depending on strategy), and valve position feedback. FMI 18 (below normal) is set when the calculated flow falls below the calibrated minimum. Plugged EGR coolers and carboned valves are common causes, but sensor bias in the flow calculation inputs can create false low-flow faults without any actual restriction.
causes: EGR valve not opening — carbon sticktion or actuator failure
Plugged EGR cooler — restriction reducing flow
Intake leakage path errors — affecting flow calculation
MAP/MAF/delta-P sensor bias — skewing flow calculation inputs
EGR cooler bypass stuck — reducing cooled EGR flow
steps: Single Action Gate — Commanded vs Actual Position
Compare commanded EGR valve position to actual position feedback. If valve is commanded open but not moving, the restriction is mechanical.
Binary Decision Gate — Flow Calculation Input Validation
Validate the sensors used in the EGR flow calculation (MAP, MAF, delta-P per OEM strategy). Sensor bias in these inputs creates false low-flow faults.
Override Manager — EGR Cooler Restriction Inspection
Inspect EGR cooler for restriction. A plugged cooler reduces flow regardless of valve position. Measure pressure drop across cooler per OEM procedure.
Safety Interceptor — Intake Integrity Check
Verify intake system integrity. Leaks in the intake path affect the flow calculation and can create false low-flow readings.
Resume Point — Delta-P / Flow PID Review
Review EGR delta-P or flow PID data under load. Compare to expected values for the operating conditions.
Verification Loop — Post-Service Flow Confirmation
After valve or cooler service, verify EGR flow PIDs return to expected range under load.
Repair Ledger Output — Cooler Replacement Decision
Replace EGR cooler only after valve and sensor inputs are proven good. Document all findings.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 2659 FMI 18 indicates a DEF dosing unit fault on Cummins engines, often leading to derate. Check for DEF contamination, dosing unit operation, and wiring integrity.
causes: DEF Contamination
Contaminated DEF fluid can clog the dosing unit, leading to ineffective operation. Always source DEF from reputable suppliers and check for tank contamination regularly.
Electrical Connection Fault
Corroded or loose electrical connections can disrupt the dosing unit's operation. Regular inspection and maintenance of wiring can prevent this.
Dosing Unit Failure
The dosing unit itself may fail due to internal mechanical issues or wear. Replacement is necessary if the unit is confirmed defective.
DEF Line Blockage
Crystallization within the DEF lines can block fluid flow. This happens more in colder climates if the system is not properly heated.
steps: Inspect DEF fluid for contamination. Use a refractometer to test fluid quality. Clear fluid indicates good quality; cloudy or debris-filled fluid suggests contamination.
Locate the DEF dosing unit, typically near the DEF tank. Check for physical damage or leaks. No leaks or damage should be visible.
Test the electrical connectors to the dosing unit using a multimeter. Ensure continuity and correct voltage (12V) when the system is active.
Check DEF lines for crystallization. Remove and clean if necessary. Lines should be clear and free of white crystal buildup.
Perform a forced regen if possible to verify dosing unit operation. Observe for proper DEF spray; it should be a fine mist.
Examine the DEF tank heater function. Use an infrared thermometer to ensure the heater is operational, especially in cold weather.
Reset the fault code using a diagnostic tool after repairs. Verify the code does not return under normal operation conditions.
symptoms: Engine derate to 5 mph, severely limiting truck speed.
Check Engine Light illuminated on the dashboard.
Frequent DEF level warnings despite a full tank.
Increased DEF consumption or no DEF usage recorded.
Harsh engine performance with possible misfires.
Unusual noises from the DEF dosing unit indicating malfunction.
Excessive white smoke from the exhaust, signaling incomplete DEF processing.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 2659 FMI 18 indicates a turbocharger speed sensor rationality fault in Detroit Diesel engines, affecting boost control and engine performance. Inspect wiring and sensor connections to resolve. The SPN 2659 FMI 18 fault code on Detroit Diesel engines signals a rationality fault with the turbocharger speed sensor. This issue can lead to suboptimal engine performance, characterized by reduced power and efficiency. Addressing this fault promptly is crucial to maintain the engine's reliability and prevent potential damage. Turbochargers play a vital role in enhancing engine performance by increasing air intake, thus improving combustion efficiency. A malfunctioning speed sensor can disrupt this process, leading to noticeable symptoms such as loss of power and increased fuel consumption. Understanding the causes and solutions for this fault code is essential for effective troubleshooting. A detailed diagnostic approach can help identify whether the issue lies within the sensor, its wiring, or the turbocharger itself.
causes: Faulty turbocharger speed sensor

The sensor itself may fail due to internal electrical faults or exposure to harsh operating conditions, leading to inaccurate readings. This can result from thermal stress or contamination affecting the sensor's internal components.
Wiring or connector issues

Damaged or corroded wiring and connectors can disrupt the signal from the sensor to the ECM, causing the fault code to trigger. Environmental factors like moisture and vibration can exacerbate these issues.
Mechanical issues within the turbocharger

Mechanical wear or damage to the turbocharger can affect its rotational speed, leading to discrepancies in sensor readings. Issues such as bearing wear or turbine imbalance can cause erratic sensor signals.
steps: Visually inspect the turbocharger speed sensor wiring and connectors for damage or corrosion. Ensure all connections are secure. Pay particular attention to any signs of wear or exposure to elements that could compromise electrical integrity.

Use a multimeter to check for proper voltage and continuity in the sensor circuit, confirming electrical integrity. Ensure the readings are within the manufacturer's specifications to rule out electrical faults.

Examine the turbocharger for any physical damage or signs of wear that may affect its performance, such as excessive play or oil leaks. Inspect the turbine blades for any foreign object damage or imbalance.
Clear the fault code using an OBD-II scanner and test drive the vehicle to see if the code returns. Monitor the engine's performance during the test drive to identify any recurring issues.

If the issue persists, consider replacing the turbocharger speed sensor with a new, OEM-approved part. Ensure the new sensor is properly calibrated and installed according to the manufacturer's guidelines.

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3250 FMI 16 – DPF Differential Pressure High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3250 FMI 16 – DPF Differential Pressure High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3250 FMI 16 indicates that the pressure difference across the Diesel Particulate Filter has exceeded the acceptable operating threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and signals that exhaust flow through the DPF is being restricted, which directly impacts engine performance and will trigger derate conditions if not addressed promptly.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF warning light illuminated 
Reduced engine power 
Engine derate condition possible Increased exhaust back pressure 
Regeneration cycles may be more frequent 
Black smoke from exhaust possible
Cause
This code triggers when the differential pressure sensor detects a pressure drop across the DPF exceeding the maximum threshold. Common causes include:
Heavily soot loaded DPF restricting exhaust flow 
High ash accumulation inside the DPF 
Failed or incomplete regeneration cycles 
Clogged or damaged DPF substrate 
Faulty differential pressure sensor or blocked sensor lines 
Engine burning excessive oil accelerating ash buildup 
Collapsed or damaged DPF internal structure
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but high differential pressure indicates severely restricted exhaust flow which reduces engine performance and can cause damage. A regeneration should be attempted immediately. If pressure remains high after a successful regen the DPF likely needs professional cleaning or replacement.
Recommended Action
Attempt a parked regeneration to reduce soot load and pressure. If the differential pressure remains high after a successful regen, inspect the sensor lines for blockages before condemning the DPF. If lines are clear the DPF should be removed for professional cleaning or inspection. Also check for excessive oil consumption that may be contributing to rapid ash accumulation.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3250 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the pressure difference across the DPF has exceeded the maximum acceptable threshold, indicating the filter is restricting exhaust flow due to soot, ash, or physical damage.
 
 
What causes SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are a heavily soot or ash loaded DPF, failed regeneration cycles, a clogged or damaged filter substrate, or a faulty differential pressure sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but high back pressure from a restricted DPF will reduce engine performance and can cause damage if ignored. Attempt a parked regen as soon as safely possible.
 
 
Will SPN 3250 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. Excessive differential pressure across the DPF will cause the ECM to trigger derate conditions to protect the engine from damage caused by high exhaust back pressure.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
Perform a parked regeneration to reduce soot load. If pressure remains elevated after regen check the sensor lines for blockages then have the DPF professionally cleaned or replaced if needed.

Detroit Diesel SPN 3250 FMI 16 indicates that the pressure difference across the Diesel Particulate Filter has exceeded the acceptable operating threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and signals that exhaust flow through the DPF is being restricted, which directly impacts engine performance and will trigger derate conditions if not addressed promptly.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF warning light illuminated 
Reduced engine power 
Engine derate condition possible Increased exhaust back pressure 
Regeneration cycles may be more frequent 
Black smoke from exhaust possible
Cause
This code triggers when the differential pressure sensor detects a pressure drop across the DPF exceeding the maximum threshold. Common causes include:
Heavily soot loaded DPF restricting exhaust flow 
High ash accumulation inside the DPF 
Failed or incomplete regeneration cycles 
Clogged or damaged DPF substrate 
Faulty differential pressure sensor or blocked sensor lines 
Engine burning excessive oil accelerating ash buildup 
Collapsed or damaged DPF internal structure
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but high differential pressure indicates severely restricted exhaust flow which reduces engine performance and can cause damage. A regeneration should be attempted immediately. If pressure remains high after a successful regen the DPF likely needs professional cleaning or replacement.
Recommended Action
Attempt a parked regeneration to reduce soot load and pressure. If the differential pressure remains high after a successful regen, inspect the sensor lines for blockages before condemning the DPF. If lines are clear the DPF should be removed for professional cleaning or inspection. Also check for excessive oil consumption that may be contributing to rapid ash accumulation.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3250 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the pressure difference across the DPF has exceeded the maximum acceptable threshold, indicating the filter is restricting exhaust flow due to soot, ash, or physical damage.
 
 
What causes SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are a heavily soot or ash loaded DPF, failed regeneration cycles, a clogged or damaged filter substrate, or a faulty differential pressure sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but high back pressure from a restricted DPF will reduce engine performance and can cause damage if ignored. Attempt a parked regen as soon as safely possible.
 
 
Will SPN 3250 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. Excessive differential pressure across the DPF will cause the ECM to trigger derate conditions to protect the engine from damage caused by high exhaust back pressure.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3250 FMI 16?
 
Perform a parked regeneration to reduce soot load. If pressure remains elevated after regen check the sensor lines for blockages then have the DPF professionally cleaned or replaced if needed.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3250 FMI 0 is a highest-severity class fault on the DPF differential pressure sensing circuit. The DPF DP sensor measures the pressure difference across the DPF to infer soot loading. A failed sensor, open or short circuit, plugged hoses creating irrational values, and connector damage are the primary causes. Hose melt or collapse from proximity to exhaust heat and water intrusion in the measurement lines are documented causes that produce irrational sensor readings. Replacing the sensor without inspecting the hoses produces repeat faults.
causes: Failed sensor — internal failure after thermal cycling
Open circuit — harness damage near aftertreatment heat
Short circuit — connector damage or chafe
Plugged hoses — soot or debris in measurement tubes
Hose melt or collapse — proximity to exhaust heat
Water in measurement lines — condensation or water ingestion
steps: Single Action Gate — Hose Condition Inspection

Inspect both measurement hoses for melt, collapse, kinking, and plugging. Hose damage from proximity to exhaust heat is a documented cause of irrational DP readings. Inspect the full hose run from sensor to DPF inlet and outlet ports.
Binary Decision Gate — Electrical Reference and Signal Check

Verify 5V reference, ground, and signal at the sensor connector. An open circuit typically produces a fixed high or low signal. A short circuit produces a signal pinned at one extreme. Confirm reference is present before condemning the sensor.
Override Manager — Key-On Baseline Check
With both hose ports open to atmosphere, check sensor baseline output. A reading significantly above or below zero with both ports equalized confirms sensor internal failure or bias.
Safety Interceptor — Connector and Harness Inspection
Inspect aftertreatment sensor harness for chafe and heat damage. The DP sensor harness runs near high-temperature aftertreatment components where heat damage is common.
Resume Point — Loaded Comparison

If safe and within OEM procedure, compare DP sensor reading to expected values at a known load point. An irrational reading at a known load confirms sensor failure after hoses and circuit are proven good.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair DP Response
After repair, verify DP sensor responds correctly to engine load changes. Confirm soot load calculation returns to expected values.
Repair Ledger Output — Sensor and Hose Service
Replace sensor and service hoses together when both are suspect. Replacing only the sensor with damaged hoses produces repeat faults.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace or reroute damaged measurement hoses.
2 . Clear water from measurement lines if water intrusion is found.
3 . Repair harness chafe or heat damage.
4 . Replace DP sensor after hose and circuit integrity are confirmed.
5 . Reroute hoses away from exhaust heat sources to prevent recurrence.
Verification Steps
Confirm DP sensor baseline reads near zero with ports equalized after repair.
Verify DP sensor responds correctly to engine load changes.
Confirm SPN 3250 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Monitor soot load calculation returns to expected values.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect DP sensor hoses for heat damage at every major aftertreatment service.
✓ Reroute hoses away from exhaust heat sources if damage is recurring.
✓ Inspect sensor connector for heat damage at every major service.
✓ Address water intrusion sources near the DP sensor measurement path.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High. Irrational DP data disrupts regen strategy and soot load management. Address promptly. Combined electrical and hose inspection takes less time than sensor replacement alone.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 1 on DPF intake pressure indicates the sensor reports below the minimum expected pressure for conditions. Sensor bias, leaking sense line, exhaust leak upstream, true low flow conditions, and wiring low-signal faults are the primary causes. Disconnected sense hoses after AT service are a documented cause of false low inlet pressure readings. An implausible low reading under load when the engine is producing exhaust flow confirms a sensing path issue rather than a true low-pressure condition.
causes: Sensor bias — pressure sensor reading below actual pressure
Leaking sense line — sense line leak producing low reading
Disconnected sense hose — hose disconnected after AT service
Exhaust leak upstream — exhaust leak reducing measured pressure
Wiring low-signal fault — low-signal circuit fault producing low reading
steps: Single Action Gate — Inspect Sense Hose Routing and Connection

Inspect the sense hose routing and connection at the DPF inlet pressure sensor. Disconnected sense hoses after AT service are a documented cause of false low inlet pressure readings. Confirm the sense hose is connected, routed correctly, and not kinked or blocked.
Binary Decision Gate — Verify Sensor Baseline at KOEO

Verify the sensor baseline at KOEO. For absolute pressure sensors, the reading should be near ambient atmospheric pressure at KOEO. An implausible low reading at KOEO confirms sensor bias or a wiring fault. A reading near ambient at KOEO with implausible low under load confirms a sense line leak or exhaust leak.
Override Manager — Compare to Outlet Pressure

Compare DPF inlet pressure to outlet pressure. One sensor disagreeing with the other while the engine is producing exhaust flow confirms the disagreeing sensor is suspect. Both sensors reading implausibly low simultaneously suggests a shared sensing path issue.
Safety Interceptor — Circuit Checks

Perform circuit checks on the DPF inlet pressure sensor if sense line and baseline checks do not identify the fault. Verify sensor power, ground, and signal integrity. A wiring low-signal fault can produce a false low reading without any sensing path issue.
Resume Point — Upstream Exhaust Leak Inspection

Inspect for exhaust leaks upstream of the DPF inlet pressure sensor. An exhaust leak upstream of the sensor reduces the measured pressure below the actual DPF inlet pressure. Inspect exhaust manifold, turbo outlet, and AT inlet connections for leaks.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Pressure Confirmation

After repair, verify DPF inlet pressure reads near ambient at KOEO and rises appropriately under load. Confirm delta-P calculation returns to normal. Monitor for return of FMI 1 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Hose, Sensor, or Exhaust Leak Decision

Reconnect or replace sense hose if disconnected or leaking. Replace sensor if bias is confirmed after sense line integrity is proven. Repair upstream exhaust leak if confirmed. Do not replace AT hardware for a sensing path fault.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3609 FMI 3 means the DPF intake pressure sensor circuit on a Freightliner (typically Detroit-powered) is reading voltage above normal, usually an open sensor or blocked sense line. It's Medium severity and inhibits DPF regeneration, though the engine keeps running. Most Freightliner Cascadias on the road run Detroit Diesel DD13 or DD15 engines, so DPF-related fault codes like SPN 3609 follow the same Detroit aftertreatment architecture. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees this fault frequently traced back to a plugged pressure sense line rather than an actual failed sensor, since the narrow sample tubes feeding these sensors are prone to soot and moisture blockage over time. Clearing the fault is usually quick once you know to check the sense line first.
causes: Plugged or kinked pressure sense line
Soot and condensation accumulate in the narrow sense tube over time, creating a false abnormal reading without any actual sensor failure.
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Vibration and heat cycling degrade the connector seal, and moisture intrusion corrodes the pin contacts.
Failed pressure sensor element
The sensor's internal pressure-sensing element can fail from extended exposure to exhaust heat and vibration.
Damaged wiring near the DPF canister from heat exposure
Insulation cracking from sustained high exhaust temperatures can eventually break the signal wire and open the circuit.
steps: Connect Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link (DDDL) or Freightliner-compatible diagnostic software and confirm SPN 3609 FMI 3, then check current soot load and regen status.
Locate the DPF intake pressure sensor and inspect the connector and pressure sense line for corrosion, disconnection, or soot blockage.
Clear any blocked sense line with a stiff wire or compressed air, since a plugged line reads as an open or abnormal signal even with a healthy sensor.
If the sense line is clear, unplug the sensor and check reference voltage and ground at the harness connector, then verify sensor resistance against spec.
Replace the sensor or repair the harness as needed, clear codes, and confirm normal regeneration resumes on the next duty cycle.
symptoms: Amber MIL illuminated
DPF regeneration inhibited or failing to complete properly
Rising soot load percentage over successive drive cycles
No immediate drivability change initially

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3609 FMI 3 on a Peterbilt means the DPF intake pressure sensor signal is above the normal 4.5 V ceiling — usually a short to Vref or an open sensor ground, not a DPF restriction. When a Peterbilt 579 or 389 logs SPN 3609 FMI 3, the aftertreatment control module has detected a DPF intake pressure sensor signal above 4.75 V — a value that cannot represent any real exhaust pressure and indicates a circuit fault. At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com we see FMI 3 on this sensor most often as a harness short or open ground, not a sensor replacement issue. The 3-wire DPF pressure sensor runs a 5 V reference supply, a 0.5 to 4.5 V signal output, and a sensor ground. FMI 3 occurs when the signal wire contacts the reference supply (short to Vref) or when the sensor ground is open and the signal floats high. Either condition produces an identical high-voltage symptom.
causes: Short from signal wire to the 5 V reference circuit in the harness

Heat cycling and vibration cause insulation to crack near DPF canister mounting points, allowing the signal wire to contact the adjacent 5 V reference wire and force the input to a high voltage state.
Open sensor ground (Pin B or Pin C depending on connector orientation)

A broken ground wire or corroded ground terminal causes the sensor output to float toward Vref due to the internal pull-up on the ACM/ECM analog input. The result is a signal above 4.75 V even if the sensor is functional.
Failed DPF intake pressure sensor with internal short to supply
The sensor's internal voltage divider circuit can fail by shorting the output to the supply rail, producing a fixed above-normal reading regardless of actual exhaust pressure.
Corroded or damaged sensor connector pins
Corrosion in the multi-pin connector can bridge the signal pin to the supply reference pin, mimicking an external harness short. Inspect the connector cavity for green or white deposits.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 to the Peterbilt DataLink connector (9-pin J1939 port under the dash). Read all active and inactive faults. If a NEXIQ USB-Link 2 adapter is used with an alternative scan application, confirm the DPF inlet pressure live data parameter. A reading above 250 kPa at idle with the engine running normally confirms FMI 3 is active.

With the key on and engine off, locate the 3-wire DPF intake pressure sensor on the DPF inlet cone or exhaust piping ahead of the filter. Back-probe the signal pin (typically Pin C or the center pin) to the sensor ground pin. If the reading exceeds 4.75 V, proceed with circuit isolation.

Disconnect the sensor connector. Measure the signal pin at the harness side to chassis ground. If the voltage remains above 0.5 V with the sensor disconnected, the harness has a short from the signal wire to the 5 V reference circuit. Inspect the harness loom near the DPF canister where heat cycling causes insulation brittleness.

If voltage drops to zero when the sensor is disconnected, the sensor itself is shorted internally. Measure the 5 V reference pin at the harness (with sensor disconnected): should read 4.95 to 5.05 V. A good reference plus a signal that goes high only when the sensor is plugged in confirms the sensor is the fault.

Replace the DPF intake pressure sensor with an OEM or approved aftermarket part. Clear the fault with PACCAR Davie4 and run a stationary regen to confirm the DPF inlet pressure rises proportionally with exhaust flow, reading 1.0 to 1.5 V at idle and 2.0 to 3.5 V during active regen.
symptoms: DPF intake pressure reading is implausibly high (above 250 kPa) in live data at idle.
Active regeneration may be inhibited or cancelled due to an unreliable inlet pressure signal.
Amber aftertreatment warning lamp illuminated on the Peterbilt cluster.
Additional DPF soot load faults or NOx efficiency faults may appear alongside SPN 3609 FMI 3.
Engine derate possible if the aftertreatment system enters a protection mode without valid pressure data.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3609 FMI 16 means DPF intake pressure is running moderately above normal, an early warning before the more severe backpressure codes. It's a medium-severity code with no derate yet - run a forced regen soon to keep it from escalating. This is the code you want to see and act on before the more dramatic severe backpressure fault shows up. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this as a straightforward proactive fix, since a forced regen at this stage usually clears it in under an hour.
causes: Building soot accumulation from incomplete regen cycles
Short trips, excessive idling, or a duty cycle that doesn't generate enough exhaust heat can prevent normal passive regeneration, letting soot build gradually.
Partial blockage in the sense line
A partially soot-clogged sense tube can produce a moderately elevated reading without a proportional real restriction.
Drifting DPF intake pressure sensor
A sensor reading slightly high independent of actual pressure is uncommon but should be checked if soot load and duty cycle history don't explain the fault.
steps: Pull the fault and check DPF soot load percentage on Volvo PTT to confirm whether accumulation is the driving factor.
Review recent duty cycle history for excessive idling or short trips that may have prevented normal regeneration.
Run a forced parked regeneration if soot load is elevated and the truck hasn't completed one recently.
Inspect the DPF intake pressure sensor's sense line for partial soot blockage, which can also cause a moderately elevated reading independent of actual restriction.
Verify the sensor's wiring and connector are free of corrosion or damage during the same inspection.
Clear the code after regen or repair and monitor intake pressure across a normal drive cycle to confirm it stays within range.
symptoms: Amber check engine lamp, typically no derate at this stage
Possible slightly elevated DPF soot load percentage
No major drivability complaint yet
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 3609 FMI 16: DPF Intake Pressure Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3609 FMI 16 means the DPF intake pressure sensor on PACCAR MX engines reads above the normal 2-5 kPa range, indicating excessive soot or ash restriction. Failed regeneration leads to progressive derate and possible five-MPH limp mode. Verify sensor zero with hoses disconnected before condemning the DPF. DPF intake pressure tells the PACCAR aftertreatment module how restricted the particulate filter has become. When SPN 3609 FMI 16 sets, exhaust flow through the DPF is impeded enough to raise inlet pressure above calibrated limits. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com recommends zero-checking the pressure sensor with hoses disconnected, then evaluating ash load with forced regen before authorizing DPF replacement on MX-11 and MX-13 trucks.
causes: Ash-loaded DPF requiring cleaning or replacement
Incombustible ash accumulates over 250,000-400,000 miles and cannot be burned during regen, permanently raising intake pressure above 8 kPa.
Failed or incomplete DPF regeneration cycles
Short-haul operation prevents reaching regen temperature thresholds, allowing soot to pack the filter and raise differential pressure.
Failed DPF intake pressure sensor or plugged sense hoses
Soot-filled pressure hoses or a drifted sensor can report falsely high pressure, though zero-check with hoses disconnected confirms sensor health.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 and monitor SPN 3609 (DPF intake pressure), SPN 4094 (soot load), and SPN 1209 (exhaust backpressure) at 1,800 RPM in neutral — intake pressure above 8 kPa with soot above 80% confirms restricted DPF.
Perform a parked forced regen and log pressure throughout — pressure should drop below 5 kPa within 30 minutes; failure to drop indicates ash-loaded DPF or failed regen.
Inspect the DPF intake pressure sensor and hose connections at the DPF inlet — verify hoses are not cracked, kinked, or filled with soot; blow through hoses with shop air to confirm free flow.
Compare intake pressure to atmospheric with hoses disconnected — sensor should read within 0.5 kPa of zero; readings above 2 kPa with hoses off indicate a failed sensor element.
If sensor and hoses check out, measure DPF outlet restriction — ash-loaded filters show less than 10 kPa drop after a complete regen, indicating the filter needs physical cleaning or replacement.
Clean or replace the DPF, verify SPN 3609 reads 2-5 kPa at cruise, and confirm soot load drops below 50% after two successful regen cycles.
symptoms: DPF intake pressure reads above 8-10 kPa at cruise on PACCAR Davie4 — normal is 2-5 kPa
Amber aftertreatment lamp with increasing soot load percentage (SPN 4094)
Reduced fuel economy and sluggish turbo response under load
Regen attempts start but fail to reduce intake pressure below 5 kPa
Progressive torque derate as soot load exceeds 80-100% threshold

procedures_full.overview: FMI 0 on DPF outlet pressure indicates the sensor reports above the maximum expected pressure for conditions. Downstream SCR or exhaust restriction, collapsed exhaust components, sensor bias high, and plugged sense line are the primary causes. Aftertreatment internal restriction beyond the DPF and damaged exhaust path after impact are documented patterns. Multi-pressure correlation is the most efficient first step — one sensor disagreeing with adjacent sensors is suspect. Replacing the DPF for a downstream restriction or sensor fault is the primary wasted-cost pattern on this fault.
causes: Downstream SCR or exhaust restriction — restriction beyond the DPF
Collapsed exhaust component — physical collapse in downstream exhaust path
Sensor bias high — outlet pressure sensor reading above actual pressure
Plugged sense line — sense line blockage producing high reading
Physical damage to exhaust path — impact damage to downstream AT or exhaust
steps: Single Action Gate — Multi-Pressure Correlation

Cross-check DPF outlet pressure against DPF inlet pressure and delta-P. One sensor reading high while adjacent sensors read normal confirms sensor bias. All pressure sensors reading high simultaneously confirms a true downstream restriction. Multi-pressure correlation is the mandatory first step before any hardware diagnosis.
Binary Decision Gate — Sense Hose and Sensor Check

Inspect the outlet pressure sense hose for blockage or kinking. A plugged sense line produces a false high reading. Verify sensor baseline at KOEO is near ambient atmospheric pressure. An implausible high reading at KOEO confirms sensor bias or a sense line fault.
Override Manager — Downstream Path Inspection

Inspect the downstream AT and exhaust path for restriction. Aftertreatment internal restriction beyond the DPF and collapsed exhaust components are documented causes of true high outlet pressure. Inspect SCR inlet, exhaust outlet, and any downstream components for restriction or physical damage.
Safety Interceptor — Impact Damage Assessment

Assess for impact damage to the downstream exhaust path. Physical damage to the exhaust system after road impact can collapse exhaust components and produce true high outlet pressure. Inspect the exhaust system for physical damage before any AT component replacement.
Resume Point — Backpressure Confirmation Under Load

Confirm backpressure under load if downstream restriction is suspected. True downstream restriction produces elevated backpressure that increases under load. A reading that is high at idle and increases under load confirms a true restriction rather than a sensor fault.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Pressure Confirmation
After repair, verify DPF outlet pressure returns to normal range. Confirm delta-P calculation returns to normal. Monitor for return of FMI 0 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Sensor, Hose, or Downstream Component Decision

Replace sensor if bias is confirmed after sense line integrity is proven. Repair or replace sense hose if blockage is confirmed. Repair or replace downstream AT or exhaust component if restriction is confirmed. Do not replace DPF for a downstream restriction or sensor fault.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair or replace plugged sense hose.
2 . Replace sensor if bias is confirmed after sense line integrity is proven.
3 . Repair or replace downstream AT or exhaust component if restriction is confirmed.
4 . Repair impact damage to downstream exhaust path if confirmed.
Verification Steps
Confirm DPF outlet pressure returns to normal range after repair.
Verify delta-P calculation returns to normal after repair.
Confirm SPN 3610 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of backpressure-related power loss after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Verify sense hose connection after every AT service.
✓ Inspect downstream exhaust path for restriction at every major service.
✓ Inspect exhaust system for impact damage after any road incident.
✓ Inspect DPF outlet pressure sensor connector for corrosion at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity

Medium to High if backpressure is truly elevated. High outlet pressure from downstream restriction reduces power and increases exhaust temperatures. Multi-pressure correlation prevents wrong-brick replacement.
symptoms: DPF outlet pressure high fault active
Downstream exhaust restriction indication
SCR or exhaust path restriction
Backpressure-related power loss
Delta-P calculation errors from high outlet pressure

field_evidence.title: 2013 International MaxxForce 7 SPN 4765 FMI 3 Sensor Voltage Issue
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2013 International MaxxForce 7 engine can experience sensor voltage issues identified by the diagnostic trouble code SPN 4765 FMI 3. This code points to a sensor circuit voltage fault, which may cause the engine sensors to display low voltage readings and struggle to detect line breaks under 1 volt. Sensor voltage readings below 1 volt often indicate a short in the circuit or a poor ground connection. These faults can stem from wiring harness problems such as corrosion, damaged wires, or continuity failures. Sensor connectors near the Diesel Oxidation Catalyst (DOC) and Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) are common locations where such issues may occur. Unplugging sensors that then show an increase in voltage up to 5 volts suggests that either the sensors themselves or their wiring harnes

dd_procedures.title: SPN 4766 FMI 31 – DPF Active Regeneration Inhibited
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
SPN 4766 FMI 31 – DPF Active Regeneration Inhibited
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 4766 FMI 31 indicates that the DPF active regeneration process is being prevented from initiating or completing due to a system condition or fault. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and means the ECM has determined that conditions are not safe or suitable for active regeneration to proceed. With regeneration blocked soot will continue to accumulate in the DPF leading to progressively more severe fault codes.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF or regen warning light illuminated 
Active regeneration not initiating 
DPF soot load continuing to rise 
Engine derate possible as soot accumulates 
Regen inhibit indicator may be illuminated on dash
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM determines one or more conditions are preventing active regeneration from proceeding. Common causes include:
Regen inhibit switch manually activated by driver 
Active fault codes preventing regeneration from initiating 
Low fuel level preventing regen from starting 
Engine operating conditions outside regen parameters 
Faulty regen related sensor preventing ECM from approving regen 
Parking brake not applied during attempted parked regen 
Multiple active fault codes creating inhibit conditions 
HC dosing system fault preventing regen from being approved
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving is possible but with active regeneration inhibited soot will continue to build in the DPF. If the inhibit condition is not resolved the DPF will reach critical soot levels triggering more severe derate conditions. Identify and resolve the inhibit cause as soon as possible.
Recommended Action
First check if the regen inhibit switch is activated and turn it off if so. Check fuel level and top up if low. Clear any active fault codes that may be creating inhibit conditions and attempt a parked regeneration. If regeneration remains inhibited have the HC dosing system, regen related sensors, and ECM conditions evaluated by a qualified diesel technician.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4766 FMI 31 mean?
 
It means the ECM is preventing active DPF regeneration from proceeding due to a system condition or fault that makes regeneration unsafe or impossible under current conditions.
 
 
What causes SPN 4766 FMI 31?
 
The most common causes are the regen inhibit switch being active, low fuel level, active fault codes creating inhibit conditions, or a faulty sensor preventing the ECM from approving regeneration.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4766 FMI 31?
 
Short distances may be possible but with regeneration inhibited soot will accumulate and more severe DPF faults will follow. Resolve the inhibit condition as soon as possible.
 
 
Will SPN 4766 FMI 31 cause a derate?
 
Not immediately but as soot accumulates from blocked regeneration more severe DPF soot codes will trigger derate conditions.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4766 FMI 31?
 
Identify and resolve the condition inhibiting regeneration — check the inhibit switch, fuel level, and any active fault codes. Once the inhibit condition is cleared and a successful active regeneration completes the code should clear.
 
 
Related codes
SPN 3826 FMI 16 
SPN 3713 FMI 16 
SPN 3713 FMI 18 
SPN 3719 FMI 0 
SPN 3556 FMI 16

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4766 FMI 3 on a Scania indicates the DOC outlet gas temperature sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage. Check for an open sensor, broken ground wire, or heat-damaged harness before condemning the sensor. Scania SPN 4766 FMI 3 flags a high-voltage condition on the DOC outlet gas temperature sensor circuit. SPN 4766 represents DOC Outlet Gas Temperature — the sensor positioned downstream of the diesel oxidation catalyst that confirms exhaust heat is sufficient to oxidize soot and hydrocarbons during active regeneration. FMI 3 means the ECU is reading a signal voltage above the calibrated maximum, which typically results from an open-circuit thermistor, a broken sensor ground, or a harness wire contacting a 12 V source. Without a valid DOC outlet temperature, Scania's aftertreatment controller cannot confirm regen completion, and the system will either inhibit regeneration or trigger a derate. Technicians at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com consistently find heat damage to the sensor pigtail as the leading cause on high-mileage DC13 and DC16 engines.
causes: Open-circuit DOC outlet temperature sensor
The thermistor element inside the sensor fails open with age or heat fatigue, forcing the signal circuit toward the supply voltage rail and triggering FMI 3.
Heat-damaged or chafed harness wiring
The sensor pigtail runs near the DPF housing. Prolonged exposure to exhaust heat breaks down insulation, creating open grounds or unintended contact with chassis voltage.
Corroded or backed-out ECU connector pin
Moisture ingress at the ECU connector oxidizes the sensor signal or ground pin, creating a high-resistance or open path that mimics an above-normal voltage condition.
steps: Connect a Texa Diagnostic Tool or Jaltest CDG unit to the Scania OBD/ATA port and read active fault codes. Confirm SPN 4766 FMI 3 is present and note any co-faults from the aftertreatment system.

Using a digital multimeter, back-probe the sensor signal pin at the ECU harness connector with the key ON and engine OFF. A reading above 4.8 V when SPN 4766 FMI 3 is active indicates an open sensor, open ground wire, or shorted signal wire.

Unplug the DOC outlet temperature sensor connector and measure resistance across the sensor pins. At ambient temperature the thermistor should read approximately 2 kΩ–5 kΩ depending on specification. An open-circuit reading (OL) confirms sensor failure.
Inspect the entire harness run from the DOC outlet sensor to the ECU connector for chafing against the exhaust pipe, heat damage, or corrosion at the pins. Repair any damaged sections and re-test.
After repair, clear faults with the Texa or Jaltest software and perform a stationary regeneration to verify the sensor returns a rising temperature reading as the DOC heats up.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp illuminated on Scania instrument cluster.
Diesel Particulate Filter regeneration inhibited or incomplete.
Engine derate limiting power or vehicle speed.
Visible black soot smoke after extended operation without successful regen.
Engine control unit stores SPN 4766 FMI 3 in active fault memory.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4766 FMI 10 means DOC outlet temperature is changing faster than the ECM allows. Capture high-speed data during doser tests and inspect thermocouple wiring before replacing parts. Cummins monitors not just absolute DOC outlet temperature but how quickly it moves — rapid spikes can indicate uncontrolled dosing or bad sensor data. SPN 4766 FMI 10 is common during regen transitions on X15 aftertreatment. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com records the fault event in INSITE first because the fix depends on whether the spike is real heat or electrical noise.
causes: Erratic HC doser injection causing sudden exothermic spikes
A sticking doser valve can dump fuel in one pulse, spiking DOC outlet temperature rate beyond calibration.
Intermittent DOC outlet thermocouple connection
Loose pins produce step changes in reported temperature that trigger FMI 10 without real heat swings.
Exhaust pulse or leak pulling cool air into sensor location
Sudden mixing at the thermocouple boss creates rapid apparent rate changes during load transitions.
ECM calibration mismatch after aftertreatment module swap
Incorrect parameter set can make normal regen temperature ramps look abnormally fast.
steps: Connect Cummins INSITE and graph SPN 4766 at high sample rate during idle, cruise, and commanded doser tests.
Inspect DOC outlet thermocouple connector for loose pins or intermittent shield ground causing data spikes.
Command HC doser on/off cycles and watch for temperature jumps that align with dosing events.
Check for exhaust leaks at the DOC outlet that cause sudden mixing of hot and cool gases at the sensor.
Compare DOC inlet and outlet rates — both spiking together suggests real heat events; outlet alone suggests wiring.
symptoms: Amber or red aftertreatment lamp with SPN 4766 FMI 10
DOC outlet temperature jumping more than 50°C per second on live data
Regen aborts logged for abnormal temperature rate
Intermittent fault that appears only during doser activation
Possible companion SPN 3242 or SPN 3246 temperature codes
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 4766 FMI 10: DOC Outlet Gas Temperature Abnormal Rate of Change

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4766 FMI 16 on Caterpillar means the DOC outlet temperature is reading above the moderately severe limit. Check the HC doser for over-fueling and inspect for oil in the exhaust before touching the temperature sensor. SPN 4766 measures the gas temperature leaving the Diesel Oxidation Catalyst — a reading that is directly tied to how well regens are executing and whether excess fuel or oil is oxidizing inside the DOC. FMI 16 means that outlet temperature is climbing into territory that can damage the DOC substrate if left unchecked. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com goes straight to the HC doser and the exhaust for oil before touching the sensor.
causes: HC doser over-fueling or stuck open during active regen (mechanical)
Very Common
A doser injector that is delivering too much or the wrong quantity of fuel during active regen causes the DOC to produce excessive exothermic heat, spiking outlet temperature above normal.
Engine oil or coolant entering the exhaust stream (mechanical)
Oil passing worn rings, a failed turbo seal, or a cracked exhaust manifold oxidizes in the DOC at very high temperatures, adding significant uncontrolled heat to the outlet reading.
Sustained high-load operation without adequate cooling periods (operational)
Extended high-RPM, high-load cycles with no passive cooling can push DOC outlet temperatures above normal bounds without any component failure.
DOC outlet temperature sensor reading high due to contamination or electrical fault (electrical)
Less Common
Soot or oil coating on the sensor thermocouple tip can cause falsely elevated readings. Sensor signal circuit faults rarely produce FMI 16 but can contribute to intermittent readings.
steps: 1. Connect Cat ET or Texa and pull all active aftertreatment faults alongside SPN 4766. Note whether HC doser-related codes or DPF soot load faults are also set.
2. Review the regen history in Cat ET — check if active regens are completing or being aborted due to overtemperature, and note the peak DOC outlet temp at abort.

3. Verify the HC (hydrocarbon) doser is not over-fueling: a stuck-open or leaking doser injector will flood the DOC with raw fuel, causing excessive exothermic oxidation and DOC outlet temps well above normal.
4. Check for oil in the exhaust — oil entering the DOC oxidizes at very high temperatures and can cause runaway DOC overtemperature that destroys the substrate and causes SPN 4766 FMI 16.

5. With Jaltest or Cat ET, scope DOC inlet and outlet temperatures simultaneously during a road test. Normal DOC temperature rise should be modest and proportional to load; a large step-up across the DOC at moderate engine load points to excessive HC in the exhaust.

6. If temperatures are consistently normal under load but FMI 16 sets intermittently, pin-test the sensor signal and reference circuit with a multimeter and check the connector for intermittent high-resistance contact.
symptoms: Aftertreatment warning or high EGT lamp illuminated
Possible power derate to reduce heat input to the aftertreatment system
Incomplete or interrupted DPF regen cycles if DOC temp exceeds safe regen limits
Possible white smoke or strong exhaust smell if HC doser is misfiring excess fuel into the DOC
High exhaust back pressure if DPF is loaded and regen is being interrupted by high DOC temp
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 4766 FMI 16: DOC Outlet Gas Temperature Above Normal Range

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4766 FMI 16 on Cummins means the DOC outlet temperature is valid but above the moderately severe limit. Inspect the HC doser for over-fueling and check for oil in the exhaust before replacing the temperature sensor. SPN 4766 measures gas temperature leaving the Diesel Oxidation Catalyst on Cummins aftertreatment systems. This reading directly controls whether active DPF regens can complete safely. When FMI 16 sets, the ECM has confirmed DOC outlet temperature exceeded the moderately severe threshold. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com goes straight to the HC doser and exhaust oil check — the sensor is usually reporting accurately.
causes: HC doser over-fueling or stuck open during active regen
Very Common
Excess hydrocarbon injection into the DOC causes uncontrolled exothermic oxidation, spiking outlet temperature above the 650°C abort threshold on X15 calibrations.
Engine oil entering the exhaust via turbo seal or worn rings
Oil oxidizing in the DOC adds heat beyond what the ECM dosing strategy expects, pushing outlet temperature into FMI 16 range.
Sustained high-load operation without cooling periods
Moderate
Extended mountain grades at high RPM without regen completion can elevate DOC outlet temperature through sheer exhaust energy input.
steps: Connect Cummins INSITE and pull all active aftertreatment faults. Log SPN 4766 alongside DOC inlet, DPF inlet (SPN 3242), and DPF outlet (SPN 3246) during a stationary regen attempt.
Review regen history in INSITE — note peak DOC outlet temperature at abort. Cummins X15 normal DOC outlet during successful regen peaks at 500°C-600°C; sustained readings above 650°C trigger FMI 16.

Command HC doser activation in INSITE at idle and monitor fuel delivery — doser should pulse defined quantities only when commanded. Continuous fuel flow when doser is commanded off indicates a stuck-open injector.
Check for engine oil in the exhaust by inspecting the turbo compressor outlet and DOC inlet for oily residue. Oil oxidation in the DOC can push outlet temperature above 700°C within minutes.

Compare DOC outlet sensor to an infrared pyrometer at the sensor boss. Variance beyond 30°C with stable mechanical temperatures suggests sensor replacement; matching high readings confirm genuine overtemperature.
symptoms: Amber or red aftertreatment lamp illuminated on the dash
DOC outlet temperature above 550°C at cruise on Cummins INSITE live data
Active or aborted DPF regen cycles with overtemperature abort reason logged
Possible white smoke during regen if HC doser is over-fueling
Companion SPN 3242 or SPN 3246 DPF temperature codes may be active
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 4766 FMI 16: DOC Outlet Gas Temperature Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4766 FMI 16 on Volvo engines means an active DPF regeneration attempt didn't reach or maintain the temperatures needed to fully burn off soot. It's a high-severity fault that can escalate to a soot-load derate if the underlying cause - often an air leak or EGT sensor issue - isn't resolved. Regeneration is a carefully choreographed thermal event, and SPN 4766 FMI 16 tells you it didn't go as planned. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com approaches this fault by pulling the freeze-frame data captured during the failed attempt rather than just clearing the code and letting the truck try again - repeatedly forcing regens without fixing the underlying restriction or leak just burns fuel and time while soot keeps accumulating toward a harder derate.
causes: Intake or exhaust air leak preventing adequate DOC/DPF temperatures
A boost leak or exhaust leak upstream of the aftertreatment introduces cool, unmetered air that keeps the system from reaching the temperatures needed for a full burn.
Damaged or drifting exhaust gas temperature sensor
If the EGT sensors feeding the regen control strategy are reading incorrectly, the ECM may end the regen early or misjudge that it failed even if the burn was progressing normally.
Restricted DOC face from soot or ash accumulation
A partially blocked DOC prevents proper light-off during the regen event, keeping temperatures below target despite normal fuel dosing.
Insufficient fuel delivery pressure during the dosing event
A weak fuel supply can prevent the doser or injector from delivering enough fuel volume to sustain the heat needed for a complete burn.
steps: Pull the fault with Volvo Premium Tech Tool and confirm SPN 4766 FMI 16 is active; review the freeze-frame data captured at the time of the incomplete regen to see which parameter (temperature, response time) fell out of range.

Inspect the entire intake and exhaust system for air leaks or damage that could prevent the aftertreatment system from reaching regen temperatures - a boost or exhaust leak upstream of the DOC is a common culprit.
Check the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) sensors before and after the DOC and DPF for damaged wiring, corrosion, or physically damaged sensor tips.
Verify fuel delivery pressure is adequate, since a starved fuel system can prevent the doser or injector from reaching the fuel volume needed to sustain regen temperatures.
If sensors and fuel delivery check out, inspect the DOC face for soot or ash blockage that could be preventing it from lighting off properly during the regen attempt.
Once the root cause is corrected, initiate a parked (stationary) regeneration through the scan tool and confirm it completes successfully before releasing the truck.
symptoms: Frequent or repeated regeneration attempts that don't seem to resolve
Rising DPF soot load percentage on the scan tool over successive drive cycles
Amber dash lamp, sometimes with a specific inducement warning as soot load climbs
Slightly reduced fuel economy as the engine keeps attempting regen cycles
Eventual power derate if soot load reaches a critical threshold without a successful regen
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 4766 FMI 16: Diagnosing an Incomplete DPF Regeneration

procedures_full.overview: FMI 0 on crankcase pressure indicates the ECM detected crankcase pressure above the calibrated limit. Plugged crankcase ventilation filter or separator, excessive ring blowby, turbo seal contribution, measurement hose restriction, and sensor bias are the primary causes. CCV filter neglect causing rising pressure and seal leaks and high-mileage blowby are documented patterns. Continued operation with high crankcase pressure can push oil past seals and create secondary failures — address promptly.
causes: Plugged CCV filter or separator — CCV filter or separator restriction preventing crankcase ventilation
Excessive ring blowby — ring wear or damage producing excessive blowby
Turbo seal contribution — turbo seal leak contributing to crankcase pressure
Measurement hose restriction — sense hose restriction producing false high reading
Sensor bias — crankcase pressure sensor bias producing false high reading
steps: Single Action Gate — Inspect CCV and Separator

Inspect the crankcase ventilation filter and separator for restriction or plugging. CCV filter neglect causing rising pressure and seal leaks is a documented pattern. A plugged CCV filter or separator prevents crankcase ventilation and produces high crankcase pressure. Service the CCV filter and separator per OEM service intervals.
Binary Decision Gate — Verify Sense Hose

Verify the crankcase pressure sense hose integrity. A sense hose that is kinked, collapsed, or restricted produces a false high pressure reading. Confirm the sense hose is clear and properly connected. A stuck sensor reading without physical pressure change is suspect — verify hose integrity before any mechanical conclusions.
Override Manager — Measure Pressure

Measure crankcase pressure with a manometer or gauge where OEM procedures allow. Compare the measured pressure to the OEM specification. A measured pressure that confirms the ECM reading confirms true high crankcase pressure. A measured pressure that is normal while the ECM reports high pressure confirms a sensing fault.
Safety Interceptor — Evaluate Blowby Per OEM Test

Evaluate blowby per OEM test procedure. A blowby test that confirms excessive blowby supports ring or cylinder wear as the source of high crankcase pressure. Compare blowby to OEM specifications for the engine mileage and duty cycle.
Resume Point — Inspect Turbo and Engine Contributors

Inspect turbo and engine contributors to crankcase pressure. A turbo seal leak contributes to crankcase pressure on some designs. Inspect for turbo seal leakage and evaluate whether the turbo contribution is within normal limits.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Pressure Confirmation
After repair, verify crankcase pressure returns to normal. Confirm SPN 101 FMI 0 does not return. Monitor for return of high crankcase pressure events over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — CCV Service, Hose, Sensor, or Engine Decision

Service CCV filter and separator if restriction is confirmed. Repair or replace sense hose if restriction is confirmed. Replace sensor if bias is confirmed by gauge comparison. Perform engine or turbo repairs only with evidence of blowby or seal failure.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1. Service CCV filter and separator if restriction is confirmed.
2. Repair or replace sense hose if restriction is confirmed.
3. Replace sensor if bias is confirmed by gauge comparison.
4. Perform engine or turbo repairs only with evidence of blowby or seal failure.
Verification Steps
Confirm crankcase pressure returns to normal after repair.
Verify SPN 101 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Confirm no oil seal leaks after repair.
Monitor for return of high crankcase pressure events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Service CCV filter and separator at OEM-specified intervals.
✓ Inspect crankcase pressure sense hose at every major service.
✓ Monitor crankcase pressure PID trend over time to identify restriction before it becomes severe.
✓ Inspect for oil seal leaks at every major service on high-mileage engines.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High. Continued operation can push oil past seals and create secondary failures. The FSM enforces ventilation-first logic before major engine conclusions.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 101 FMI 3 on Caterpillar engines means crankcase pressure sensor voltage is above the normal range, typically a short to 5V or power. The ECM may ignore blow-by data and apply limp strategies. Test the harness with the sensor unplugged before assuming engine wear. Crankcase pressure codes scare owners into engine-rebuild quotes, but ProfessionalDieselRepair.com finds FMI 3 on Cat platforms is overwhelmingly a wiring or sensor fault. Voltage-above-normal FMI codes point at the circuit, not necessarily worn rings.
causes: Signal wire shorted to 5V supply or battery positive
Chafed harness near the valve cover or turbo plumbing contacts a power feed, pulling signal voltage high.
Failed crankcase pressure sensor internal short
Moisture intrusion or age cracks the sensor element, shorting the output high regardless of actual blow-by.
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Oil mist and road salt create conductive paths between supply and signal pins at the Deutsch connector.
steps: Connect via Jaltest or Cat ET and read freeze-frame voltage on SPN 101; values above 4.8V at idle confirm FMI 3.
Disconnect the crankcase pressure sensor at the valve cover. Key on, measure supply pin for 5.0V +/- 0.25V and signal pin; above 4.5V with sensor unplugged indicates a shorted signal wire.
Inspect harness routing along the valve cover and turbo feed lines for rubbed-through insulation contacting exhaust heat shields.
Measure sensor resistance pin-to-pin per Cat spec, typically 1-5k ohms; open or shorted element sets voltage faults.
Repair harness or replace sensor, then run a crankcase pressure functional test in ET to confirm 0-8 inH2O range at idle.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with active SPN 101 FMI 3 in ET or Jaltest
Crankcase pressure reading pegged high or flat-lined in live data
Possible rough idle if ECM enters limp strategy for sensor plausibility
No physical crankcase breather overflow despite high reported pressure
Fault present key-on engine-off with sensor unplugged may clear

procedures_full.overview: SPN 101 FMI 16 means Caterpillar crankcase pressure is reading above normal at a moderately severe level, usually from a clogged breather or excessive blow-by. It is High severity and can push oil out of seals if ignored, though it doesn't force a shutdown. Crankcase pressure is one of those readings that tells you a lot about internal engine health without ever opening it up, and SPN 101 FMI 16 is the Cat ECM's way of flagging that pressure has climbed higher than it should during normal operation. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always tells techs to resist the urge to assume the worst here - a plugged crankcase breather filter causes this exact same symptom as genuine piston ring or turbo seal blow-by, and it costs a fraction as much to fix. Working through the diagnostic steps in order from cheapest to most invasive saves a lot of unnecessary teardown time.
causes: Clogged or oil-soaked crankcase breather filter
The breather element restricts crankcase ventilation as it accumulates oil mist and debris over normal service life, raising internal pressure.
Kinked or frozen breather hose
A collapsed hose or ice buildup in cold climates blocks the ventilation path just as effectively as a clogged filter.
Excessive piston ring blow-by
Worn piston rings or cylinder liners allow combustion gases to leak into the crankcase in volumes beyond what the ventilation system was designed to handle.
Failing turbocharger seal allowing boost pressure into the crankcase
A failed turbo shaft seal can push charged air into the crankcase, raising pressure without any actual combustion blow-by involved.
symptoms: Amber diagnostic lamp illuminated
Oil leaks appearing at seals or gaskets that weren't leaking before
Visible mist or oil residue around the crankcase breather outlet
Possible slight power reduction on some engine calibrations
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 101 FMI 16: Crankcase Pressure Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 101 FMI 16 on Volvo engines means crankcase pressure is above the normal operating range with a valid sensor reading. High blow-by, a restricted breather, or turbo drain issues can trigger derate. Inspect the breather system and confirm mechanical blow-by before major engine work. High crankcase pressure on a Volvo D13 can mean anything from a clogged breather to tired rings. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com starts every SPN 101 FMI 16 diagnosis with inexpensive restriction checks because the FMI confirms the sensor data is believable.
causes: Restricted crankcase breather filter or hose
Oil-soaked or carbon-clogged breathers trap pressure in the crankcase even when ring seal is acceptable.
Turbocharger oil drain restriction or failure
Oil backing up through the turbo seal pressurizes the crankcase without true cylinder blow-by.
Excessive cylinder blow-by from worn rings or liners
High-mileage engines pass combustion gases into the crankcase, raising measured pressure at all speeds.
steps: Read SPN 101 live data in Jaltest at idle and 1200 RPM; Volvo spec is typically below 6-8 inH2O at idle on healthy engines.
Inspect the crankcase breather filter and hose for blockage, kinks, or oil sludge saturation.
Remove the oil fill cap at idle briefly; excessive blow-by puffing confirms mechanical leakage beyond sensor error.
Check the turbocharger oil drain line for restriction; a plugged drain raises crankcase pressure without ring wear.
If mechanical blow-by is confirmed, perform a cylinder cutout test and compression check before authorizing an in-frame overhaul.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with elevated crankcase pressure in MID or Jaltest
Oil seepage at valve cover gaskets or breather hose connections
Loss of power or mild derate under load
Blue smoke at idle on high-mileage engines with real blow-by
Oil residue in the crankcase filter housing or breather separator

steps: Low Speed Check (Low Box)
Inspect the entire air intake system for leaks and/or restrictions.
If leaks or restrictions are found, repair as necessary. Refer to "27.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no air intake system leaks or restrictions are found, go to step 2.
Connect to DDDL 7.0
Turn the ignition ON (key On, engine OFF).
Perform the DDDL Turbo Hysteresis Test.
If the test passed, replace the Turbo Speed Sensor (TSS). Refer to "27.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the test failed, refer to "6.5 Turbocharger (Diesel)"
6.5 in the Series 60 Service Manual
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

causes: This diagnosis is typically circuit failed low.‪
steps: Short Circuit Check
Check for short as follows:‪
Disconnect the Turbo Speed Sensor (TSS).
Disconnect the 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance across pins 1 and 2 of the TSS connector.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short between the 120–pin MCM connector wires 50 and 51. Refer to "27.3.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 4.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 of the TSS harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short between pin 1 of the TSS harness connector and ground. Refer to "27.3.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 5.
Measure the resistance between pin 2 of the TSS harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short between pin 2 of the TSS harness connector and ground. Refer to "27.3.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, refer to "27.3.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

This code is triggered when the Engine Control Module (ECM) detects that the EGR valve is not responding as quickly as expected, which can affect engine performance and emissions. What SPN 3058 FMI 10 Means The SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code specifically points to a slow response in the EGR system. The EGR valve is responsible for recirculating a portion of the engine's exhaust back into the intake air to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions. When the ECM commands the EGR valve to open or close, it expects a certain response time. If the valve is sluggish or fails to reach the desired position promptly, this fault code is set. Common Causes of This Fault Code EGR valve sticking or carbon buildup EGR cooler blockage Faulty EGR position sensor EGR actuator malfunction Restricted or damaged EGR piping Symptoms Drivers May Notice When the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code is active, drivers may notice a decrease in engine performance, increased exhaust emissions, or a check engine light. In some cases, the engine may experience rough idling or hesitation during acceleration. How Technicians Diagnose This Fault Technicians begin diagnosing this fault with a visual inspection of the EGR valve and piping for signs of carbon buildup or physical damage. Using a scan tool, they command the EGR valve to open and close, observing the response time and position feedback. The EGR position sensor readings are checked for accuracy and consistency. Technicians also inspect the EGR cooler for blockages or leaks and perform a pressure test on the EGR system to identify any restrictions. Electrical diagnostics include checking battery voltage, verifying sensor power supply and ground circuits, and inspecting the wiring harness for damage, corrosion, or loose connectors. Signal readings are verified using a scan tool or multimeter before considering sensor or module replacement. Common Misdiagnosis Technicians often misdiagnose this fault by assuming a faulty EGR valve without checking for carbon buildup. Replacing the EGR position sensor without verifying the sensor signal integrity is another common mistake. Additionally, overlooking EGR cooler issues can lead to a misdiagnosis of the slow response problem. Can You Keep Driving? While it may be possible to continue driving with the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code active, it is not advisable. The fault can lead to increased emissions and potential engine derate or protection mode, which can affect vehicle performance and fuel efficiency. Addressing the issue promptly is recommended to avoid further complications. Mechanic's Diagnostic Tip When diagnosing the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code, always check for carbon buildup in the EGR valve and cooler before replacing any components. Carbon buildup is a common cause of slow EGR response and can often be resolved with cleaning rather than part replacement. Frequently Asked Questions Q: What tools are needed to diagnose SPN 3058 FMI 10? A: A scan tool, multimeter, and pressure testing equipment are essential for diagnosing this fault code. Q: Can a faulty EGR position sensor cause SPN 3058 FMI 10? A: Yes, a faulty EGR position sensor can cause this fault if it provides inaccurate feedback to the ECM. Q: Is it necessary to replace the EGR valve if SPN 3058 FMI 10 is active? A: Not necessarily. Always perform a thorough diagnostic to determine if cleaning or other repairs can resolve the issue before replacing the EGR valve. This code is triggered when the Engine Control Module (ECM) detects that the EGR valve is not responding as quickly as expected, which can affect engine performance and emissions. What SPN 3058 FMI 10 Means The SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code specifically points to a slow response in the EGR system. The EGR valve is responsible for recirculating a portion of the engine's exhaust back into the intake air to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions. When the ECM commands the EGR valve to open or close, it expects a certain response time. If the valve is sluggish or fails to reach the desired position promptly, this fault code is set. Common Causes of This Fault Code EGR valve sticking or carbon buildup EGR cooler blockage Faulty EGR position sensor EGR actuator malfunction Restricted or damaged EGR piping Symptoms Drivers May Notice When the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code is active, drivers may notice a decrease in engine performance, increased exhaust emissions, or a check engine light. In some cases, the engine may experience rough idling or hesitation during acceleration. How Technicians Diagnose This Fault Technicians begin diagnosing this fault with a visual inspection of the EGR valve and piping for signs of carbon buildup or physical damage. Using a scan tool, they command the EGR valve to open and close, observing the response time and position feedback. The EGR position sensor readings are checked for accuracy and consistency. Technicians also inspect the EGR cooler for blockages or leaks and perform a pressure test on the EGR system to identify any restrictions. Electrical diagnostics include checking battery voltage, verifying sensor power supply and ground circuits, and inspecting the wiring harness for damage, corrosion, or loose connectors. Signal readings are verified using a scan tool or multimeter before considering sensor or module replacement. Common Misdiagnosis Technicians often misdiagnose this fault by assuming a faulty EGR valve without checking for carbon buildup. Replacing the EGR position sensor without verifying the sensor signal integrity is another common mistake. Additionally, overlooking EGR cooler issues can lead to a misdiagnosis of the slow response problem. Can You Keep Driving? While it may be possible to continue driving with the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code active, it is not advisable. The fault can lead to increased emissions and potential engine derate or protection mode, which can affect vehicle performance and fuel efficiency. Addressing the issue promptly is recommended to avoid further complications. Mechanic's Diagnostic Tip When diagnosing the SPN 3058 FMI 10 fault code, always check for carbon buildup in the EGR valve and cooler before replacing any components. Carbon buildup is a common cause of slow EGR response and can often be resolved with cleaning rather than part replacement. Frequently Asked Questions Q: What tools are needed to diagnose SPN 3058 FMI 10? A: A scan tool, multimeter, and pressure testing equipment are essential for diagnosing this fault code. Q: Can a faulty EGR position sensor cause SPN 3058 FMI 10? A: Yes, a faulty EGR position sensor can cause this fault if it provides inaccurate feedback to the ECM. Q: Is it necessary to replace the EGR valve if SPN 3058 FMI 10 is active? A: Not necessarily. Always perform a thorough diagnostic to determine if cleaning or other repairs can resolve the issue before replacing the EGR valve. SPN_3058.pgn_description: NOTE - Retarder can be disabled by commanding a torque limit of 0%. Use of the limit mode allows the use of the retarder only up to the limit specified in the request. This can be used to permit retarding of up to 50%, for example, if that limit is required by some device such as an EBS, or it can disable the use of the retarder by others, as when an ABS controller detects wheel slip. Note that the 10 ms transmission repetition rate is intended for temporary powertrain control (P32 of SPN 3350).

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 0 is a critical code meaning exhaust backpressure has reached a severely high level, almost always from a plugged DPF. Expect an active power derate - check soot load and attempt a forced regen before assuming filter replacement is needed.
causes: Heavily soot-loaded DPF that missed its regeneration window
Frequent short trips or excessive idling prevent the DPF from completing normal passive or active regeneration, letting soot accumulate past safe limits.
Physically damaged or collapsed DPF substrate
Internal structural damage from a prior overtemp event or impact can create a permanent restriction that a regen cycle can't clear.
Blocked backpressure sensor sense line
Soot accumulation in the sense line itself can produce a falsely high backpressure reading independent of the actual exhaust restriction.
steps: Pull freeze-frame backpressure data on Volvo PTT and note the pressure reading against the OEM most-severe threshold.
Check DPF soot load percentage on the same scan to confirm whether the filter itself is the restriction source.
Attempt a forced parked regeneration through PTT if soot load is high and the truck's duty cycle hasn't allowed a normal regen to complete.
Inspect the exhaust piping and DPF housing for any physical damage or collapsed internal structure if regen doesn't resolve the pressure.
Verify the backpressure sensor itself and its sense line are not blocked with soot, which can cause a falsely high reading independent of actual restriction.
If a forced regen fails to reduce backpressure, the DPF likely needs to be removed for cleaning or replacement rather than continuing to force regens.
symptoms: Red stop engine or amber lamp with active power derate
Noticeable loss of power, especially under load or acceleration
Excessive heat buildup near the DPF and exhaust piping
Possible unusual exhaust smell or visible smoke if soot loading is extreme

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 0 means exhaust backpressure is far above normal, most often from a heavily loaded DPF or a VGT stuck toward closed. It's a Critical fault that commonly triggers a power derate until the restriction is cleared.
causes: Heavily soot-loaded or ash-loaded DPF
A mechanical/aftertreatment restriction. The filter simply can't pass exhaust volume anymore, and backpressure climbs upstream of it exactly as the sensor reports.
VGT actuator or unison ring stuck toward closed
A mechanical failure inside the turbocharger. Carbon buildup on the vanes or a seized actuator prevents the turbo from opening up to relieve pressure.
Blocked or kinked backpressure sensor sense tube
This one is a sensor/plumbing fault rather than a true restriction - soot packed in the small sense line can make the ECM read a false high pressure.
Failed exhaust backpressure sensor
A straightforward electrical fault where the sensor itself reports incorrectly high pressure despite a clear exhaust path.
steps: Pull the full active fault list in Cummins INSITE - SPN 1209 almost never appears alone; look for a companion SPN 3251 (DPF differential pressure) code.
Check DPF soot load percentage and differential pressure in live data; a soot load reading above 100% confirms a plugged filter as the primary restriction.
Command a VGT sweep test through INSITE and watch actual vs. commanded turbo vane position - vanes that lag or won't reach commanded position point to a stuck actuator or soot-packed unison ring.
Inspect the exhaust backpressure sensor's sense tube for carbon blockage, since a plugged tube can make a healthy exhaust system look restricted.
If the DPF is confirmed loaded, perform a stationary forced regen; if regen won't complete or the filter is ash-loaded rather than soot-loaded, remove it for cleaning or replacement.
symptoms: Noticeable loss of power, especially climbing grades or under load
Active power derate accompanied by a check engine or stop engine lamp
Excessive exhaust smoke or a burnt smell if the DPF is severely loaded
Engine runs hotter than normal at the exhaust manifold
