procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 0 on International trucks means exhaust gas pressure is at the critical most-severe-high threshold. Before ordering any parts, disconnect the pressure sense tube and check for carbon packing. A blocked sense tube is the most common cause of this critical fault and costs nothing to fix.
causes: Carbon-packed exhaust pressure sense tube (mechanical)

The small-bore sense tube connecting the exhaust manifold tap or DPF inlet to the exhaust pressure sensor accumulates carbon deposits over thousands of miles of operation. When sufficiently packed, it traps pressure and presents a false-high reading to the sensor, triggering an FMI 0 critical fault without any actual exhaust restriction.
Severely plugged DPF (aftertreatment)
Moderate

Extreme soot or ash overload in the DPF creates real backpressure that the sense tube faithfully reports. At FMI 0 levels, actual DPF restriction is severe and a forced regen or physical DPF cleaning is required.
Collapsed or kinked exhaust flex pipe (mechanical)
Moderate

The corrugated stainless exhaust flex section between the turbo outlet and main exhaust run can collapse internally, particularly on high-vibration applications. The internal collapse blocks flow like a pinched hose while the external appearance remains normal.
Exhaust pressure sensor failure (electrical)
Less Common

The exhaust pressure sensor itself can fail in a high-reading direction, reporting extreme pressure when the exhaust system is clear. Confirmed by verifying sense tube is clear and mechanical gauge reads near zero while sensor reads high.
steps: 1. Connect Navistar Diamond Logic / ServiceMaxx and read live SPN 1209 exhaust pressure. At idle, exhaust backpressure should be under 0.5 kPa (0.07 psi). At rated load, typically under 6 kPa (0.87 psi). Values above 15-20 kPa at load are severe restriction territory; a reading above 30 kPa is extreme and may indicate the sense tube is packed rather than a real restriction of that magnitude.

2. Disconnect the mechanical sense tube at the exhaust pressure sensor and inspect it for carbon packing. Insert a wire or blow compressed air through the tube toward the exhaust manifold/DPF tap. Carbon that was blocking the tube often falls out immediately. Reconnect and recheck SPN 1209 — if the reading drops to near zero, the sense tube was the fault.

3. Tee a mechanical exhaust backpressure gauge (rated for exhaust gas, minimum 100 kPa / 15 psi range) into the exhaust upstream of the DPF to independently confirm whether real restriction exists. A mechanical reading near zero while ServiceMaxx reads high confirms a sense tube or sensor issue. Equal readings confirm a real mechanical restriction.

4. If real exhaust backpressure is confirmed high, check DPF differential pressure via ServiceMaxx (SPN 4094 soot load and DPF differential pressure parameters). Attempt a stationary forced regen to reduce soot load and recheck backpressure. A successful regen that drops backpressure confirms the DPF was the restriction.

5. If backpressure remains high after a successful regen, inspect the exhaust system from the turbo outlet to the tail pipe for a collapsed flex pipe, kinked pipe run, packed catalytic muffler, or physical DPF damage. Use Jaltest or Snap-on NEXIQ for additional live data cross-reference.
symptoms: Critical derate or engine protection shutdown event
ServiceMaxx or Jaltest showing SPN 1209 exhaust pressure far above 15-20 kPa at load
Possible black smoke from DPF backpressure affecting combustion
Turbocharger whine or surge if real backpressure is starving the exhaust side
Power loss proportional to the degree of real restriction

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 3 means the exhaust backpressure sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage, an electrical fault rather than a genuine restriction event. It's a medium-severity code with no derate - check the harness before replacing the sensor. Don't confuse this circuit fault with a genuinely plugged DPF - the fix here is almost always electrical. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always confirms the fault is a wiring issue before assuming the exhaust system itself is restricted.
causes: Chafed or heat-damaged signal wire near the exhaust system
Prolonged heat exposure can degrade wire insulation over time, allowing the signal wire to short against a powered or grounded surface.
Corroded connector pin
Moisture intrusion at the connector can corrode pins, producing an intermittent high-voltage reading.
Internally failed sensor
Heat cycling can degrade the sensor's internal element, presenting as an open circuit that mimics the same fault.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on Mercedes-Benz Xentry to confirm the reading is pinned at an unrealistic high value.
Locate the exhaust backpressure sensor and its sense line, typically mounted near the DPF, and unplug the connector.
Back-probe signal and ground with a multimeter, key on engine off - a reading near 5V with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness-side fault.
Inspect the signal wire for chafing or heat damage along its routing near the exhaust system.
Verify the sense line itself is not damaged or disconnected, which can also affect sensor accuracy independent of the electrical circuit.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor as needed, then clear the code and confirm a plausible reading returns.
symptoms: Check engine lamp illuminated, typically no derate
No noticeable drivability change in most cases
Possible delayed or irregular regen scheduling

procedures_full.overview: PACCAR SPN 1209 FMI 16 means exhaust backpressure is above the normal operating range, signaling DPF restriction on MX-13 or MX-11 engines. This High-severity fault escalates to a derate if the DPF is not serviced. Diagnose with PACCAR Davie4 live data and a parked regen attempt before recommending any hardware replacement. PACCAR SPN 1209 FMI 16 is a High-severity aftertreatment fault on MX-13 and MX-11 engines indicating the exhaust gas backpressure parameter is reporting a data-valid above-normal value. Unlike a sensor circuit fault (FMI 3 or FMI 4), FMI 16 means the data itself is valid - the exhaust system has a genuine restriction causing elevated pressure upstream of the DPF outlet. On PACCAR platforms, the primary cause is DPF soot or ash accumulation. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com recommends using PACCAR Davie4 and Diesel Laptops to review regen history and attempt a parked regen before scheduling DPF cleaning. Many SPN 1209 FMI 16 cases on city-cycle trucks resolve with a single completed parked regen and a driver reminder to allow regens to finish.
causes: DPF soot overloading from incomplete regeneration cycles
Very Common

Short-haul or urban duty cycles repeatedly abort regens before completion, allowing soot to accumulate beyond what a single regen can clear. PACCAR Davie4 regen history will show multiple incomplete regens preceding the SPN 1209 FMI 16 event.
Ash accumulation in DPF after extended service

Non-combustible ash from engine oil additives accumulates permanently in the DPF over time. After 300,000+ miles without cleaning, ash restriction is the dominant contribution to elevated backpressure and forced regens no longer resolve the condition.
Exhaust backpressure sensor drift or plumbing blockage

The sensor or its pressure tap hose can become clogged with soot deposits, causing an artificially high reading. Comparing the sensor output to a T-fitting mechanical gauge at the same location confirms whether the sensor is accurate.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 diagnostic software via a Diesel Laptops USB-Link 2 or compatible J1939 adapter. Navigate to Engine > Aftertreatment and read SPN 1209 live data. At idle with a healthy DPF, exhaust backpressure should read below 10 kPa. FMI 16 sets when pressure exceeds the upper normal threshold, typically around 20-25 kPa depending on engine speed and load.

Check DPF regen history in Davie4. If the last several regens were incomplete or aborted, the filter has accumulated excess soot and a parked regen is the first intervention. Initiate a parked regen using the Davie4 service function and monitor SPN 1209 during and after the regen to confirm backpressure drops below 10 kPa.

If a parked regen does not reduce backpressure, the DPF may be ash-loaded beyond what passive or active regen can clear. Use Davie4 to review ash accumulation data. At over 300,000 miles since last DPF cleaning, physical cleaning or replacement is likely required.

Inspect the exhaust backpressure sensor (located in the exhaust pipe or DOC inlet housing on the MX-13). Unplug the sensor connector and measure signal voltage at key-on engine-off: normal range is 0.5-4.5 V. A sensor stuck reading above 4.0 V at idle with no load may be drifted high; compare to a known good T-fitting mechanical gauge reading to verify.

If backpressure is confirmed high by both the sensor and a T-fitting mechanical gauge, proceed with DPF cleaning or replacement. Use Diesel Laptops to access PACCAR service reset procedures after DPF service to reset the soot and ash counters.
symptoms: Amber Check Engine and aftertreatment lamps active; possible derate at elevated backpressure.
Engine power feels slightly down at highway speed, especially under load.
DPF regeneration indicator may be active or recently completed without resolving the backpressure.
Exhaust restriction audible as slightly labored engine note at highway cruise.
Fuel economy deterioration proportional to the degree of DPF restriction severity.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 16 on International engines means exhaust gas pressure is above the normal range with valid sensor data. DPF restriction, stuck VGT vanes, or plugged sensor tubes can trigger derate. Compare backpressure to DPF differential pressure in JPRO before replacing components. High exhaust backpressure is the engine telling you it cannot exhale. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com starts International SPN 1209 FMI 16 diagnosis with DPF soot load and a sensor tube inspection because valid data means the ECM believes the restriction is real.
causes: Plugged or overloaded DPF with incomplete regen history
Soot and ash accumulation raise exhaust backpressure until the ECM derates power to protect the turbo.
Stuck VGT turbo vanes or failed actuator
Vanes stuck toward closed increase drive pressure even when the DPF is partially clean.
Carbon-plugged exhaust pressure sensor sense tube
A blocked tube reports falsely high pressure, though FMI 16 usually reflects genuine restriction when confirmed mechanically.
steps: Pull full fault list in Noregon JPRO; SPN 1209 FMI 16 often pairs with SPN 3251 DPF differential pressure codes.
Monitor DPF soot load and differential pressure; soot above 100 percent or DP above 8-10 inH2O indicates restriction.
Command a forced regen through ServiceMaxx or JPRO; abort or incomplete regen confirms heavy soot loading.
Inspect the exhaust backpressure sensor tube for carbon plugging; blow through with regulated shop air below 30 psi.
Check VGT actuator movement versus commanded position; stuck closed vanes raise backpressure without a full DPF plug.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with active SPN 1209 FMI 16 in ServiceMaxx or JPRO
Noticeable power loss climbing grades or under heavy load
Excessive exhaust smoke during regen attempts
High exhaust temperature readings alongside elevated backpressure
Audible exhaust restriction or turbo whine change under load

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1209 FMI 16 on Volvo engines means exhaust backpressure is moderately above the expected level. It's a medium-severity fault that usually points to a clogged sense tube, a soot-loaded DPF, or a physical exhaust restriction. Exhaust pressure faults like SPN 1209 FMI 16 sit in a gray area on Volvo engines - not an immediate derate, but a sign something's restricting flow through the exhaust path. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this as a triage code: check the cheap and common cause first (a plugged sensor sense line) before assuming the DPF or exhaust piping is physically restricted. Left unaddressed, sustained high backpressure works against the turbo and accelerates soot accumulation, so it's worth a proper look even without a hard fault light on the dash.
causes: Clogged or disconnected exhaust pressure sensor sense tube
Soot and condensation build up in the small sense line over time, producing an artificially high pressure reading with no actual restriction.
Elevated DPF soot load
A DPF nearing its regeneration threshold restricts exhaust flow and drives up measured backpressure ahead of the filter.
Physical exhaust restriction (damaged pipe, aftermarket muffler, or collapsed liner)
Mechanical damage or a non-OEM exhaust component can restrict flow enough to read as elevated backpressure under load.
Faulty exhaust pressure sensor
Internal sensor drift can produce a false high reading even with clean sense lines and normal actual pressure.
steps: Connect Volvo's Premium Tech Tool (or a Jaltest heavy-duty interface) and confirm whether SPN 1209 FMI 16 is active and check the logged exhaust pressure value against the expected range for current RPM and load.
Visually inspect the exhaust system from the turbo outlet back through the DOC and DPF for any obvious dents, kinks, or aftermarket exhaust modifications that could restrict flow.
Check the DPF differential pressure (SPN 3251) alongside this code - if soot load is climbing, the DPF itself is the likely source of the added backpressure rather than the exhaust piping.
Verify the exhaust pressure sensor's sense tube isn't cracked, disconnected, or plugged with soot - a blocked sense line will read artificially high even with normal actual backpressure.
If the sensor and lines check out and soot load is within range, inspect the DPF for physical damage or a partially melted substrate using a borescope through the inlet.
Clear the code, run a road test under load, and compare live exhaust pressure readings to a known-good baseline before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Slight reduction in power or fuel economy that builds gradually

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3363 FMI 16 – DEF Pump Pressure High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3363 FMI 16 – DEF Pump Pressure High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3363 FMI 16 indicates that the DEF pump is generating pressure above the acceptable operating range. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and signals a problem within the DEF supply system that can prevent proper dosing and lead to SCR system faults and engine derate if not resolved.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF or SCR warning light illuminated 
Engine derate possible 
DEF system operating abnormally 
Possible DEF leaks from pressurized components
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM detects DEF pump pressure exceeding the specified threshold. Common causes include:
Blocked or restricted DEF return line 
Clogged DEF filter Faulty DEF pressure relief valve 
Failed DEF pump delivering excessive pressure 
Pinched or kinked DEF lines restricting flow 
Faulty DEF pressure sensor giving false high readings
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but excessive pressure in the DEF system can cause damage to lines, fittings, and the dosing injector. Address this fault promptly to avoid more costly repairs to the aftertreatment system.
Recommended Action
Start by inspecting the DEF filter and replacing it if clogged. Check the DEF return line for blockages, kinks, or restrictions. If the filter and lines are clear, have the DEF pump, pressure relief valve, and pressure sensor inspected by a qualified diesel technician.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3363 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the DEF pump is generating pressure above the acceptable operating range, which can disrupt proper DEF dosing and damage system components.
 
 
What causes SPN 3363 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are a clogged DEF filter, a blocked DEF return line, a faulty pressure relief valve, or a failing DEF pump producing excessive pressure.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3363 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but continued operation with excessive DEF system pressure risks damaging lines, fittings, and the dosing injector.
 
 
Will SPN 3363 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
It can if the high pressure condition prevents proper DEF dosing and the SCR system cannot meet emissions thresholds as a result.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3363 FMI 16?
 
Inspect and replace the DEF filter, check the return line for restrictions, and have the DEF pump and pressure relief valve tested. Once pressure returns to normal operating range the code should clear.

SPN 4094 FMI 18 
SPN 3364 FMI 2 
SPN 3936 FMI 1

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 1 means DEF pump pressure is critically low on your Caterpillar engine. This is a high-severity code that leads to an inducement derate if not resolved - check DEF quality, tank heating, and lines before replacing the pump. A weak DEF pump doesn't announce itself the way a mechanical failure does, but it starts an inducement clock the moment it can't reliably dose. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees this most often tied to frozen DEF in cold climates rather than an actual failed pump module, so start there before ordering an expensive part.
causes: Frozen or gelled DEF in the tank or suction lines
DEF freezes around 12F and requires proper tank heating; a failed heater circuit in cold weather causes the pump to draw against frozen or partially frozen fluid.
Air trapped in the DEF supply lines
Recent service work or running the DEF tank dry can introduce air that prevents the pump from building adequate pressure until purged.
Contaminated or off-spec DEF fluid
Diluted, contaminated, or expired DEF can cause the pump to cavitate or the system to reject the fluid as unreliable.
Failed DEF pump module
Internal pump wear or motor failure directly reduces achievable pressure and typically requires module replacement.
steps: Pull the fault on Cat ET and check freeze-frame DEF pump pressure against the specification, typically in the 60-100 PSI range depending on Cat platform and duty cycle.
Verify DEF tank level and fluid quality with a refractometer - low fluid or off-spec concentration can cause the pump to cavitate.
Inspect the DEF suction line and filter/strainer inside the tank for frozen or gelled fluid, especially in cold weather without proper tank heating.
Check the DEF pump's electrical connector and wiring for corrosion or damage using a multimeter for voltage and continuity.
Bleed air from the DEF lines if the system was recently run dry or serviced, since trapped air prevents the pump from building proper pressure.
If pressure remains low after ruling out fluid, lines, and electrical issues, the pump module itself likely needs replacement.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp with DEF system icon
Countdown warning toward speed limitation if not addressed
Possible DEF pump audible cycling or clicking noise
Increasing NOx efficiency-related codes if DEF dosing is inadequate for an extended period
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 3363 FMI 1: DEF Pump Pressure Below Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 1 on Volvo trucks means the DEF tank heater (coolant-based) is not achieving minimum temperature — most severe level. Check the DEF tank coolant control valve and temperature sensor before replacing the DEF tank. This is a heater circuit fault, not a DEF pump pressure fault. SPN 3363 on a Volvo is not about DEF pump pressure — it is about the coolant-fed heater circuit that keeps your DEF tank from freezing. When the heater system can't maintain minimum DEF temperature, the SCR system loses the ability to dose properly in cold conditions. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com works this code systematically: confirm the coolant valve is opening, confirm coolant is flowing through the DEF tank coil, and then isolate whether the valve, the coil, or just the temperature sensor is the problem.
causes: DEF tank coolant heater control valve failed or stuck closed (electrical/mechanical)

The solenoid-controlled coolant valve that routes hot engine coolant through the DEF tank heating coil can fail with the valve in the closed position, completely cutting coolant flow to the tank heater regardless of ambient temperature.
Coolant circuit restriction to DEF tank heater (mechanical)
Moderate
Scale buildup, a pinched coolant hose, or debris in the coolant circuit serving the DEF tank heater can restrict flow enough that the heating coil cannot transfer adequate heat to the DEF tank.
DEF tank temperature sensor failure (electrical)
Moderate

If the DEF tank temperature sensor fails and reads falsely low (below actual temperature), the AFTCU calculates insufficient heating even when the coolant heater is operating normally. This causes FMI 1 in warm weather — a diagnostic clue that the system itself may be functional.
Failed internal DEF tank heating coil (mechanical)
Less Common

The heating coil inside the DEF tank can corrode, crack, or become blocked with DEF scale or urea crystallization, preventing coolant from flowing through the coil even when the control valve is open.
steps: 1. Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and navigate to the AFTCU (Aftertreatment Control Unit) data. Check live DEF tank temperature (SPN 3363-related parameter). Target operating temperature is >5°C (41°F). Note ambient temperature to establish whether the heater should be active.

2. Locate the DEF tank coolant heater control valve — on Volvo D13 platforms it is typically on the engine or chassis coolant circuit near the firewall or cab-back area. With the engine at operating temperature (coolant >70°C), the valve should open and route coolant through the DEF tank heating coil. Use PTT to command the valve active and observe whether DEF tank temperature rises over 5-10 minutes.

3. Feel the coolant supply hose to the DEF tank heater inlet and the return hose from the heater outlet. If the inlet hose is hot but the outlet hose remains cold, either the control valve is not opening or the heater coil inside the DEF tank is blocked. A hot inlet and hot outlet with a cold tank suggests the coil is bypassed or the tank temperature sensor is faulty.

4. Test the heater control valve electrically with a multimeter: check coil resistance across the solenoid terminals (typically 10-20 ohms for a 12V solenoid) and verify 12V supply and a switched ground on the control side. Apply 12V directly to confirm the valve shifts mechanically.

5. If coolant flow through the heater coil is confirmed and DEF tank temperature is still reading cold, suspect the DEF tank temperature sensor. Compare the DEF tank temperature reading in PTT against the actual ambient temperature and a calibrated thermometer placed at the tank — a sensor reading significantly below ambient in a warm environment confirms sensor failure.
symptoms: SCR or DEF warning lamp illuminated with associated derate
DEF tank temperature reading below minimum threshold (typically below 5°C/41°F) in Volvo PTT live data
SCR system may suspend dosing if DEF is suspected frozen or below temperature
Fault most common in sub-freezing ambient temperatures but can occur in moderate temps with a failed coolant valve
DEF system rattle or reduced dosing if partial freeze is present in tank
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 3363 FMI 1: DEF Tank Heater Below Normal — Most Severe

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 1 on a Scania engine means the DEF tank coolant heater is confirmed operating at critically insufficient output. The coolant-fed heat exchanger that prevents AdBlue from freezing is not receiving adequate coolant flow. Check the heater solenoid control valve with SDP3 actuator test before ordering a full heater assembly. Scania SPN 3363 FMI 1 is a DEF system thermal protection fault—the AdBlue tank heater has confirmed critically below-normal output at the most severe level. On Scania DC13 and DC09 trucks, the DEF tank is heated by a dedicated coolant circuit that routes hot engine coolant through a heat exchanger integrated with the tank assembly. A solenoid valve controls coolant flow to the exchanger based on tank temperature. When the heater circuit fails to deliver adequate heat (FMI 1), the ECM flags the most severe level because a frozen DEF tank is a direct path to SCR system failure and a non-compliance derate in cold-weather operation. The Scania SDP3 actuator test on the heater solenoid—covered in detail at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com—pinpoints whether the fault is electrical (valve coil) or mechanical (coolant flow).
causes: Failed DEF tank heater coolant solenoid valve (electrical/sensor)
High

The solenoid coil on the coolant control valve for the Scania DEF tank heater is prone to burnout after repeated thermal cycling and continuous-duty operation in cold climates. An open-circuit coil leaves the valve in the normally-closed (no-flow) position, completely blocking coolant to the heat exchanger and producing FMI 1.
Coolant control valve stuck closed due to mineral scale (mechanical)
Medium

Silicate-based coolant inhibitor deposits can accumulate on the internal valve spool and seat, mechanically preventing the valve from opening even when the solenoid is energized. This failure produces a valve that passes the electrical resistance test but fails the actuator flow test—coolant flow through the heater remains zero despite a functioning solenoid coil.
Restricted or blocked coolant supply hose to the DEF heater (mechanical)
Medium

The small-diameter coolant hose that feeds the DEF tank heat exchanger can develop internal collapse (hose age/heat fatigue), kinking from improper routing after a repair, or external blockage at a fitting. A restricted hose reduces heat exchanger output below the minimum acceptable level at low ambient temperatures.
Failed DEF tank heater heat exchanger (mechanical)
Low–Medium

The heat exchanger passages can become internally blocked with coolant scale or AdBlue crystal deposits over extended service. Heat exchanger failure is typically a secondary cause after years of neglected coolant maintenance—the scale that builds up in the heat exchanger is the same scale that blocks the control valve.
DEF tank temperature sensor drift reading falsely low (electrical/sensor)
Low

The DEF tank temperature sensor that provides feedback to the ECM can develop a negative offset, causing the ECM to see a critically low tank temperature even when the heater is functioning and actual tank temperature is adequate. SDP3 comparison of the tank temp sensor reading vs. ambient temperature at cold startup can identify a sensor with excessive offset.
symptoms: Yellow or amber malfunction indicator with SPN 3363 FMI 1 logged in Scania SDP3
DEF tank temperature reading critically low—at or below ambient in cold conditions
AdBlue quality or temperature warning displayed in the Scania instrument cluster
DEF system may request inhibited injection if tank temperature falls below freeze point (12°F / -11°C)
Possible SCR-related secondary faults if DEF cannot be dispensed due to freezing

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 3 means the DEF tank heater circuit voltage is high. Find the short or stuck relay before replacing the heater element, especially before cold weather trips. Mack Anthem and Granite trucks store SPN 3363 FMI 3 until the first hard freeze exposes the real problem—no DEF tank heating. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com recommends fixing FMI 3 before winter because frozen DEF triggers a chain of derates unrelated to the original electrical fault.
causes: Heater harness short to battery power
Tank strap rub-through or road debris damage forces heater voltage high even when the ECM commands off.
Stuck DEF heater relay
Relay contacts weld closed, keeping heater power applied and setting FMI 3 protection logic.
Failed heater element shorted internally
Element insulation breakdown shorts the coil and pulls the control circuit high.
steps: Read commanded vs actual DEF tank heater status in ServiceMaxx with key on; FMI 3 often shows heater off with high circuit voltage.
Locate the DEF tank heater relay and fuse per MP wiring diagram—replace only blown fuses after finding the short.
Disconnect the heater element at the tank and ohm the heater coil; typical resistance is 2-8 Ω depending on tank size—open or shorted coil needs element replacement.
Inspect harness along the tank strap for pinches that short heater power to chassis; repair with 12 AWG heat-shrink splices rated for underbody exposure.
After repair, verify heater current draw stays within spec (often 8-15 A) during a cold-soak test above 32 °F tank temperature threshold.
symptoms: DEF system warning lamp with SPN 3363 FMI 3 active in ServiceMaxx or JPRO
Heater commanded off while tank temperature drops in cold weather
Blown DEF heater fuse or visible heat damage at the tank harness
DEF level or quality messages may appear after heater circuit faults
Voltage on heater control circuit reads near battery voltage when off
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 3363 FMI 3: DEF Tank Heater Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: Cummins SPN 3363 FMI 9 indicates an issue with the EGR valve position circuit. Check for wiring issues, sensor faults, or valve blockages. Immediate attention prevents significant performance loss. In the bay, when a Cummins engine throws a SPN 3363 FMI 9 code, you're looking at an EGR valve position circuit error. Drivers usually notice a drop in power, and sometimes a check engine light, before limping into the shop. This page is your go-to for diagnosing the problem, understanding what's at stake, and deciding whether it's a DIY fix or time to call in the pros. This fault affects the EGR system, critical for controlling emissions and maintaining engine efficiency. Ignoring it can lead to an engine derate, leaving trucks crawling at 5 mph. We'll walk you through common symptoms, root causes, and the steps to troubleshoot and resolve this EGR valve issue. Before you throw a sensor or valve at it, get the full picture here. You might save time, money, and a lot of headache. The EGR system isn't just about emissions; it's about keeping your engine running smoothly. A blocked valve can cause improper exhaust gas recirculation, which affects combustion and can lead to overheating. Understanding the nuances of this system is crucial for any diesel tech dealing with Cummins engines.
causes: Wiring Harness Damage

Harness damage is frequent due to vibration and proximity to hot components. Inspect for chafing or cuts, especially near the EGR valve and ECM. Repair with high-temperature resistant tape or replace sections as necessary.
EGR Valve Carbon Buildup

Carbon can obstruct valve movement, leading to position errors. Regular cleaning can prevent this, but severe buildup might require replacement. Use an EGR cleaning kit or have the valve professionally serviced.
Faulty EGR Position Sensor
The sensor may fail due to internal damage or corrosion on the connector. A multimeter can confirm if the sensor is operating within specs. Replace if readings are erratic.
ECM Software Glitch
Software bugs can occasionally cause false readings. Updating the ECM software to the latest version can resolve these issues. Check with Cummins for any TSBs related to the EGR system.
steps: Use a multimeter to check the EGR valve position sensor's voltage. Located on the valve itself, normal operation should show a smooth voltage increase with valve movement.
Inspect wiring harness for chafing, especially near tank straps and engine mounts. Repair any damaged wires with appropriate connectors and insulation.
Remove the EGR valve and inspect for carbon buildup. Use a soft brush and EGR cleaner to remove deposits, ensuring the valve moves freely.
Check the EGR position sensor connector for corrosion. Clean contacts with electrical cleaner and ensure tight, secure connections.
Access the ECM and verify the EGR position signal using a diagnostic tool. Look for consistent readings that match the valve's physical position.
Perform an EGR valve actuation test with a diagnostic tool. Listen for smooth operation without hesitation or binding.
Replace the EGR valve if mechanical failure or excessive wear is evident. Ensure the new valve is OEM or equivalent quality.
symptoms: Engine derate to 5 mph, often after a failed regeneration cycle.
Check engine light illuminated with decreased throttle response.
Rough idling or stalling during low-speed operations.
Increased black smoke due to improper EGR functioning.
Noticeable decrease in fuel efficiency as the engine compensates.
Engine overheating under load due to improper exhaust gas recirculation.
Frequent need for manual regeneration if the EGR is stuck closed.
Unusual noises from the EGR valve area, indicating possible mechanical failure.
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 3363 FMI 9 EGR Valve Fault Diagnosis

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 16 means the DEF tank heater on Volvo D13 and D11 engines is reporting above the ECM normal range. Overheating DEF degrades urea quality and can trigger SCR derate or five-MPH limp mode. Check heater resistance at 8-15 ohms and verify the coolant valve cycles off above 86°F tank temperature. The DEF tank heater keeps diesel exhaust fluid above freezing so the SCR dosing pump can deliver accurate urea quantity. When SPN 3363 FMI 16 sets on a Volvo, the heater is running hotter than intended, which breaks down DEF and poisons the SCR catalyst over time. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com advises testing heater resistance and coolant valve operation on PTT before replacing the entire DEF tank assembly.
causes: Stuck-open coolant control valve to DEF tank heater
A valve that fails open passes continuous engine coolant through the heater coil, pushing tank temperature above 95°F even in mild weather.
Shorted DEF tank heater element
Internal heater short drops resistance below 2 ohms, increasing current draw and producing excessive heat the ECM flags as above normal.
Failed DEF tank temperature sensor reading low
A sensor that reads artificially cold prevents the ECM from shutting off the heater at the 86°F cutoff, causing continuous heating.
steps: Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and monitor SPN 3363 (DEF tank heater) and DEF tank temperature — heater should cycle on below 12°F and off below 86°F tank temp; continuous heating above 95°F indicates a stuck heater or failed thermostat.
Locate the DEF tank heater element and coolant-control valve on the DEF tank — inspect wiring for chafing and verify the heater relay clicks off when tank temperature exceeds 86°F.
With the key off, measure heater element resistance — most Volvo DEF heaters read 8-15 ohms; below 2 ohms indicates a shorted element that draws excessive current and overheats.

Check coolant flow to the DEF tank heater valve — supply line should be warm (120-180°F) when the engine is at operating temperature; a stuck-open valve passes continuous hot coolant through the heater.
Test the heater control signal at the ECM — PWM duty cycle should drop to 0% when tank temp exceeds 86°F; a stuck 100% duty cycle confirms ECM or wiring fault.
Replace the heater element or coolant valve, refill DEF tank with fresh 32.5% urea solution, and verify tank temperature stabilizes between 40-86°F during a cold-soak test.
symptoms: DEF tank temperature reads above 95°F on Volvo PTT when ambient is below 40°F
Ammonia odor from the DEF tank area indicating urea decomposition
Amber MIL with SCR efficiency warnings and progressive torque derate
DEF level gauge may fluctuate or show quality warnings
Heater relay clicking rapidly or DEF tank surface feels excessively hot to touch
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 3363 FMI 16: DEF Tank Heater Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3363 FMI 16 on Mack engines means DEF pump pressure is moderately above the expected range. It's a high-severity fault that risks dosing inaccuracy and an SCR inducement countdown if the underlying blockage or contamination isn't addressed. The DEF pump has to maintain precise pressure to keep dosing accurate, and SPN 3363 FMI 16 means it's running higher than it should. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this as a fault worth catching early - dosing accuracy directly affects SCR efficiency, and Mack's inducement escalation for SCR-related faults gets progressively more restrictive the longer it's ignored. Most cases trace back to a partial blockage or crystallization in the doser line rather than the pump itself failing.
causes: Crystallized or partially blocked DEF doser/injector line
DEF crystallizes when it dries out, and a partial blockage downstream of the pump creates backpressure that reads as an overpressure fault.
Stuck or malfunctioning check valve in the DEF supply module
A check valve that isn't releasing pressure properly can cause the pump circuit to run persistently high.
Contaminated or over-concentrated DEF fluid
Fluid outside the proper urea concentration range can behave differently under pump pressure, occasionally triggering this fault.
Faulty DEF pressure sensor
A sensor reading falsely high independent of actual pump pressure is possible but less common than a genuine blockage.
steps: Pull the fault with PACCAR Davie4 or Jaltest and confirm SPN 3363 FMI 16 is active; log the reported DEF pump pressure against the expected operating range for the current dosing state.
Inspect the DEF supply module and pump for any recent service or contamination that could cause abnormal pressure buildup, such as a stuck check valve.
Check the DEF injector/doser line for a partial blockage or crystallization that could cause backpressure to build in the pump circuit.
Verify the DEF pressure sensor's wiring and connector for corrosion, which could produce a falsely high reading independent of actual pump performance.
Test DEF quality with a refractometer to rule out contaminated or overly concentrated fluid, which can affect both dosing accuracy and system pressure readings.
Clear the code and monitor live DEF pump pressure through a dosing cycle to confirm it stabilizes within the normal range before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Amber dash lamp, sometimes escalating to a countdown warning message
No immediate power loss in early stages
Possible increased DEF consumption as the system compensates for pressure inaccuracy
Reduced SCR efficiency reflected in NOx sensor data over time if dosing accuracy suffers
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 3363 FMI 16: Diagnosing High DEF Pump Pressure

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically a short to power/open.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically a short to power/open.‪
steps: Short to Power/Open Check
Disconnect the Grid Heater connector.
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Measure the voltage between pins 2 and 4 of the Grid Heater connector. See Figure
"Grid Heater Wiring".
Figure 1. Grid Heater Wiring
If the voltage is greater than 11.5 volts, go to step 5.
If the voltage is less than 11.5 volts, go to step 4.
Measure the voltage between pin 2 of the Grid Heater connector and ground.
If the voltage is greater than 11.5 volts, repair the open between pin 4 of the Grid Heater connector and pin 95 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "75.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the voltage is less than 11.5 volts, repair the open between pin 2 of the Grid Heater connector and pin 41 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "75.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance between pins 2 and 3 of the Grid Heater connector.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 8.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short between Grid Heater pins 2 and 3 and pins 41 and 92 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "75.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the resistance between pin 3 of the Grid Heater connector and pin 92 of the 120–pin MCM connector.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, repair the open between pin 3 of the Grid Heater connector and pin 92 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "75.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, replace the Grid Heater.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: MBE 4000 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 75.1 SPN 729/FMI 3 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

This code suggests that the Engine Control Module (ECM) has detected an issue with the ACC, which could involve the radar sensor, wiring, or control module. What SPN 1590 FMI 19 Means SPN 1590 FMI 19 is a diesel engine fault code that signifies a general error within the Adaptive Cruise Control system. The ECM interprets this fault when it receives an unexpected signal or no signal from the ACC components, indicating a potential malfunction in the system's ability to maintain safe following distances. Common Causes of This Fault Code Failed radar sensor Wiring harness damage Connector corrosion Defective control module Voltage reference faults Symptoms Drivers May Notice When the SPN 1590 FMI 19 fault code is active, drivers may notice that the adaptive cruise control system is not functioning properly. The system may fail to engage, disengage unexpectedly, or not maintain the set following distance. Additionally, a warning light may illuminate on the dashboard. How Technicians Diagnose This Fault Technicians begin diagnosing this fault with a visual inspection of the radar sensor for any physical damage or obstructions. Next, they check the wiring harness for signs of damage, corrosion, or loose connections. Using a multimeter, they test for proper voltage and continuity in the wiring harness. A diagnostic tool is then connected to verify if there are any additional fault codes related to the ACC system. Finally, the control module is inspected for signs of water ingress or physical damage. Common Misdiagnosis Technicians often misdiagnose this fault by assuming the issue lies with the engine control module (ECM) instead of the ACC system. Another common mistake is replacing the radar sensor without checking the wiring harness for faults. Additionally, overlooking software updates that may resolve the fault code can lead to unnecessary part replacements. Can You Keep Driving? While the truck can continue operating with the SPN 1590 FMI 19 fault code active, it is not advisable to rely on the adaptive cruise control system. The fault may not lead to an immediate engine derate or protection mode, but it compromises the safety feature designed to maintain safe following distances. Mechanic's Diagnostic Tip Before replacing any components, ensure that all electrical connections are clean and secure. Often, poor connections or corroded terminals are the root cause of the fault. Always verify the integrity of the wiring harness and connectors before considering sensor or module replacement. Frequently Asked Questions Q: Can a software update fix the SPN 1590 FMI 19 fault code? A: Yes, sometimes a software update can resolve the fault if it addresses known issues with the ACC system. Q: Is it safe to drive with this fault code active? A: While the vehicle can be driven, the adaptive cruise control system may not function correctly, affecting safety features. Q: What tools are needed to diagnose this fault? A: A multimeter and a diagnostic scan tool are essential for testing voltage, continuity, and retrieving fault codes. A: Yes, recalibration may be necessary to ensure the sensor is accurately detecting objects and communicating with the ECM. procedures_full.overview: FMI 0 on charging system potential indicates the system voltage is above the maximum calibrated threshold. Failed regulator, incorrect alternator application, open sense circuit causing overcharge on some designs, and wiring faults are the primary causes. Overcharge damaging batteries and sensitive modules is a documented consequence — diagnose immediately when overvoltage is confirmed. Confirming true overvoltage with a meter at the batteries and alternator before parts replacement prevents replacing batteries for a regulator fault.
causes: Failed regulator — voltage regulator failure producing uncontrolled output
Incorrect alternator application — wrong alternator installed producing incorrect voltage
Open sense circuit — open sense circuit causing overcharge on some regulator designs
Wiring faults — wiring fault producing false high voltage reading
steps: Single Action Gate — Meter Verification at Batteries and Alternator

Confirm true overvoltage with a meter at the batteries and at the alternator output. Compare to ECM reported voltage. A meter reading that matches the ECM reported overvoltage confirms true overvoltage. A meter reading that is normal while the ECM reports overvoltage confirms a sensing or wiring fault.
Binary Decision Gate — Sense Circuit Checks

Check sense circuit integrity. An open sense circuit causes overcharge on some regulator designs — the regulator increases output to compensate for the missing sense feedback. Inspect the sense wire connection and circuit integrity before any alternator replacement.
Override Manager — Alternator Bench or Vehicle Test

Perform an alternator bench or vehicle test. Confirm the alternator output voltage under load. An alternator that produces above-specification voltage under load with a confirmed intact sense circuit confirms regulator failure.
Safety Interceptor — Inspect Batteries for Damage

Inspect batteries for damage from overcharge. Overcharging can cause battery electrolyte loss, swelling, and internal damage. Inspect batteries for physical damage and test battery capacity after any confirmed overcharge event.
Resume Point — Verify Correct Alternator Application

Verify the alternator application is correct for the platform. An incorrect alternator installed during a previous repair can produce incorrect voltage regulation. Confirm the alternator part number matches the OEM specification for the platform.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Voltage Confirmation
After repair, verify charging system voltage meets specification under all load conditions. Confirm SPN 167 FMI 0 does not return. Monitor for return of overvoltage events over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Regulator, Sense Circuit, or Battery Decision

Replace alternator or regulator if regulator failure is confirmed. Repair sense circuit if open sense is confirmed. Replace batteries if overcharge damage is confirmed. Verify correct alternator application before installation.

Repair Steps
1 . Replace alternator or regulator if regulator failure is confirmed.
2 . Repair sense circuit if open sense is confirmed.
3 . Replace batteries if overcharge damage is confirmed.
4 . Verify correct alternator application before installation.
Verification Steps
Confirm charging system voltage meets specification after repair.
Verify SPN 167 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Confirm no module failures or battery damage after repair.
Monitor for return of overvoltage events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect alternator sense wire connection at every major service.

✓ Inspect batteries for overcharge damage at every major service.

High. Overvoltage can destroy electronics. Diagnose immediately. Confirming true overvoltage before parts replacement prevents replacing batteries for a regulator fault.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 1 on charging system potential indicates the system voltage is below the minimum while the engine is running. Failed alternator or regulator, belt slip, poor battery cable connections, sense wire issues, and excessive load are the primary causes. High-resistance cables causing module low-voltage faults while the alternator is actually outputting correctly are a documented pattern. Voltage-drop tests on positive and ground cables under load identify high-resistance cable faults that produce low-voltage symptoms without any alternator failure.
causes: Failed alternator or regulator — alternator or regulator failure producing low output
Belt slip — belt slipping on alternator pulley
Poor battery cable connections — high-resistance cable connections reducing charging voltage
Sense wire issues — sense wire fault causing incorrect voltage regulation
Excessive load — excessive electrical load exceeding alternator capacity
steps: Single Action Gate — Belt Condition Check

Inspect the alternator belt condition and tension. A slipping belt prevents the alternator from reaching full output speed. Inspect for belt wear, glazing, and proper tension. A slipping belt produces low charging voltage that increases with load.
Binary Decision Gate — Running Voltage Measurement

Measure battery voltage with the engine running. A running voltage below the minimum specification confirms the charging system is not maintaining adequate voltage. Measure at the battery posts and at the alternator output to identify where the voltage loss occurs.
Override Manager — Voltage-Drop Tests on Positive and Ground Cables

Perform voltage-drop tests on the positive and ground cable paths under load. High-resistance cables causing module low-voltage faults while the alternator is actually outputting correctly are a documented pattern. Measure voltage drop on the alternator B+ cable and the battery negative to engine block and frame ground paths.
Safety Interceptor — Alternator Output Test

Perform an alternator output test. Measure alternator output voltage and current under load. An alternator that produces correct output voltage at the alternator output but low voltage at the battery confirms a cable voltage-drop fault. An alternator that produces low output voltage confirms alternator or regulator failure.
Resume Point — Sense Circuit Integrity Check

Check sense circuit integrity if voltage regulation appears incorrect. A sense wire fault causes incorrect voltage regulation — the alternator may undercharge or overcharge based on incorrect sense voltage. Inspect the sense wire connection and circuit integrity.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Charging Confirmation

After repair, verify charging system voltage meets specification under all load conditions. Confirm SPN 167 FMI 1 does not return. Monitor for return of module resets or low-voltage events over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Cable, Belt, or Alternator Decision

Repair or replace high-resistance cables or terminals if voltage-drop confirms cable fault. Replace belt or tensioner if belt slip is confirmed. Replace alternator if output test confirms alternator or regulator failure. Do not replace alternator for a cable voltage-drop fault.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair or replace high-resistance cables or terminals.
2 . Replace belt or tensioner if belt slip is confirmed.
3 . Repair sense wire fault if confirmed.
4 . Replace alternator if output test confirms alternator or regulator failure.
Verification Steps
Confirm charging system voltage meets specification under all load conditions after repair.
Verify SPN 167 FMI 1 does not return after repair.
Confirm no module resets or low-voltage events after repair.
Monitor for return of charging system faults over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect alternator belt condition and tension at every major service.
✓ Inspect battery cable terminals for corrosion at every major service.
✓ Perform voltage-drop tests on charging system cables at every major service on high-mileage systems.
✓ Inspect alternator sense wire connection at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity
High reliability risk. Can progress to no-start or uncontrolled shutdowns. Voltage-drop-first method prevents unnecessary alternator replacement.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 2 on crankshaft speed and position indicates the CKP signal is erratic or inconsistently timed. Failing CKP sensor, damaged tone ring or reluctor, harness intermittents, connector oil or moisture intrusion, improper air gap, and loose sensor mount are the primary causes. Heat-soak stalls, tone ring damage after transmission R&R, and connector fretting are documented patterns. A scope is the most effective tool for capturing CKP dropouts — DVOM alone may miss intermittent signal loss. Do not dispatch a truck with an active erratic crank signal fault — an intermittent crank signal can stall a loaded truck.
causes: Failing CKP sensor — sensor degradation producing intermittent signal
Damaged tone ring or reluctor — missing or damaged teeth producing erratic pattern
Harness intermittents — intermittent connection at sensor connector or harness flex point
Connector oil or moisture intrusion — oil or moisture at sensor connector
Improper air gap — sensor air gap outside specification
Loose sensor mount — sensor movement producing intermittent signal
steps: Single Action Gate — Visual Mount and Connector Inspection

Inspect the CKP sensor mount and connector. A loose sensor mount produces intermittent signal from sensor movement. Inspect the connector for oil intrusion, moisture, and fretting corrosion. Confirm the connector is fully latched and the lock tab is engaged.
Binary Decision Gate — Harness Wiggle Hot

Perform a harness wiggle test with the engine at operating temperature. Heat-soak stalls are a documented CKP pattern — the fault may only appear when the harness is hot. Wiggle the harness near bellhousing and front cover routing chafe points while monitoring the CKP PID for dropouts.
Override Manager — Pattern and PID Integrity While Cranking

Monitor CKP pattern and PID integrity while cranking. A scope is the most effective tool for capturing CKP dropouts. Dropouts on a scope are definitive — a clean pattern at cranking speed with an erratic fault at operating speed confirms a heat-related intermittent.
Safety Interceptor — Tone Ring Inspection

Inspect the tone ring or reluctor for damage. Tone ring damage after transmission R&R is a documented cause of erratic CKP signal. Inspect for missing, bent, or damaged teeth. A damaged tone ring produces a repeating pattern error at the damaged tooth location.
Resume Point — Air Gap Verification
Verify sensor air gap per OEM specification. An improper air gap produces weak or erratic signal, especially at low RPM. Confirm the air gap meets OEM specification before sensor replacement.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Signal Stability Confirmation
After repair, verify CKP signal is stable at operating temperature under load. Confirm SPN 636 FMI 2 does not return. Monitor for return of intermittent stall or hot no-start complaints.
Repair Ledger Output — Sensor, Harness, or Tone Ring Decision

Replace CKP sensor after mount, connector, harness, and tone ring integrity are confirmed and sensor failure is proven. Repair harness intermittent if flex point break is found. Service tone ring if damage is confirmed. Do not replace ECM for erratic crank data without exhausting sensor, harness, and tone ring diagnosis.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness intermittent at flex point near bellhousing or front cover.
2 . Service tone ring if damage is confirmed.
3 . Replace CKP sensor after mount, connector, harness, and tone ring integrity are confirmed.
4 . Correct air gap if outside specification.
Verification Steps
Confirm CKP signal is stable at operating temperature under load after repair.
Verify SPN 636 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Confirm no intermittent stall or hot no-start complaints after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect tone ring for damage after every transmission R&R.
✓ Inspect CKP sensor connector for oil intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect CKP harness for heat brittleness at every major service.
✓ Verify CKP sensor air gap after any front engine service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity
High. Intermittent crank signal can stall a loaded truck. Do not dispatch until isolated. The hot intermittent process prevents random ECM replacement.
symptoms: SPN 636 FMI 2 crank sensor erratic
Intermittent stall under load
Hot no-start after heat soak
Crank signal dropout
Intermittent sync loss
Cam-crank correlation fault following CKP erratic

procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 2 means the crankshaft position sensor signal is erratic or inconsistent. This is a high-severity code since it can cause rough running or stalling - inspect the toothed ring and wiring before replacing the sensor. Because this signal underpins injection timing, an erratic reading deserves prompt diagnosis rather than a wait-and-see approach. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always wiggle-tests the harness first, since a chafed wire producing an intermittent fault is more common than an outright failed sensor.
causes: Chafed or intermittent signal wiring
A wire with partial insulation damage can produce a signal that drops in and out under vibration, mimicking a sensor fault.
Damaged or debris-packed toothed ring
A chipped tooth or metal debris near the sensor tip disrupts the expected magnetic pulse pattern.
Incorrect sensor air gap
An air gap outside specification produces a weak or inconsistent signal that the ECM flags as erratic.
Internally failing sensor
Heat and vibration exposure over time can degrade the sensor's internal components, producing an unstable signal even with a healthy ring.
steps: Pull the fault on DDDL and check occurrence count and freeze-frame data to determine if the fault correlates with a specific engine condition.
Inspect the crankshaft position sensor connector near the front of the engine for corrosion, looseness, or heat damage.
Verify the sensor's air gap to the toothed ring with a non-magnetic feeler gauge if the sensor design allows for adjustment.
Inspect the toothed ring for damaged teeth or metal debris that could disrupt the magnetic pulse pattern.
Check the signal wiring for chafing along its routing back to the ECM, since erratic signals are frequently traced to intermittent wiring faults.
Replace the sensor only after confirming the toothed ring and wiring are sound, since a new sensor on a damaged ring will reproduce the same fault.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp with possible rough idle or hesitation
Intermittent stalling, especially at idle or during deceleration
Hard or extended cranking on startup attempts
Erratic tachometer behavior on the dash
procedures_full.source_title: Freightliner SPN 636 FMI 2: Crankshaft Position Signal Erratic

procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 2 means the crankshaft position sensor signal is erratic or intermittent rather than a clean steady pulse. It's a High severity fault that can cause random stalling or hard starting, and in rare cases a complete signal loss can shut the engine down while driving. The crankshaft position sensor is what tells the Cummins ECM exactly where each piston is in its stroke, which is critical for firing injectors at the right instant. SPN 636 FMI 2 specifically flags an erratic or noisy signal, distinct from a total signal loss, which is why the symptoms are often intermittent rather than a hard no-start. This guide from ProfessionalDieselRepair.com walks through separating a genuinely bad sensor from the far more common culprits: a widened air gap after service work or a chafed harness near the timing case.
causes: Chafed crank sensor harness near the timing cover
Engine vibration wears the harness against the timing case or accessory bracket, introducing intermittent noise into the signal.
Incorrect sensor air gap after service
If the sensor wasn't properly shimmed or torqued after a timing cover or gear train repair, the air gap can be too wide, producing a weak, erratic signal.
Failing crank sensor
Internal degradation of the sensor element itself, often heat-related, causes intermittent dropouts especially once the engine reaches operating temperature.
Damaged or missing teeth on the reluctor/tone wheel
Physical damage to the toothed wheel the sensor reads creates a genuinely erratic mechanical signal that no amount of sensor or wiring repair will fix.
steps: Connect Cummins INSITE and check the freeze-frame data for when the fault set - a hot-engine intermittent points toward heat-related sensor failure or connector expansion.
Inspect the crank sensor connector for corrosion, and check that the sensor is seated fully against its mounting boss with the correct air gap per the service manual.

With the connector unplugged, measure sensor resistance across its terminals with a multimeter and compare to the Cummins spec (most Hall-effect crank sensors read in the 500-900 ohm range, magnetic pickup types vary more).
Inspect the wiring harness from the sensor back to the ECM for chafing near the front gear cover or timing case, a common wear point from engine vibration.
Clear the code, road test while monitoring live crank signal quality on INSITE, and confirm the fault does not return under varying RPM and load.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 2 on Mercedes-Benz means the crank sensor signal is erratic or internally inconsistent. Check the harness for abrasion, the tone wheel for damage, and scope the signal before swapping the sensor. An erratic crank signal is one of the more frustrating intermittent faults in the shop because it comes and goes with heat, vibration, and load. SPN 636 FMI 2 on a Mercedes-Benz heavy-duty is the ECM telling you the signal is there — it just doesn't trust it. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com systematically works from harness to tone wheel to sensor, in that order.
causes: Chafed or intermittently open signal harness (electrical)
Very Common
The crank sensor harness runs near chassis members and heat shields where vibration-induced abrasion creates an intermittent open that produces exactly the FMI 2 erratic pattern.
Damaged or debris-packed tone wheel / trigger ring gear (mechanical)
Missing teeth or packed metallic debris on the ring gear distorts the pulse pattern, causing the ECM to reject the signal as erratic even though the sensor itself is fine.
Failing crankshaft position sensor (internal weak magnet or cracked housing)
A sensor that is on its way out produces variable amplitude output — enough signal for FMI 2, not consistent enough for FMI 12 or FMI 3.
Loose ECM connector terminal on the crank signal pin (electrical)
Less Common
A pin that has backed out slightly in the ECM connector causes a vibration-sensitive intermittent open that only triggers under load or rough road conditions.
steps: 1. Connect Mercedes-Benz Xentry or Jaltest and read freeze-frame data — note RPM, coolant temp, and load at the moment FMI 2 set.
2. Inspect the crankshaft position sensor and its trigger wheel: pull the sensor, check the tip for cracks or physical damage, and look at the ring gear teeth for chips or packed debris.
3. Measure sensor resistance across the signal terminals with a multimeter and compare to spec; then check for intermittent opens by wiggling the harness while monitoring resistance.

4. Inspect harness routing from the sensor back to the ECM connector for abrasion points on chassis members or heat shield edges — FMI 2 is notorious for harness-chafe faults that only show up on the road.

5. Use Texa or Jaltest to scope the crank signal pattern at cranking speed and verify the waveform amplitude and tooth-gap pattern are consistent — a dropout or distorted pulse confirms a failing sensor or damaged tone wheel.
6. Confirm connector terminal tension at the ECM end; a loose pin on the crank signal circuit can produce exactly this erratic FMI 2 pattern.
symptoms: Intermittent rough running or sudden misfires
Engine stall that may restart after a cool-down
Hard no-start if the signal becomes completely unreliable during cranking
MIL illuminated with possible torque reduction
Erratic RPM reading on the instrument cluster
procedures_full.source_title: Mercedes-Benz SPN 636 FMI 2: Crankshaft Position Sensor Erratic or Intermittent

procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 2 on a Mack engine means the crankshaft position sensor is sending an erratic or intermittent signal—not missing entirely, but inconsistent. This causes stall events, rough running, and hard start conditions on MP7 and MP8 platforms. Check the connector, air gap, and reluctor ring before touching the sensor. Mack SPN 636 FMI 2 is the ECM telling you it can't trust the crankshaft position signal—it's getting something, but what it's getting doesn't consistently match the expected reluctor ring pattern. On MP7 and MP8 engines, the crankshaft position sensor is a passive variable reluctance (VR) pickup reading a 60-2 tooth reluctor ring. FMI 2 ('erratic, intermittent, or incorrect') means the signal is either dropping in and out of range, producing tooth-count mismatches, or showing noise spikes that corrupt the injection timing calculation. The connector, air gap, and reluctor ring integrity are the first three things to check—ProfessionalDieselRepair.com has the MP7/MP8 crank sensor air gap procedure with feeler gauge specs.
causes: Backed-out or corroded sensor connector terminal (electrical/sensor)
High

The crankshaft position sensor connector on MP7/MP8 engines is exposed to vibration, heat cycles, and oil splash. A terminal that has partially backed out of the connector housing creates an intermittent contact that drops the signal under vibration or heat expansion—exactly the FMI 2 erratic pattern. This is the most common cause and requires only connector inspection and terminal reseating.
Incorrect air gap between sensor tip and reluctor ring (mechanical)
Medium–High

The passive VR sensor generates signal voltage from reluctor ring tooth proximity—a gap wider than the 0.060 in. maximum produces a signal amplitude too low for the ECM to reliably decode, causing erratic tooth-count readings. Gap drift occurs after sensor replacement if the correct spacer or shimming procedure was not followed.
Ferrous debris on sensor tip (mechanical)
Medium

Metal filings from normal engine wear accumulate on the magnetic sensor tip, filling the gap between the sensor and reluctor ring. This changes the effective sensor-to-ring distance and creates signal irregularity—most common in engines that have had recent bearing or ring wear generating metallic debris.
Damaged or missing reluctor ring tooth (mechanical)
Medium

A missing or bent tooth on the crankshaft reluctor ring produces a repeating dropout at a specific crank angle—the ECM receives no signal for that angular window and flags the timing pattern as erratic. The 60-2 tooth pattern relies on the two-tooth gap for TDC reference; any additional missing tooth creates a false reference that corrupts injection timing.
Chafed or damaged sensor wiring harness (electrical/sensor)
Medium

The wiring harness routing from the sensor to the ECM passes near the block, frame rail, and heat sources. Chafed insulation that grounds intermittently under vibration produces noise spikes on the signal line that the ECM interprets as extra teeth—an 'incorrect' tooth count that triggers FMI 2.
steps: 1. Connect Mack Premium Tech Tool (PTT) or Snap-on NEXIQ and pull all active and inactive codes. Note whether SPN 636 FMI 2 is active constantly or only under specific conditions (hot, cold, high vibration).

2. With the engine off and key off, visually inspect the crankshaft position sensor connector and wiring harness at the sensor mounting boss. Look for chafed insulation, oil-soaked connectors, or a backed-out terminal pin.

3. Measure the air gap between the sensor tip and the reluctor ring tooth with a feeler gauge (access through the sensor bore). Mack MP7/MP8 spec: 0.030–0.060 in. (0.76–1.52 mm). A gap outside this range produces erratic signal amplitude.

4. Inspect the reluctor ring (crankshaft tone ring) through the sensor bore with a flashlight while rotating the engine by hand. Look for a missing tooth, bent tooth, or surface rust that could cause a drop-out in the signal pattern.
5. Check for ferrous debris on the sensor tip—metal filings attracted to the magnetic sensor body fill the gap and corrupt the reluctor signal. Clean the tip and recheck the air gap.

6. With a multimeter, perform an oscilloscope or AC millivolt test on the sensor signal wire while cranking. A healthy magnetic pickup (passive VR sensor) on Mack MP7 produces a clean sinusoidal signal at 0.5–5V AC amplitude at cranking RPM. A signal that drops out or shows noise spikes during cranking confirms a wiring or sensor issue.

7. Use Jaltest or Mack PTT to monitor the crankshaft signal quality parameter if available—some MP8 calibrations report a crank signal 'tooth error count' that pinpoints a specific tooth gap position as the source.
symptoms: Yellow or red check engine lamp with SPN 636 FMI 2 logged
Intermittent stall or stumble, especially at low RPM transitions
Hard start—engine cranks but may not fire if crank signal is absent at key-on
Rough running or erratic idle with RPM fluctuating on the tachometer
Fault may be active only under vibration or specific temperature conditions (wiring intermittent)

procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 3 means the crankshaft position sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage, an electrical fault that can cause rough running or hard starting. Pin test the harness before replacing the sensor. Even though this is an electrical circuit fault rather than a mechanical failure, it strikes at one of the ECM's most fundamental inputs. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always pin-tests the connector first, since a chafed wire is a more common cause than an actually failed sensor.
causes: Chafed signal wire shorting to a powered circuit
Heat and vibration wear through insulation over time, allowing the signal wire to contact a powered source near the front of the engine.
Corroded connector pin
Moisture intrusion at the connector can corrode pins, producing an intermittent high-voltage reading.
Internally failed sensor
Heat cycling can degrade the sensor's internal element, presenting as an open circuit that mimics the same fault.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on PACCAR Davie4 to confirm the signal is pinned at an unrealistic value.
Locate the crankshaft position sensor near the front of the engine and unplug the connector.
Back-probe signal and ground with a multimeter, key on engine off - a reading near 5V with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness-side fault.
Trace the signal wire for chafing along its routing back to the ECM, since a short to a powered circuit is a common cause.
Inspect the toothed ring and sensor mounting for any physical issue that could also affect signal quality.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor as needed, then clear the code and confirm a clean, stable signal returns during cranking.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp with possible rough idle
Hard starting or extended cranking
Possible intermittent stalling
Erratic tachometer behavior on the dash

procedures_full.overview: International SPN 636 FMI 5 means the crankshaft position sensor circuit has an open circuit or current below normal. This is a CRITICAL no-start fault on Maxxforce and A26 engines - the ECM cannot authorize fuel injection without CKP signal. Test sensor winding resistance (400-1,000 ohms) and harness continuity with Jaltest or Diesel Laptops before replacing the sensor.
causes: Chafed CKP sensor wiring harness under oil pan

The sensor harness routing under the Maxxforce oil pan contacts the block over time. Repeated vibration wears through the insulation and eventually severs the conductor, creating an open circuit that prevents the ECM from receiving any speed signal.
Failed CKP sensor (open sensor winding)

The magnetic pickup coil inside the sensor fails open from vibration fatigue or contamination. Infinite resistance at the sensor terminals confirms the open winding. Replacement is straightforward and low cost.
Corroded sensor connector causing open circuit

Moisture ingress into the sensor connector oxidizes the terminals, creating a high-resistance open circuit. Cleaning and re-seating the terminals or fitting a new connector pigtail resolves the fault without sensor replacement.
steps: Connect Jaltest or Diesel Laptops diagnostic interface to the J1939 data link. Navigate to Engine > Speed Sensors and read SPN 636 FMI 5. Use the software to observe engine RPM signal during cranking - zero RPM with active cranking confirms CKP signal loss.

Locate the crankshaft position sensor on the International Maxxforce 13 or A26 engine (typically on the front of the engine block near the crankshaft reluctor wheel, accessible from below with the engine running protection). Inspect the connector for corrosion, bent pins, or chafed wiring near the block.

Unplug the CKP sensor connector and measure resistance between the two signal pins (or signal and shield on a 3-pin sensor). A healthy Maxxforce CKP sensor reads approximately 400-1,000 ohms at room temperature (NTC magnetic pickup). Infinite resistance confirms an open sensor winding.

If sensor resistance is normal, measure continuity on both signal wires from the sensor connector back to the ECM. FMI 5 requires an open in the circuit. Check harness routing under the oil pan where the wires commonly contact the block and abrade through the insulation over time.

Replace the sensor if internal resistance is infinite (torque to 18-20 ft-lb), or repair the wiring open. Clear faults with Jaltest or Diesel Laptops, crank the engine, and confirm live RPM appears in the diagnostic software immediately on engine start.
symptoms: Engine cranks but will not start - the ECM cannot confirm crank position or speed to authorize fuel injection.
Engine may start and immediately stall as the CKP signal is lost within the first few crankshaft revolutions.
Red Stop Engine lamp active when the fault sets during a running engine event.
No engine speed reading on the tachometer even during active cranking.
Possible simultaneous cam sensor fault (SPN 637) if the CKP failure also disrupts ECM timing synchronization.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 8 on crankshaft speed indicates the CKP signal frequency is outside the expected range, suggesting noise, missing teeth detection errors, or signal integrity problems. Shield or ground issues, damaged reluctor, intermittent contact, electromagnetic noise, and loose sensor mount are the primary causes. False overspeed or underspeed events from a noisy CKP signal are a documented pattern. A scope is preferred over DVOM for frequency diagnosis — spikes or dropouts that indicate integrity issues are visible on a scope but may be missed by DVOM. Shield continuity and clean sensor return grounds are critical for CKP signal integrity.
causes: Shield or ground issues — CKP shield or return ground fault producing noise
Damaged reluctor — damaged tone ring teeth producing frequency errors
Intermittent contact — intermittent sensor contact producing frequency spikes
Electromagnetic noise — external noise source coupling into CKP circuit
Loose sensor mount — sensor movement producing frequency errors
steps: Single Action Gate — Secure Mount and Inspect Target

Confirm the CKP sensor mount is secure and inspect the tone ring or reluctor. A loose sensor mount produces frequency errors from sensor movement. Inspect the tone ring for damaged, missing, or bent teeth. A damaged tone ring produces repeating frequency errors at the damaged tooth location.
Binary Decision Gate — Shield and Ground Integrity

Check CKP shield continuity and sensor return ground integrity. Shield continuity and clean sensor return grounds are critical for CKP signal integrity. A shield fault or poor return ground allows electromagnetic noise to couple into the CKP circuit and produce frequency errors.
Override Manager — Scope the CKP Signal

Scope the CKP signal at operating speed. Frequency should track engine speed cleanly. Spikes or dropouts indicate integrity issues. A scope is preferred over DVOM for frequency diagnosis — spikes that indicate noise are visible on a scope but may be missed by DVOM.
Safety Interceptor — Compare Crank and Cam Correlation

Compare crank and cam correlation. A crank frequency fault with a clean cam signal confirms the fault is isolated to the crank sensing path. A crank frequency fault with a simultaneous cam fault suggests a shared circuit or ground fault.
Resume Point — Wiring Repair Before ECM Conclusions

Repair wiring shield and ground faults before any ECM conclusions. A noisy CKP signal from a shield or ground fault produces frequency errors that appear as sensor failure. Confirm wiring integrity before sensor or ECM replacement.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Frequency Stability Confirmation
After repair, verify CKP frequency tracks engine speed cleanly at all operating speeds. Confirm SPN 636 FMI 8 does not return. Monitor for return of false overspeed or underspeed events.
Repair Ledger Output — Shield, Ground, Sensor, or Tone Ring Decision

Repair shield or ground fault if confirmed. Service tone ring if damage is confirmed. Replace CKP sensor after shield, ground, and tone ring integrity are confirmed and sensor failure is proven. Do not replace ECM for frequency errors without exhausting wiring and target diagnosis.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair CKP shield or return ground fault.
2 . Service tone ring if damage is confirmed.
3 . Replace CKP sensor after shield, ground, and tone ring integrity are confirmed.
4 . Identify and eliminate external electromagnetic noise source if confirmed.
Verification Steps
Confirm CKP frequency tracks engine speed cleanly after repair.
Verify SPN 636 FMI 8 does not return after repair.
Confirm no false overspeed or underspeed events after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect CKP shield and ground connections at every major service.
✓ Inspect tone ring for damage after every transmission R&R.
✓ Inspect CKP sensor mount security at every major service.
✓ Identify and eliminate external electromagnetic noise sources near CKP circuit.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High depending on stall or misfire behavior from frequency errors. Noise-versus-mechanical target branch control prevents replacing the sensor for a shielding or ground fault.
symptoms: SPN 636 FMI 8 crank abnormal frequency
CKP noise or signal integrity fault
False RPM spike or underspeed event
Sync error from frequency fault
Cam-crank correlation fault following frequency fault
