procedures_full.overview: SPN 636 FMI 8 means the crankshaft position sensor's frequency signal is abnormal on your PACCAR MX engine. This is a high-severity code since it can cause rough running or stalling - check the toothed ring and air gap before replacing the sensor. This fault strikes at one of the ECM's most fundamental inputs, so it's worth diagnosing promptly rather than ignoring an intermittent stall complaint. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always checks the toothed ring condition before assuming the sensor itself has failed.
causes: Damaged, chipped, or debris-packed toothed ring
A physically damaged tooth or metal debris near the sensor tip disrupts the magnetic pulse pattern the sensor reads.
Incorrect sensor air gap
An air gap outside MX engine specification produces a weak or inconsistent signal flagged as abnormal frequency.
Corroded or damaged connector
A degraded connection introduces signal noise that disrupts the expected pulse pattern.
Internally failed sensor
Heat and vibration exposure over time can degrade the sensor's internal windings, producing an abnormal signal even with a healthy ring.
steps: Pull the fault on PACCAR Davie4 and check the occurrence count and freeze-frame data to establish whether the fault is constant or intermittent.
Inspect the crank sensor connector near the front of the engine for corrosion, looseness, or heat-related damage.
Check the sensor's air gap to the toothed ring using a non-magnetic feeler gauge and compare against MX engine specification.
Inspect the toothed ring for damaged or missing teeth, or metal debris that would disrupt the expected pulse pattern.
Back-probe the signal wires with a multimeter set to AC volts while cranking to check for a clean, consistent waveform amplitude.
Replace the sensor only after confirming the toothed ring and wiring are in good condition, since replacing the sensor alone won't fix a damaged ring.
symptoms: Amber or red warning lamp with rough idle or hesitation
Intermittent stalling, particularly at idle or during deceleration
Extended cranking time on startup
Erratic tachometer behavior

SPN_2791.description_en: ECU internal EGR valve driver chip overtemperature
causes: In Deutz TCD 6.1 engines, a known issue is the EGR valve actuator firmware not matching the ECM software version, causing data format mismatches
Always verify the calibration part number against the engine serial number
Upon activation, the ECM enters a safety fallback: EGR valve is forced to 50% open, and torque is derated linearly from 100% to 75% over 30 seconds
Fuel injection timing is retarded by 3° to reduce peak cylinder pressure and NOx formation
Long-term strategy: After replacing the EGR valve or sensor, perform a 'valve learn' procedure using OEM

[FMI 3 katalog] Aktüatör besleme hattında aşırı gerilim/kısa devre olup olmadığını ölçün. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 4 katalog] Aktüatör besleme hattında gerilim düşüklüğü ve şasi teması arayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

[FMI 7 katalog] Aktüatör itici kollarını, mekanik bağlantıyı ve hava/yağ tahrik hatlarını kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

[FMI 12 katalog] Aktüatör sürücü modülünün beslemesini ve haberleşmesini kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 2791 FMI 2 indicates EGR actuator control response or data erratic. Intermittent power or ground, failing actuator electronics, harness heat damage, and mechanical binding varying with temperature are the primary causes. Heat-soak intermittent EGR faults after extended road loads are a documented pattern. Replacing the EGR actuator cold and releasing the vehicle without hot verification is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Intermittent power or ground — intermittent power or ground producing erratic actuator control
Failing actuator electronics — failing actuator electronics producing erratic control response
Harness heat damage — harness heat damage producing intermittent signal
Mechanical binding varying with temperature — mechanical binding varying with temperature producing erratic response
steps: Step 1 — Hot Duplicate Conditions

Duplicate the fault conditions while hot. Heat-soak intermittent EGR faults after extended road loads are a documented pattern. Perform hot wiggle tests at the actuator connector and nearest harness clips. Electrical dropouts are instant; binding is often temperature and load related.
Step 2 — Power and Ground Stability

Check power and ground stability while hot. An intermittent power or ground producing erratic actuator control requires circuit repair. Verify power and ground stability at the actuator connector under hot operating conditions.
Step 3 — Command and Response Graphing

Graph command and response while hot. Watch command and response while hot. A command that is present with no response confirms a mechanical or actuator fault. A command that produces erratic response confirms a sensor or circuit fault.
Step 4 — Inspect Mechanical Binding
Inspect for mechanical binding. Mechanical binding varying with temperature producing erratic response is a documented cause. Inspect the EGR valve and actuator for binding at operating temperature.
Step 5 — Repair Based on Evidence

Repair based on confirmed evidence. Repair the harness if heat damage is confirmed. Replace the actuator or valve assembly if failure is confirmed. Clean the valve if binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved per OEM procedure.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness if heat damage is confirmed.
2 . Replace actuator or valve assembly if failure is confirmed.
3 . Clean valve if binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved per OEM procedure.
Verification Steps
Confirm EGR actuator control is stable after repair.
Verify SPN 2791 FMI 2 does not return after repair under hot operating conditions.
Confirm EGR flow is correct after repair.
Monitor for return of erratic actuator control events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGR actuator connector for heat damage at every major service.
✓ Inspect EGR harness for heat damage at every major service.
✓ Inspect EGR valve for binding at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium — can affect emissions and soot production if unresolved Severity
Medium. Can affect emissions and soot production if unresolved. Erratic EGR actuator faults often require hot verification.
symptoms: EGR actuator intermittent
EGR control unstable
Actuator response erratic
Intermittent EGR code
Heat-soak EGR fault after road load

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically short to ground.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically short to ground.‪
steps: Check for Short
Disconnect EGR valve connector.
Disconnect 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 of the EGR valve connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short circuit between pin 1 of the EGR valve connector and ground. Refer to "93.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, replace the EGR valve.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 7 is the mechanical not-responding class. The ECM commands EGR valve movement and the position feedback does not track within calibrated tolerance. On Detroit DD platforms, carbon buildup and actuator wear are the dominant patterns. On Cummins, soot stiction after short-trip duty cycles is common. PACCAR MX engines see actuator response lag and cooler contribution. Volvo/Mack platforms show position feedback drift. Universal causes include carbon packing, failed actuator, wiring faults, and mechanical binding. Replacing the assembly without proving movement and circuit integrity is the most common misdiagnosis on this fault.
causes: Carbon packing — soot stiction holding valve in position
Failed actuator — motor or electronics not driving valve
Wiring fault — open or high-resistance actuator circuit
Mechanical binding — physical obstruction or seized shaft
Position feedback drift — sensor not tracking actual position
EGR cooler restriction — contributing to system abnormality
steps: Single Action Gate — Record Desired vs Actual EGR Position

Log commanded EGR position vs actual position feedback on scan tool. A large steady gap confirms the valve is not following commands. A gap that appears only under certain conditions suggests intermittent binding or feedback drift.
Binary Decision Gate — Command Movement Test

Use scan tool to command EGR valve through full range where supported by OEM procedure. Observe actual position response. No movement with valid power and ground confirms mechanical binding or actuator failure.
Override Manager — Carbon Binding Inspection

Remove EGR valve and inspect for carbon packing. On Cummins and Detroit platforms, soot stiction after short-trip duty is a primary cause. Carbon-packed valves often move freely after cleaning without requiring actuator replacement.
Safety Interceptor — Actuator Circuit Verification
Verify actuator power, ground, and control signal integrity. Inspect connector for heat damage, oil contamination, and weak pin tension. Check for chafe near hot-side plumbing and clamp edges.
Resume Point — EGR Cooler and Passage Restriction
Evaluate EGR cooler and passage restriction as a contributing factor. Restricted cooler flow can affect valve authority and system response on some platforms.
Verification Loop — Post-Service Movement Confirmation
After cleaning or repair, command valve through full range and confirm actual position tracks commanded position within OEM tolerance.
Repair Ledger Output — Assembly Replacement Decision
Replace actuator or full valve assembly only after movement proof and circuit integrity are confirmed failed. Note: some platforms require position relearn after replacement.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Clean EGR valve and passages if carbon binding is found.
2 . Repair any actuator circuit wiring faults found.
3 . Replace actuator assembly if electrical failure is confirmed after circuit proof.
4 . Replace full valve assembly if mechanical failure is confirmed.
5 . Service EGR cooler and passages as needed.
6 . Perform position relearn if required by OEM after replacement.
Verification Steps
Confirm EGR actual position tracks commanded position after repair.
Verify no EGR flow or position faults return after repair.
Monitor NOx output returns to normal after repair.
Confirm derate condition clears after root cause is fixed.
Preventative Measures
✓ Perform EGR valve cleaning per OEM service intervals.
✓ Avoid excessive short-trip duty cycles that accelerate soot stiction.
✓ Address EGR cooler leaks promptly to prevent contamination.
✓ Inspect EGR actuator connector for heat damage at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. Often still drivable with derate risk. Extended operation with a non-responding EGR valve increases soot production and NOx instability. Address before long dispatch.
symptoms: EGR valve not responding active
Stuck EGR position
EGR actuator fault
Derate with EGR code
Rough running with EGR fault
Elevated NOx from EGR failure

procedures_full.overview: SPN 2791 FMI 7 means the EGR valve isn't moving to its commanded position, most often from carbon coking. It's a High severity fault that hurts performance and emissions until the valve is freed or replaced. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats EGR coking like a maintenance item rather than a one-time repair on trucks that run a lot of city or short-haul duty cycles - it's worth setting that expectation with the customer up front.
causes: Carbon-coked EGR valve or seat
A mechanical restriction where hardened carbon deposits physically prevent the valve from reaching its commanded position.
Failing EGR valve actuator motor
An electromechanical component wearing out, unable to produce enough force to move even a clean valve through its full range.
Corroded actuator electrical connector
An electrical/wiring fault that can mimic a mechanical failure even when the valve itself moves freely on the bench.
EGR cooler restriction limiting valve travel indirectly
A related mechanical restriction upstream of the valve that can affect how it responds under commanded movement.
steps: Connect Volvo Tech Tool (PTT) and run the EGR valve sweep test to command the valve through its full range of travel.
Watch actual valve position feedback against commanded position - a lag or a hard stop partway through indicates mechanical binding.
With the engine off and cool, remove the EGR valve and visually inspect the valve and seat for hard carbon coking that would prevent full closure or opening.
Check the valve's electrical connector and actuator motor wiring for corrosion, since a good mechanical valve can still fault from a bad electrical connection.
If carbon buildup is confirmed, clean or replace the valve - a valve with heavy coking rarely responds to cleaning alone and often needs replacement.
symptoms: Rough or unstable idle, particularly when cold
Check engine light with reduced power in some cases
Elevated intake manifold temperatures under load
Possible failed emissions inspection due to abnormal EGR flow

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically the EGR valve is in an incorrect position.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically the EGR valve is in an incorrect position.‪
steps: EGR Valve Position Check
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Using DDDL 7.0, monitor the EGR actual position while activating active PWM1 to 50% for 15 seconds.
Is the EGR actual position reading between 42% and 58%?
If yes, go to step 6.
If no, go to step 4.
Remove the EGR valve.
Inspect the EGR valve butterfly for signs of excessive soot or white residue.
If white residue is found, repair the cause/source of coolant contamination and possible EGR cooler failure. Also replace the EGR valve. Refer to "93.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If excessive soot residue is found, correct the cause of soot contamination and any possible CAC system leaks. Repair the source of soot contamination and replace the EGR valve. Refer to "93.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no contamination is found, replace the EGR valve. Refer to "93.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the EGR valve connector.
Inspect the connector for bent, spread or corroded pins.
If connector damage is found, repair as necessary. Refer to "93.4.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no damage is found, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800 for further assistance.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 12 is the bad device/component failure class. The ECM has determined through internal diagnostics or repeated control failures that the EGR valve or actuator has failed as a component. True causes include failed motor or actuator electronics, severe mechanical seizure, internal position sensor failure, and repeated overtemperature exposure. However, false FMI 12 codes from open power feeds, grounded signals, and water intrusion at connectors are common. Replacing the assembly without confirming power, ground, and mechanical freedom is the primary misdiagnosis path on this fault.
causes: Failed motor or actuator electronics — internal component failure
Severe mechanical seizure — physical binding preventing all movement
Internal position sensor failure — feedback circuit inside assembly
Repeated overtemperature exposure — heat cycling damage
Open power feed — false bad device from supply fault
Water intrusion at connector — corrosion causing false failure classification
steps: Single Action Gate — Power and Ground Verification

Verify actuator supply voltage and ground integrity under load before any other step. An open power feed or high-resistance ground can trigger FMI 12 without any internal component failure. Check supply voltage at the actuator connector with the key on.
Binary Decision Gate — Command Movement Test

With valid power and ground confirmed, command EGR valve movement via scan tool. No movement with valid power and ground supports true component failure. Movement with valid power and ground contradicts the FMI 12 classification.
Override Manager — Mechanical Binding Inspection
Inspect for mechanical binding before condemning the actuator electronics. Severe carbon seizure can prevent movement and trigger component failure classification without any electronic failure.
Safety Interceptor — Connector and Harness Inspection
Inspect connector for water intrusion, corrosion, and heat damage. Water intrusion at the EGR actuator connector is a documented cause of false FMI 12 on multiple platforms.
Resume Point — Internal Test Procedures
Follow OEM internal test procedures for the specific platform. Some OEMs provide resistance and response specifications for the actuator assembly.
Verification Loop — Post-Replacement Confirmation
After replacement, confirm valve responds to commands and position feedback tracks correctly. Perform position relearn if required by OEM.
Repair Ledger Output — Assembly Replacement
Replace EGR valve or actuator assembly only after power, ground, and mechanical binding are proven not to be the cause. Note programming or relearn requirements for the platform.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair any power feed or ground faults found before replacing the assembly.
2 . Repair connector water intrusion or corrosion.
3 . Clean mechanical binding if carbon seizure is found.
4 . Replace EGR valve or actuator assembly after circuit and mechanical proof.
5 . Perform position relearn or adaptation if required by OEM.
6 . Clear related NOx and flow faults after repair.
Verification Steps
Confirm EGR valve responds to commands after repair.
Verify position feedback tracks commanded position.
Confirm FMI 12 does not return after repair.
Monitor NOx output returns to normal after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGR actuator connector seals at every major service.
✓ Address coolant and oil leaks near EGR plumbing promptly.
✓ Perform EGR valve cleaning per OEM service intervals.
✓ Verify actuator connector integrity after any EGR system service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium to High depending on derate strategy. Address promptly. Extended operation with failed EGR increases NOx output and can trigger progressive derate strategies.

EGR component failure code
EGR actuator not responding
Permanent EGR derate
Elevated NOx from EGR failure

procedures_full.overview: The EGR valve controls exhaust gas recirculation flow for NOx reduction. FMI 13 (out of calibration) is set when the valve position feedback does not match the commanded position within the calibrated tolerance. Heavy carbon soot sticktion after short-trip cycles and actuator gear wear are the most common causes. Replacing the full assembly without verifying movement and feedback wastes money.
causes: Carbon sticktion — heavy soot buildup preventing valve movement
Failed EGR actuator — gear wear or motor failure
Position sensor bias — feedback signal not tracking commanded position
Wiring fault — actuator connector corrosion or pin tension issue
EGR cooler restriction contributing to control error
steps: Single Action Gate — Command EGR Movement
Use scan tool to command EGR valve to open and close positions. Verify the valve physically moves through its range. No movement with command confirms stuck or failed actuator.
Binary Decision Gate — Carbon Deposit Inspection
Inspect EGR valve for carbon deposits. Heavy soot sticktion is the most common cause of calibration faults on short-trip or high-idle applications.
Override Manager — Position Feedback Verification
Monitor position feedback signal while commanding valve movement. Feedback should track smoothly with command. Erratic or non-tracking feedback indicates sensor or actuator fault.
Safety Interceptor — Actuator Connector Check
Inspect actuator connector for corrosion, heat damage, or poor pin tension. Connector issues after service are a common cause of calibration faults.
Resume Point — EGR Cooler Contribution Check
Inspect EGR cooler for restriction or leakage. A restricted cooler can affect EGR flow and contribute to valve control errors.
Verification Loop — Post-Clean Recalibration
After cleaning or service, perform EGR valve recalibration per OEM procedure if required. Verify calibration completes successfully.
Repair Ledger Output — Assembly Replacement Decision
Replace EGR valve/actuator assembly only after movement, feedback, and connector are proven. Document all findings.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Clean EGR valve of carbon deposits if sticktion is found.
2 . Replace EGR actuator if movement is confirmed stuck or gear is worn ($400–$1,800).
3 . Repair actuator connector if corrosion or pin tension issue is found.
4 . Service or replace EGR cooler if restriction is found.
5 . Perform OEM recalibration procedure after any EGR valve service.
Verification Steps
Confirm EGR valve moves through full range after repair.
Verify position feedback tracks commanded position smoothly.
Confirm EGR calibration completes successfully.
Monitor for return of SPN 2791 FMI 13 over 50+ miles.
Verify DPF soot loading rate is normal after EGR repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect and clean EGR valve at every major service on short-trip applications.
✓ Avoid excessive idle time that accelerates EGR carbon buildup.
✓ Address EGR cooler leaks promptly.
✓ Inspect actuator connector at every EGR service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium severity. May derate power. Prolonged EGR issues affect emissions compliance and accelerate DPF soot loading. Address promptly to prevent secondary aftertreatment faults.
symptoms: EGR valve calibration fault active
EGR stuck open or closed
Derate from EGR fault
Rough running with EGR codes
Increased DPF soot loading from EGR abnormality

procedures_full.overview: This fault typically results from high load operation in high ambients. No action is necessary (this is a “silent” fault, the fan will be turned on).‪
causes: This fault typically results from high load operation in high ambients. No action is necessary (this is a “silent” fault, the fan will be turned on).‪
steps: Note: This fault is a concern only if the fan on times are excessive but coolant temperatures are in the normal operating range.
Check for multiple codes:
If SPN 110/FMI 0 is also present, repair the cooling system first. Refer to "97.9.1 Verify Repairs".
If only SPN 2791/FMI 15 is present, go to the next step.
Visually inspect for signs of exhaust leak in the area of the actuator.
If exhaust leaks are present, repair as necessary. Refer to "97.9.1 Verify Repairs".
If no exhaust leaks are present, go to the next step.
Remove and inspect the actuator cooler lines and fittings.
If coolant lines or fittings are kinked or plugged, repair/replace the damaged component. Refer to "97.9.1 Verify Repairs".
If coolant lines are not damaged and problem still persists, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
ENGINE EXHAUST

Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 58 - Output Shaft Speed Sensor
dd_procedures.overview: This fault code indicates an electrical problem in the Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit. The signal from the sensor did not match the current operating conditions When troubleshooting an Inactive code See "Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode"
causes: Transmission Harness Output Shaft Speed Sensor Various transmission components Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Failed or loose Tone Wheel
Note: If troubleshooting an UltraShift PLUS model transmission’s Output Shaft Speed Sensor, which is a directional sensor, go to Step E; otherwise, start at Step A
steps: A. Measure Output Shaft Speed Sensor resistance and test for short to ground through Transmission Harness. Key off. Disconnect negative battery cable. Disconnect the Transmission Harness 38-way connector. Measure resistance between the Transmission Harness 38-way connector pins: 23 and 24 23 and ground If resistance between Pin 23 and Pin 24 is 2K to 4.5K ohm and between Pin 23 to ground is OL , Go to Step B If resistance is outside of the range, Go to Step C

B. Visually inspect Output Shaft Speed sensor for contamination and damage. Inspect Output Shaft Speed Sensor for contamination or damage. If no problem found, (if fault code is Active) replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Heavy-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Go to Step V If problem is found or you were sent here from Step C or D, replace the: Medium-Duty Output Shaft Speed Sensor Heavy-Duty Output Shaft Speed Sensor Inspect the tone wheel for damage, looseness or corrosion. Go to Step V

C. Measure Output Shaft Speed Sensor resistance. Disconnect the Transmission Harness from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor. Measure resistance between Output Shaft Speed Sensor Pin A and Pin B. If resistance is 2K to 4.5K ohm, Go to Step D If resistance is outside of range, Go to Step B

D. Test for shorts to ground of the Output Shaft Speed sensor. Measure resistance between Output Shaft Speed Sensor Pin A and ground. If resistance is OL, replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Harness Heavy-Duty Transmission Harness Go to Step V If resistance is less than 10K ohm, Go to Step B

E. UltraShift PLUS transmission only: Measure voltage supply to Output Shaft Speed Sensor. Key off. Disconnect the Transmission Harness from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor. With key on, measure voltage from Transmission Harness connector 1 and 2. If voltage is within 4.9 - 5.1volts, replace the: Medium-Duty Output Shaft Speed Sensor Heavy-Duty Output Shaft Speed Sensor Go to Step V If voltage is out of range, Go to Step F

F. Verify continuity of the Output Shaft Speed Sensor wiring. Key off. Disconnect negative battery cable. Disconnect the Transmission Harness 38-way connector. Check for connector damage and measure resistance between: Transmission Harness 38-way connector Pin 22 and Pin 1. Transmission Harness 38-way connector Pin 21 and Pin 2. If harness connections are in good condition and resistance of both circuits measure between 0 to 0.3 ohms, (if fault code is Active) replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Heavy-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) and Go to Step V If damaged or failed harness connectors are found, or if either or both circuits are out of range, replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Harness Heavy-Duty Transmission Harness Go to Step V

V. Verify repair. Key off. Reconnect all connectors and the negative battery cable. Verify proper installation of speed sensor. Key on. Clear fault codes. Drive the vehicle and attempt to reset the fault code. Check for fault codes. If no fault codes, test complete. If Fault Code 58 appears Go to Step A to find error in testing. If fault code other than 58 appears, See "Fault Code Isolation Procedure Index"

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 58: Output Shaft Speed Sensor
dd_procedures.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with electronic speed sensors. The Input Shaft, Main Shaft and Output Shaft Speed Sensors are used to calculate gear ratios within the transmission. The Input Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the Input Shaft, taken from the upper countershaft drive gear. The Main Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the transmission gearing exiting the main case, taken from the auxiliary upper countershaft gear. The Output Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed and direction of the output shaft, taken from the Tone Wheel.
causes: internal failure Tone Wheel loose or broken

1. 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector 2. Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) 3. 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector Body 4. 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector 5. 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor 1. Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) 2. 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector 3. 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector 4. 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor
steps: A. Check for Active or Inactive fault codes. Record the transmission fault codes, FMIs, occurrences, and timestamps from the Service Activity Report created during the Diagnostic Procedure. If Fault Code 58 FMI 5, 6 or 10 is Inactive, Go to Step B If Fault Code 58 FMI 5, 6, 10 is Active, Go to Step F If Fault Code 58 FMI 2 is Active or Inactive, Go to Step D If Fault Code 58 FMI 8, 11 is Active or Inactive, Go to Step I

B. Use Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode to locate intermittent failures. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Place transmission in PD Mode. See more about Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode . Note: Transmission does not enter PD Mode when Active fault codes exist. Wiggle wiring and connections of the Transmission Harness from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor to the TECU. Look for signs of pinched or chafed wiring. Verify all connections are clean and tight. Exit PD Mode by powering down. Notice Allow 2-3 minutes for the TECU to perform a complete power-down sequence before proceeding. If any fault code set Active while wiggling the Transmission Harness, replace Transmission Harness . Go to Step V If no fault codes set Active, Go to Step C

C. Check tightness of Output Shaft End Yoke. Key off. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Attempt to move the Output Yoke at the rear of the transmission both vertically and horizontally. Look and feel for any play. Verify that Tone Wheel is clean, free of debris or damage and does not spin freely by hand. Remove Output Shaft Speed Sensor and inspect for any damage or signs of wear (cracks, broken pickup, etc.). If play is present in Output Shaft End Yoke, Go to Step E If Output Shaft Speed Sensor is damaged, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor . Go to Step V If no play is present and no damage found, Go to Step F

D. Check tightness of Output Shaft End Yoke. Key off. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Attempt to move the Output Yoke at the rear of the transmission both vertically and horizontally. Look and feel for any play. Verify that Tone Wheel is clean, free of debris or damage and does not spin freely by hand. Remove Output Shaft Speed Sensor and inspect for any damage or signs of wear (cracks, broken pickup, etc.). If play is present in Output Shaft End Yoke, Go to Step E If no play is present, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor . Go to Step V

E. Inspect auxiliary case of transmission. Drain transmission of lubricant into a clean pan for re-use. Note how much lubricant comes out and if significant metal fragments appear in the oil. Remove the auxiliary case of the transmission and inspect for signs of damage, specifically inspecting the Auxiliary Output Bearing for signs of failure. Inspect Output Shaft Bearing for any damage or wear. If metal fragments are found, or if damage is found in the auxiliary case, repair or replace auxiliary case components as necessary. Go to Step V If no metal fragments are found, replace Auxiliary Output Bearing and reinstall auxiliary case. Go to Step V

F. Verify 5-volt reference at Output Shaft Speed Sensor. Key on with engine off. Disconnect 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor. Inspect 2-Way Connector body for damage and bent, spread, corroded or loose terminals. Inspect 2-Way Connector and Transmission Harness for any signs of cut, chafed or damaged wiring. Measure voltage between the 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector Pin 1 and ground. Compare reading(s) in table. If readings are in range, Go to Step H If readings are out of range, Go to Step G Pins Range Reading(s) 1 to Ground 4.5-6.0 V

G. Verify continuity of Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit. Key off. Disconnect 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector from the TECU. Inspect 38-Way Connector body for damage and bent, spread, corroded or loose terminals. Measure resistance between 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector Pin 22 and 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector Pin 1. Record reading(s) in table. Measure resistance between 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector Pin 22 and ground. Record reading(s) in table. Compare reading(s) in table. If readings are in range, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor and Transmission Harness . Go to Step V If readings are out of range, replace Transmission Harness . Go to Step V Pins Range Reading(s) 22 to 1 0.0-0.3 Ohms 22 to Ground Open Circuit (OL)

H. Verify continuity of Output Shaft Speed Sensor ground circuit. Key off. Disconnect 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector at TECU. Inspect 38-Way Connector body for damage and bent, spread, corroded or loose terminals. Measure resistance between 38-Way Transmission Harness Connector Pin 21 and 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor Connector Pin 2. Compare reading(s) in table. If readings are in range, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor . Go to Step V If readings are out of range, replace Transmission Harness . Go to Step V Pins Range Reading(s) 21 to 2 0.0-0.3 ohms

I. Verify condition of Output Shaft Speed Sensor connector. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Key off. Disconnect the 2-Way Output Speed Sensor. Inspect the 2-Way Output Speed Sensor Connector, verify the connector is free from contamination and corrosion; the terminals are not bent, spread or loose; and there is no damage to the connector body. Inspect the Transmission Harness side of the 2-Way Output Speed Sensor Connector, verify the connector is free from contamination and corrosion; the terminals are not bent, spread or loose; and there is no damage to the connector body. If no contamination and damage is found, replace the Output Shaft Speed Sensor . Go to Step V If contamination or damage is found, replace the Output Shaft Speed Sensor and Transmission Harness . Go to Step V

V. Verify repair. Key off. Reconnect all connectors and verify that all components are properly installed. Key on with engine off. Clear fault codes using ServiceRanger. Drive vehicle and attempt to reset the code or duplicate the previous complaint. Check for fault codes using ServiceRanger. If no fault codes set and vehicle operates properly, test complete. If Fault Code 58 sets Active during the test drive, Go to Step A If a fault code other than 58 sets, troubleshoot per Fault Code Isolation Procedure Index .

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 375: Output Speed
dd_procedures.overview: The Endurant HD transmission is equipped with speed sensors to monitor input, Countershaft and output speeds. The speed sensors provide rotational speed inputs to the Transmission Control Module (TCM) to verify clutch operation and calculate gear ratios. The Output Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed and direction of the Planetary Output Shaft Assembly. The Output Speed Sensor is mounted externally and connects at the Mechatronic Transmission Module (MTM) Housing. The 3-Way Output Speed Sensor Connector connects to the TCM at the 74-Way Transmission Harness Connector.
causes: MTM - Output Speed Sensor Internal failure Damaged Internal Transmission Mechanical failure TCM Software issue Internal failure FMI 3: TCM Software issue Internal failure FMI 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10: MTM - Output Speed Sensor Internal failure Damaged Output Speed Sensor Harness Wiring shorted to power, shorted to ground or open MTM - Transmission Harness Wiring shorted to power, shorted to ground or open TCM Software issue Internal failure Additional Tools Endurant HD Service Manual TRSM0950 3-Way Eaton Diagnostic Adapter - RR1060TR Eaton Breakout Box with 74-Way Eaton Diagnostic Adapter - RR1029TR Digital Volt/Ohm Meter (DVOM)

steps: A. Check for active or inactive fault codes. Set vehicle parking brake and chock wheels. C. Verify condition of 74-Way Transmission Harness Connector. Key off. Remove the TCM from the MTM with the 20-Way TCM Vehicle Harness Connector and 20-Way TCM Body Harness Connector connected. Reference Endurant HD Service Manual TRSM0950, Transmission Removal Service Procedure. If readings are out of range, replace the Transmission Control Module (TCM) . Go to Step V Ignition State Pins Range Reading(s) Key on 52 to 64 4.75-5.25 V

E. Check for active or inactive fault codes. Confirm a Service Activity Report was downloaded and sent to Eaton. Retrieve and record the transmission fault codes and FMI’s, and their occurrences and timestamps. If Fault Code 375 FMI 3 is Active or Inactive, replace Transmission Control Module (TCM) . Go to Step V

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 375: Output Speed
dd_procedures.overview: The Procision transmission is equipped with speed sensors to monitor: Engine, Primary Input, Secondary Input, and Output speeds. The speed sensors provide rotational speed inputs to the Transmission Control Module (TCM) for the purpose of verifying Primary and Secondary Clutch engagement, making shift decisions, and confirming gear engagement. The Output Speed Sensor is mounted in the Main Housing and captures rotational speed and direction of the Main shaft from 6th Drive Gear. The Output Speed Sensor is integrated into the Transmission Harness, connecting it to the TCM.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Will cleaning the sensor fix SPN 191 FMI 8 permanently?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: If metallic debris was the cause, cleaning the sensor face can restore normal operation. However, rapid re-accumulation of metallic debris can indicate abnormal internal wear. Change the transmission fluid and inspect the magnetic drain plug material if the debris was significant.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can SPN 191 FMI 8 affect the truck's ABS system?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: Possibly. Some vehicles use the transmission output shaft speed as a secondary input for ABS and stability control modules. An erratic transmission speed signal could create a disagreement between systems. If ABS codes appear alongside this code, the transmission sensor should be confirmed first before assuming ABS hardware is at fault.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Does this code appear in Eaton Endurant HD transmissions the same way as older UltraShift models?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The SPN and FMI are consistent across Eaton automated transmission families that use J1939 reporting. ServiceRanger is the correct tool for all Eaton AMT models; some model-specific diagnostic procedures differ between Gen 3 AutoShift/UltraShift PLUS and the Endurant HD, so use the appropriate service documentation.

oem_troubleshooting.title: Eaton UltraShift SPN 191 FMI 8 �?Output Shaft Speed Sensor Erratic | Truck Fault Codes

troubleshooting_faq.question: Is the output shaft speed sensor on the Eaton UltraShift Plus the same as on the older Fuller automated transmissions?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The UltraShift Plus and the earlier Fuller AutoShift use similar speed sensor architectures �?a magnetic pickup or Hall-effect sensor reading a tone wheel �?but the specific sensor part numbers, tone wheel configurations, and mounting details may differ between transmission generations. ServiceRanger part look-up or the Roadranger service portal can confirm the correct part for the specific transmission model.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can a worn transmission output seal affect the tone wheel and cause SPN 191 FMI 8 on the Eaton UltraShift?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: A worn output seal can allow lubricant to contaminate the sensor area, which may foul the sensor face and produce erratic readings. Inspecting the sensor for oil contamination alongside checking the tone wheel condition is worthwhile during diagnosis.

troubleshooting_faq.question: How does the Eaton UltraShift use output shaft speed data compared to vehicle speed from the ABS?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The Eaton UltraShift TCM uses its own output shaft speed sensor for primary shift control. It may also receive vehicle speed data from the ABS via J1939 as a reference. When both sources are available and agree, shift control is optimal. When the transmission output sensor is faulted, the TCM may attempt to use the J1939 vehicle speed as a fallback, but this depends on the specific transmission generation and calibration.

oem_troubleshooting.title: ZF AS-Tronic / TraXon SPN 191 FMI 8 �?Output Shaft Speed Sensor Erratic | Truck Fault Codes

troubleshooting_faq.question: What is the difference between the ZF AS-Tronic and ZF TraXon in terms of speed sensor design?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The ZF TraXon is the current-generation automated transmission platform that superseded the AS-Tronic for new applications. Both use output shaft speed sensors for shift control, but the sensor types, connector formats, and tone wheel designs differ between generations. ZF Testman covers both platforms with specific procedures for each model.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can the ZF TraXon transmission enter a safe mode if SPN 191 FMI 8 is active?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: Yes. If the TCM cannot determine vehicle speed accurately from the output sensor and no alternative speed reference is available, the TraXon may restrict certain operating modes or gear ranges as a protective measure. The specific response depends on the severity of the signal fault and the transmission calibration.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Is ZF Testman or WABCO Toolbox required to diagnose SPN 191 FMI 8 on the ZF AS-Tronic?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: While the fault code itself is readable with any J1939-capable scan tool, ZF Testman provides the live data parameters �?output shaft speed, sensor signal quality, and bidirectional tests �?needed to effectively characterize the fault. Generic scan tools typically cannot access these specific ZF live data channels.

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 58: Output Shaft Speed Sensor
procedures_full.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with electronic speed sensors. The Input Shaft, Main Shaft and Output Shaft Speed Sensors are used to calculate gear ratios within the transmission. The Input Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the Input Shaft, taken from the upper countershaft drive gear. The Main Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the transmission gearing exiting the main case, taken from the auxiliary upper countershaft gear. The Output Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed and direction of the output shaft, taken from the Tone Wheel. The Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) compares these speeds to calculate the gear ratios of the main case, auxiliary case and overall transmission. The Output Shaft Speed Sensor transmits a digital signal to the TECU based on the rotational speed of the Output Shaft Tone Wheel. The TECU compares Main Shaft Speed to Output Shaft Speed to confirm the gear ratio of the auxiliary case and compares Input Shaft Speed to Output Shaft Speed to confirm the overall transmission gear ratio. Fault Code 58 indicates an electrical fault within the Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit or a speed value
procedures_full.detection: The TECU compares the values of the three speed sensors to determine sensor validity. The TECU also monitors the Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit for any shorts to power, shorts to ground, open circuits or incorrect rotational direction of the Output Shaft.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The system can detect Output Shaft Speed Sensor faults when one of the following conditions is present for 1 second or longer: FMI 2 – Data Erratic: TECU detects data from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor does not match the current gear ratio. FMI 5 – Current Below Normal or Open Circuit: TECU detects an open circuit or the Output Shaft Speed Sensor has high resistance. FMI 6 – Current Above Normal or Grounded Circuit: TECU detects a short to power in the circuit. FMI 8 – Abnormal Frequency: TECU detects an incorrect rotational direction from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor. FMI 10 – Abnormal Rate of Change: TECU detects an excessive rate change. FMI 11 – Root Cause Unknown: TECU detects a speed sensor error.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: All FMIs: TECU receives a valid signal from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor and detects no electrical open or short circuits for 2 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: All FMIs “F” flashes in gear display. Service light flashes (if equipped). If fault occurs in low range, transmission still shifts up and down within low range, but will not complete the shift to high range. If fault occurs while in high range, the transmission still shifts up and down within high range. Once low range is reached, the transmission will not complete the shift back to high range. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive All FMIs: TECU receives a valid signal from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor and detects no electrical open or short circuits for 2 seconds.

steps.B:
B. Use Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode to locate intermittent failures. 
 Set parking brake and chock wheels. 
 Place transmission in PD Mode. See more about Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode . 
 Note: Transmission does not enter PD Mode when Active fault codes exist. 
 Wiggle wiring and connections of the Transmission Harness from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor to the TECU. Look for signs of pinched or chafed wiring. Verify all connections are clean and tight. 
 Exit PD Mode by powering down. 
 Notice
 Allow 2–3 minutes for the TECU to perform a complete power-down sequence before proceeding. 
 If any fault code set Active while wiggling the Transmission Harness, replace Transmission Harness . Go to Step V 
 If no fault codes set Active, Go to Step C
steps.C:
C. Check tightness of Output Shaft End Yoke. 
 Key off. 
 Set parking brake and chock wheels. 
 Attempt to move the Output Yoke at the rear of the transmission both vertically and horizontally. Look and feel for any play. 
 Verify that Tone Wheel is clean, free of debris or damage and does not spin freely by hand. 
 Remove Output Shaft Speed Sensor and inspect for any damage or signs of wear (cracks, broken pickup, etc.). 
 If play is present in Output Shaft End Yoke, Go to Step E 
 If Output Shaft Speed Sensor is damaged, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor D . Go to Step V 
 If no play is present and no damage found, Go to Step F
steps.D:
D. Check tightness of Output Shaft End Yoke.

 Verify that Tone Wheel is clean, free of debris or damage and does not spin freely by hand. 
 Remove Output Shaft Speed Sensor and inspect for any damage or signs of wear (cracks, broken pickup, etc.). 
 If play is present in Output Shaft End Yoke, Go to Step E 
 If no play is present, replace Output Shaft Speed Sensor D . Go to Step V
steps.E:
E. Inspect auxiliary case of transmission. 
 Drain transmission of lubricant into a clean pan for re-use. Note how much lubricant comes out and if significant metal fragments appear in the oil. 
 Remove the auxiliary case of the transmission and inspect for signs of damage, specifically inspecting the Auxiliary Output Bearing for signs of failure. 
 Inspect Output Shaft Bearing for any damage or wear. 
 If metal fragments are found, or if damage is found in the auxiliary case, repair or replace auxiliary case components as necessary. Go to Step V 
 If no metal fragments are found, replace Auxiliary Output Bearing and reinstall auxiliary case. Go to Step V
steps.F:
F. Verify 5-volt reference at Output Shaft Speed Sensor. 
 Key on with engine off. 
 Disconnect 2-Way Output Shaft Speed Sensor.

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 58: Output Shaft Speed Sensor
procedures_full.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with electronic speed sensors. The Input Shaft, Main Shaft and Output Shaft Speed Sensors are used to calculate gear ratios within the transmission. The Input Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the Input Shaft, taken from the upper countershaft drive gear. The Main Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed of the transmission gearing exiting the main case, taken from the auxiliary upper countershaft gear. The Output Shaft Speed Sensor measures the rotational speed and direction of the output shaft, taken from the Tone Wheel. The Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) compares these speeds to calculate the gear ratios of the main case, auxiliary case and overall transmission. The Output Shaft Speed Sensor transmits a digital signal to the TECU based on the rotational speed of the Output Shaft Tone Wheel. The TECU compares Main Shaft Speed to Output Shaft Speed to confirm the gear ratio of the auxiliary case and compares Input Shaft Speed to Output Shaft Speed to confirm the overall transmission gear ratio. Fault Code 58 indicates an electrical fault within the Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit or a speed value
procedures_full.detection: The TECU compares the values of the three speed sensors to determine sensor validity. The TECU also monitors the Output Shaft Speed Sensor circuit for any shorts to power, shorts to ground, open circuits or incorrect rotational direction of the Output Shaft.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The system can detect Output Shaft Speed Sensor faults when one of the following conditions is present for 1 second or longer: FMI 2 – Data Erratic: TECU detects data from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor does not match the current gear ratio. FMI 5 – Current Below Normal or Open Circuit: TECU detects an open circuit or the Output Shaft Speed Sensor has high resistance. FMI 6 – Current Above Normal or Grounded Circuit: TECU detects a short to power in the circuit. FMI 8 – Abnormal Frequency: TECU detects an incorrect rotational direction from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor. FMI 10 – Abnormal Rate of Change: TECU detects an excessive rate change. FMI 11 – Root Cause Unknown: TECU detects a speed sensor error.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: All FMIs: TECU receives a valid signal from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor and detects no electrical open or short circuits for 2 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: All FMIs “F” flashes in gear display. Service light flashes (if equipped). If fault occurs in low range, transmission still shifts up and down within low range, but will not complete the shift to high range. If fault occurs while in high range, the transmission still shifts up and down within high range. Once low range is reached, the transmission will not complete the shift back to high range. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive All FMIs: TECU receives a valid signal from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor and detects no electrical open or short circuits for 2 seconds.

procedures_full.overview: The Endurant XD Series transmissions are equipped with speed sensors to monitor Input, Countershaft, and Output speeds. The speed sensors provide rotational speed inputs to the Transmission Control Module (TCM) for the purpose of verifying clutch engagement, making shift decisions, and confirming gear engagements. procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 58 - Output Shaft Speed Sensor
procedures_full.overview: The Output Shaft Speed Sensor is located on the rear bearing cover at the 12 o’clock position. The sensor is a magnetic pickup that produces an AC voltage as the tone wheel teeth moves past the end of the sensor. At idle, the Speed Sensor output is low and it increases as the speed of the output shaft increases.
procedures_full.detection: The following preconditions must be met before the system detects the fault: Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) ignition voltage is greater than 7 volts and less than 16 volts. FMI 2 does not set if there is already an Active FMI 5 for the Input or Output Shaft Speed Sensors.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The following conditions must be met to set the fault code Active: FMI 2 is set when the TECU output shaft speed is compared to the input shaft speed and it produces an inconsistent reading for 1 second or greater. FMI 3, 4 are set when the TECU detects a short to ground, short to battery, or the output shaft speed is 0 for 1 second or greater. FMI 5 is set when the TECU detects an open and the Output Shaft Speed Sensor is 0 for 1 second or greater.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: Only Inactive faults can be cleared from the TECU or HCM history using ServiceRanger. The TECU automatically clears faults from history after 200 hours. The HCM automatically clears a fault from history after that fault has been Inactive for 200 hours.

procedures_full.overview: The Procision transmission is equipped with speed sensors to monitor: Engine, Primary Input, Secondary Input, and Output speeds. The speed sensors provide rotational speed inputs to the Transmission Control Module (TCM) for the purpose of verifying Primary and Secondary Clutch engagement, making shift decisions, and confirming gear engagement. The Output Speed Sensor is mounted in the Main Housing and captures rotational speed and direction of the Main shaft from 6th Drive Gear. The Output Speed Sensor is integrated into the Transmission Harness, connecting it to the TCM.
procedures_full.detection: The TCM monitors the Output Speed signal. If a system failure is detected, the fault is set Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 2 – Data Erratic: Output Speed signal out of range for 2 seconds. FMI 4 – Voltage Below Normal or Shorted Low: Output Speed Sensor circuit shorted to ground for 2 seconds. FMI 5 – Current Below Normal or Open Circuit: Output Speed Sensor circuit open or shorted to power for 2 seconds. FMI 6 - Current Above Normal or Shorted Circuit: Output Speed sensor power supply out of normal operating voltage (4.25 to 6.25 volts) for 2 seconds. FMI 8 – Abnormal Frequency: Output Speed signal abnormal pulse width for 2 seconds. FMI 14 – Special Instructions: Output Speed signal less than J1939 Front Axle Speed and calculated Output Speed (based on input speed and gear ratio) for 1 second. FMI 20 – Data Drifted High: Output Speed signal greater than calculated Output Speed (based on Primary and Secondary Input Speeds and gear ratio) for 1 second. FMI 21 – Data Drifted Low: Output Speed signal less than calculated Output Speed (based on Primary and Secondary Input Speeds and gear ratio) for 1 second. FMI 31 – Condition Exists: Output Speed signal greater than J1939 Front Axle Speed and calculated Output Speed (based on Input Speed and gear ratio) for 1 second.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: FMI 2: Output Speed signal in range for 10 seconds. FMI 4: Output Speed Sensor circuit not shorted to ground for 10 seconds. FMI 5: Output Speed Sensor circuit not open or shorted to power for 10 seconds. FMI 6: Output Speed Sensor power supply voltage between 4.25 and 6.25 volts for 10 seconds. FMI 8: Output Speed signal pulse width correct for 10 seconds. FMI 14, 31: Output Speed signal matches J1939 Front Axle Speed and calculated Output Speed for 10 seconds. FMI 20, 21: Output Speed signal matches calculated Output Speed for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: All FMIs: Amber warning lamp on No degraded performance Note: If speed substitution is not available: Only engaged gears allowed PTO Mode prohibited Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive FMI 2: Output Speed signal in range for 10 seconds. FMI 4: Output Speed Sensor circuit not shorted to ground for 10 seconds. FMI 5: Output Speed Sensor circuit not open or shorted to power for 10 seconds. FMI 6: Output Speed Sensor power supply voltage between 4.25 and 6.25 volts for 10 seconds. FMI 8: Output Speed signal pulse width correct for 10 seconds. FMI 14, 31: Output Speed signal matches J1939 Front Axle Speed and calculated Output Speed for 10 seconds. FMI 20, 21: Output Speed signal matches calculated Output Speed for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.possible_causes: All FMIs: Output Speed Sensor Internal failure Damaged Transmission Harness Wiring shorted to power, shorted to ground or open Mechanical failure TCM Internal failure

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 58 - Output Shaft Speed Sensor Fault
procedures_full.overview: The Output Shaft Speed Sensor is located at 12 o’clock on the Rear Bearing Cover. It is a magnetic pickup that produces an AC voltage as the Tone Wheel teeth move past the end of the sensor. The amount of AC voltage output from the Output Shaft Speed Sensor increases and decreases in correlation with the speed of the Output Shaft.
procedures_full.detection: Fault is detected when: Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) ignition voltage is greater than 7 volts and less than 16 volts. FMI 2 sets if an Active FMI 5 for the Input or Output Shaft Speed Sensors already exists.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The following conditions may set the fault Active: FMI 2 is set when the TECU detects a difference between the Output Shaft speed and the Input Shaft speed for 1 second or greater. FMI 3, 4 are set when the TECU detects a short to ground, short to battery or the Output Shaft speed is 0 for 1 second or greater. FMI 5 is set when the TECU detects an open circuit and the Output Shaft Speed Sensor is 0 for 1 second or greater. Note: When troubleshooting an Inactive code refer to the Product Diagnostic Mode (PDM) .
procedures_full.fallback: When Fault Code 58 is set the following conditions occur: Red “Service” light illuminates and an “F” flashes in the gear display. Fault is stored in TECU memory. Operation mode changes to AutoShift Fallback. If this fault occurs while moving, the transmission remains in the current gear and the clutch opens when the vehicle stops.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 3 on the APP2 circuit indicates the secondary pedal channel signal is above the valid maximum voltage range. On dual-path APP systems, APP2 should remain mathematically correlated to APP1 throughout the pedal travel range. An open APP2 signal circuit, failed pedal track B, and connector cavity issues specific to the APP2 channel are the primary causes. Single-track failures inside pedal potentiometer assemblies are a documented pattern on high-mileage vehicles. Channel-specific isolation prevents replacing the entire harness for a single-channel fault.
causes: Open APP2 signal circuit — signal floating toward reference voltage
Failed pedal track B — single-track failure inside potentiometer
Connector cavity issue — APP2 pin pullout or corrosion
Stretched APP2 conductor — firewall routing damage
Pedal assembly wear — track B failure under vibration
steps: Single Action Gate — Channel Graphing

Graph APP1 and APP2 channels simultaneously. APP2 should remain mathematically correlated to APP1 throughout the pedal travel range. APP2 high with APP1 normal confirms a channel-specific fault on the APP2 path.
Binary Decision Gate — Pin-Level Inspection of APP2 Cavity

Inspect the APP2 connector cavity specifically. Pin pullout, corrosion, and stretched conductors are channel-specific faults that do not affect APP1. Inspect the APP2 cavity at both the pedal connector and the ECM connector.
Override Manager — APP2 Circuit Continuity

Perform continuity test on the APP2 signal wire only. An open APP2 signal wire confirms a harness fault rather than pedal failure. Confirm APP2 reference and ground are present before evaluating the pedal.
Safety Interceptor — Harness Wiggle on APP2 Path

Wiggle the harness specifically along the APP2 path while monitoring APP2 PIDs. Stretched conductors from pedal travel and firewall routing damage are documented causes of intermittent APP2 high-voltage faults.
Resume Point — Pedal Assembly Evaluation

If APP2 circuit integrity is confirmed and the fault persists, evaluate the pedal assembly. Single-track failures inside pedal potentiometer assemblies are a documented pattern — APP2 track failure with APP1 intact.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Channel Confirmation
After repair, verify APP1 and APP2 are correlated and within OEM specification throughout the pedal travel range. Confirm limp mode does not activate during a test drive.
Repair Ledger Output — Pedal or Harness Decision
Replace pedal assembly after APP2 circuit integrity is confirmed and pedal track B failure is proven. Repair harness if open wire or terminal issue is found on the APP2 path.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair APP2 connector pin pullout or corrosion.
2 . Repair open APP2 signal wire.
3 . Replace pedal assembly after APP2 circuit proof confirms track B failure.
4 . Verify APP1 and APP2 are correlated after repair.
Verification Steps
Confirm APP1 and APP2 are correlated and within OEM specification after repair.
Verify limp mode does not activate during a test drive.
Confirm SPN 2623 FMI 3 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of power limit from APP2 fault.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect APP connector for pin tension and corrosion at every major service.
✓ Inspect APP harness routing for stretch damage at every major service.
✓ Address APP faults promptly — limp mode is a safety risk in traffic.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High Severity
High for response reliability. Limp mode from APP2 fault is a safety risk in traffic. Channel-specific isolation avoids whole-harness guesswork.

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3509 FMI 16 – DEF Concentration Out of Range
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3509 FMI 16 – DEF Concentration Out of Range (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3509 FMI 16 indicates that the DEF fluid concentration is outside the acceptable range. Proper DEF must contain 32.5% urea and 67.5% deionized water. When the ECM detects the concentration is off on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines, the SCR system cannot function correctly and a derate condition will follow.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF or SCR warning light illuminated 
Engine derate condition 
Reduced vehicle speed 
SCR system performance degraded
Cause
This code triggers when the DEF quality sensor detects that the urea concentration in the tank does not meet the required 32.5% standard. Common causes include:
Wrong fluid added to DEF tank (water, diesel, or other fluid) 
Poor quality or off-brand DEF with incorrect concentration 
DEF that has degraded due to age or heat exposure 
Contaminated DEF tank Faulty 
DEF quality sensor giving incorrect readings
Can You Keep Driving?
The engine will enter a derate condition fairly quickly with this fault active. The SCR system requires correct DEF concentration to control emissions. Continued operation without addressing the fluid quality will result in progressive power reduction.
Recommended Action
Drain the DEF tank completely and refill with fresh, quality DEF that meets ISO 22241 standards. After refilling, clear the fault codes and allow the system to verify the new fluid. If the code returns after refilling with quality DEF, have the DEF quality sensor inspected and replaced if necessary.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3509 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the DEF fluid in the tank does not have the correct urea concentration and the SCR system cannot operate properly as a result.
 
 
What causes SPN 3509 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are poor quality DEF, wrong fluid added to the DEF tank, degraded DEF, or a faulty DEF quality sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3509 FMI 16?
 
Not recommended. The engine will derate and power will be progressively reduced until the DEF concentration issue is resolved.
 
 
Will SPN 3509 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. Incorrect DEF concentration prevents the SCR system from controlling NOx emissions and the ECM will trigger a derate condition.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3509 FMI 16?
 
Drain and replace the DEF with fresh fluid meeting ISO 22241 standards. Clear the fault codes and allow the system to verify fluid quality. If the code persists with fresh DEF, inspect the DEF quality sensor.

SPN 3936 FMI 1 
SPN 4334 FMI 16

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3509 FMI 3 on a Mercedes-Benz means the ECU's 5V sensor reference supply is reading above normal. Expect multiple simultaneous sensor faults — isolate the shorted sensor pulling the rail high before replacing anything. Mercedes-Benz SPN 3509 FMI 3 is a 5V sensor reference supply voltage fault. SPN 3509 (Sensor Supply Voltage 1) is the shared 5-volt reference rail that the ECU provides to power numerous sensors — boost pressure, fuel delivery pressure, EGT, and more. When FMI 3 (above normal voltage) is logged, the ECU has detected the rail voltage exceeding its upper calibration limit, typically 5.25–5.5 V depending on ECU firmware. The most common cause is a sensor with an internal short that forces the supply rail upward, dragging every sensor on that circuit to an abnormally high reading and generating a storm of secondary fault codes. Technicians at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com stress that this fault must be diagnosed as a system-level supply problem — not as a collection of individual sensor failures — to avoid a parts-cannon replacement cycle.
causes: Internally shorted sensor on the 5V supply rail

A failed MAP, boost pressure, or EGT sensor with an internal short between its signal wire and the 5V supply pin pulls the entire reference rail above normal, triggering SPN 3509 FMI 3 plus multiple secondary codes.
Harness short between 5V supply and signal wires
Insulation damage caused by heat or chafing allows the 5V reference wire to contact a signal wire, creating a feedback path that raises the measured rail voltage.
ECU internal 5V regulator fault
In rare cases the voltage regulator circuit inside the ECU fails, outputting more than 5 V on the reference rail regardless of external circuit condition. This requires ECU replacement or rebuild.
steps: Connect a Texa or Jaltest diagnostic tool to the vehicle's diagnostic port and read all active fault codes. List every code simultaneously present — multiple sensor faults sharing SPN 3509 FMI 3 point to a supply rail problem rather than individual sensor failures.

With the ignition ON and engine OFF, use a digital multimeter to probe the 5V reference pin on one of the sensors sharing the rail (such as a MAP or boost sensor). A reading above 5.3 V confirms the rail is high; a reading at 0 V confirms an open supply wire.

Disconnect sensors on the 5V rail one at a time and re-measure the supply voltage after each disconnection. When the voltage returns to 5.0 V after removing a specific sensor, that sensor has an internal short pulling the rail high.
Inspect all harness connectors on the 5V supply circuit for pushed-back pins, spread terminals, or moisture bridging the 5V supply pin to an adjacent signal pin.

After identifying and replacing the shorted sensor or repairing the harness fault, clear all codes with the Texa or Jaltest tool and verify 5V rail stability across the operating temperature range before returning the vehicle to service.
symptoms: Multiple sensor fault codes active simultaneously across different systems.
Erratic pressure and temperature gauge readings on the instrument cluster.
Engine derate or reduced power mode active.
Amber MIL (Malfunction Indicator Lamp) illuminated.
Aftertreatment regeneration inhibited due to invalid sensor data.
procedures_full.source_title: Mercedes-Benz SPN 3509 FMI 3: 5V Sensor Supply Voltage Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3509 FMI 4 means the 5-volt reference supply feeding a group of Cummins sensors has dropped low, almost always from a short to ground. It is High severity and commonly triggers multiple sensor codes at once, though the engine keeps running. SPN 3509 covers Sensor Supply Voltage 1, one of several regulated 5-volt reference circuits the Cummins ECM uses to power analog sensors like TPS, MAP, and various pressure transducers. When FMI 4 sets, the ECM has detected that this shared supply rail has sagged below its normal 5.0-volt window, which is a strong signal that something on the circuit is shorted to ground rather than any single sensor simply failing. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com gets a lot of calls on this one because shops sometimes chase four or five sensor codes individually before realizing they're all fed off the same shorted circuit. Once you understand the supply-sharing layout, tracking down the actual short becomes a straightforward process of elimination.
causes: Chafed sensor harness shorting to ground
Any sensor wire on the shared 5-volt bus rubbing through to bare metal against the block or chassis will pull the whole reference circuit down.
Water-intruded sensor connector
Corrosion inside a connector can create a low-resistance path from the 5-volt pin to a ground pin, especially on sensors mounted low near the frame.
Internally shorted sensor
A sensor with a failed internal circuit board can short its own 5-volt supply pin to its ground pin, pulling the whole shared circuit down.
ECM internal regulator fault
The ECM's own 5-volt regulator stage can fail, but this should only be suspected after every sensor on the circuit has tested clean.
steps: Pull codes with Cummins INSITE and note every SPN that shares the 3509 sensor supply circuit - this narrows down which sensor group to inspect first.
With the key on and engine off, back-probe the 5-volt reference wire at the ECM connector and verify you have 4.9-5.1 volts DC with a multimeter.
Unplug sensors on that supply circuit one at a time while watching the reference voltage - when the short disappears, you've isolated the offending sensor or its harness leg.
Inspect the isolated harness section for chafing against the block, frame rail, or turbo heat shield, and check connectors for water intrusion.
Repair or replace the damaged harness section, reconnect all sensors, and confirm 5.0 volts is restored before clearing codes.
symptoms: Multiple unrelated sensor fault codes appearing at the same time
Amber MIL illuminated
Rough idle or erratic throttle response if affected sensors include TPS or MAP
Engine may enter a limp or default-value operating mode

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3509 FMI 4 on Mack means the 5V sensor reference supply is shorted low, typically pulling multiple sensors to incorrect readings simultaneously. Find the short in the supply bus — do not start replacing individual sensors. When SPN 3509 FMI 4 shows up on a Mack, it usually brings a crowd of other fault codes with it. That is not a coincidence — the 5V sensor supply circuit feeds multiple sensors from one reference voltage, so a single short to ground shows up as every sensor on that bus reporting low or erratic values. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com works the supply wire, not the sensor list.
causes: Sensor body internally shorted to ground dragging the supply bus down (electrical)
Very Common

An internally failed sensor with a short between its supply pin and case ground pulls the entire shared 5V bus toward 0V, causing cascading low-voltage faults on every sensor connected to that reference.
Harness abrasion grounding the 5V supply wire to chassis metal (electrical)
The sensor supply wire running through tight routing areas near brackets, the firewall, or exhaust contact points can abrade through insulation and ground through the chassis.
Water intrusion in a sensor connector causing a ground path through moisture (electrical)
Moisture in a sensor connector creates a low-resistance path from the supply pin to the connector shell/ground, effectively shorting the supply bus.
steps: 1. Connect Mack Premium Tech Tool or Snap-on NEXIQ and document ALL active and pending fault codes — a long list of sensor faults with FMI 3 or FMI 4 pointing at multiple different sensors strongly suggests a supply voltage fault rather than multiple independent sensor failures.
2. Locate the SPN 3509 sensor supply voltage circuit in the wiring diagram and identify which sensors are fed from this reference bus for your engine family (MP8/MP7/MP10).

3. With the key on and engine off, measure voltage at the supply reference wire of each sensor on this bus with a multimeter — all should read approximately 5V. A reading near 0V or less than 4V on the supply wire confirms the bus is being pulled down.

4. Disconnect sensors from this supply bus one at a time, checking bus voltage after each disconnection. When voltage recovers to approximately 5V after disconnecting a particular sensor, that sensor body is shorted to ground internally and is pulling the bus down.

5. Walk the sensor supply harness for abrasion points where the 5V reference wire could be grounding through the chassis — wiring that routes near the firewall, exhaust, or engine brackets is most vulnerable.
6. After repairing the short, clear all fault codes, start the engine, and confirm all sensors return to normal readings in PTT live data before releasing the truck.
symptoms: Multiple sensor fault codes active at the same time (temperature, pressure, position sensors)
Erratic or zeroed-out sensor readings in PTT live data across several parameters
Possible engine derate as the ECM loses confidence in multiple sensor inputs simultaneously
MIL and potentially other warning lamps active from the cascade of sensor faults
Sensors that share the SPN 3509 reference bus all reading at the low end of their range

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3509 FMI 16 means the ECM 5V sensor supply 1 circuit on Freightliner trucks reads above the 5.2V maximum. Overvoltage biases every sensor on that branch, causing multiple false readings and cascading derate codes. Measure supply voltage at the ECM connector before replacing individual sensors. Sensor supply voltage 1 feeds a shared 5V reference to multiple engine and aftertreatment sensors on Freightliner Cascadia and Coronado trucks. When SPN 3509 FMI 16 sets, the reference is too high, and every sensor on that branch reports skewed data. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com advises measuring supply voltage at the ECM first and isolating shorted sensors one at a time rather than replacing parts based on companion codes alone.
causes: Internal short in a sensor on the supply 1 branch
A failed sensor with internal short to the reference pulls supply voltage above 5.2V, corrupting readings from all other sensors on the same branch.
Chafed harness shorting supply 1 to battery voltage
Rubbing at firewall grommets or frame clips can short the 5V reference to 12-14V battery positive, producing readings of 5.5-6.0V or higher.
ECM internal voltage regulator failure
A failed regulator inside the ECM can output excessive reference voltage, though this is far less common than sensor or harness faults.
steps: Connect Detroit DDDL or Cummins INSITE and read SPN 3509 (sensor supply 1 voltage) with key on — spec is 4.8-5.2V; readings above 5.3V confirm overvoltage on the reference circuit.
Identify all sensors on supply 1 by pulling the wiring diagram for your engine platform — typically includes oil temp, intake pressure, and one or more aftertreatment sensors.
With the key on, back-probe supply 1 at the ECM connector (usually pin C3-58 on DD15, varies by platform) and measure voltage — compare to voltage at each sensor connector on the same branch.

Disconnect sensors one at a time on the supply 1 branch and monitor SPN 3509 — if voltage drops to normal when a specific sensor is unplugged, that sensor has an internal short to the reference circuit.
Inspect the harness for chafed wires where supply 1 shorts to battery voltage (12-14V) — common rub points include the firewall grommet and frame rail clips.
Repair the shorted sensor or harness, verify supply 1 reads 4.9-5.1V with all sensors connected, clear all companion codes, and confirm no sensors re-fault within 30 minutes of idle.
symptoms: Multiple sensor faults set simultaneously — temperature, pressure, and position sensors on supply 1 branch
Sensor supply 1 voltage reads 5.5-6.0V on Detroit DDDL or Cummins INSITE
Erratic gauge readings on dash for oil temp, boost, and DEF level
Amber MIL with rapid accumulation of companion SPN faults within one key cycle
Possible torque derate as ECM receives conflicting sensor data from the same supply branch
