procedures_full.overview: SPN 3510 FMI 3 indicates sensor supply bank 1 voltage above the valid maximum. Short to higher voltage on the Supply 1 branch, failed supply regulator, and miswire after service are the primary causes. Bank-specific cascades where only one reference family fails is a documented pattern. Replacing sensors from the healthy supply bank while the Supply 1 fault remains is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Short to higher voltage on Supply 1 branch — harness short to battery or ignition voltage on Supply 1 branch
Failed supply regulator — failed Supply 1 regulator producing above-normal reference
Miswire after service — miswire after service feeding higher voltage into Supply 1 branch
steps: Step 1 — Identify Supply 1 Sensors

Identify which sensors share Supply 1. Map which sensors are on the Supply 1 bank using the OEM wiring diagram. Inspect that branch only first. Bank-specific cascades where only one reference family fails is a documented pattern.
Step 2 — Measure Supply 1 Voltage

Measure Supply 1 voltage at a known sensor on that bank. Compare to Supply 2 if available. A Supply 1 voltage significantly above OEM specification confirms a Supply 1 fault. A Supply 2 voltage that is normal confirms the fault is isolated to Supply 1.
Step 3 — Isolate Branch

Isolate the Supply 1 branch. Disconnect Supply 1 sensors one group at a time. If the voltage drops when a branch is disconnected, the voltage source is external to the ECM. A short to higher voltage on the Supply 1 branch requires harness repair.
Step 4 — Repair Short or Miswire

Repair the short or miswire. Confirm the Supply 1 branch is clean before any ECM assessment. ECM replacement is only indicated if the unloaded Supply 1 voltage remains incorrect after all loads are removed and power and grounds are perfect.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness short to higher voltage if confirmed on Supply 1 branch.
2 . Repair miswire if confirmed after service.
3 . Replace ECM if Supply 1 regulator failure is confirmed after harness proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm Supply 1 voltage returns to specification after repair.
Verify SPN 3510 FMI 3 does not return after repair.
Confirm all Supply 1 sensor codes clear after repair.
Confirm Supply 2 remains healthy after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Verify connector pin assignments after any harness repair.
✓ Inspect Supply 1 branch after any harness work.
✓ Use OEM wiring diagrams for all harness repairs.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High when multiple controls lose trust. Severity
High when multiple controls lose trust. Supply 1 high is a bank isolation problem, not a single-sensor guess.

procedures_full.source_title: SPN 3510 FMI 3 — Sensor Supply Voltage 1 Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3510 FMI 3 means the second 5-volt reference supply feeding a group of PACCAR sensors has risen above its normal range, usually from a short to a higher voltage source. It is High severity and commonly triggers multiple sensor codes at once, though the engine keeps running. SPN 3510 covers Sensor Supply Voltage 2, a separate 5-volt reference circuit from SPN 3509 that the PACCAR MX engine ECM uses to power a different group of analog sensors. FMI 3 flags voltage above normal, meaning the reference has been pulled high rather than pulled low, usually from a short to a stronger voltage source somewhere along that circuit. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees shops waste time chasing individual sensor codes on this fault before realizing they're all sourced from the same compromised supply rail.
causes: Chafed sensor harness shorting to a higher voltage circuit
Any wire on the shared 5-volt bus rubbing against a battery-fed or ignition-fed wire will pull the whole reference circuit above its normal range.
Open ground reference on the sensor supply circuit
A broken or corroded ground connection can cause the reference voltage to float higher than expected on some sensor supply designs.
Internally shorted sensor
A sensor with a failed internal circuit board can short its 5-volt supply pin to a higher voltage source internally.
ECM internal regulator fault
The ECM's own 5-volt regulator stage can fail, but this should only be suspected after every sensor on the circuit has tested clean.
steps: Pull codes with PACCAR Davie4 and note every SPN that shares the 3510 sensor supply circuit to narrow down which sensor group to inspect.
With the key on and engine off, back-probe the sensor supply wire at the ECM connector and verify you have 4.9-5.1 volts DC rather than an elevated reading.
Check for a chafed wire shorting the 5-volt supply to a higher-voltage circuit such as battery power, which would explain the voltage-above-normal condition.
Unplug sensors on that supply circuit one at a time while monitoring the reference voltage to isolate which sensor or harness leg is causing the fault.
Repair or replace the damaged harness section, reconnect all sensors, and confirm 5.0 volts is restored before clearing codes.
symptoms: Multiple unrelated sensor fault codes appearing together
MIL illuminated
Erratic readings on sensors sharing the affected supply circuit
Possible rough idle or throttle response issues depending on which sensors are affected

steps: Erratic Data Check
Disconnect the Accelerator Pedal (AP).
Turn the ignition ON.
Measure the voltage between pins 1 and 3 of the AP harness connector. See Figure
"Accelerator Pedal Assembly Installation".
Figure 1. Accelerator Pedal Assembly Installation
If the voltage is between 4.5 and 5.5 volts, go to step 5.
If the voltage is less than 4.5, go to step 4.
Measure the voltage between pins 1 of the AP harness connector and ground.
If the voltage is between 4.5 and 5.5 volts, repair the open circuit between pin 3 of the AP harness connector and pin 4 of the CPC #1 connector. Refer to "109.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the voltage is less than 4.5, repair the open circuit between pin 1 of the AP harness connector and pin 8 of the CPC #1 connector. Refer to "109.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the CPC #1 connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 2 of the AP harness connector and pin 7 of the CPC #1 connector.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, repair the open between pin 2 of the AP harness connector and pin 7 of the CPC #1 connector. Refer to "109.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the Accelerator Pedal. Refer to "109.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".

Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.

dd_procedures.title: Detroit Diesel SPN 4334 FMI 16 – SCR Conversion Efficiency Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 4334 FMI 16 – SCR Conversion Efficiency Low (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 4334 FMI 16 indicates that the SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction) system is not converting NOx emissions efficiently enough to meet required thresholds. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and is a moderate severity warning that can escalate to a derate if left unaddressed.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
SCR or DEF warning light illuminated 
Possible reduction in engine performance Increased 
NOx emissions Engine derate may follow if efficiency continues to drop
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM detects that the SCR catalyst is not reducing NOx at the required efficiency level. Common causes include:
Low quality or contaminated 
DEF fluid Faulty NOx sensor (upstream or downstream) 
Worn or damaged SCR catalyst 
DEF dosing system malfunction 
Exhaust leaks affecting sensor readings
Can You Keep Driving?
Short term driving is possible but this code typically escalates. If the SCR system efficiency continues to fall, the engine will enter a progressive derate. Address this promptly to avoid a more severe code or breakdown.
Recommended Action
Start by checking DEF fluid quality — contaminated or diluted DEF is a very common cause. If DEF quality is good, have the NOx sensors, DEF dosing system, and SCR catalyst inspected by a qualified diesel technician.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4334 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the SCR system is operating but not converting NOx emissions at the required efficiency level, triggering a moderate severity fault.
 
 
What causes SPN 4334 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are poor quality or contaminated DEF, a failing NOx sensor, a worn SCR catalyst, or a DEF dosing system fault.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4334 FMI 16?
 
Limited driving is possible but the code is likely to escalate to a more severe fault and derate if the underlying issue is not addressed.
 
 
Will SPN 4334 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes, if SCR efficiency continues to drop the ECM will trigger progressive derate conditions to reduce emissions output.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4334 FMI 16?
 
Inspect and replace DEF if quality is suspect, then have the NOx sensors and SCR system diagnosed. The code will clear once the system confirms acceptable conversion efficiency.

Yes. If not repaired, the engine control module may limit vehicle speed to comply with emissions regulations.

Inspect DEF quality, test NOx sensors, check for exhaust leaks, and perform SCR system diagnostics to determine the root cause.

Yes, if SCR efficiency continues to drop the ECM will trigger progressive derate conditions to reduce emissions output.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4334 FMI 16?
 
Inspect and replace DEF if quality is suspect, then have the NOx sensors and SCR system diagnosed. The code will clear once the system confirms acceptable conversion efficiency.

Detroit Diesel SPN 4334 FMI 18 indicates that the SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction) system conversion efficiency is below acceptable limits. This fault is commonly associated with emissions system performance issues.
Symptoms
Check engine light illuminated
Aftertreatment warning
DEF system alerts
Reduced engine power
Progressive derate countdown
Cause
This code is typically caused by failed NOx sensors, contaminated DEF fluid, clogged SCR catalyst, exhaust leaks, or improper DEF dosing.
Can You Keep Driving?

Recommended Action
Inspect DEF quality and dosing system operation. Check NOx sensors and perform SCR efficiency diagnostics. Replace faulty components as necessary.
What causes SPN 4334 FMI 18?
 
Common causes include failed NOx sensors, contaminated DEF, clogged SCR catalyst, improper DEF dosing, or exhaust leaks.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4334 FMI 18?
 
Driving may be possible temporarily, but unresolved SCR efficiency faults can trigger progressive engine derate.
 
 
Will SPN 4334 FMI 18 cause a speed restriction?
 
Yes. If not repaired, the engine control module may limit vehicle speed to comply with emissions regulations.
 
 
How do I fix SPN 4334 FMI 18?
 
Inspect DEF quality, test NOx sensors, check for exhaust leaks, and perform SCR system diagnostics to determine the root cause.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 18 is the data-valid-but-below-normal class. The DEF pressure sensor reports a valid but insufficient pressure during commanded pump operation. A weak pump, clogged suction filter, air intrusion in the suction line, leaking pressure line, and failed pressure sensor are the primary causes. Repeated low pressure after partial thaw events in cold climates is a documented fleet pattern. Validating the sensor against a known-good pressure source before major pump work is the critical first gate.
causes: Weak pump — pump performance degraded below minimum
Clogged suction filter — restriction reducing pump inlet flow
Air intrusion — suction line leak allowing air into pump
Leaking pressure line — pressure loss before dosing injector
Failed pressure sensor — reading low without true low pressure
Partial thaw damage — cold climate freeze-thaw cycle damage
steps: Single Action Gate — Visual Leak Inspection

Inspect all DEF lines and fittings for leaks. A leaking pressure line prevents pressure buildup regardless of pump condition. Inspect the dosing injector, pressure line fittings, and return line connections.
Binary Decision Gate — Suction Filter Inspection
Inspect the pump suction filter for restriction and contamination. A clogged suction filter is a common cause of low DEF pressure that is resolved by filter replacement without pump replacement.
Override Manager — Commanded Pressure Test
Command pump operation and observe pressure PID versus OEM minimum specification. Compare reported pressure to expected values at the commanded pump duty cycle.
Safety Interceptor — Pump Feed Voltage Drop Test
Measure voltage drop on the pump power feed under operation. A voltage drop greater than OEM specification reduces pump output and can cause low pressure without any pump failure.
Resume Point — Pressure Sensor Correlation
Evaluate pressure sensor correlation. If pressure PID reads low but system appears to be dosing correctly, the sensor may be biased low. Compare to dosing quantity data for plausibility.
Verification Loop — Post-Service Pressure Confirmation
After repair, command pump and verify pressure meets OEM minimum specification. Confirm dosing quantity returns to expected levels.
Repair Ledger Output — Pump Replacement Decision
Replace pump only after suction filter, line leaks, voltage drop, and sensor correlation are all proven not to be the cause.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace suction filter if restriction is found.
2 . Repair any DEF line leaks found.
3 . Repair pump power feed voltage drop if found.
4 . Replace pressure sensor if bias is confirmed.
5 . Replace pump module after supply-side proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm pressure meets OEM minimum specification after repair.
Verify dosing quantity returns to expected levels.
Confirm SPN 4334 FMI 18 does not return after repair.
Monitor SCR efficiency returns to normal after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Replace DEF suction filter per OEM service intervals.
✓ Inspect DEF lines for leaks at every major service.
✓ Inspect pump power feed connections for corrosion.
✓ Address partial thaw damage before returning to service in cold climates.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. Insufficient DEF pressure reduces dosing quantity and SCR efficiency. Address before inducement cascade begins. Supply-side diagnosis is faster and less expensive than pump replacement.
symptoms: DEF pressure low fault active
Weak DEF pump indication
Dosing pressure insufficient
SCR efficiency declining from low dosing
Inducement risk from dosing failure

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4334 FMI 31 warns that SCR catalyst NOx conversion efficiency has dropped, most often from bad DEF quality or a dosing problem, and will lead to a derate if not corrected. This code is your last warning before the SCR inducement system starts limiting engine performance. Because DEF quality is the most common cause and the cheapest fix, always rule that out before assuming the catalyst itself has failed.
causes: Diluted or contaminated DEF
Fluid that's out of spec reduces the SCR system's ability to convert NOx, even with a perfectly healthy catalyst.
DEF injector/doser clogging or poor spray pattern
Inconsistent dosing means the catalyst doesn't get the reagent volume it needs at the right time.
Degraded SCR catalyst (age or thermal damage)
Catalysts lose efficiency over very high mileage or after exposure to excessive exhaust temperatures.
NOx sensor drift or failure
A miscalibrated sensor can report false inefficiency even when the catalyst is working normally.
steps: Check DEF quality with a refractometer if available, or at minimum confirm the fluid was purchased from a sealed, reputable source - diluted or contaminated DEF is a leading cause.
Inspect the DEF tank for any signs of water intrusion or use of the wrong fluid (some drivers mistakenly add diesel or windshield washer fluid).
Check the DEF injector/doser for clogging or poor spray pattern, since inconsistent dosing reduces conversion efficiency.
Verify the NOx sensors upstream and downstream of the SCR catalyst are reading plausible, differing values - if they read identically, the catalyst may be failing.
Review recent fault history for DEF quality or dosing codes that may have preceded this efficiency warning.
symptoms: Amber warning lamp, often paired with a dash message about emissions system performance
No immediate performance loss, but a countdown to derate if uncorrected
Possible increase in DEF consumption as the system tries to compensate
May follow shortly after a DEF refill with contaminated or diluted fluid

dd_procedures.title: Detroit Diesel SPN 100 FMI 1 – Engine Oil Pressure Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 27 FMI 9 – EGR Valve Position Error (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 27 FMI 9 indicates that the EGR valve position is not matching the commanded position from the ECM. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and means the exhaust gas recirculation system is not responding correctly, which can affect emissions control, engine performance, and combustion efficiency.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
EGR or emissions warning light illuminated 
Rough idle or unstable engine operation 
Reduced engine performance Engine derate possible Increased 
NOx emissions 
Black smoke from exhaust possible
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM detects a discrepancy between the commanded EGR valve position and the actual position reported by the valve sensor. Common causes include:
Excessive carbon deposits in the EGR system
Carbon buildup on the EGR valve preventing proper movement
Stuck or seized EGR valve
Failed EGR valve position sensor
Damaged EGR valve actuator motor
Wiring or connector fault at the EGR valve
EGR cooler restriction affecting valve operation
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but an EGR valve position error affects combustion efficiency and emissions control. Engine performance will be impacted and a derate condition may follow if the fault persists. Address this promptly to avoid further carbon buildup or component damage.
Recommended Action
Inspect the EGR valve for carbon buildup and clean if necessary. Check the valve actuator and position sensor for proper operation. Inspect wiring and connectors at the EGR valve for damage or corrosion. If cleaning does not resolve the issue the EGR valve assembly may need to be replaced.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 27 FMI 9 mean?
 
It means the EGR valve is not moving to the position commanded by the ECM, indicating a mechanical, electrical, or carbon buildup issue with the valve or its control system.
 
 
What causes SPN 27 FMI 9?
 
The most common causes are carbon buildup preventing valve movement, a stuck or seized EGR valve, a failed position sensor, or a wiring fault at the valve connector.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 27 FMI 9?
 
Short distances may be possible but EGR valve position errors affect combustion and emissions control. A derate condition may follow if not addressed promptly.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 27 FMI 2 indicates EGR position feedback unstable or implausible. Failing position sensor, carbon-induced unstable movement, harness intermittents, and poor reference or ground are the primary causes. Carbon sticktion misread as pure sensor failure and both coexisting are documented patterns. Replacing the EGR assembly before proving feedback and movement is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Failing position sensor — failing EGR position sensor producing unstable feedback
Carbon-induced unstable movement — carbon binding producing unstable valve movement and feedback
Harness intermittents — harness intermittents producing unstable position signal
Poor reference or ground — poor reference voltage or ground producing unstable sensor readings
steps: Step 1 — Graph Desired vs Actual

Graph desired and actual EGR position. Desired and actual should track smoothly. Abrupt dropouts are electrical; slow sticking is mechanical carbon. Carbon sticktion misread as pure sensor failure is a documented pattern — both can coexist.
Step 2 — Command Sweep

Command a sweep of the EGR valve through its full range. A valve that does not respond to command confirms a mechanical or actuator fault. A valve that responds to command but produces erratic feedback confirms a sensor or circuit fault.
Step 3 — Electrical Reference and Ground Checks

Check the electrical reference voltage and ground at the actuator connector. Actuator connector heat damage and pin fretting are documented causes. Verify reference voltage stability and ground integrity.
Step 4 — Inspect Carbon Binding

Inspect for carbon binding. Carbon sticktion producing unstable valve movement is a documented cause. Inspect the EGR valve for carbon buildup. Clean the valve if carbon binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved per OEM procedure.
Step 5 — Repair Based on Evidence

Repair based on confirmed evidence. Clean or service the valve if carbon binding is confirmed. Repair the connector or harness if electrical fault is confirmed. Replace the valve or actuator assembly if wear or failure is confirmed ($400–$1,800).

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Clean or service EGR valve if carbon binding is confirmed.
2 . Repair connector or harness if electrical fault is confirmed.
3 . Replace valve or actuator assembly if wear or failure is confirmed ($400–$1,800).
Verification Steps
Confirm EGR position feedback is stable after repair.
Verify SPN 27 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Confirm EGR flow is correct after repair.
Monitor for return of erratic EGR position events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGR valve for carbon buildup at every major service.
✓ Inspect actuator connector for heat damage at every major service.
✓ Inspect EGR harness for intermittents at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. Erratic EGR position is feedback integrity plus possible carbon binding.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 27 FMI 3 means the EGR valve position sensor circuit is electrically shorted high, most often from heat-damaged wiring near the exhaust manifold. The EGR valve's proximity to exhaust heat makes wiring damage the leading cause here, well ahead of an actual failed sensor or valve.
causes: Heat-damaged wiring near the EGR valve or cooler
Sustained exhaust heat degrades insulation faster in this area than almost anywhere else on the engine.
Corroded connector from underhood washing
Water intrusion can bridge pins and mimic an internal short.
Failed sensor internally shorted
Less common than wiring damage but possible on higher-mileage units.
steps: Locate the EGR valve position sensor, typically integrated into the EGR valve assembly on top of or near the intake manifold.
Backprobe the signal wire with key on, engine off - a voltage pegged near sensor supply voltage confirms the short-high condition.
Inspect the harness for heat damage near the exhaust manifold or EGR cooler, a common chafe and heat-degradation point.
Check the connector for corrosion, especially if the truck has seen recent underhood pressure washing.
Replace the EGR valve assembly only after confirming the wiring is clean, since some designs integrate the sensor into a non-serviceable valve unit.
symptoms: Possible rough idle or slightly reduced performance since the ECM can't verify EGR valve position
Amber check-engine lamp
Occasional increase in NOx-related aftertreatment activity if EGR flow can't be properly controlled
No dramatic power loss in most cases
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 27 FMI 3: EGR Valve Position Sensor Shorted High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 27 FMI 3 on a PACCAR MX-13 engine means the EGR valve position sensor signal is above 4.75 V — indicating a short to Vref or open sensor ground. Isolate the circuit with PACCAR Davie4 before ordering the EGR assembly. When a PACCAR MX-13 or MX-11 engine logs SPN 27 FMI 3, the ECM has detected an EGR valve position feedback voltage above the normal 4.5 V ceiling, which cannot represent any real valve position and points to a circuit fault. The EGR position sensor is a potentiometer integrated into the EGR valve actuator, ranging from 0.5 V (fully closed) to 4.5 V (fully open). At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com, FMI 3 on this sensor splits roughly 50/50 between a harness short near the EGR cooler (where heat cycling cracks the insulation) and an internal failure of the EGR actuator position sensor. The PACCAR Davie4 bi-directional EGR sweep test is the fastest way to confirm whether the fault follows the actuator or the harness.
causes: Internal failure of the EGR actuator position sensor (shorted to supply)
The potentiometer wiper or resistor track inside the EGR actuator fails by shorting to the 5 V supply rail, producing a fixed high-voltage output regardless of valve position.
Short from signal wire to the 5 V reference wire in the EGR harness
Heat cycling near the EGR cooler cracks the signal wire insulation, allowing it to contact the adjacent 5 V reference wire in the wiring loom and forcing the ECM input above 4.75 V.
Open EGR position sensor ground wire
A broken or corroded ground wire causes the sensor output to float toward the 5 V supply rail through the ECM input pull-up resistance, mimicking a short-to-Vref fault.
Corroded or spread connector pins in the EGR valve connector
Moisture and exhaust heat corrode the multi-pin EGR valve connector, sometimes bridging the signal pin to the reference supply pin and producing a fixed high-voltage fault.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 to the truck diagnostic port (Kenworth T680, T880, or Peterbilt 579, 567). Navigate to engine live data and select the EGR valve position parameter. A reading above 100 percent position or a raw voltage above 4.75 V with the engine at idle confirms FMI 3 is active. Diesel Laptops with a NEXIQ USB-Link 2 adapter can also read the EGR position parameter for a cross-check.

With the key on and engine off, locate the EGR valve assembly on the MX-13 engine (left-side intake manifold area). Back-probe the position sensor signal wire at the EGR valve connector. The EGR valve 3-pin or 5-pin connector provides a 5 V reference, signal output, and ground — verify pin assignment using the PACCAR service manual or ProfessionalDieselRepair.com wiring diagrams. If the signal reads above 4.75 V, the circuit is shorted high.

Use PACCAR Davie4 bi-directional controls to command the EGR valve sweep from 0 to 100 percent while monitoring the position feedback. If the feedback voltage stays fixed above 4.75 V throughout the sweep regardless of commanded position, the sensor is failed or the circuit has a permanent short.

Disconnect the EGR valve connector. Measure the signal pin at the harness side to the sensor ground pin. If voltage remains above 0.5 V with the connector unplugged, the harness has a short from the signal wire to the 5 V reference circuit. Inspect the loom near the EGR cooler where heat cycling causes insulation brittleness.

If voltage drops to zero with the connector unplugged, the EGR actuator assembly has an internal sensor short. On PACCAR MX-13, the position sensor is integrated into the EGR valve actuator assembly and is not sold separately — replace the EGR valve assembly. Torque the mounting flange bolts to 25 Nm and clear the fault with PACCAR Davie4.
symptoms: EGR valve position reads above 100 percent or shows an implausibly high voltage in PACCAR Davie4 live data.
Engine derate or rough running as the ECM enters a default EGR position due to invalid feedback.
Increased NOx emissions may occur if the EGR valve defaults to a closed position due to invalid position data.
Amber check engine lamp illuminated with possible torque limitation on Kenworth and Peterbilt models.
PACCAR Davie4 displays SPN 27 FMI 3 as active with an EGR position circuit fault.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 4 indicates the EGR position sensor signal is below the expected voltage range. On electronic EGR position-equipped engines, the position sensor is typically a 5V ratiometric device. A signal pinned near 0V with the 5V reference present indicates a signal short to ground or a failed sensor. An open 5V reference causes the signal to collapse regardless of sensor condition. Harness damage after EGR cooler service is a documented cause — the harness runs near hot-side plumbing and bracket edges where chafe damage is common.
causes: Signal short to ground — wire damage or connector corrosion
Failed position sensor — internal short or open
Open 5V reference — supply circuit fault
Damaged connector — heat damage, oil contamination, or weak pin tension
Harness chafe — rubbed-through insulation near bracket edges and heat shields
steps: Single Action Gate — 5V Reference Verification

Measure 5V reference at the EGR position sensor connector. If 5V reference is absent, the signal will be low regardless of sensor condition. Trace the 5V reference circuit back to the ECM before condemning the sensor.
Binary Decision Gate — Signal and Ground Check

With 5V reference confirmed present, measure signal voltage. A signal pinned near 0V with valid reference indicates signal short to ground or failed sensor. Measure ground integrity at the sensor connector.
Override Manager — Sensor Disconnect Test

Disconnect the sensor and re-evaluate the circuit. If signal rises toward reference voltage with sensor disconnected, the sensor has an internal short. If signal remains low with sensor disconnected, the fault is in the harness or ECM.
Safety Interceptor — Harness Inspection

Inspect harness for chafe near bracket edges, heat shields, and EGR plumbing. Harness damage after EGR cooler service is a documented cause. Look for rubbed-through insulation at clamp edges and hot-side plumbing contact points.
Resume Point — Continuity and Short Tests
Perform continuity test on signal wire from sensor connector to ECM connector. Perform short-to-ground test on signal wire. Document findings before any component replacement.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Signal Confirmation
After repair, verify 5V reference, ground, and signal are all within OEM specification at the sensor connector. Confirm position feedback tracks commanded EGR position.
Repair Ledger Output — Sensor or Harness Decision
Replace position sensor only after circuit is proven good and sensor disconnect test confirms internal failure. Repair harness if chafe or short is found in the wiring.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair any harness chafe or short-to-ground found.
2 . Repair 5V reference circuit if open is found.
3 . Replace position sensor if internal short is confirmed by disconnect test.
4 . Replace full EGR valve assembly only if position sensor is integral and cannot be replaced separately.
5 . Seal harness routing against future heat damage near EGR plumbing.
Verification Steps
Confirm 5V reference, ground, and signal are within spec after repair.
Verify EGR position feedback tracks commanded position.
Confirm SPN 27 FMI 4 does not return after repair.
Monitor EGR flow faults do not follow from position feedback loss.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect EGR harness routing after any EGR cooler or valve service.
✓ Secure harness away from bracket edges and heat shields.
✓ Inspect sensor connector for heat damage at every major EGR service.
✓ Address EGR cooler leaks promptly to prevent oil contamination of connectors.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. EGR control is degraded from position feedback loss. Address before extended operation. Circuit diagnosis takes less time than assembly replacement and resolves most cases.
symptoms: EGR position sensor low voltage fault active
EGR electrical fault
EGR signal short indication
EGR not responding from position feedback loss
Derate from EGR control loss

procedures_full.overview: SPN 27 FMI 7 on Cummins means the EGR valve is not responding to the ECM's commands. Remove and inspect for carbon seizure before ordering a new valve — cleaning fixes the majority of these faults. FMI 7 is the EGR valve telling you it received the command but cannot follow through. On Cummins ISX, ISB, and ISL engines, that almost always translates to a pintle buried in carbon deposits. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com has cleaned more FMI 7 valves than it has replaced — pull it, clean it, and prove it before you spend $500 on a new assembly.
causes: Heavy carbon buildup preventing valve movement (mechanical)
Very Common
EGR recirculates hot, soot-laden gas which deposits carbon on the valve bore and pintle over time. Thick deposits physically prevent the actuator from moving the valve to the commanded position.
Failed EGR valve actuator motor (mechanical/electrical)
The electric actuator motor that drives the valve shaft can fail internally, losing torque output. The motor may test open or draw abnormal current.
EGR cooler failure causing increased deposit rate (mechanical)
A leaking EGR cooler deposits scale and steam residue on the valve, dramatically accelerating carbon accumulation and shortening valve life.
Damaged valve actuator position sensor (electrical)
Less Common
If the position feedback sensor inside the actuator is faulty, the ECM receives incorrect position data and cannot close the control loop, triggering FMI 7.
steps: 1. Connect Cummins INSITE or Snap-on NEXIQ and command the EGR valve through a relative actuator test — monitor commanded vs actual position in live data to confirm the mismatch.
2. Inspect the EGR valve and cooler for heavy carbon buildup — on ISB, ISL, and ISX engines, carbon-loaded valves are the leading cause of FMI 7 because the deposits physically prevent movement.
3. With the valve removed, test the actuator motor resistance and check for free mechanical movement through the full stroke by hand. A valve that is seized by carbon will resist or stick midrange.

4. Check the EGR actuator harness connector for moisture, spread terminals, and continuity through the control circuit — a high-resistance connection can prevent the actuator from producing enough torque to overcome moderate carbon buildup.
5. Inspect the EGR cooler for external leaks or coolant weeping — a failed EGR cooler can deposit steam and scale on the valve, accelerating seizure.
6. If cleaning and reinstalling the valve does not resolve the fault, test actuator motor current draw under commanded movement; a motor drawing outside normal range indicates an internal fault.
symptoms: High exhaust temperatures under load
Black smoke at part throttle as EGR flow is disrupted
Rough running or stumble if the valve is stuck partially open
MIL illuminated with possible torque derate
Failed emissions testing due to NOx rise with EGR inoperative
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 27 FMI 7: EGR Valve Mechanical System Not Responding

procedures_full.overview: SPN 27 FMI 7 on International engines means the EGR valve isn't mechanically reaching the position the ECM commands. It's a medium-severity fault most commonly caused by carbon buildup binding the valve rather than an electrical failure. FMI 7 faults are different from a typical sensor circuit code - they mean the ECM commanded a mechanical action and didn't get the expected physical response. For SPN 27, that means the EGR valve itself isn't moving the way it should, and ProfessionalDieselRepair.com finds carbon buildup is the culprit far more often than a truly failed valve assembly. A thorough cleaning resolves this fault in the majority of cases without needing a full replacement.
causes: Carbon buildup binding the valve pintle or body
EGR valves accumulate carbon deposits over time from recirculated exhaust gas, especially on trucks with significant idle time, eventually restricting or preventing full valve travel.
Corroded or seized linkage/actuator mechanism
Beyond carbon buildup, mechanical corrosion in the actuator linkage itself can prevent the valve from responding to commands even after cleaning.
Failed valve actuator motor
The electric motor or solenoid that physically moves the valve can fail internally, producing a genuine mechanical non-response independent of carbon fouling.
Damaged position sensor giving inaccurate feedback
If the position sensor itself is inaccurate, the ECM may believe the valve isn't reaching commanded position even if it actually is, though this is less common than a genuine mechanical issue.
steps: Pull the fault with Diesel Laptops or Jaltest and confirm SPN 27 FMI 7 is active; use the scan tool's EGR valve command test to sweep the valve through its full range and watch for a sluggish or incomplete response.
Remove the EGR valve and visually inspect the valve body and pintle for carbon buildup that could be preventing full travel.
Clean the valve thoroughly using an appropriate carbon-safe solvent, being careful not to damage the pintle seat or position sensor during cleaning.
Inspect the valve's linkage or actuator mechanism for binding, corrosion, or physical damage beyond just carbon buildup.
Reinstall the valve with a new gasket and verify it seats properly, then run the actuator sweep test again to confirm smooth, full-range movement.
Clear the code and monitor EGR position tracking during a drive cycle to confirm the fault doesn't return before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Amber dash lamp, sometimes with a specific EGR-related message
Rough idle or slight hesitation if the valve is stuck significantly out of position
Possible increase in NOx-related aftertreatment activity as the ECM compensates
No dramatic power loss in most cases since EGR faults are primarily emissions-related

procedures_full.overview: FMI 2 on the kickdown or secondary pedal switch indicates the switch data is erratic or inconsistently matches expected values. Failed switch, harness intermittents, water intrusion, and pedal assembly wear are the primary causes. Moisture in pedal connectors on open cab environments is a documented pattern. Some MD/HD and vocational platforms use kickdown or discrete pedal switches with electronic APP — the switch should change state cleanly through pedal travel. Shift quality complaints and power request behavior changes from erratic kickdown data are often misdiagnosed as transmission internal faults when the pedal switch is the root cause.
causes: Failed switch — switch not changing state cleanly through pedal travel
Harness intermittents — intermittent connection at pedal connector or firewall transition
Water intrusion — moisture in pedal connector on open cab environment
Pedal assembly wear — worn switch mechanism in pedal assembly
Firewall transition damage — harness damage at firewall pass-through
steps: Single Action Gate — Monitor Switch PID Through Pedal Travel

Monitor the kickdown switch PID while pressing the pedal through its full travel. The switch should change state cleanly at the kickdown point. An erratic or intermittent state change confirms switch or circuit fault. A switch that never changes state confirms an open or failed switch.
Binary Decision Gate — Wiggle Test at Pedal Connector

Perform a harness wiggle test at the pedal connector while monitoring the switch PID. Moisture in pedal connectors on open cab environments is a documented cause of intermittent switch faults. A PID change during wiggle confirms a connector or harness intermittent.
Override Manager — Continuity Checks
Perform continuity tests on the kickdown switch circuit. Inspect the firewall transition for harness damage. Confirm switch circuit continuity from the pedal connector to the ECM connector.
Safety Interceptor — APP Signal Correlation

Correlate the kickdown switch state with the APP position signal. The kickdown switch should change state at a specific APP percentage. A kickdown switch that changes state at an implausible APP position confirms switch or pedal assembly wear.
Resume Point — Pedal Assembly Replacement Assessment

If switch failure is confirmed by PID monitoring and continuity checks, assess whether the switch can be replaced separately or requires pedal assembly replacement. Some platforms allow switch-only replacement; others require the pedal assembly.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Switch State Confirmation

After repair, verify the kickdown switch changes state cleanly through pedal travel. Confirm shift quality and power request behavior return to normal. Monitor for return of FMI 2 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Switch, Harness, or Pedal Assembly Decision

Replace switch or pedal assembly after circuit proof confirms switch failure. Repair harness if intermittent is found at connector or firewall transition. Address moisture intrusion source if water is found in pedal connector.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace switch or pedal assembly after circuit proof confirms switch failure.
2 . Repair harness intermittent at pedal connector or firewall transition.
3 . Address moisture intrusion source in pedal connector.
4 . Repair harness damage at firewall pass-through.
Verification Steps
Confirm kickdown switch changes state cleanly through pedal travel after repair.
Verify shift quality and power request behavior return to normal after repair.
Confirm SPN 558 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of transmission kickdown complaints over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect pedal connector for moisture intrusion at every major service on open cab environments.
✓ Inspect firewall harness transition for damage at every major service.
✓ Verify kickdown switch state change through pedal travel at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. Can affect shift quality and power request behavior. Pedal switch verification takes minutes and prevents unnecessary transmission diagnosis.

causes: This fault is a typically incorrect wiring of the Idle Validation Switch (IVS).‪
steps: Check Idle Validation Switch Wiring
Connect the diagnostic tool
Turn ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Monitor IVS #1 and IVS #2 with the throttle pedal in the idle position.
If IVS #1 reads OFF and IVS #2 reads ON, verify the proper wire pin outs.
IVS #1 should be routed from Idle Validation Switch pin 5 to pin 6 of the CPC #1 connector.
IVS #2 should be routed from Validation Switch pin 6 to pin 3 of the CPC #1 connector.
If wiring checks OK, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center (313–592–5800).

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1347 FMI 5 is a fuel pump or fuel delivery control circuit open or low-current class fault depending on OEM mapping. Open control wire, failed relay coil, blown fuse, unplugged pump connector, and failed pump motor open are the primary causes. No-start after pump connector left unplugged and intermittent open at relay bases are documented patterns. Replacing the supply pump before verifying command voltage and power feed is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Open control wire — open control wire producing no command path to pump
Failed relay coil — failed relay coil producing no pump command
Blown fuse — blown fuse producing no power to pump circuit
Unplugged pump connector — unplugged pump connector producing open circuit
Failed pump motor open — failed pump motor internal open producing open circuit
steps: Step 1 — Verify Command Present

Verify command voltage is present during key-on, prime, and run events. No-start after pump connector left unplugged is a documented pattern — always inspect the pump connector and circuit after any recent filter service. Confirm the ECM is commanding the pump.
Step 2 — Check Fuse and Relay Feed

Check the fuse and relay feed. Inspect the pump connector, relay base, fuse and junction power feeds, and ground studs. A blown fuse or failed relay coil producing no pump command requires fuse or relay replacement.
Step 3 — Voltage at Pump Under Command

Measure voltage at the pump under command. Confirm command voltage is present at the pump connector during key-on prime. A voltage fault at the pump under command confirms a power feed or relay fault.
Step 4 — Ground Integrity
Verify ground integrity at the pump circuit. A ground fault producing no pump operation requires ground circuit repair. Measure voltage drop on the pump ground circuit.
Step 5 — Pump Replace Only If Power and Ground Are Good
Replace the pump only if power and ground are confirmed good. A pump replaced without power and ground proof may replace a good pump into a circuit fault that will fail the new pump.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace relay or fuse if relay or fuse fault is confirmed.
2 . Repair harness if open circuit is confirmed.
3 . Replace supply pump if power and ground are confirmed good and pump fails ($150–$600+ typical).
Verification Steps
Confirm fuel pump operates correctly after repair.
Verify SPN 1347 FMI 5 does not return after repair.
Confirm no-start or fuel starvation condition is resolved after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect pump connector after any filter service.
✓ Inspect relay base for intermittent contact at every major service.
✓ Inspect fuse and junction power feeds at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High if no-start or fuel starvation under load Severity
High if no-start or fuel starvation under load. Fuel delivery control open is an electrical command-path diagnosis first.

Lift pump not running
Fuel delivery control open
No-start fuel pump electrical

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1347 FMI 6 is a fuel delivery control circuit current above normal or short class fault. Shorted pump motor, harness short to ground or power, water-intruded connectors, and pinched loom are the primary causes. Repeat fuse failures after pump-only replacement when the harness short remains is a documented pattern. Replacing the pump without isolating the short source is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Shorted pump motor — shorted pump motor producing above-normal current
Harness short to ground or power — harness short producing above-normal current
Water-intruded connectors — water intrusion producing short circuit
Pinched loom — loom pinched at frame-rail or battery-box transition producing short circuit
steps: Step 1 — Remove Pump Load

Remove the pump load from the circuit. Disconnect the pump and check if the high-current fault clears. A fault that clears with the pump disconnected confirms a pump fault. A fault that remains with the pump disconnected confirms a harness fault.
Step 2 — Check Harness Shorts

Check the harness for shorts. Inspect frame-rail chafe, battery-box transitions, and pump connector moisture. A harness short to ground or power producing above-normal current requires harness repair. Water intrusion producing a short circuit requires connector service.
Step 3 — Measure Pump Resistance and Current
Measure pump resistance and current draw. Low resistance on the pump circuit supports a shorted pump motor. Current draw above OEM limits supports a failed pump. Compare to OEM specification.
Step 4 — Repair Circuit Before New Pump If Needed

Repair the circuit before installing a new pump if a harness fault is confirmed. A new pump installed into a harness short will fail the new pump and may blow the fuse again. Confirm the harness is clean before any pump replacement.
Step 5 — Replace Pump After Circuit Proof
Replace the pump after circuit proof. Confirm the harness is clean and the short is resolved before pump replacement. Replace relay and fuse as collateral damage if they were damaged by the short.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness if short is confirmed in the harness.
2 . Service connector if water intrusion is confirmed.
3 . Replace pump if pump fault is confirmed after circuit proof.
4 . Replace relay and fuse as collateral damage if damaged.
Verification Steps
Confirm fuel pump operates correctly after repair.
Verify SPN 1347 FMI 6 does not return after repair.
Confirm fuse does not blow after repair.
Confirm no-start or fuel starvation condition is resolved after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect pump harness for chafe at frame-rail and battery-box transitions at every major service.
✓ Inspect pump connector for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect loom routing after any major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High operational impact if fuel delivery is lost Severity
High operational impact if fuel delivery is lost. High-current fuel control codes need short isolation before another pump is installed.
symptoms: Fuel pump circuit shorted
Lift pump high current
Fuel control short
Fuse blows fuel pump circuit
Intermittent no-start from pump circuit fault

When the commanded duty cycle (PWM) produces a current reading below 0.5 A for 2 consecutive seconds, the
Heater Element Open: Open circuit in the heater coil caused by thermal cycling or manufacturing defect, verified by resistance check
Driver Circuit Failure: Internal short or open in the ECM's low-side driver for heater 2, requiring ECM replacement or repair

steps: Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor Check
Disconnect the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor.
Inspect the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor connectors for bent, damaged or corroded pins.
If damaged pins are found, repair as necessary. Refer to "84.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no damage is found, replace the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor. Refer to "84.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: This code is typically sensor or circuit failed high.‪
causes: This code is typically sensor or circuit failed high.‪
steps: Open Circuit Check
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Check for multiple codes.
If 1172/3, 3250/3, 3242/3 and 3246/3 are present, go to step 3.
If only 1172/3 is present, go to step 5
Disconnect the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor (TCI Sensor).
Measure the voltage between pin 1 of the TCI Sensor and ground.

If the voltage is greater than 2.75 volts, repair the short to power between pin 88 of the 120–pin MCM connector and the TCI Sensor, DOC Inlet Temperature Sensor, DOC Outlet Temperature Sensor and the DPF Outlet Temperature Sensor. Refer to "84.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If no voltage is present on pin 1 of the Intake Air Temperature Sensor, repair the open between pin 88 of the 120–pin MCM connector and the TCI Sensor, DOC Inlet Temperature Sensor, DOC Outlet Temperature Sensor and the DPF Outlet Temperature Sensor. Refer to "84.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor.
Measure the voltage between pin 1 and pin 2 of the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor.
If the voltage is less than 2.75 volts, go to step 7.
If the voltage is greater than 2.75 volts, replace the sensor. Refer to "84.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the voltage between pin 2 of the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor and ground.
If the voltage is less than 2.75 volts, repair the open between pin 2 of the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor and pin 86 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "84.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the voltage is greater than 2.75 volts, repair the open between pin 1 of the Turbo Compressor Inlet Temperature Sensor and pin 86 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "84.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

SPN_5394.pgn_rate: To engine or positive torque producing devices: Control Purpose dependent or 10 ms To retarder or negative torque producing devices: 50 ms
SPN_5394.pgn_description: NOTE - Retarder can be disabled by commanding a torque limit of 0%. Use of the limit mode allows the use of the retarder only up to the limit specified in the request. This can be used to permit retarding of up to 50%, for example, if that limit is required by some device such as an EBS, or it can disable the use of the retarder by others, as when an ABS controller detects wheel slip. Note that the 10 ms transmission repetition rate is intended for temporary powertrain control (P32 of SPN 3350).

procedures_full.overview: SPN 5394 FMI 3 means the DEF tank heater circuit is electrically shorted high, mainly affecting cold-weather DEF thaw performance. A low-priority code most of the year but worth fixing proactively before the first hard freeze.
causes: Chafed harness near the tank bracket
Frame flex wears insulation thin at consistent contact points.
Corroded low-mounted connector
Road spray and salt exposure corrode connector pins over time.
Stuck heater driver circuit
A stuck relay or module output can mimic this fault.
steps: Locate the DEF tank heater connector at the tank base.
Backprobe the circuit with key on, engine off - a voltage pegged high with heater off confirms a short.
Inspect harness routing near the tank bracket for chafing.
Check the connector for corrosion from road spray.
Verify the heater driver circuit isn't stuck providing constant voltage.
symptoms: No noticeable effect in warm weather
Slower DEF thaw in cold weather
Amber check-engine lamp
May cluster with other DEF system codes
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 5394 FMI 3: DEF Tank Heater Circuit Shorted High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 5394 FMI 3 means the DEF tank heater circuit is electrically shorted high, which won't affect summer driving but can slow DEF thawing in cold weather if left unrepaired. This is a low-urgency code most of the year, but it's exactly the kind of fault that should be fixed proactively before winter rather than after a driver reports a frozen-DEF startup delay.
causes: Chafed harness near the tank mounting bracket
Frame-mounted tanks flex the harness with chassis movement, wearing insulation over time.
Corroded low-mounted connector
The DEF tank sits low and is exposed to road spray and salt, which corrodes connector pins.
Stuck heater relay or driver circuit
A relay or control module output stuck on can produce a similar constant-high voltage reading.
steps: Locate the DEF tank heater connector, typically at the base of the tank or integrated with the tank sending unit.
Backprobe the heater circuit with key on, engine off - a voltage pegged high with the heater not commanded on confirms a short.
Inspect the harness for chafing near the tank mounting bracket or frame rail where it could contact a higher-voltage circuit.
Check the connector for corrosion or bridged pins from road spray, since the DEF tank sits low on the frame.
Verify the heater relay or driver circuit at the ECM/body control module isn't stuck providing constant voltage.
symptoms: No noticeable performance impact in warm weather
In cold weather, DEF may take longer than normal to thaw, delaying full engine power availability at startup
Amber check-engine lamp
Possible DEF-related fault cluster if the tank freezes solid without heater function
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 5394 FMI 3: DEF Tank Heater Circuit Shorted High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 5394 FMI 4 means the DEF tank heater circuit is shorted to ground, mainly affecting cold-weather DEF thaw times if left unrepaired. This is a low-urgency, seasonal code. Address it in the shoulder seasons rather than waiting for the first hard freeze to expose the problem.
causes: Chafed harness near the tank bracket
Frame-mounted tank harnesses flex with chassis movement, wearing insulation thin.
Corroded or moisture-intruded connector
The low-mounted connector is exposed to road spray and salt.
Internally shorted heater element
Less common than wiring but does occur with age.
steps: Locate the DEF tank heater connector at the base of the tank or integrated sending unit.
Backprobe the heater circuit with key on, engine off - a voltage pegged near zero with the heater commanded on confirms a short to ground.
Inspect the harness for chafing near the tank mounting bracket or frame rail.
Check the connector for corrosion or moisture intrusion that could bridge the circuit to ground.
Verify the heater element itself isn't internally shorted by testing resistance once disconnected from the harness.
symptoms: No noticeable effect in warm weather
Slower DEF thaw times in cold weather, delaying full power availability at startup
Amber check-engine lamp
May appear alongside other cold-weather DEF system codes

procedures_full.overview: The DEF dosing (metering) valve isn't responding mechanically to ECM commands. DEF can't be metered correctly, SCR efficiency drops, and a derate follows. Crystallization or a clogged/failed dosing valve is the usual culprit.
procedures_full.severity_action: Power derate likely — plan to stop soon
causes: DEF crystallization clogging the dosing valve/injector
Failed dosing valve (electrical or mechanical)
Low DEF supply pressure or air in the line
Wiring/connector fault to the dosing valve
first_moves: Look for white DEF crystals around the dosing valve, line, and decomposition tube.
Check DEF supply pressure and confirm the supply module is building pressure.
Inspect the dosing-valve connector and wiring for faults.
Check for companion dosing/quality codes (SPN 3361 / 4094) to confirm the picture.
common_misdiagnoses: Replacing the whole SCR/DEF module when the dosing valve just needed cleaning/replacement.
Blaming DEF quality when the supply pump can't build pressure.
Letting crystallization return because the root leak/clog wasn't fixed.

SPN_188.pgn_description: This map describes the stationary behavior of the engine and the speed dependent available indicated torque. This map should reflect the effect of changes due to barometric pressure, engine temperature, and any other stationary changes (sensor failures, etc.) which influence the engine torque curve more than 10%. This map is only valid for maximum boost pressure. At low boost pressures the torque limit may be much lower. The map is the sum of the net torque map and the static friction torque map

procedures_full.overview: The Hybrid Control Module (HCM) controls engine torque and speed for transmission shifting by communicating with the engine Electronic Control Unit (ECU) over the J1939 Data Link.
procedures_full.detection: Fault is detected when: HCM ignition voltage is greater than 7 volts and less than 16 volts. J1939 Communication Link Fault (HCM) not Active. J1939 Engine Message Fault (HCM) not Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The following conditions may set the fault Active: FMI 7 is set when the HCM-commanded engine torque is less than 80% max engine torque. HCM-commanded engine torque is greater than 100 lb-ft, and the difference between commanded engine torque and engine torque feedback is greater than 80 lb-ft for more than 1 second. Engine speed or torque maps are received with an error.
procedures_full.fallback: When Fault Code 70 is set the following conditions occur: Amber “Check Hybrid” light illuminates. Fault is stored in HCM memory. If the fault is set while driving, the vehicle may experience shifting problems.

field_evidence.title: Freightliner Cascadia 2015 Won't Crank: SPN 677 FMI 4 Diagnosis
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2015 Freightliner Cascadia can experience intermittent no-crank issues, often linked to starter relay or ignition switch failures. When this truck won't crank and displays the SPN 677 FMI 4 fault code, it signals a problem in the starter circuit. SPN 677 FMI 4 specifically points to a fault within the starter circuit. Even if the starter motor and general switches have been replaced, the problem can still persist due to wiring harness issues such as corrosion or loose connections. These electrical faults can interrupt the starter solenoid circuit, leading to intermittent cranking failures. To address this issue, it is important to inspect the wiring harnesses for any signs of corrosion or looseness. Checking the starter relay and verifying ground points under the hood is also recommend

SPN_677.pgn_description: NOTE - Retarder can be disabled by commanding a torque limit of 0%. Use of the limit mode allows the use of the retarder only up to the limit specified in the request. This can be used to permit retarding of up to 50%, for example, if that limit is required by some device such as an EBS, or it can disable the use of the retarder by others, as when an ABS controller detects wheel slip. Note that the 10 ms transmission repetition rate is intended for temporary powertrain control (P32 of SPN 3350).

procedures_full.overview: SPN 677 FMI 3 indicates starter relay control circuit voltage above the valid maximum — typically an open or high-signal class on the control side. Open control wire, failed relay coil open, unplugged relay, blown control fuse, and poor ignition feed to the control side are the primary causes. No-crank after body or alarm installs that open the starter control circuit is a documented pattern. Replacing the starter motor before proving the control path is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Open control wire — open control wire producing high-voltage reading on control side
Failed relay coil open — failed relay coil open producing high-voltage reading
Unplugged relay — unplugged relay producing open circuit
Blown control fuse — blown control fuse producing open circuit
Poor ignition feed — poor ignition feed to control side producing open circuit
steps: Step 1 — Confirm Start Request and Interlocks

Confirm a start request is present and all interlocks are satisfied. Verify interlock status PIDs before condemning the relay. No-crank after body or alarm installs that open the starter control circuit is a documented pattern — always inspect for aftermarket starter interrupt devices.
Step 2 — Check Control Power at Relay

Check control power at the relay. Verify ignition feed voltage is present at the relay base control terminal. A blown control fuse or poor ignition feed to the control side produces an open circuit. Inspect the relay base terminals and control-side wiring.
Step 3 — Continuity on Control Wire

Check continuity on the control wire. Verify continuity through the control wire from the ECM or ignition feed to the relay base. An open control wire producing a high-voltage reading confirms a harness fault.
Step 4 — Relay Coil Test

Test the relay coil. Measure coil resistance versus OEM specification. A failed relay coil open producing a high-voltage reading confirms a relay fault. Replace the relay if coil resistance is out of specification.
Step 5 — Starter Power-Side Tests Only After Control Path Is Proven

Perform starter power-side tests only after the control path is proven. Confirm interlock, control power, control wire continuity, and relay coil integrity before any starter power-side assessment. A starter replaced before proving the control path will not resolve a control circuit fault.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Remove faulty aftermarket starter interrupt if confirmed.
2 . Replace blown control fuse if confirmed.
3 . Repair open control wire if confirmed.
4 . Replace relay if coil failure is confirmed ($20–$80).
5 . Repair ignition feed if poor feed is confirmed.
Verification Steps
Confirm starter relay engages correctly after repair.
Verify SPN 677 FMI 3 does not return after repair.
Confirm no-crank condition is resolved after repair.
Monitor for return of starter relay circuit faults over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect relay base terminals and control-side wiring after any body or alarm install.
✓ Inspect control fuses at every major service.
✓ Verify interlock status PIDs after any transmission or clutch service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High operational impact — no-crank. Not an overheat code by itself. Severity
High operational impact. No-crank. Not an overheat code by itself. Starter relay high-voltage codes are control-circuit open diagnostics first.
symptoms: Starter relay high voltage
Starter control open
No crank relay circuit
ECM starter enable fault
No-crank after body or alarm install

procedures_full.overview: SPN 677 FMI 4 indicates starter relay control circuit voltage below the minimum — typically a shorted or low class. Control wire short to ground, failed relay coil short, water-intruded relay centers, and crushed harness are the primary causes. Repeat relay failures when the harness short is never isolated is a documented pattern. Installing a new relay into an unrepaired short is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Control wire short to ground — control wire shorted to ground producing low-voltage reading
Failed relay coil short — failed relay coil shorted producing low-voltage reading
Water-intruded relay centers — water intrusion producing short circuit in relay center
Crushed harness — harness crushed at cab-mount pinch points producing short to ground
steps: Step 1 — Remove Relay and Measure Coil
Remove the relay and measure coil resistance. Coil resistance below OEM minimum supports a failed relay coil short. Confirm coil resistance versus OEM specification before any further diagnosis.
Step 2 — Short-Check Control Wire

Short-check the control wire with the relay removed. A short that remains with the relay removed confirms a harness fault. Inspect cab-mount pinch points, battery-box looms, and wet relay panels for harness damage.
Step 3 — Inspect Panel Heat Damage

Inspect the relay panel for heat damage. Water-intruded relay centers and crushed harness producing short to ground are documented causes. Inspect the relay base and surrounding panel for heat damage, water intrusion, and corrosion.
Step 4 — Repair Circuit Before Installing New Relay

Repair the circuit before installing a new relay. Repeat relay failures when the harness short is never isolated is a documented pattern. Confirm the control wire short is repaired and the relay panel is clean before installing a new relay.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness if control wire short is confirmed.
2 . Service relay panel if water intrusion or heat damage is confirmed.
3 . Replace relay after circuit repair is confirmed ($20–$80).
4 . Weather-seal relay center if water intrusion is confirmed.
Verification Steps
Confirm starter relay engages correctly after repair.
Verify SPN 677 FMI 4 does not return after repair.
Confirm no repeat relay failures after repair.
Monitor for return of starter relay circuit faults over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect relay panel for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect harness at cab-mount pinch points at every major service.
✓ Weather-seal relay centers in wet environments.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High safety concern if starter engagement behavior is abnormal. Diagnose before repeated start attempts. Severity
High safety concern if starter engagement behavior is abnormal. Diagnose before repeated start attempts. Starter relay low-voltage codes need short isolation before another relay is installed.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 5 on the starter relay indicates the ECM control circuit is open or not loading the driver as expected. Open control wire, failed relay coil, poor ignition or ECM enable feed, blown fuse, and neutral safety or clutch interlock preventing command are the primary causes. Aftermarket starter interfaces and poor grounds causing intermittent no-crank are documented patterns. The interlock status must be verified before condemning the relay — an interlock preventing the start command produces the same symptom as a failed relay.
causes: Open control wire — open between ECM and relay coil
Failed relay coil — open coil resistance
Poor ignition or ECM enable feed — no power to relay feed circuit
Blown fuse — fuse in relay feed circuit
Neutral safety or clutch interlock — interlock preventing start command
Aftermarket alarm interrupt — aftermarket device interrupting start circuit
steps: Single Action Gate — Verify Start Request and Interlocks

Verify the start request is being generated and all interlocks are satisfied. Check neutral safety switch, clutch switch, and any other interlock PIDs with the scan tool. An interlock preventing the start command produces the same symptom as a failed relay. Confirm interlock status before any relay work.
Binary Decision Gate — Check Power at Relay Feed

Verify power at the relay feed circuit during a start request. A blown fuse or open feed circuit prevents the relay from energizing regardless of coil condition. Confirm power is present at the relay feed before measuring the coil control signal.
Override Manager — Measure Coil Control Signal

Measure the coil control signal at the relay during a start request. The ECM should pull the control circuit low to energize the relay. No control signal with confirmed power at the feed confirms an open control wire or ECM output fault.
Safety Interceptor — Relay Test and Replacement

Test the relay coil resistance versus OEM specification. An open coil confirms relay failure. Replace the relay and retest. Confirm the relay base is not damaged from previous overcurrent events before installing a new relay.
Resume Point — Aftermarket Interface Inspection

Inspect for aftermarket starter interfaces and alarm systems that may interrupt the start circuit. Aftermarket devices creating open conditions in the start circuit are a documented cause of intermittent no-crank with relay codes.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Start Confirmation
After repair, verify the engine cranks normally. Confirm no-crank does not recur. Monitor for return of FMI 5 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Relay, Wiring, or Interlock Decision

Replace relay if coil failure is confirmed. Repair control wiring if open wire is found. Repair fuse or junction if feed circuit is open. Repair interlock switch if interlock is preventing start command. Proceed to starter cable voltage-drop only after relay path is proven.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace relay if coil failure is confirmed.
2 . Repair open control wire between ECM and relay.
3 . Replace blown fuse in relay feed circuit.
4 . Repair interlock switch if interlock is preventing start command.
5 . Repair aftermarket interface interrupting start circuit.
Verification Steps
Confirm engine cranks normally after repair.
Verify no-crank does not recur after repair.

procedures_full.overview: FMI 6 on the starter relay indicates the ECM control circuit is drawing above-normal current. Control wire short to ground or power depending on driver type, failed relay coil short, and water-intruded relay centers are the primary causes. Water entry in relay panels after washes and melted relay bases from chronic overcurrent are documented patterns. Crushed looms near cab mounts and battery boxes are a documented harness short cause. Replacing the relay without isolating the short source produces repeat failures and can create a safety concern if the starter engages unexpectedly.
causes: Control wire short to ground — insulation damage on control wire
Control wire short to power — insulation damage creating high-side short
Failed relay coil short — internal coil short producing low resistance
Water-intruded relay center — moisture bridging relay terminals
Crushed loom — loom crushed near cab mount or battery box
steps: Single Action Gate — Remove Relay and Measure Coil Resistance

Remove the relay and measure coil resistance versus OEM specification. Low coil resistance below the minimum specification confirms an internal coil short. A coil resistance within specification with the relay removed confirms the harness is the short source.
Binary Decision Gate — Control Wire Short Checks

With the relay removed, check the control wire for short-to-ground and short-to-power. Inspect harness near cab mounts and battery boxes for crushed looms. A short on the control wire with the relay removed confirms a harness fault.
Override Manager — Relay Panel and Base Inspection

Inspect the relay panel and base for heat damage from chronic overcurrent. A melted relay base indicates the short has been present for an extended period. Repair the base and panel before installing a new relay.
Safety Interceptor — Water Intrusion Inspection

Inspect the relay center for water intrusion. Water entry in relay panels after washes is a documented cause of high-current relay faults. Inspect relay center seals and address water entry paths before installing a new relay.
Resume Point — Harness Repair Before New Relay
Repair the harness short before installing a new relay. Installing a new relay into a shorted harness produces repeat failure and risks unintended starter engagement.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Current Confirmation
After repair, verify the relay control circuit current is within normal range. Confirm no unintended starter engagement occurs. Monitor for return of FMI 6 over extended operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Relay, Harness, or Panel Decision

Replace relay if coil short is confirmed. Repair harness short if control wire short is found. Repair relay base and panel if heat damage is found. Address water intrusion source before closing the repair.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace relay if coil short is confirmed.
2 . Repair control wire short-to-ground or short-to-power.
3 . Repair relay base and panel if heat damage is found.
4 . Address water intrusion source in relay center.
5 . Repair crushed loom near cab mount or battery box.
Verification Steps
Confirm relay control circuit current is within normal range after repair.
Verify no unintended starter engagement occurs after repair.
Confirm SPN 677 FMI 6 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of repeat relay failure over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect relay center seals for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect harness near cab mounts and battery boxes for crush damage at every major service.
✓ Address water entry paths near relay centers promptly.
✓ Replace relay base if heat damage is found — do not install new relay in damaged base.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High safety concern Severity
High safety concern if starter engagement behavior is abnormal. Diagnose before further start attempts. Short isolation is required before installing a new relay.
