procedures_full.overview: FMI 5 on the DEF line heater indicates the circuit is open or drawing below-normal current. Broken heater wire, unplugged inline connector, failed heater element, and open fuse or driver are the primary causes. Lines damaged during tank or aftertreatment R&R and connectors not fully reconnected are documented patterns. Inline connectors along the frame rail are prone to abrasion at clamps and corrosion from DEF leaks. Replacing all heated lines without isolating the open segment wastes parts cost when only one segment is failed.
causes: Broken heater wire — wire break at clamp or abrasion point
Unplugged inline connector — connector not reconnected after AT or tank R&R
Failed heater element — open element resistance in line heater
Open fuse or driver — fuse in line heater circuit
DEF leak corrosion — urea corrosion at inline connector from DEF leak
steps: Single Action Gate — Visual Connector Audit

Audit all inline connectors along the DEF line heater circuit. Lines damaged during tank or aftertreatment R&R and connectors not fully reconnected are documented causes. Inspect inline connectors along the frame rail for proper engagement and pin condition.
Binary Decision Gate — Resistance Test

Measure line heater circuit resistance versus OEM specification. Infinite resistance or OL indicates an open circuit. Compare resistance across individual line segments to identify the open segment. A reading within specification on one segment with OL on another confirms the open segment location.
Override Manager — Command Voltage Check

Verify command voltage at the line heater circuit when the heater is commanded. No voltage at the line heater feed confirms an open feed circuit or blown fuse. Voltage present with no heater response confirms an open element or circuit downstream of the feed.
Safety Interceptor — Abrasion and DEF Leak Inspection

Inspect inline connectors along the frame rail for abrasion at clamps and corrosion from DEF leaks. DEF leak corrosion at inline connectors is a documented cause of open heater circuits. Clean or replace corroded connectors before any line replacement.
Resume Point — Open Segment Isolation

Isolate the open segment by testing resistance across individual line segments. Replace only the segment with confirmed open resistance. Replacing all heated lines without segment isolation wastes parts cost when only one segment is failed.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Heater Operation Confirmation

After repair, verify DEF line heater operation in cold ambient conditions. Confirm DEF line temperature rises appropriately with heater active. Monitor for return of FMI 5 over extended cold-weather operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Connector, Segment, or Full Line Decision

Repair connector if found unplugged or corroded. Replace the open line segment if element failure is confirmed. Replace full heated line assembly only if multiple segments are failed or the line is physically damaged.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Reconnect inline connector if found unplugged after AT or tank R&R.
2 . Repair DEF leak corrosion at inline connector.
3 . Replace the open line segment after resistance test confirms the open location.
4 . Replace blown fuse in line heater circuit.
5 . Replace full heated line assembly only if multiple segments are failed or physically damaged.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF line heater operation in cold ambient conditions after repair.
Verify DEF line temperature rises appropriately with heater active.
Confirm SPN 4340 FMI 5 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of frozen line indication over extended cold-weather operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Verify all inline DEF line heater connectors after every AT or tank R&R.
✓ Inspect inline connectors for abrasion at clamps at every major service.
✓ Address DEF leaks near inline connectors promptly to prevent corrosion.
✓ Inspect line heater circuit fuse at every major service.

Medium in cold climates Severity
Medium in cold climates. Can block dosing and lead toward inducement if unresolved. Address before cold-weather operation.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3598 FMI 0 indicates controller power output supply above the calibrated maximum. Failed regulator inside the ECM, short to higher voltage source in the harness, and incorrect jump or miswire after service are the primary causes. Mis-pinned connectors after repairs feeding battery voltage into reference circuits is a documented pattern. Replacing the ECM without proving the harness voltage intrusion is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Failed regulator inside ECM — failed ECM internal regulator producing above-normal reference voltage
Short to higher voltage source in harness — harness short to battery or ignition voltage producing above-normal reference
Incorrect jump or miswire after service — mis-pinned connector after service feeding battery voltage into reference circuit
steps: Step 1 — Measure Reference at ECM and at Sensors

Measure reference voltage at the ECM and at multiple sensors on the same bus. Reference significantly above approximately 5V or OEM specification is abnormal. Confirm at multiple sensors on the same bus to distinguish a bus-wide fault from a single-sensor fault.
Step 2 — Inspect Recent Harness Work

Inspect recent harness work. Mis-pinned connectors after repairs feeding battery voltage into reference circuits is a documented pattern. Inspect any recent harness repairs for mis-pinned connectors or incorrect wire routing. Look for sensor reference bundled into battery or ignition shorts after harness repairs.
Step 3 — Disconnect Loads to Identify External Voltage Source

Disconnect loads to identify whether the voltage source is external. Disconnect sensors and branches one group at a time. If the reference voltage drops when a branch is disconnected, the voltage source is external to the ECM. A short to higher voltage source in the harness requires harness repair.
Step 4 — ECM Decision Only After Harness Proof

Make the ECM decision only after harness proof. Confirm the harness is clean and no external voltage source is present before any ECM replacement. ECM replacement or programming is only indicated if the internal regulator is proven failed after harness proof.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair harness miswire if mis-pinned connector is confirmed.
2 . Repair harness short to higher voltage if confirmed.
3 . Replace and reprogram ECM if internal regulator failure is confirmed after harness proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm reference voltage returns to specification after repair.
Verify SPN 3598 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Confirm all related sensor codes clear after repair.
Monitor for return of reference overvoltage events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Verify connector pin assignments after any harness repair.
✓ Inspect sensor reference circuits after any harness work.
✓ Use OEM wiring diagrams for all harness repairs.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High. Overvoltage on sensor supplies can damage multiple components. Severity
High. Overvoltage on sensor supplies can damage multiple components. High reference supply is a harness-versus-ECM regulator diagnosis.
symptoms: Sensor reference voltage high
5V supply high
Sensor readings irrational high
Reference overvoltage
Multiple high-voltage sensor codes

procedures_full.overview: This fault indicates the Proportional Valve Bank 2 circuit has failed low.‪
causes: This fault indicates the Proportional Valve Bank 2 circuit has failed low.‪
steps: Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the Rear Valve Cover Injector Harness connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 14 on the engine side of the Valve Cover Injector Harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between the Rear Valve Cover Injector Harness and the medium (rear) engine brake solenoid.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to the next step.
Disconnect the EGR Valve connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 of the EGR Valve and ground.
Note: This measurement is ON the EGR Valve.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, replace the EGR Valve. Refer to "117.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to the next step.
Disconnect the MCM 120–pin connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 1 of the EGR Valve Harness connector and ground.

If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 62 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the EGR Valve/Rear Valve Cover Injector Harness connectors. Refer to "117.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to the next step.
Disconnect the Fuel Cutoff Valve connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 2 of the Fuel Cutoff Valve Harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, go to the next step.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, replace the Doser Block Assembly. Refer to "117.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the Electronic Dosing Valve connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 2 of the Electronic Dosing Valve connector and ground.

If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 64 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the Electronic Dosing Valve/Fuel Cutoff Valve connector.Refer to "117.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, replace the Doser Block Assembly. Refer to "117.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
ENGINE EXHAUST
To avoid injury from inhaling engine exhaust, always operate the engine in a well-ventilated area. Engine exhaust is toxic.‪
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1322 FMI 31 means the ECM has detected misfire on more than one cylinder on an International A26. It's a High severity fault - the truck is drivable but running rough, and the cause is usually a shared fuel, air, or wiring issue. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com applies the same discipline to this A26 code as any other platform's multi-cylinder misfire fault - the code is telling you the problem is shared, not isolated to one injector.
causes: Restricted or contaminated fuel supply
A mechanical fuel delivery issue - low or fluctuating supply pressure can starve several injectors at once, especially under load.
Chafed or corroded shared harness ground or power feed
An electrical fault where a single damaged wire on a shared circuit causes intermittent misfire signatures across multiple cylinders.
Marginal crankshaft or camshaft position sensor signal
A sensor/signal-quality issue rather than a true combustion problem - a noisy timing signal can cause false misfire logging across cylinders.
Air intake restriction or boost leak
A mechanical airflow issue that can cause lean misfire conditions spread across multiple cylinders.
steps: Pull the full fault list with a scan tool - look for which specific cylinder SPNs are logging alongside this multi-cylinder code.
Check fuel supply pressure and filter condition first, since a restricted supply commonly affects multiple cylinders at once rather than just one.
Inspect the injector harness and connectors for a shared ground or power wire that could affect several cylinders if chafed or corroded.
Run individual injector cutout tests to see if misfires cluster on one bank or side, which often points to a harness or fuel rail issue on that side.
If cylinders are scattered with no pattern, check crankshaft and camshaft position sensor signal quality, since a marginal timing signal can register as false misfire across multiple cylinders.
symptoms: Rough idle or a noticeable shake felt through the cab
Check engine light, often with individual cylinder misfire codes alongside it
Loss of power and poor fuel economy
Excessive white or black smoke depending on which cylinders are affected

procedures_full.overview: Freightliner SPN 3464 FMI 10 indicates an abnormal rate of change in the SCR catalyst temperature. This often results from issues like sensor faults, catalyst inefficiency, or exhaust leaks. Diagnose using live data and inspect components for damage. When a Freightliner truck displays SPN 3464 FMI 10, it signals an abnormal rate of change in the SCR catalyst temperature. This fault code is crucial to address promptly as it can affect the efficiency of the aftertreatment system, leading to increased emissions and potential engine derate. The Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system is vital for reducing NOx emissions, which are harmful pollutants that contribute to smog and acid rain. Anomalies in the catalyst temperature can indicate problems such as a malfunctioning temperature sensor, catalyst inefficiency, or exhaust leaks. Understanding the root cause is essential for maintaining engine performance and compliance with emissions standards. Ignoring this issue can result in failed emissions tests, hefty fines, and damage to the vehicle's engine and aftertreatment components. In this guide, we'll walk through the symptoms, common causes, and step-by-step diagnostics to resolve this issue effectively. Whether you're a fleet manager or a driver, this comprehensive overview will equip you with the knowledge to tackle SPN 3464 FMI 10 confidently, ensuring your Freightliner remains roadworthy and environmentally friendly.
causes: Faulty Temperature Sensor

Temperature sensors in the SCR system may fail or become inaccurate over time. This can lead to incorrect temperature readings, triggering the fault code. Regular checks and calibration can prevent this issue.
Exhaust Leaks
Leaks in the exhaust system can cause incorrect temperature readings by allowing cooler air to enter the system. Inspect all connections and joints for signs of leakage.
SCR Catalyst Inefficiency

If the SCR catalyst becomes inefficient due to age or contamination, it may not effectively reduce NOx emissions, leading to abnormal temperature changes. Regular maintenance and inspections are crucial.
DEF Quality Issues
Poor quality or contaminated DEF can affect the SCR system's performance, leading to incorrect temperature regulation. Always use high-quality DEF from reputable sources.
steps: Connect a diagnostic scanner to the OBD port to retrieve fault codes and freeze-frame data. Look for related codes that might indicate sensor or catalyst issues.
Inspect the SCR temperature sensors for damage or disconnection. Use a multimeter to check continuity and resistance values against specifications.
Examine the exhaust system for leaks, focusing on joints, clamps, and flexible sections. Use a smoke machine if necessary to identify elusive leaks.
Check the SCR catalyst for physical damage or signs of melting. Ensure that the catalyst is not clogged or contaminated.
Review live data to monitor SCR inlet and outlet temperatures. Compare these readings to expected values under different operating conditions.
Test the NOx sensors upstream and downstream of the SCR catalyst. Ensure they are functioning correctly and providing accurate readings.
Inspect the DEF injection system for blockages or malfunctions that could affect catalyst efficiency.
Perform a manual regeneration if safe and recommended, to clear any accumulated soot and verify system operation.
symptoms: Engine warning light illuminated due to aftertreatment system faults.
Noticeable decrease in engine performance and possible derate.
Increased emissions, potentially leading to failed emissions tests.
Unusual exhaust noises indicating possible leaks or blockages.
Frequent regeneration cycles or inability to complete regeneration.
Temperature sensor readings that fluctuate or appear inconsistent.
Excessive DEF consumption without corresponding emissions reduction.
Visible damage or corrosion on SCR components upon inspection.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3464 FMI 31 indicates an intake throttle actuator condition exists. The OEM defines the exact trigger — position error, control fault, or inhibit class. Carboned plate, failed actuator, position feedback fault, wiring issues, and software adapts lost after service are the primary causes. Carbon buildup after short-trip service cycles and connector unplugged after intake work are documented patterns. Replacing the throttle body assembly before cleaning and verifying control is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Carboned plate — carbon buildup on throttle plate producing binding and position error
Failed actuator — failed actuator producing no movement or erratic response
Position feedback fault — position feedback fault producing position error
Wiring issues — wiring issues producing control fault
Software adapts lost after service — software adapts lost after service producing position error
steps: Step 1 — Command Sweep

Command a sweep of the intake throttle through its full range. Binding shows lag; electrical faults show dropout or no movement with good power. Carbon buildup after short-trip service cycles is a documented cause — inspect for carbon if binding is confirmed.
Step 2 — Inspect Carbon

Inspect the throttle body for carbon buildup. Carbon buildup after short-trip service cycles is a documented pattern. Inspect the throttle plate and bore for carbon deposits. Clean the throttle body if carbon binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved per OEM procedure.
Step 3 — Circuit Checks

Perform circuit checks. Connector unplugged after intake work is a documented pattern — always inspect the throttle body connector after any recent intake service. Verify throttle body connector integrity, reference voltage, ground, and signal circuit.
Step 4 — Clean vs Replace Decision Based on Wear and Response

Make the clean vs replace decision based on wear and response. Clean the throttle body if carbon binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved. Replace the throttle assembly if actuator or sensor failure is confirmed after cleaning and circuit proof ($300–$1,200).

Repair Steps
1 . Clean throttle body if carbon binding is confirmed and cleaning is approved per OEM procedure.
2 . Repair connector or harness if circuit fault is confirmed.
3 . Replace throttle assembly if actuator or sensor failure is confirmed ($300–$1,200).
Verification Steps
Confirm intake throttle operates correctly after repair.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3511 FMI 4 indicates sensor supply bank 2 voltage below the minimum. Shorted sensor on Supply 2, harness short to ground on that bank, and failed supply driver are the primary causes. One shorted sensor creating a family of codes only on the Supply 2 bank is a documented pattern. Replacing sensors from the Supply 1 bank while the Supply 2 fault remains is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Shorted sensor on Supply 2 — one shorted sensor on Supply 2 pulling down the bank reference
Harness short to ground on Supply 2 bank — harness short to ground on Supply 2 branch producing below-normal reference
Failed supply driver — failed Supply 2 supply driver producing below-normal reference
steps: Step 1 — Measure Supply 2 KOEO

Measure Supply 2 voltage key-on engine-off. Supply 2 should be near OEM reference specification. A Supply 2 voltage significantly below specification confirms a Supply 2 fault. Confirm Supply 1 is healthy to distinguish a bank-specific fault from a system-wide fault.
Step 2 — Branch Isolation

Disconnect Supply 2 sensors one group at a time until reference recovers. Recovery after disconnecting one sensor or branch identifies the offender. One shorted sensor creating a family of codes only on the Supply 2 bank is a documented pattern.
Step 3 — Repair Shorted Sensor or Harness
Repair the shorted sensor or harness within the identified branch. Replace the shorted sensor if sensor failure is confirmed. Repair the harness section if harness short to ground is confirmed.
Step 4 — Reconfirm Supply 1 Remains Healthy

Reconfirm Supply 1 remains healthy after repair. Confirm Supply 2 returns to specification after repair. Confirm Supply 1 is not affected by the repair. ECM replacement is only indicated if the Supply 2 bus remains dead with all loads removed and power and grounds are perfect.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace shorted sensor if sensor failure is confirmed on Supply 2 branch.
2 . Repair harness section if harness short to ground is confirmed.
3 . Replace ECM if Supply 2 driver failure is confirmed after all loads are removed.
Verification Steps
Confirm Supply 2 voltage returns to specification after repair.
Verify SPN 3511 FMI 4 does not return after repair.
Confirm all Supply 2 sensor codes clear after repair.
Confirm Supply 1 remains healthy after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect Supply 2 sensor connectors for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect Supply 2 harness for damage at every major service.
✓ Verify Supply 2 voltage at every major service on high-mileage engines.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High due to multi-signal failure potential. Severity
High due to multi-signal failure potential. Supply 2 low voltage is resolved by isolating the shorted branch or sensor.
symptoms: 5V supply 2 low
Sensor Vref 2 collapsed
Multiple low-voltage codes supply 2
Bank-specific sensor cascade
Supply 2 sensor readings stuck low

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3597 FMI 1 indicates controller power output supply to sensors or actuators below normal — commonly the 5V reference network. One shorted sensor on the supply bus, damaged harness loading the supply, failed ECM supply driver (less common), and water intrusion are the primary causes. One shorted MAP, rail, or TPS-style sensor creating a cascade of codes is a documented pattern. Replacing the ECM for multiple simultaneous sensor codes without isolating the shared bus is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Shorted sensor on supply bus — one shorted sensor pulling down the shared reference supply
Damaged harness loading supply — harness damage loading the reference supply below normal
Failed ECM supply driver — failed ECM supply driver producing below-normal reference (less common)
Water intrusion — water intrusion producing short circuit on reference bus
steps: Step 1 — Measure Reference Voltage KOEO

Measure reference voltage key-on engine-off. A significantly low reference voltage under key-on indicates bus loading or a short. One shorted MAP, rail, or TPS-style sensor creating a cascade of codes is a documented pattern. Confirm the reference voltage is below specification before proceeding.
Step 2 — Disconnect Branch Isolation

Disconnect sensors and branches one group at a time until voltage recovers. Any sensor on the shared reference can pull the bus down. Use isolation by disconnect groups. The branch that restores reference voltage when disconnected contains the fault.
Step 3 — Locate Shorted Sensor or Harness

Locate the shorted sensor or harness within the identified branch. Disconnect individual sensors within the identified branch until the shorted device is isolated. A shorted sensor or harness section producing below-normal reference confirms the fault source.
Step 4 — Repair and Confirm All Related Codes Clear

Repair the shorted sensor or harness and confirm all related codes clear after repair. Confirm reference voltage returns to specification after repair. Confirm all cascade codes clear after repair. ECM replacement is only indicated if the supply remains dead with all loads removed and power and grounds are perfect.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace shorted sensor if sensor failure is confirmed.
2 . Repair harness section if harness short is confirmed.
3 . Service connector if water intrusion is confirmed.
4 . Replace ECM only if supply remains dead with all loads removed and power and grounds are perfect.
Verification Steps
Confirm reference voltage returns to specification after repair.
Verify SPN 3597 FMI 1 does not return after repair.
Confirm all cascade sensor codes clear after repair.
Monitor for return of reference voltage faults over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect sensor connectors for water intrusion at every major service.
✓ Inspect sensor harness for damage at every major service.
✓ Verify reference voltage at every major service on high-mileage engines.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
High due to multi-system trust loss and possible derate or no-start. Severity
High due to multi-system trust loss and possible derate or no-start. Low ECU supply voltage is shared-bus isolation work first.
symptoms: Sensor supply voltage low
ECU 5V supply low
Multiple sensor codes at once
Reference voltage collapsed
Cascade of sensor codes from one shorted device

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically proportional valve bank 1 circuit failed low.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically proportional valve bank 1 circuit failed low.‪
steps: Circuit Check
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Monitor the active codes.
Disconnect the rear valve cover injector harness.
Does SPN 3597/FMI 3 become inactive?
If yes, go to step 5.
If no, go to step 9.
Reconnect the rear valve cover injector harness.
Remove the upper valve cover.
Disconnect the rear Jake Brake® solenoid.
Does SPN 3597/FMI 3 become inactive?
If yes, replace the rear Jake Brake solenoid. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no, replace the injector wiring harness. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the turbo actuator.
Does SPN 3597/FMI 3 become inactive?
If yes, replace the turbo actuator. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no, go to step 11.
Disconnect the fan control solenoid.
Does SPN 3597/FMI 3 become inactive?
If yes, replace the fan control solenoid. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no, go to step 13.
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the MCM 120–pin connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 91 of the MCM 120–pin connector and ground.

If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 91 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the rear injector valve cover connector, turbo actuator connector and or fan control solenoid. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 16.
Measure the resistance between pin 93 of the MCM 120–pin connector and ground.

If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 93 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the rear injector valve cover connector, turbo actuator connector and or fan control solenoid. Refer to "114.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800 for MCM replacement.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: Series 60 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 114.1 SPN 3597/FMI 3 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically Proportional Valve Bank 1 circuit failed low.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically Proportional Valve Bank 1 circuit failed low.‪
steps: Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the front valve cover injector harness connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 14 on the valve cover side of the injector harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, go to step 4.
If resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 6.
Remove the valve cover and disconnect the wires from the low engine brake solenoid.
Measure the resistance between pin 14 on the valve cover side of the injector harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, replace the solenoid.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, replace the front under valve cover injector harness.
Disconnect the MCM 120–pin connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 14 on the engine harness side of the injector harness connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, go to the next step.
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 10.
Disconnect the engine 31–pin connector.
Again measure the resistance between pin 14 on the engine harness side of the injector harness connector and ground.

If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair short to ground between pin 91 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the valve cover injector harness connector or the 31 pin connector. Refer to "116.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, repair short to ground between pin 22 of the 31–pin connector on the vehicle side of the harness and the fan control solenoid. Refer to "116.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the Air Seal Pressure Regulator Valve connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 2 of the Air Seal Pressure Regulator Valve connector and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair short to ground between pin 93 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the Air Seal Pressure Regulator Valve connector. Refer to "116.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If resistance is greater than 5 Ω, replace the Air Seal Pressure Regulator Valve.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
ENGINE EXHAUST
To avoid injury from inhaling engine exhaust, always operate the engine in a well-ventilated area. Engine exhaust is toxic.‪
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically injector #1, 2, or 3 spill control valve circuit is shorted to battery/power.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically injector #1, 2, or 3 spill control valve circuit is shorted to battery/power.‪
steps: Short to Battery/Power Check
Disconnect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector.
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Measure the voltage between pin 2 on the MCM side of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground.
If there is voltage present, repair the short to power between pin 2 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and pin 14 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "130.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If there is no voltage present, go to step 4.
Measure the voltage between pin 4 on the MCM side of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground.
If there is voltage present, repair the short to power between pin 4 of the Front Injector Harness connector and pin 10 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "130.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If there is no voltage present, repair the short to power between pin 6 of the Front Injector Harness connector and pin 12 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "130.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: Series 60 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 130.1 SPN 4258/FMI 3 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically injector #1, 2, or 3 spill control valve circuit is shorted to ground.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically injector #1, 2, or 3 spill control valve circuit is shorted to ground.‪
steps: Short to Ground Check
Disconnect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector.
Inspect the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector for bent or spread pins, inspect the connector seal for damage (signs of water or oil intrusion).
If the water or oil intrusion, bent or spread pins are found, repair as necessary.
If connector shows no signs of damage, go to step 3.
Measure the resistance between pin 9 on the valve cover side of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground. If you are using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #1 pin 3 and ground.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, go to step 11.
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 4.
Remove the valve cover.
Disconnect injector #1.
Measure the resistance between pin 9 on the valve cover side of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground. If you are using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #1 pin 3 and ground.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the #1 injector. Refer to "130.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 7.
Disconnect injector #2.
Measure the resistance between pin 9 of the valve cover side on the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground. If you are using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #2 pin 3 and ground.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the #2 injector. Refer to "130.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, go to step 9.
Disconnect injector #3.
Measure the resistance between pin 9 on the valve cover side of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground.
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, replace the #3 injector. Refer to "130.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, replace the under valve cover Injector Harness. Refer to "130.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance between pin 9 on the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector and ground. If you are using J-48671–10 , measure between injector #3 pin 3 and ground.

If the resistance is less than 3 Ω, repair the short to ground between pin 11 of the MCM 120–pin connector and pin 9 of the Front Injector Harness 12–pin connector. Refer to "130.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 3 Ω, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800 for MCM replacement authorization.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: Series 60 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 130.2 SPN 4258/FMI 4 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

field_evidence.title: Cummins ISB No Start Issue with SPN 1347 FMI 3 Code
field_evidence.excerpt: The Cummins ISB engine can experience a no start condition associated with the SPN 1347 FMI 3 fault code. This code indicates a fuel system issue that is often related to the fuel pump actuator or its wiring. Common problems with ISB engines include water in fuel sensor faults and fuel pump actuator failures, both of which can contribute to this no start condition. Even after replacing components like the water separator and fuel filter, problems such as poor injector control or faulty actuator signals may still cause symptoms like low idle and engine stalling. To address this issue, it is important to check the voltage and ground connections at the fuel pump actuator and inspect the wiring harness for any damage. Testing the actuator’s mechanical function is also a useful diagnostic step.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 0 indicates outlet NOx related high condition or contribution class depending on OEM mapping. DEF chemistry issues, dosing quantity problems, NOx sensor bias, exhaust leaks, degraded SCR catalyst, and high engine-out NOx from combustion faults are the primary causes. Catalyst replaced before DEF and dosing proof is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern. The SCR catalyst is the last component to assess after all upstream causes are eliminated.
causes: DEF chemistry issues — DEF chemistry fault producing reduced NOx conversion
Dosing quantity problems — dosing quantity fault producing insufficient urea injection
NOx sensor bias — NOx sensor bias producing false high outlet NOx reading
Exhaust leaks — exhaust leak producing false high outlet NOx reading
Degraded SCR catalyst — degraded SCR catalyst producing reduced NOx conversion
High engine-out NOx — combustion fault producing high engine-out NOx that exceeds SCR conversion capacity
steps: Step 1 — DEF Chemistry Check

Check DEF chemistry with a refractometer. DEF chemistry issues producing reduced NOx conversion are a documented cause. Verify the DEF concentration is within specification. Drain and refill with fresh OEM-specification DEF if quality is suspect.
Step 2 — Dosing Pressure and Quantity Check

Check dosing pressure and quantity. A dosing quantity fault producing insufficient urea injection reduces NOx conversion. Verify dosing system operation per OEM procedure. Confirm dosing pressure and quantity meet specification.
Step 3 — NOx Sensor Plausibility Check

Check NOx sensor plausibility. A NOx sensor bias producing a false high outlet NOx reading confirms a sensing fault. Compare upstream and downstream NOx sensor readings. A downstream reading that is implausibly high relative to upstream confirms a sensor fault.
Step 4 — Engine-Out NOx Contributors

Evaluate engine-out NOx contributors. High engine-out NOx from combustion faults that exceeds SCR conversion capacity produces high outlet NOx. Evaluate EGR system operation and combustion health. Address engine-out NOx contributors before SCR catalyst assessment.
Step 5 — Catalyst Assessment Last

Assess the SCR catalyst only after all upstream causes are eliminated. A catalyst replaced before DEF and dosing proof is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern. Confirm DEF chemistry, dosing quantity, NOx sensor plausibility, and engine-out NOx are all within specification before any catalyst assessment.
Step 6 — Verify After Repair
Verify outlet NOx readings are within specification after repair. Confirm SPN 4363 FMI 0 does not return. Monitor for return of high outlet NOx events over extended operation.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Drain and refill with fresh OEM-specification DEF if quality is suspect.
2 . Repair dosing system if dosing fault is confirmed.
3 . Repair NOx sensor circuit if sensor bias is confirmed.
4 . Address engine-out NOx contributors if combustion fault is confirmed.
5 . Replace SCR catalyst only after all upstream causes are eliminated.
Verification Steps
Confirm outlet NOx readings are within specification after repair.
Verify SPN 4363 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Confirm SCR efficiency returns to normal after repair.
Monitor for return of high outlet NOx events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Use OEM-specification DEF only.
✓ Inspect dosing system operation at every major service.
✓ Inspect NOx sensor connectors at every major service.
✓ Monitor engine-out NOx trend over time on high-mileage engines.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High with progressive derate risk Severity
Medium to High with progressive derate risk. High outlet NOx is a conversion-system diagnosis, not automatic catalyst failure.
symptoms: High outlet NOx
SCR not converting NOx
Efficiency failure from high NOx
Aftertreatment NOx high
Progressive derate from high outlet NOx

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 0 is a critical code meaning SCR catalyst outlet temperature has exceeded the most severe threshold. Expect an active power derate - address the heat source immediately to avoid permanent catalyst damage.
causes: Stuck-open or malfunctioning DEF/HC doser during regen
Excess unburned fuel or improper DEF dosing timing lets exhaust temperature climb unchecked as it passes through the SCR section.
Upstream DPF regeneration running excessively hot
A hot or prolonged DPF regen event can push elevated exhaust temperatures downstream into the SCR catalyst.
Failed SCR outlet temperature sensor
A sensor reading falsely high without a genuine overtemp condition is possible but should only be assumed after cross-checking against the SCR intake sensor.
steps: Do not continue heavy-load operation once this code is active - pull over and let the aftertreatment system cool if temperatures are climbing rapidly.
Pull freeze-frame data on DDDL comparing SCR intake and SCR outlet temperatures to determine whether excess heat is generated upstream or specific to the catalyst itself.
Check for a stuck-open HC doser or over-fueling regen event driving excess heat into the SCR section.
Inspect the DEF doser injector for proper spray pattern; a malfunctioning doser can allow excess exhaust heat to reach the SCR without adequate cooling from DEF injection.
Verify the SCR outlet temperature sensor itself with a resistance check against the OEM chart to rule out a sensor-level fault.
If temperatures are genuinely excessive, do not clear the code and return to service - have the SCR catalyst inspected for thermal damage before continued operation.
symptoms: Red stop engine or check engine lamp with active derate
Strong exhaust heat and possible visible heat shimmer near the SCR canister
Reduced power that worsens the longer the condition continues
Possible accompanying DEF dosing or NOx sensor codes
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 4363 FMI 0: Critical SCR Outlet Overtemperature

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 1 on a Mack means the SCR outlet gas temperature is reading below normal range. Compare inlet vs outlet temperatures during regen with Jaltest before replacing the sensor. When a Mack MP8 or MP7 truck logs SPN 4363 FMI 1, the aftertreatment control module has determined the SCR outlet gas temperature is below the expected range for current operating conditions. Unlike SPN 4363 FMI 3 (voltage above normal), FMI 1 means the reading is in a valid but below-normal range — which on a hot engine under load or during active regen points to sensor failure rather than actual cold exhaust. At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com, the most reliable diagnostic step is comparing the SCR inlet temperature (SPN 4360) against the outlet (SPN 4363) using Jaltest during a commanded stationary regen. If the inlet climbs normally but the outlet stays near ambient temperature, the outlet sensor has failed. If both stay low, the regen process itself is incomplete due to a DEF or fuel doser issue.
causes: Failed NTC thermistor in the SCR outlet sensor (open or degraded)
The thermistor element degrades from long-term exposure to high-temperature exhaust gases. An open thermistor causes the ACM to read an implausibly low temperature, setting FMI 1.
DEF or exhaust condensation contaminating the sensor connector
The SCR outlet is downstream of the DEF dosing point. DEF vapor or condensation migrates into the sensor connector, creating partial grounds that pull the signal below the FMI 1 threshold.
Exhaust system air leak upstream of the SCR outlet sensor

A gasket failure or loose clamp between the SCR catalyst outlet and the sensor mounting point allows ambient air to cool the exhaust stream near the sensor, producing a genuinely low temperature reading during light-load operation.
Incomplete regeneration lowering actual SCR outlet temperature

If a fuel doser or DEF dosing fault prevents the regen from reaching full temperature, the outlet sensor may read correctly but below the expected regen temperature, triggering FMI 1 as a secondary fault.
steps: Connect Jaltest Trucks diagnostic software to the Mack 9-pin diagnostic port. Navigate to the aftertreatment module data and command a stationary regeneration test. Monitor SPN 4363 (SCR outlet temperature) during the regen cycle. If the outlet temperature fails to climb above 200 degrees C while the SCR inlet (SPN 4360) is reading above 350 degrees C, the outlet sensor circuit is suspect.

After the regen test with the engine off and exhaust cooled for at least 45 minutes, disconnect the SCR outlet temperature sensor connector. Measure resistance between the sensor pins. For Mack MP8 NTC thermistors, expect 50 to 120 kOhm at ambient temperature (25 degrees C). An open reading (OL) or a reading above 500 kOhm confirms thermistor failure. Use Diesel Laptops with a J1939 adapter for a pre-test and post-test parameter comparison.

If resistance is in spec, inspect the connector for DEF crystallization, corrosion, or physical damage. The SCR outlet sensor is located downstream of the DEF injection point, where DEF vapor can migrate into the connector cavity. Clean with electrical contact cleaner and re-test resistance.

Back-probe the signal pin to sensor ground with the connector attached and key on (engine off). The voltage should reflect the current ambient temperature on the NTC curve. A signal below 0.2 V with a confirmed 5 V reference on the supply pin indicates a short-to-ground path in the connector or harness.

If the connector is clean and the harness is intact, replace the SCR outlet temperature sensor. Use Jaltest to command another stationary regen and confirm the outlet temperature rises to the expected 400 to 600 degrees C range during peak regen activity.
symptoms: SCR outlet temperature reads below 150 degrees C during a commanded regeneration event.
Active regeneration fails to complete, leaving the DPF at elevated soot load.
Amber aftertreatment lamp and possible derate warning if the incomplete regen cycle accumulates.
Diesel Laptops or Jaltest live data shows SPN 4363 value significantly lower than SPN 4360 (inlet) during regen.
Mack instrument cluster may display a service aftertreatment system message.
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 4363 FMI 1: SCR Outlet Temperature Below Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 3 means the International SCR catalyst outlet temperature sensor circuit is reading voltage above normal, usually an open sensor or broken wire. It is Medium severity and affects DEF dosing confidence, though the engine keeps running normally. The SCR catalyst outlet temperature sensor completes the temperature picture the International ECM needs to verify the catalyst is properly converting NOx with DEF, working alongside its intake counterpart at SPN 4360. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees SPN 4363 FMI 3 most commonly from heat-damaged wiring given the sensor's location right at the hottest part of the aftertreatment system, and while there's no immediate drivability symptom, letting this fault linger can gradually undermine SCR dosing accuracy.
causes: Heat-damaged sensor wiring near the SCR canister
Extended exposure to high exhaust temperatures cracks wire insulation over time, eventually breaking the conductor and opening the circuit.
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Vibration and thermal cycling loosen connector locks, and moisture intrusion corrodes the pin contacts over time.
Failed internal sensor element
The temperature sensing element inside the sensor can fail from repeated extreme heat cycling near the SCR catalyst.
Damage during a previous aftertreatment repair
Sensor bungs or wiring can be accidentally damaged during SCR component service if care isn't taken during reassembly.
steps: Connect a compatible diagnostic tool and confirm SPN 4363 FMI 3, then check current SCR system status and dosing activity.
Locate the SCR outlet temperature sensor at the rear of the SCR catalyst canister and inspect the connector for corrosion or heat-damaged wiring.
Unplug the sensor and verify reference voltage and ground are present at the harness connector.
Check sensor resistance with a multimeter against spec at ambient temperature to confirm whether the sensor itself is open.
Replace the sensor or repair the harness as needed, clear codes, and confirm normal SCR dosing resumes on the next drive cycle.
symptoms: Amber MIL illuminated
Possible changes to DEF dosing rate or dosing suspension
No immediate drivability change in most cases
Potential future SCR efficiency codes if left unresolved
procedures_full.source_title: International SPN 4363 FMI 3: SCR Outlet Temp Sensor High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 3 means the SCR outlet gas temperature sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage, an electrical fault rather than an actual overtemp event. It's a medium-severity code with no derate - check the harness near the aftertreatment canister first. Don't confuse this circuit fault with a genuine overtemp condition - the fix here is almost always electrical, not aftertreatment-related. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always pin-tests the connector before assuming the sensor itself needs replacement.
causes: Chafed or heat-damaged signal wire near the aftertreatment canister
Extended exposure to exhaust heat can degrade wire insulation over time, allowing the signal wire to short against a powered or grounded surface.
Corroded connector pin
Moisture intrusion at the aftertreatment sensor connector can corrode pins, producing an intermittent high-voltage signature.
Internally failed sensor element
A cracked thermocouple or thermistor inside the sensor housing can present as an open circuit, mimicking the same fault.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on Mack Premium Tech Tool to confirm the outlet temperature reading is pinned at an unrealistic high value.
Locate the SCR outlet temperature sensor at the aftertreatment canister and unplug the connector.
Back-probe signal and ground with a multimeter, key on engine off - a reading near 5V with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness-side fault.
Trace the signal wire for chafing or heat damage along its routing near the aftertreatment canister and exhaust piping.
Test sensor resistance at the connector against Mack's published temperature/resistance chart to rule out an internally open sensor.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor as needed, then clear the code and confirm a plausible reading returns.
symptoms: Check engine lamp illuminated, typically no derate
No noticeable drivability change in most cases
Possible related NOx efficiency monitoring limitations
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 4363 FMI 3: SCR Outlet Temperature Circuit Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4363 FMI 16 on Kenworth means the SCR catalyst outlet gas temperature is valid but above the moderately severe limit. Check DEF dosing, regen history, and SCR brick condition before replacing the outlet temperature sensor. Kenworth trucks running PACCAR MX-13 or Cummins X15 engines rely on SCR outlet temperature to verify the catalyst is operating within safe thermal limits after NOx reduction. SPN 4363 FMI 16 tells you that outlet reading has crossed the moderately severe threshold. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats this as a system fault — doser, DEF quality, and upstream regen behavior — not an isolated sensor problem in most cases.
causes: Excessive DEF dosing from stuck doser or incorrect ACM calibration
Very Common
Over-injection of urea into a hot SCR brick drives exothermic reactions that spike outlet temperature beyond the ECM safe window.
SCR catalyst substrate damage from prior overtemperature event
A melted or collapsed SCR brick restricts flow and retains heat, keeping outlet temperature elevated even at moderate engine loads.
Incomplete regen leaving elevated exhaust heat in the aftertreatment stream
Moderate
Aborted DPF regens that spike DOC temperatures propagate residual heat to the SCR outlet for 10-20 minutes after the regen stops.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 (MX-13) or Cummins INSITE (X15) and log SPN 4363 alongside SCR intake (SPN 4360), DEF flow rate, and outlet NOx sensor readings during a 15-minute loaded drive.
Normal SCR outlet temperature at 55 mph cruise on MX-13 is typically 220°C-380°C. Readings sustained above 450°C at moderate load confirm genuine SCR overtemperature.
Command a stationary SCR test in Davie4 and monitor DEF dosing quantity — MX-13 dosers should deliver 0-2.5 L/h at idle test; continuous flow above spec indicates a stuck doser valve.

Inspect the SCR outlet thermocouple connector at the OneBox or standalone SCR module for soot contamination. Compare sensor reading to an infrared pyrometer at the boss — acceptable variance is within 25°C.

If outlet temp is high with normal SCR intake, inspect the SCR brick for face plugging or substrate damage using borescope access ports. Clear codes only after temperatures stabilize below 400°C at cruise for two complete drive cycles.
symptoms: Amber MIL and possible aftertreatment inducement countdown on late-model Kenworth dashboards
SCR outlet temperature reading above 500°C at highway cruise on PACCAR Davie4 live data
White exhaust vapor or ammonia odor if DEF is over-dosing into an overheated SCR brick
Possible companion SPN 4364 SCR NOx efficiency codes
Fuel economy drop if ECM reduces load to protect aftertreatment

dd_procedures.title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3936 FMI 1 – DEF Level Low
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3936 FMI 1 – DEF Level Low (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3936 FMI 1 indicates that the Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) level in the tank has dropped below the minimum threshold. This code commonly appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and will trigger derate conditions if DEF is not added promptly.
Symptoms
DEF warning light illuminated 
Check engine light on 
Audible warning chime 
Engine derate may begin if DEF level continues to drop
Cause
This code is triggered when the DEF level sensor detects fluid below the minimum required level. Common causes include normal DEF consumption without refilling, a slow DEF leak, or a faulty DEF level sensor giving a false low reading.
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving is possible but the engine will begin to derate — typically reducing power to 55 mph or less — if DEF is not added. Continued operation without addressing the code can result in a complete engine derate to 5 mph.
Recommended Action
Add DEF fluid immediately. If the warning clears after refilling, no further action is required. If the code persists after filling the tank, have the DEF level sensor and wiring inspected for faults.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3936 FMI 1 mean?
 
It means the DEF tank level has dropped below the minimum required threshold and the engine is at risk of entering a derate condition.
 
 
What causes SPN 3936 FMI 1?
 
Most commonly, the DEF tank simply needs to be refilled. It can also be caused by a DEF leak or a faulty DEF level sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3936 FMI 1?
 
You can drive short distances but the engine will progressively derate if DEF is not added. Do not ignore this code.
 
 
Will SPN 3936 FMI 1 cause a derate?
 
Yes. Detroit Diesel engines are programmed to derate engine power and eventually limit speed to 5 mph if DEF level remains critically low.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3936 FMI 1?
 
Add DEF to the tank to bring it above the minimum level. The code should clear on its own once the sensor reads an acceptable level. If it persists, inspect the DEF level sensor.
 
 
Related codes
SPN 3364 FMI 2 
SPN 520372 FMI 16 
SPN 4334 FMI 18
Need Immediate Help With This Fault Code?
If your engine is derating, losing power, or unable to complete regeneration, don’t risk further damage or costly downtime.
Use 4RoadService to locate mobile truck repair, dealer diagnostics, or emergency roadside assistance near your location.

Important Notice
The information provided above is for general informational purposes only and should not replace official OEM service procedures. Always consult the manufacturer’s service manual or a qualified diesel technician before performing repairs. Operating a vehicle with active fault codes may result in further damage.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3936 FMI 0 means the SCR system isn't converting NOx efficiently enough, based on inlet vs. outlet sensor readings. It's a High severity fault that can escalate toward an inducement derate if not resolved. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always starts SCR efficiency diagnosis at the DEF tank, not the sensors - it's the fastest, cheapest thing to rule out and it resolves a surprising share of these calls on its own.
causes: Diluted, contaminated, or expired DEF
A fluid quality issue rather than a mechanical or electrical fault - even a healthy SCR system can't hit conversion targets with bad DEF.
Clogged or uneven DEF doser spray pattern
A mechanical restriction that reduces effective NOx conversion despite good DEF quality.
Aging or degraded NOx sensors
An electrical/sensor accuracy issue that can either cause a false efficiency reading or reflect a genuinely developing catalyst problem.
Degraded SCR catalyst
A true mechanical/aftertreatment failure where the catalyst itself has lost conversion capacity, often from age or thermal exposure.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 and test DEF quality with a refractometer, since diluted or contaminated DEF is the single most common cause of this fault.
Compare inlet and outlet NOx sensor readings side by side under steady-state driving conditions to confirm a genuine conversion gap.
Inspect the DEF doser injector for a clogged or uneven spray pattern using the OEM spray test procedure.
Check for exhaust leaks between the inlet and outlet NOx sensors, since fresh air infiltration can throw off the calculated conversion efficiency.
If DEF, doser, and exhaust integrity all check out normal, the SCR catalyst itself may be degraded and require professional inspection.
symptoms: Check engine light with SCR system warning message
No immediate power loss at this stage, but a countdown risk if ignored
Possible slightly elevated DEF consumption
Companion NOx sensor or DEF quality codes may also be present

← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 1569 FMI 31 indicates an engine protection derate condition. The ECM has limited engine power to protect critical components due to an active fault.
Symptoms
Reduced engine power
Limited vehicle speed
Check engine light illuminated
Possible shutdown warning
Cause
SPN 1569 FMI 31 is typically triggered when a critical engine fault has occurred. This may include high coolant temperature, low oil pressure, aftertreatment system issues, or DEF system faults.
Can You Keep Driving?
Driving may be possible at reduced power, but continued operation without diagnosing the underlying fault may lead to further engine damage.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Will SPN 1569 FMI 31 clear on its own once the engine cools down?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: The derate condition may clear if a temperature-related trigger drops back within range, but the underlying problem will likely cause the code to return under similar operating conditions. Clearing codes without repairing the root cause is not a solution.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Can SPN 1569 FMI 31 appear without any other fault codes?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: It's uncommon but possible if the triggering code was already cleared or if the protection activated from a parameter that was briefly out of range. In those cases, reviewing freeze-frame data and inactive code history in Cummins Insite is important.

troubleshooting_faq.question: Does engine protection derate indicate the engine is already damaged?
troubleshooting_faq.answer: Not necessarily �?the system is designed to prevent damage by reducing load before a threshold that would cause harm. Whether damage occurred depends on how long and how severely the protected condition was present. A shop inspection is warranted to assess component condition.

procedures_full.overview: A general engine-protection derate is active. The ECM has pulled power to protect the engine because another monitored parameter — coolant temp, oil pressure, aftertreatment, or boost — is out of range. SPN 1569/FMI 31 tells you a derate is on; it does not by itself say why.
procedures_full.severity_action: Power derate likely — plan to stop soon
causes: Aftertreatment fault (DPF/DEF/SCR) commanding a derate
High coolant temperature or low coolant level
Low oil pressure protection
Boost/turbo or intake-air fault the ECM is guarding against
first_moves: Read the COMPANION active codes — SPN 1569 alone won't tell you the trigger; the partner code will.
Check the dash: coolant temp, oil pressure, and DEF/check-engine lamps.
If gauges are normal, suspect an aftertreatment-driven derate and inspect for DPF/DEF codes.
Don't keep pushing a derated truck under load — it can escalate to a no-start or engine damage.
common_misdiagnoses: Treating 1569 as the root cause instead of reading the companion fault that triggered it.
Assuming it's always emissions — overheating and low oil pressure trigger the same derate flag.
Clearing the derate without addressing the underlying parameter that's out of range.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1569 FMI 31 means Cummins engine protection has tripped shutdown or severe derate. Find and repair the underlying fault with INSITE before clearing.
causes: Coolant over-temperature or failed coolant sensor
High coolant temp or erratic sensor input triggers shutdown to prevent head gasket or piston damage.
Low oil pressure or failed oil pressure sensor
Oil pressure below calibrated minimum at RPM causes immediate protection activation.
Turbo overspeed or charge-air over-temp protection
Boost overspeed or high turbine inlet temp can arm shutdown on tuned or restricted exhaust trucks.
steps: Connect Cummins INSITE or Noregon JPRO and read the full active fault list — SPN 1569 is a result code, not the root cause.
Check coolant level, oil level, and oil pressure at idle (target 25–40 PSI on most X15/ISX at operating temp).
Verify coolant temp sensor plausibility against a mechanical gauge — erratic readings above 220°F trigger protection.
Inspect turbo oil supply line and charge-air cooler for leaks that could cause over-temp or overspeed protection.
After root fault repair, use INSITE to verify protection status cleared before attempting restart.
symptoms: Red stop engine lamp or flashing shutdown warning
Engine shuts down or refuses to restart after stop
Severe power derate before shutdown on some calibrations
Active protection fault stacked with coolant, oil, or turbo codes
INSITE shows Engine Protection Shutdown active
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 1569 FMI 31: Engine Protection Shutdown Active

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1569 FMI 31 means engine protection is actively cutting torque in response to a separate underlying fault - find and fix the accompanying code.
causes: High coolant temperature triggering thermal protection
Overheating is one of the most frequent derate triggers.
Low engine oil pressure
Insufficient lubrication pressure triggers an aggressive protective derate.
Excessive DPF soot load
A filter loaded beyond its safe threshold forces a performance limit.
steps: Pull the full active fault list - SPN 1569 never appears alone.
Prioritize checking coolant temp, oil pressure, and DPF soot load codes first.
Check for SCR inducement codes if the derate feels gradual rather than sudden.
Review fault history timeline to see which code logged first.
Fix the root-cause code directly rather than attempting to clear SPN 1569 itself.
symptoms: Noticeable, often severe power loss
Red warning lamp typically active
Truck limited to a low fixed speed
Always accompanied by a more specific fault code
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 1569 FMI 31: Engine Protection Torque Derate

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1569 FMI 31 means the ECM has cut torque to protect the engine from an unresolved fault. It's a Critical code, but the real fix is finding and repairing whatever triggering fault set alongside it.
causes: Active DEF quality or SCR system fault
A mechanical/aftertreatment issue - poor DEF quality or a failing SCR component triggers the engine's protection strategy to limit emissions impact.
Low engine oil pressure or high coolant temperature
A genuine mechanical protection trigger, where the ECM derates torque specifically to reduce heat and load on a stressed engine.
NOx sensor circuit fault
An electrical/sensor issue that, left unresolved, escalates into the same protection-level derate as a true emissions failure.
Multiple stacked companion faults
A combination issue where fixing one trigger reveals another that was masked underneath it.
steps: Connect Volvo Tech Tool (PTT) and pull the complete active and inactive fault list - SPN 1569 will always be accompanied by the actual triggering fault.
Sort the fault list by timestamp to identify which code set first, since that's almost always the real root cause driving the derate.
Check common triggers first: DEF quality, NOx sensor faults, low oil pressure, or high coolant temperature, since these are the most frequent causes of a protection derate.
Once the root fault is identified and repaired, clear all codes and perform a road test while monitoring for the derate code returning.
If the derate persists after the primary fault is cleared, check for a secondary fault that only appears once the first is resolved - some ECMs stack protection triggers.
symptoms: Noticeable and sudden loss of power under acceleration or load
Amber or red warning lamp with a torque limitation message on the dash
Engine feels 'capped' well below normal power output regardless of throttle input
One or more additional fault codes active alongside this one
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 1569 FMI 31: Engine Protection Torque Derate

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1569 FMI 31 means the engine protection system is actively cutting torque in response to a separate underlying fault - find and fix the accompanying code, not this one.
causes: High coolant temperature triggering thermal protection
Overheating is one of the most frequent reasons the ECM invokes a protective derate.
Low engine oil pressure
Insufficient lubrication pressure triggers an aggressive derate to prevent bearing or component damage.
Excessive DPF soot load
A filter that's loaded beyond its safe threshold forces a performance limit until it's cleared.
SCR inducement escalation
Unresolved DEF quality or dosing faults progress through inducement stages, eventually invoking this derate.
steps: Pull the full active fault list on a scan tool - SPN 1569 never appears alone, so identify the specific accompanying code causing the derate.
Prioritize investigating coolant temperature, oil pressure, and DPF soot load codes first, since these are the most common derate triggers.
Check for any DEF/SCR inducement codes if the derate feels gradual rather than sudden, since inducement derates ramp up in stages.
Review the ECM's fault history timeline to see which code logged first - that's almost always the true root cause.
Address the root-cause code directly rather than attempting to clear or bypass SPN 1569 itself.
symptoms: Noticeable, often severe loss of power
Red stop lamp typically active alongside the amber warning
Truck may be limited to a low fixed speed or unable to maintain highway speed on grades
Always accompanied by at least one other, more specific fault code

field_evidence.title: 2016 Freightliner Cascadia Forced Regen Failure SPN 4077 FMI 14
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2016 Freightliner Cascadia can experience forced regeneration failures indicated by the diagnostic trouble code SPN 4077 FMI 14. This issue generally relates to problems with the dosing block or injector during the forced regen process. Common problems in the Cascadia include forced regen interruptions and malfunctioning injector dosing blocks, which contribute to incomplete regeneration cycles. Even after replacing components such as the doser block and the 7th injector, carbon buildup may still cause the regen to fail. To address this issue, it is important to thoroughly clean the injectors and carefully inspect the wiring harnesses for any damage or poor connections. Additionally, verifying that the regen system’s sensors and pressure lines are clear helps maintain proper function.

Both issues can be linked to disruptions in sensor wiring harnesses or connectors located near the Engine Control Module (ECM). It is important to check whether any programming resets have reversed the DEF delete modifications, as such reversions can trigger these fault codes. procedures_full.overview: FMI 31 is the condition-exists class on the DEF heater relay, indicating the relay state is outside expected parameters. Failed relay, open heater circuit, blown fuse, failed tank or line heater element, and connector corrosion from urea are the primary causes. Winter faults after relay contact failure and line heater open circuits are documented patterns. Urea-contaminated connectors at the tank and line heaters are a documented cause of intermittent heater faults. Replacing the DEF tank assembly without proving relay and element integrity is the most expensive misdiagnosis on this fault.
causes: Failed relay — relay contact failure in cold weather
Open heater circuit — open in tank or line heater circuit
Blown fuse — fuse in heater circuit
Failed tank or line heater element — open element resistance
Connector corrosion from urea — urea contamination corroding heater connectors
steps: Single Action Gate — Confirm Ambient and DEF Temperature Context

Confirm ambient temperature and DEF temperature context. DEF heater faults in cold ambient conditions are expected to be active — the heater system is designed to warm frozen DEF. Confirm whether the fault is in a context where the heater should be active before any component diagnosis.
Binary Decision Gate — Command Heater and Measure Relay Output Voltage

Command the DEF heater and measure voltage at the heater feeds. Relay output voltage present with no heater response confirms an open heater element or circuit. No relay output voltage with a confirmed command confirms a relay or feed circuit fault.
Override Manager — Element Resistance Checks

Measure tank and line heater element resistance per OEM specification. An open element resistance confirms element failure. Current draw tests identify open elements when resistance measurement is not practical. Compare element resistance to OEM specification for the specific heater component.
Safety Interceptor — Urea-Contaminated Connector Inspection

Inspect heater connectors at the tank and line heaters for urea contamination. Urea-contaminated connectors create intermittent heater faults that appear as relay or element failures. Clean or replace urea-contaminated connectors before any component replacement.
Resume Point — Relay Center and Fuse Inspection

Inspect the relay center and fuse for the DEF heater circuit. A blown fuse or failed relay contact prevents heater operation regardless of element condition. Replace fuse and relay before element replacement if feed circuit faults are found.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Heater Operation Confirmation

After repair, verify DEF heater operation in cold ambient conditions. Confirm DEF temperature rises appropriately with heater active. Monitor for return of FMI 31 over extended cold-weather operation.
Repair Ledger Output — Relay, Fuse, Harness, or Element Decision

Replace relay or fuse if feed circuit fault is confirmed. Repair harness or connector if open circuit or urea contamination is found. Replace tank header heater or line heaters if element failure is confirmed. Do not replace DEF tank assembly without element and circuit proof.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace relay if contact failure is confirmed.
2 . Replace blown fuse in heater circuit.
3 . Repair urea-contaminated connector terminals.
4 . Replace tank header heater if element failure is confirmed.
5 . Replace line heaters if element failure is confirmed.
6 . Do not replace DEF tank assembly without element and circuit proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF heater operation in cold ambient conditions after repair.
Verify DEF temperature rises appropriately with heater active.
Confirm SPN 4077 FMI 31 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of DEF heater fault over extended cold-weather operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect DEF heater connectors for urea contamination at every major aftertreatment service.
✓ Inspect relay center for contact failure at every major service.
✓ Inspect heater circuit fuse at every major service.
✓ Address DEF leaks near heater connectors promptly to prevent urea contamination.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity
Medium. In freeze conditions dosing may be inhibited until heaters restore. Address before cold-weather operation to prevent DEF dosing inhibition.
symptoms: DEF heater relay fault active
DEF tank heater not working
Cold weather DEF code
Frozen DEF lines indication
DEF dosing inhibited in cold conditions

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 32 - Loss of Switch Ignition Power Test
dd_procedures.overview: This fault code indicates a loss of Switched Ignition Power to the Transmission Electronic Control Unit. When troubleshooting an Inactive code, See "Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode"
causes: Ignition switch is turned off during operation Ignition power is lost during operation
steps: A. Measure batter voltage. Visually inspect the batteries, inline fuse, power, ground supplies to TECU. Key off. Inspect starter/battery and inline fuse holder connections for integrity. Measure voltage across batteries. If voltage is 11 to 13 volts on a 12-volt system or 22 to 26 on a 24-volt system, proceed with battery load test. Repair or replace batteries as required. Go to Step B If voltage is outside of range, repair or replace batteries and charging system as required. Repeat this step.

B. Verify proper ground path at 4-way diagnostic port. Locate diagnostic port on Transmission Harness. Key on. Measure voltage between Pin C and the battery negative post. If voltage between Pin C and battery negative post is 0.70 volts or less, Go to Step C If voltage is outside of range, repair battery ground supply to TECU. Repeat test.

C. Measure battery voltage at 4-way diagnostic port. Locate diagnostic port on Transmission Harness. Key on. Measure voltage between Pin B and Pin C. If voltage is within 0.6 volts of battery voltage, Go to Step D If voltage is outside of range, repair battery power supply to TECU. Fuse may be blown. Repeat test.

D. Measure ignition voltage at 4-way diagnostic port. Key on. Measure voltage between Pin A and Pin C. If voltage is within 0.6 volts of battery voltage, Go to Step V If voltage is outside of range, repair ignition power supply to TECU. Fuse may be blown. Repeat test.

V. Verify repair. Drive vehicle and attempt to reset codes. Retrieve codes. See "Fault Code Retrieval/Clearing" If code 32 is Inactive, This code indicates a loss of ignition switched power to the TECU during operation. Verify the key was not turned off during operation. Inspect ignition circuit for intermittent open.

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 67: Gen1 ECA Ignition Voltage
procedures_full.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with an Electronic Clutch Actuator (ECA) that controls the position of the clutch assembly. The ECA requires a 12-volt ignition supply from the Transmission Control Unit (TCU) via the Transmission Harness to initiate ECA operation when the key is on. Fault Code 67 indicates an issue with the ignition supply voltage to the ECA.
procedures_full.detection: After power up, the ECA monitors the ignition voltage from the TCU. If the ECA loses ignition voltage, but maintains battery voltage and High Integrity Link (HIL) communication, that information is broadcast to the TCU and the fault code sets Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 3 – Voltage Above Normal or Shorted High: ECA ignition voltage is shorted high for 2 seconds during key on operation. FMI 4 – Voltage Below Normal or Shorted Low: ECA ignition voltage is shorted to ground or open for 2 seconds or longer during key on operation.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: All FMIs: Ignition voltage signal is within range for 6 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: All FMIs: “F” flashes in gear display. Service light flashes (if equipped). Engine does crank but the transmission cannot engage a start gear from neutral. If failure occurs during operation transmission shift quality is not affected by the fault until the vehicle ignition switch is turned off and TCU powers down. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive All FMIs: Ignition voltage signal is within range for 6 seconds.
procedures_full.possible_causes: ALL FMIs: Transmission Harness Damage to wiring between the TCU and ECA Bent, spread, corroded or loose terminals Wiring shorted to ground or open ECA Internal failure TCU Internal failure Vehicle Harness Wiring shorted to ground or shorted to power Component Identification 1.
