procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 32: Loss of Switched Ignition Voltage
procedures_full.overview: The Medium Duty 4-Speed EV Transmission is equipped with a Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) and requires a key on battery voltage ignition supply. The ignition voltage initiates TECU operation at and during key on. The ignition voltage circuit is contained within the 38-Way TECU Vehicle Harness Connector. This fault code indicates a loss of Switched Ignition Power to the TECU.
procedures_full.detection: The TECU monitors Ignition Power during normal operation. If Ignition power is lost to the TECU during operation a fault is logged.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 2 – Data Erratic: TECU has lost ignition voltage for 2 seconds or longer. J1939 devices are still communicating with the TECU.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: FMI 2: TECU detects ignition voltage for 2 seconds more.
procedures_full.fallback: FMI 2 Service light flashes (if equipped). Motor may not operate. Transmission may not engage a gear from neutral. Transmission may not attempt to shift. Until the fault becomes inactive, driver may have to shut off motor with transmission gear. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive FMI 2: TECU detects ignition voltage for 2 seconds more.
procedures_full.possible_causes: All FMIs Ignition switch keyed off during operation Ignition switch failure Vehicle Harness Wiring shorted to ground or open Terminals bent, spread, corroded or loose

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 8 - Loss of Switched Ignition Power
procedures_full.overview: The Hybrid Control Module (HCM) is mounted to the transmission and contains all of the software to control both the hybrid power electronics as well as the transmission operation. The HCM ignition power is a fused, single 12-volt feed that runs through the HCM 38-Way Vehicle Connector.
procedures_full.detection: The following preconditions must be met before the system detects the fault: Output Shaft speed must be greater than 0 RPM.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: The following conditions must be met to set the fault code Active: FMI 4 is set when the HCM loses ignition power during operation for 2 seconds or greater. Note: When troubleshooting an Inactive code refer to the Product Diagnostic Mode (PDM) .
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: Only Inactive faults can be cleared from the TECU or HCM history using ServiceRanger. The TECU automatically clears the faults from history after 200 hours. The HCM automatically clears a fault from history after that fault has been Inactive for 200 hours.
procedures_full.fallback: When Fault Code 8 is set the following conditions occurs: Amber “Check Hybrid” light illuminates only if the vehicle is moving. Fault is stored in HCM memory. Red “Service” light illuminates and an “F” flashes in the gear display, if the fault occurs prior to power up. Fault is stored in Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) memory due to lack of communication with the HCM. If fault occurs while the vehicle is moving, the transmission remains in place and the clutch opens when the vehicle comes to an idle. The clutch closes and the vehicle will operate in 1st and reverse from stop. If this fault occurs at power up, the vehicle does not crank. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive Only Inactive faults can be cleared from the TECU or HCM history using ServiceRanger. The TECU automatically clears the faults from history after 200 hours. The HCM automatically clears a fault from history after that fault has been Inactive for 200 hours.
procedures_full.possible_causes: This fault code can be caused by any of the following: FMI 4 Ignition Power Supply to HCM HCM

procedures_full.eaton_fault_code: Fault Code 32 - Loss of Switch Ignition Power Test
procedures_full.overview: This fault code indicates a loss of Switched Ignition Power to the Transmission Electronic Control Unit. When troubleshooting an Inactive code, See "Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode"
procedures_full.detection: The TECU monitors Ignition Power during normal operation. If Ignition power is lost to the TECU during operation a fault is logged.
procedures_full.fallback: This fault causes an In-Place fallback while moving.

steps.A:
A. Measure batter voltage. Visually inspect the batteries, inline fuse, power, ground supplies to TECU. 
 Key off. 
 Inspect starter/battery and inline fuse holder connections for integrity. 
 Measure voltage across batteries. 
 If voltage is 11 to 13 volts on a 12-volt system or 22 to 26 on a 24-volt system, proceed with battery load test. Repair or replace batteries as required. Go to Step B 
 If voltage is outside of range, repair or replace batteries and charging system as required. Repeat this step.
steps.B:
B. Verify proper ground path at 4-way diagnostic port. 
 Locate diagnostic port on Transmission Harness. 
 Key on. 
 Measure voltage between Pin C and the battery negative post. 
 If voltage between Pin C and battery negative post is 0.70 volts or less, Go to Step C 
 If voltage is outside of range, repair battery ground supply to TECU. Repeat test.
steps.C:
C. Measure battery voltage at 4-way diagnostic port. 
 Locate diagnostic port on Transmission Harness. 
 Key on. 
 Measure voltage between Pin B and Pin C. 
 If voltage is within 0.6 volts of battery voltage, Go to Step D 
 If voltage is outside of range, repair battery power supply to TECU. Fuse may be blown. Repeat test.
steps.D:
D. Measure ignition voltage at 4-way diagnostic port. 
 Key on. 
 Measure voltage between Pin A and Pin C. 
 If voltage is within 0.6 volts of battery voltage, Go to Step V 
 If voltage is outside of range, repair ignition power supply to TECU. Fuse may be blown. Repeat test.
steps.V:
V. Verify repair. 
 Drive vehicle and attempt to reset codes. 
 Retrieve codes. See "Fault Code Retrieval/Clearing" 
 If code 32 is Inactive, This code indicates a loss of ignition switched power to the TECU during operation. Verify the key was not turned off during operation. Inspect ignition circuit for intermittent open.

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 28: J1939 Auxiliary I/O Message
dd_procedures.overview: The Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) receives the Auxiliary Input/Output (I/O) message over the J1939 Data Link. This information is used to determine transmission operation.
causes: Vehicle Components Vehicle ECU(s) J1939 Data Link Additional Tools None
steps: A. Check for Active or Inactive fault codes. Set vehicle parking brake and chock wheels. Record the transmission fault codes, FMIs, occurrences, and timestamps from the Service Activity Report created during the Diagnostic Procedure. If Fault Code 28 FMI 9 is Inactive and there are other Active vehicle or transmission fault codes, troubleshoot all Active fault codes. Go to Step V If Fault Code 28 FMI 9 is Inactive, Go to Step B If Fault Code 28 FMI 9 is Active, refer to OEM guidelines regarding Auxiliary I/O message repair or replacement. Go to Step V

B. Use Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode to locate intermittent failures. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Place transmission in PD Mode. Reference Identifying a Problem in PD Mode . Note: Transmission does not enter PD Mode when Active fault codes exist. Note: The vehicle J1939 Data Link and connectors between the vehicle Auxiliary I/O message ECU and TECU is OEM proprietary. Refer to OEM wiring diagrams, harness routing, connector view and pin locations. Wiggle the J1939 Data Link and connections between vehicle Auxiliary I/O message ECU and 38-Way TECU Vehicle Harness Connector. Look for signs of rubbing or chafing. Exit PD Mode by powering down. Notice Allow 2-3 minutes for the TECU to perform a complete power-down sequence before proceeding. If Fault Code 28 FMI 2 became Active while wiggling the J1939 Data Link, refer to OEM guidelines for repair or replacement of harness. Go to Step V If Fault Code 28 is Inactive, no fault was found. The intermittent nature of the fault makes it likely that the problem is in the J1939 Data Link between the 38-Way TECU Vehicle Harness Connector and vehicle Auxiliary I/O message ECU Connector. Refer to OEM guidelines for repair or replacement of the J1939 Data Link. Go to Step V

V. Verify Repair. Key off. Reconnect all connectors and verify that all components are properly installed. Key on with engine off. Connect ServiceRanger. Go to “Fault Codes”. Select “Clear All Faults”. Operate vehicle and attempt to reset the fault code or duplicate the previous complaint. Check for fault codes using ServiceRanger. If no fault codes set and the vehicle operates properly, test complete. If Fault Code 28 sets Active, Go to Step A If a fault code other than 28 sets Active, troubleshoot per See "Fault Code Isolation Procedure Index"

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically circuit failed high.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically circuit failed high.‪
steps: High Circuit Check
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Check for multiple codes.
If 1176/3, 1172/3, 100/3 and 175/3 are present, repair the open between pin 105 on the 120–pin MCM connector and the associated sensors. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If 1176/3 and 1172/3 are present, go to step 7.
If only 1176/2 is present, go to step 4.
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor.
Disconnect the 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance between pins 1 and 2 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor harness connector.

If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, repair the short to power on the circuit between pin 120 of the 120–pin MCM connector and pin 1 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor harness connector. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 5 Ω, repair the short between pins 120 and 85 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Disconnect the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor.
Measure the resistance between pins 2 and 4 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor.
If the resistance is greater than 140 Ω, replace the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 140 Ω, go to step 9.
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Measure the voltage between pin 2 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor and ground.
If the voltage is greater than 2.75 volts, repair the open circuit between pin 105 of the 120–pin MCM connector and pin 4 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the voltage is less than 2.75 volts, repair the open circuit between pin 85 of the 120–pin MCM connector and pin 2 of the Turbo Pressure/Temp Sensor. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: MBE 4000 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 83.1 SPN 1176/FMI 3 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

This error can stem from NOx sensor failures, issues with sensor wiring, or poor connections within the circuit. dd_procedures.title: SPN 4375 FMI 18 – DEF Doser Valve Response Fault
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 4375 FMI 18 – DEF Doser Valve Response Fault (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 4375 FMI 18 indicates that the DEF doser valve is not responding as commanded by the ECM. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and means the aftertreatment system cannot accurately control DEF delivery to the SCR catalyst, which will affect emissions performance and can lead to a derate condition if not resolved.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF or SCR warning light illuminated 
Engine derate condition possible 
Reduced aftertreatment system performance 
May appear alongside other DEF dosing related codes
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM sends a command to the DEF doser valve and does not receive the expected response. Common causes include:
Stuck or seized doser valve due to DEF crystallization 
Electrical fault at the doser valve solenoid 
Damaged or corroded wiring harness to the valve 
Failed doser valve unable to open or close correctly 
DEF contamination causing valve to stick 
ECM communication fault with the doser valve circuit
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but without proper doser valve response the SCR system cannot control DEF delivery accurately. The engine will likely enter a derate condition if the fault persists. Address this promptly to prevent further aftertreatment damage.
Recommended Action
Inspect the DEF doser valve for signs of crystallization or physical damage. Check the valve wiring and connector for corrosion or damage. If the valve is crystallized it may be cleanable but replacement is often the more reliable fix. Have the valve solenoid tested for proper electrical response before condemning the part.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4375 FMI 18 mean?
 
It means the DEF doser valve is not responding correctly to ECM commands, preventing accurate control of DEF delivery to the SCR catalyst.
 
 
What causes SPN 4375 FMI 18?
 
The most common causes are a stuck or crystallized doser valve, an electrical fault at the valve solenoid, or damaged wiring in the doser valve circuit.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4375 FMI 18?
 
Short distances may be possible but without proper doser valve function the SCR system cannot operate correctly and a derate condition is likely to follow.
 
 
Will SPN 4375 FMI 18 cause a derate?
 
Yes. If the ECM cannot control DEF dosing through the valve the SCR system will fail to meet emissions thresholds and a derate will be triggered.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4375 FMI 18?
 
Inspect, clean, or replace the DEF doser valve and verify wiring integrity. Once the valve responds correctly to ECM commands and the SCR system confirms proper DEF delivery the code should clear.
 
 
Related codes

SPN 4094 FMI 18 
SPN 3362 FMI 1 
SPN 3363 FMI 16

steps: DEF dozaj valfini kristalleşme veya fiziksel hasar belirtileri açısından inceleyin.

[FMI 0 katalog] Aktüatörün komut aldığı halde hareket etmediğini doğrulayın; mekanik sıkışma arayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

[FMI 4 katalog] Aktüatör besleme hattında gerilim düşüklüğü ve şasi teması arayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

[FMI 12 katalog] Aktüatör sürücü modülünün beslemesini ve haberleşmesini kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

field_evidence.title: 2009 Freightliner Cascadia Intake Air Pressure Sensor Code SPN 3563 FMI 4
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2009 Freightliner Cascadia frequently experiences issues related to the intake air pressure sensor, which can lead to engine performance problems. One common diagnostic code encountered is SPN 3563 FMI 4, which specifically points to a low or shorted voltage condition from the Engine Intake Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) sensor. This sensor code can stem from several underlying causes. Damage or corrosion in the MAP sensor wiring harness may disrupt voltage signals. Additionally, leaks in the intake manifold can alter sensor accuracy, contributing to faults. Voltage irregularities detected on the sensor output are often an indicator of these issues. To address Code SPN 3563 FMI 4, it is advisable to inspect the MAP sensor wiring harness thoroughly for any signs of wear or corrosion.

field_evidence.title: 2013 Freightliner Cascadia SPN 679-FMI 7 Pressure Valve Issue
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2013 Freightliner Cascadia is known to experience pressure limiting valve failures, particularly indicated by the diagnostic code SPN 679-FMI 7. This fault code signals that the pressure limiting valve is failing to close properly, which can result in a noticeable loss of power once the engine warms up. This issue in Cascadia models often stems from the valve's inability to regulate pressure as expected. However, replacing the valve alone does not always resolve the problem. Additional factors may contribute, such as potential faults within the electronic control module (ECM), wiring harness problems, or issues in the transmission control system and hydraulic pressure sensors. field_evidence.excerpt: The 2014 Freightliner Cascadia equipped with the DD15 engine may display the SPN 70 FMI 19 engine code, which relates to a turbocharger boost pressure fault. procedures_full.overview: The Transmission Control Module (TCM) receives the vehicle’s Brake Pedal Position message from a vehicle Electronic Control Unit (ECU) over the Primary Data Link (J1939A). This information is used to determine transmission operation.
procedures_full.detection: The TCM monitors Brake Pedal Position messages. If messages are not available or are invalid, the fault is set Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 13 - Out of Calibration: Brake Pedal Position message not available for 10 seconds. FMI 19 – Received Network Data in Error: Brake Pedal Position messages invalid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: FMI 13, 19: Brake Pedal Position messages available and valid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: FMI 13, 19: If Fault Code 156, 161 and 163 are all Active: Amber warning lamp on Urge to Move and Creep Mode prohibited Hill Start Aid prohibited Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive FMI 13, 19: Brake Pedal Position messages available and valid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.possible_causes: FMI 13, 19: Vehicle Components Brake Pedal Position message not enabled Other vehicle ECU(s) faulted Vehicle Harness - Primary Data Link (J1939A) Wiring shorted to power, shorted to ground or open Terminals bent, spread, corroded, or loose Note: Refer to OEM for troubleshooting a failed system.

steps.A:
A. Check for Active or Inactive fault codes. 
 Set vehicle parking brake and chock wheels. 
 Record transmission fault codes, FMIs, occurrences, and timestamps from Service Activity Report created during the Diagnostic Procedure. 
 If Fault Code 156 is Inactive and there are other Active vehicle or transmission fault codes, troubleshoot all Active fault codes. Go to Step V 
 If Fault Code 156 FMI 9, 19 is Active or Inactive, refer to OEM guidelines for repair of the vehicle Brake Pedal Position message (SPN 521). Go to Step V 
 If Fault Code 156 FMI 13 is Active, refer to OEM and enable vehicle Brake Pedal Position message (SPN 521). Go to Step V 
 If Fault Code 156 FMI 13 is Inactive, Go to Step V
steps.V:

 Key off. 
 Reconnect all connectors and verify all components are properly installed. 
 Key on with engine off. 
 Connect ServiceRanger. 
 Go To “Fault Codes”. 
 Select “Clear All Faults”. 
 Operate vehicle and attempt to reset the fault code or duplicate the previous complaint. 
 Check for fault codes using ServiceRanger. 
 If no fault codes set and vehicle operates properly, test complete. 
 If Fault Code 156 sets Active, Go to Step A 
 If a fault code other than 156 sets Active, troubleshoot per Fault Code Isolation Procedure Index .

Code SPN-3510 points to a sensor supply voltage problem, which often arises from faults in the wiring or the sensor itself. Meanwhile, SPN-723 relates to errors in the engine speed sensor signal. Both issues can be linked to disruptions in sensor wiring harnesses or connectors located near the Engine Control Module (ECM). It is important to check whether any programming resets have reversed the DEF delete modifications, as such reversions can trigger these fault codes. procedures_full.overview: The Transmission Control Module (TCM) receives the vehicle's Engine Speed message from a vehicle Electronic Control Unit (ECU) over the Primary Data Link (J1939A). This information is used to determine transmission operation. The TCM also receives the Engine Speed message over the Secondary Data Link (J1939B). The Secondary Data Link is used in the event that the Primary Data Link is inoperative and allows the transmission to operate in a degraded mode. The Primary Data Link (J1939A) is connected to the TCM at the 20-Way TCM Vehicle Harness Connector. The Secondary Data Link (J1939B) is connected to the TCM at the 20-Way TCM Body Harness Connector.
procedures_full.detection: The TCM monitors Engine Speed messages on the Secondary Data Link (J1939B). If messages are not received or are invalid, the fault is set Active.

procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: FMI 9, 13, 19: Engine Speed messages received and valid for 10 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: FMI 9, 13, 19: Amber warning lamp on If Fault Code 115, 165, 171, or 185 is Active: Coast Mode and Neutral Coast prohibited Urge to Move and Creep Mode prohibited Inertia Brake activation prohibited Upshifts prohibited Clutch engagements prohibited Non-Neutral modes prohibited PTO mode prohibited Hill Start Aid prohibited If vehicle is moving: Red stop lamp on Note: Vehicle may have additional fallback modes. SPN_1073.description_en: Internal brake valve 2 drive circuit short circuit
causes: Short to Battery: Solenoid coil wire or connector pin chafed against 12/24V supply line
Open Ground Path: High-side driver sees no return path, causing floating voltage above threshold
Failed Solenoid Coil: Coil internal short or open winding alters back-EMF, raising sensed voltage
ECM Driver Damage: Internal MOSFET shorted high due to previous overcurrent or thermal stress
Advanced Technical Analysis The ECM microcontroller executes a
German OEM specifications typically require 12V nominal with ±10% tolerance for reliable solenoid operation
Circuit analysis reveals that intermittent electrical breakdowns often occur at connector interfaces where moisture ingress creates variable resistance paths
The ECM employs sophisticated debouncing algorithms with 50-100ms filtering periods to prevent false triggering from electrical noise

SPN_1073.pgn_description: NOTE - Retarder can be disabled by commanding a torque limit of 0%. Use of the limit mode allows the use of the retarder only up to the limit specified in the request. This can be used to permit retarding of up to 50%, for example, if that limit is required by some device such as an EBS, or it can disable the use of the retarder by others, as when an ABS controller detects wheel slip. Note that the 10 ms transmission repetition rate is intended for temporary powertrain control (P32 of SPN 3350).

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically a short to power.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically a short to power.‪
steps: Short to Power Check
Disconnect the Brake Gate solenoid.
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Measure the voltage between pin 1 of the Brake Gate harness connector and ground.
If the voltage is greater than 11.5 volts, repair the short to power between pin 1 of the Brake Gate harness connector and pin 96 of the 120–pin MCM connector. See Figure
"Brake Gate"
. Refer to "81.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Figure 1. Brake Gate
If the voltage is less than 11.5 volts, go to step 4.
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the 120–pin MCM connector.
Measure the resistance between pins 1 and 2 of the Brake Gate harness connector.
If the resistance is greater than 5Ω, reconnect the 120–pin MCM connector and repeat steps 2 through 6
. If the results are the same, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center (313–592–5800).
If the resistance is less than 5Ω, repair the short between pins 1 and 2 of the Brake Gate harness connector and pins 91 and 96 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "81.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: MBE 4000 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 81.1 SPN 1073/FMI 3 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

procedures_full.overview: This fault code indicates that the Jake Brake Stage 2 circuit failed low.‪
causes: This fault code indicates that the Jake Brake Stage 2 circuit failed low.‪
steps: Short to Ground Check
Disconnect the front injector valve cover harness.
Measure resistance between pin 12 and ground on the front injector valve cover harness connector. If you are using J-48671–10 , measure across the rear Jake pins.

If the resistance is greater than 15 Ω, repair short to ground between pin 12 of the front injector valve cover harness connector and pin 32 of the 120–pin MCM connector. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the less is greater than 5 Ω, go to step 3.
Remove the upper valve cover.
Disconnect the Front Jake Brake Harness
Measure resistance between either terminal on the Jake Brake solenoid and ground.
If the resistance is less than 5 ohms, replace the Jake Brake solenoid. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is greater than 5 Ω, repair the short to ground between pins 11 and 12 of the front injector valve cover harness. Refer to "83.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.

procedures_full.overview: This fault code indicates that the Jake Brake Stage 2 circuit failed open.‪

steps: Open Circuit Check
Check for multiple codes.
If SPN 1073/5 and SPN 2791/5 are active repair the open between the pin 62 of the 120–pin MCM connector and the front Jake Brake and fan control solenoids.
If only SPN 1073/5 is active, go to step 2.

Remove the upper valve cover.
Measure the resistance across the front Jake Brake solenoid.
If the resistance is greater than 15 Ω, replace the Jake Brake solenoid. Refer to "83.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the resistance is less than 15 Ω, repair the open between pins 11 and 12 of the front injector valve cover harness connector and the Jake Brake solenoid. Refer to "83.2.1.1 Verify Repairs".

Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.

Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

steps: Temperature Check

Note: Prior to performing this diagnostic procedure the engine must have a minimum of a three hour soak (cool down).
Connect DDDL 7.0.
Turn the ignition ON (key ON, engine OFF).
Monitor the intake manifold, engine oil, engine coolant, EGR and turbo outlet temperature parameters.
Are any of the temperature readings 15°F greater or less than that of the other sensors?

Review the intake manifold, engine oil, engine coolant, EGR and turbo outlet temperature parameters on snapshot.
Are any of the temperature readings 20°F greater or less than that of the other sensors?

procedures_full.overview: SPN 2629 FMI 0 indicates compressor inlet temperature above the calibrated limit. Hot-air reversion from poor duct sealing, engine-bay heat soak, restricted fresh-air path, sensor bias high, and extreme ambient load are the primary causes. Missing air cleaner seals recirculating engine-bay heat are a documented pattern. Pursuing turbo hardware conclusions for a duct sealing or sensor fault is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Hot-air reversion from poor duct sealing — poor duct sealing allowing hot engine-bay air to recirculate to compressor inlet
Engine-bay heat soak — engine-bay heat soak producing elevated inlet temperature
Restricted fresh-air path — restricted fresh-air path producing elevated inlet temperature
Sensor bias high — sensor bias high producing false above-normal reading
Extreme ambient load — extreme ambient temperature and load producing elevated inlet temperature
steps: Step 1 — Sensor Correlation to Ambient

Correlate the sensor reading to ambient temperature. Cold soak near ambient is expected. A large offset between the sensor reading and ambient supports a sensor fault. Rising far above ambient at speed suggests ducting or heat issues.
Step 2 — Inspect Air Filter Housing Seals

Inspect air filter housing seals. Missing air cleaner seals recirculating engine-bay heat are a documented pattern. Inspect the air filter housing seals for missing, damaged, or improperly seated seals. Replace seals if missing or damaged.
Step 3 — Duct Integrity Check

Check duct integrity. Inspect the intake ducting from the air filter to the compressor inlet for cracks, loose connections, and missing seals. A duct integrity fault allowing hot engine-bay air to recirculate requires duct repair.
Step 4 — Cooling Package Airflow Around Inlet Path

Evaluate cooling package airflow around the inlet path. A debris-packed cooling package reducing airflow around the inlet path produces elevated inlet temperature. Inspect the cooling package for debris and restriction.
Step 5 — Sensor Replacement After Proof

Replace the sensor after proof of sensor fault. Confirm duct sealing and inlet path integrity before any sensor replacement. A sensor replaced without proof may replace a good sensor into a duct or heat fault.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Replace air filter housing seals if missing or damaged.
2 . Repair duct integrity if duct fault is confirmed.
3 . Clean cooling package if debris restriction is confirmed.
4 . Replace sensor if sensor fault is confirmed after duct and path proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm compressor inlet temperature is within specification after repair.
Verify SPN 2629 FMI 0 does not return after repair.
Confirm no power loss in heat after repair.
Monitor for return of high inlet temperature events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect air filter housing seals at every major service.
✓ Inspect intake ducting for cracks and loose connections at every major service.
✓ Inspect cooling package for debris at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High under heavy load and heat Severity
Medium to High under heavy load and heat. High compressor inlet temp is often duct sealing or sensing, not automatic turbo failure.

Compressor inlet overtemp
Hot air ingestion turbo
Derate intake temp
Power loss in heat from inlet temp fault

procedures_full.overview: This diagnosis is typically Low Air Flow.‪
causes: This diagnosis is typically Low Air Flow.‪
steps: Low Air Flow
Inspect air filter and air inlet piping to turbocharger for blockage or leaks.
If blockage or leakage is found, repair as necessary.
If no blockage or leakage is found, go to next step.

Check VPOD for the correct part number and proper air line supply installation and configuration (PWM 10 in MCM Group PGR001_Prop Valve must be configured to “Turbo control”). Is the VPOD installed and configured correctly?
Yes, go to next step.
No, correct the VPOD installation and/or configuration.
Note: Be sure to also inspect turbo inlet seal, intake manifold and EGR hoses and clamps.
Perform CAC inspection and leak test. Refer to OEM literature for procedure.
If inspection and/or leak test fails, repair as necessary.
If CAC inspection passes, go to next step.
Using the AMA service routine, select “Set fault” and perform an air mass adaptation.
Turn the ignition ON, (key ON, engine OFF).
Check EGR valve operation. Using Activate Outputs Service Routine, command PWM1 to 50% while monitoring EGR actual position. Does EGR actual position read between 47-54%?
Yes, go to next step.
No, go to step 8.
Command PWM1 to 90% while monitoring EGR actual position. Does the EGR actual position read between 87-94%?
Yes, go to step 12.
No, go to next step.
Turn the ignition OFF.
Disconnect the EGR valve harness connector.
Inspect connector for damaged, corroded or spread pins.
If damage is found, repair as necessary.
If no damaged pins are found, go to next step.
Remove the EGR valve, inspect valve for heavy soot or coolant contamination or leakage.
If contamination is found, repair root cause as necessary, and replace the EGR Valve.
If no contamination is found, replace the EGR Valve.
With Ignition ON, engine OFF, compare the intake manifold pressure to the compressor inlet pressure. Are the pressures within 0.6 psi of each other?
Yes, go to next step.
No, replace suspect sensor.
Check the inlet air Delta P Sensor, with the ignition ON (key ON engine OFF). Does the inlet air Delta P pressure read 0?
Yes, go to next step.
No, remove and inspect the inlet air Delta P sensor including the systek sensor; look for damaged O-rings or plugged orifices. If no damage is found, replace the inlet air Delta P sensor.
Start the engine.
Check the VPOD (wastegate) operation.
Using Activate Outputs Service Routine, command PWM 10 to 30%; no movement of wastegate actuator rod should be seen.
Command the PWM 10 to 70%; wastegate actuator rod should begin to move.
Command the PWM 10 to 90%; wastegate actuator rod should be fully open. Go to next step.
If the actuator fails to move, verify air supply pressure equals truck air pressure. If pressure is OK, replace the VPOD.
Check the brakegate actuator.
Using the Activate Outputs Service Routine, command SW 4 to ON then OFF.
The brakegate actuator should be fully extended when ON and fully retracted when OFF. Go to next step.
If the actuator does not operate, verify air supply. If OK, inspect the brakegate and actuator arm.
Perform a parked regeneration.
After the parked regen completes, monitor the DPF Inlet Pressure with the engine running at 1500 rpm with no load. Is the DPF Inlet Pressure greater than 2 psi?
Yes, remove and inspect DOC and DPF for blockage/obstruction. If blockage/obstruction is found, replace the suspect component as necessary.
No, obtain a DDDL log file showing the active code and contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center (313–592–5800).

dd_procedures.title: SPN 3480 FMI 16 - DPF Ash Load High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 3480 FMI 16 – DPF Ash Load High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3480 FMI 16 indicates that the ash load inside the Diesel Particulate Filter has accumulated beyond the acceptable threshold. Unlike soot, ash is a non-combustible byproduct of engine oil consumption and cannot be removed through regeneration. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and typically means the DPF requires professional cleaning or replacement.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF warning light illuminated 
Reduced engine performance 
Increased exhaust back pressure 
Regeneration cycles becoming more frequent 
Engine derate possible Regen completing but codes returning quickly
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM calculates that ash accumulation inside the DPF has exceeded the acceptable level based on engine hours and oil consumption data. Common causes include:
Normal long term ash accumulation over high mileage 
Excessive engine oil consumption accelerating ash buildup 
Wrong engine oil specification causing higher ash content 
Worn piston rings or valve seals increasing oil burning 
Extended oil change intervals contributing to higher ash deposits 
DPF approaching end of service life
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but ash cannot be burned off through regeneration like soot can. The DPF will continue to restrict exhaust flow as ash builds up, leading to increased back pressure, more frequent regens, and eventual derate. The DPF needs to be cleaned or replaced to resolve this condition.
Recommended Action
Have the DPF removed and professionally cleaned using a DPF cleaning machine to remove ash deposits. If the filter is too heavily loaded or damaged it will need to be replaced. Also investigate engine oil consumption — if the engine is burning excessive oil the root cause should be addressed to prevent rapid ash reaccumulation after cleaning.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 3480 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means the DPF has accumulated too much ash, which is a non-combustible byproduct of oil combustion that cannot be removed through normal regeneration and requires professional cleaning or filter replacement.
 
 
What causes SPN 3480 FMI 16?
 
The most common cause is normal long term ash accumulation over high mileage. Excessive engine oil consumption, wrong oil specification, or worn piston rings can accelerate ash buildup significantly.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 3480 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but ash accumulation will not improve on its own. Continued operation will lead to increased back pressure, more frequent regeneration cycles, and eventual derate.
 
 
Will SPN 3480 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. As ash continues to restrict exhaust flow through the DPF the ECM will trigger derate conditions due to excessive back pressure and reduced aftertreatment performance.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 3480 FMI 16?
 
The DPF must be removed and professionally cleaned or replaced. Simply performing a regeneration will not remove ash. Once the cleaned or new filter is reinstalled and the ECM confirms acceptable ash and back pressure levels the code should clear.
 
 
Related codes

SPN 3713 FMI 18 
SPN 3719 FMI 0 
SPN 3251 FMI 18

← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3480 FMI 16 indicates that the ash load inside the Diesel Particulate Filter has accumulated beyond the acceptable threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and typically means the DPF requires professional cleaning or replacement.

DPF warning light illuminated 
Reduced engine performance 
Increased exhaust back pressure 
Regeneration cycles becoming more frequent 
Engine derate possible Regen completing but codes returning quickly
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM calculates that ash accumulation inside the DPF has exceeded the acceptable level based on engine hours and oil consumption data. Common causes include:
Normal long term ash accumulation over high mileage 
Excessive engine oil consumption accelerating ash buildup 
Wrong engine oil specification causing higher ash content 
Worn piston rings or valve seals increasing oil burning 
Extended oil change intervals contributing to higher ash deposits 
DPF approaching end of service life

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3480 FMI 1 means HC doser fuel supply pressure is below normal during regen. Verify pump voltage, filter restriction, and mechanical pressure before replacing the doser supply module. International LT and RH Series trucks set SPN 3480 FMI 1 when regen fuel pressure cannot support the seven-point doser spray pattern. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com ties this code to clogged doser fuel filters and weak supply pumps more often than failed doser valves.
causes: Clogged HC doser fuel filter or restricted supply line
Low flow at the doser pump drops supply pressure below the moderately severe threshold during regen.
Weak HC doser supply pump
Worn pump internals cannot maintain 400+ kPa when the doser valve opens during active regen.
Air ingestion at doser fuel line fittings
Loose banjo bolts or cracked hoses introduce air that collapses pressure spikes the ECM monitors.
steps: Connect ServiceMaxx or Noregon JPRO and read SPN 3480 live pressure during a commanded regen attempt.
Verify the HC doser fuel supply pump fuse and relay, then measure supply voltage at the pump: 12.4-14.2 V during crank and regen command.
Inspect the doser fuel filter and replace if differential pressure exceeds 15 psi; prime until ServiceMaxx shows stable supply above 400 kPa.
Check for leaking doser fuel lines at the metering pump and one-way check valve—air ingestion drops pressure below FMI 1 limits.
If mechanical pressure at the test port stays low with a new filter, test pump output flow at 0.3-0.5 L/min spec and replace the HC supply pump module if below minimum.
symptoms: Check engine and HEST lamps with failed or aborted stationary regen events
SPN 3480 pressure reading below OEM minimum—often under 350 kPa on A26—in ServiceMaxx
Increasing DPF soot load percentage with SPN 4094 companion codes
White smoke or fuel smell near the doser valve during regen attempts
Progressive derate when regen cannot complete multiple times
procedures_full.source_title: International SPN 3480 FMI 1: HC Doser Fuel Supply Pressure Low

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3480 FMI 1 on Detroit DD13/DD15 engines means the hydrocarbon doser's fuel supply pressure has been below the minimum specification for an extended period. It's a high-severity fault because the doser needs that fuel pressure to inject the heat source for DPF regeneration. The hydrocarbon doser injects fuel directly into the exhaust stream to help generate the heat needed for active DPF regeneration, and it needs stable, adequate fuel pressure to do that job. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats SPN 3480 FMI 1 as a fault that demands prompt attention because a doser that can't get proper fuel pressure means regeneration events won't complete, and soot load will keep climbing in the background. The fix depends heavily on whether the truck has a two-filter or three-filter fuel system, so confirming that configuration is the first real diagnostic step.
causes: Restricted or overdue HC doser fuel filter (three-filter systems)
A dedicated filter feeding the doser circuit can plug up independently of the main engine fuel filters, starving the doser of adequate pressure.
Kinked or blocked doser fuel line or needle valve return line
Physical damage or blockage in the dedicated doser plumbing restricts flow even when the main fuel system is healthy.
Faulty fuel compensation pressure sensor
A sensor reading falsely low can trigger this fault without an actual pressure deficiency, though it's less common than a real restriction.
Weak main fuel system supply pressure
If the primary engine fuel supply itself is deficient, the doser circuit that draws from it will also run low, though this typically shows up as other fuel-related codes as well.
symptoms: Failed or incomplete DPF regeneration attempts
Amber dash lamp, often alongside a related regeneration fault code
Rising DPF soot load over successive drive cycles
No direct drivability symptom outside of aftertreatment performance
procedures_full.source_title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3480 FMI 1: Diagnosing Low HC Doser Fuel Supply Pressure

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3480 FMI 1 on a Cummins engine means the hydrocarbon doser fuel supply pressure is below minimum. Start with the HC doser fuel filter and supply line before testing or replacing the dosing pump. Cummins SPN 3480 FMI 1 indicates that the HC doser fuel supply pressure is reading below the ECM's calibrated lower limit during active regeneration. SPN 3480 is the HC Doser Fuel Supply Pressure parameter — monitoring the fuel supply to the hydrocarbon dosing injector used to elevate exhaust temperatures for DPF regeneration. When this pressure falls below the threshold, the dosing system cannot effectively heat the DOC and DPF, causing regeneration to fail or not initiate at all. A rising DPF soot load combined with SPN 3480 FMI 1 is a precursor to forced derate and eventual shutdown if the soot load reaches a critical percentage. Technicians at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com recommend a systematic supply-circuit approach — filter, line, pump — before any component replacement.
causes: Clogged HC doser fuel filter
The in-line fuel filter in the HC doser supply circuit becomes restricted over time, reducing fuel flow to the dosing pump below the pressure threshold required for FMI 1.
Failing HC doser fuel pump
The electric dosing fuel pump loses output pressure as its impeller or check valve wears, preventing it from reaching operating pressure during regen commands.
Restricted or kinked supply line
A pinched or incorrectly routed supply line reduces flow to the pump, producing below-normal pressure readings even when the pump itself is functional.
steps: Connect Cummins INSITE software or a Diesel Laptops diagnostic adapter to read active fault codes. Confirm SPN 3480 FMI 1 and check DPF soot load percentage and HC doser operational status in live data.

Locate the HC doser fuel filter in the supply circuit (typically a small in-line filter near the dosing pump). Remove and inspect the filter element for restriction or contamination. A heavily discolored or clogged filter is a primary cause of FMI 1.

Using a fuel pressure gauge with the correct fitting adapter, measure HC doser supply pressure with the dosing pump active during a commanded regen cycle. Compare to the specification in the Cummins service manual — typically 60–100 PSI depending on engine calibration.
Inspect the supply line from the main fuel circuit to the dosing pump for kinks, cracking, or improper routing that could restrict flow. Also inspect the dosing pump inlet screen for debris.

If supply line and filter are clear but pressure remains low, perform an HC doser pump output test using Cummins INSITE or Diesel Laptops active test function to confirm whether the pump generates rated pressure on command.
symptoms: Active regeneration failures with DPF soot load continuing to rise.
SPN 3480 FMI 1 logged alongside DPF soot load or backpressure fault codes.
Engine derate or regeneration inhibit warning on the instrument cluster.
Fuel smell from the exhaust during attempted regen cycles.
Increased DPF backpressure and possible forced parked regen requests.
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 3480 FMI 1: HC Doser Fuel Supply Pressure Below Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3480 FMI 16 means the hydrocarbon doser fuel supply pressure on Mack MP7 and MP8 engines exceeds the ECM maximum, typically above 90 psi during regeneration. Over-dosing raises DPF outlet temperature past safe limits and can trigger immediate derate or shutdown. Verify doser pressure stays within 70-85 psi before clearing the code.
causes: Stuck-open HC doser solenoid or failed pressure regulator
A solenoid that fails to close or a regulator stuck open delivers continuous fuel above 90 psi, overdosing the exhaust during regen.
Carbon-fouled doser nozzle with stuck pintle
Crystallized carbon holds the nozzle open, producing a fuel stream instead of a mist and raising exhaust temperature beyond safe limits.
Pinched or restricted doser return line raising supply pressure
A kinked return line prevents pressure relief, causing supply pressure to climb above the 85 psi maximum even with a functioning regulator.
steps: Connect Mack Premium Tech Tool and log SPN 3480 (HC doser pressure), SPN 3246 (DPF outlet temp), and SPN 3242 (DPF intake temp) during a forced regen — pressure above 90 psi with outlet temp climbing past 1,150°F confirms over-dosing.
Inspect the HC doser fuel supply line from the fuel rail to the 7th injector/doser — check for pinched lines, failed pressure regulator, or a stuck-open doser solenoid.
Install a mechanical fuel pressure gauge at the doser supply port and command a parked regen — pressure should hold 70-85 psi; readings above 95 psi indicate regulator or solenoid failure.
Remove and inspect the HC doser injector nozzle for carbon buildup or stuck pintle — spray pattern should be a fine mist, not a steady stream; clean with OEM-approved solvent or replace if dripping.
Check the doser control solenoid resistance — most Mack doser solenoids read 2-5 ohms; below 1 ohm indicates internal short causing continuous fuel flow.
Replace the pressure regulator, doser nozzle, or solenoid as needed, then perform a controlled regen confirming SPN 3480 stays below 85 psi and outlet temp remains under 1,100°F.
symptoms: HC doser fuel pressure reads above 90 psi on Mack Premium Tech Tool during regen — normal is 70-85 psi
DPF outlet temperature (SPN 3246) climbs above 1,150°F during parked regen
White or blue exhaust smoke during active regeneration
Amber aftertreatment lamp with rapid torque derate
Fuel odor from the exhaust outlet and possible visible glow on exhaust pipe at night

procedures_full.overview: FMI 18 on DEF temperature indicates the DEF is below the minimum expected temperature for normal dosing operation. Failed tank heater, coolant control valve issues on coolant-heated systems, extreme ambient cold, temperature sensor bias, and wiring to the heater are the primary causes. Winter no-dose conditions from frozen DEF and heater element failures are the most common fleet patterns. Replacing the tank header assembly without proving heater operation and sensor plausibility is the primary misdiagnosis.
causes: Failed tank heater — heater element failure
Coolant control valve fault — coolant-heated systems not supplying heat
Extreme ambient cold — DEF frozen below heater capacity
Temperature sensor bias — reading low without true low temperature
Wiring to heater — open or high-resistance heater circuit
steps: Single Action Gate — DEF Temperature vs Ambient Comparison

Compare DEF temperature reading to ambient temperature and operating history. If DEF temperature matches ambient after a cold soak, the heater has not operated. If DEF temperature is significantly below ambient during operation, the heater is not functioning.
Binary Decision Gate — Heater Command Test
Command heater operation via scan tool where supported. Verify heater activates. On coolant-heated systems, verify coolant flow to the DEF tank heater circuit.
Override Manager — Heater Circuit Power and Ground
Verify heater circuit power and ground integrity. Measure heater current draw per OEM specification. An open heater circuit or failed element produces no current draw with valid supply voltage.
Safety Interceptor — Coolant Supply Inspection
On coolant-heated DEF systems, inspect coolant supply valve and lines to the DEF tank heater. A failed coolant control valve prevents heat transfer to the DEF regardless of heater circuit integrity.
Resume Point — Temperature Sensor Plausibility
Evaluate temperature sensor plausibility. If DEF is confirmed warm by other means but sensor reads low, the sensor is biased. Compare to ambient temperature and heater operation history.
Verification Loop — Post-Repair Temperature Confirmation
After repair, verify DEF temperature rises to operating range during normal operation. Confirm dosing resumes after DEF temperature reaches threshold.
Repair Ledger Output — Tank Header or Sensor Decision
Replace tank header assembly only after heater circuit and coolant supply are proven failed. Replace temperature sensor only after heater operation is confirmed and sensor bias is proven.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Repair heater circuit power or ground faults if found.
2 . Replace heater element if current draw confirms element failure.
3 . Repair coolant control valve on coolant-heated systems if failed.
4 . Replace temperature sensor if bias is confirmed after heater operation is verified.
5 . Replace tank header assembly only after circuit and coolant supply proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF temperature rises to operating range after repair.
Verify dosing resumes after DEF temperature reaches threshold.
Confirm SPN 3515 FMI 18 does not return after repair.
Monitor SCR efficiency returns to normal after dosing resumes.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect DEF tank heater circuit at every pre-winter service.
✓ Verify coolant supply to DEF heater on coolant-heated systems before winter.
✓ Park in heated facilities in extreme cold to prevent DEF freeze.
✓ Address heater faults before winter operation begins.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium Severity

Medium. In severe cold, dosing may be inhibited until DEF thaws or heater is repaired. Address before extended cold-weather operation. A non-dosing SCR system will trigger efficiency and inducement faults.
symptoms: DEF temp low fault active
DEF tank frozen indication
Cold weather DEF code
Dosing disabled from cold DEF
SCR efficiency declining from dosing inhibit

To address Code SPN 3563 FMI 4, it is advisable to inspect the MAP sensor wiring harness thoroughly for any signs of wear or corrosion.

6.5 in the Series 60 Service Manual

Disconnect the Intake Manifold Pressure Sensor.
Inspect the Intake Manifold Pressure Sensor connector for bent, spread or corroded pins.

dd_procedures.title: Detroit Diesel SPN 3720 FMI 16 – DPF Soot Load Percent High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
SPN 3720 FMI 16 – DPF Soot Load Percent High
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 3720 FMI 16 indicates that the calculated soot load percentage inside the Diesel Particulate Filter has exceeded the acceptable threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and represents the ECM’s percentage based calculation of DPF soot loading. When this percentage rises above acceptable limits regeneration is required to prevent derate conditions and potential DPF damage.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF or regen warning light illuminated 
Regeneration request active Reduced engine performance 
Engine derate possible if soot percentage continues to rise 
May appear alongside DPF differential pressure codes
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM calculates the DPF soot load percentage has risen above the acceptable threshold based on differential pressure readings and engine operating data. Common causes include:
Frequent short trips preventing passive regeneration 
Excessive idling not allowing exhaust temperatures to reach regen levels

dd_procedures.title: SPN 4360 FMI 18 - Aftertreatment SCR Inducement Active
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 4360 FMI 18 – Aftertreatment SCR Inducement Active (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 4360 FMI 18 indicates that the SCR inducement system has been activated on the engine. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and is the ECM’s way of enforcing compliance with emissions requirements by progressively limiting engine performance when the SCR system has been operating outside acceptable parameters for an extended period.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
SCR and DEF warning lights illuminated 
Significant engine derate active 
Vehicle speed may be limited 
Multiple SCR and NOx related codes likely present 
Engine power noticeably reduced
Cause
SCR inducement is triggered after the ECM has detected ongoing SCR system issues that have not been addressed within the allowed timeframe. Common causes include:
Extended operation with low or empty DEF tank 
Prolonged SCR efficiency faults left unresolved 
Repeated DEF quality faults not corrected 
DEF dosing system failure over extended period 
Tampered or missing SCR components 
Accumulated fault counts exceeding ECM thresholds
Can You Keep Driving?
The engine is already in an active derate condition with this fault. Vehicle speed and power will be significantly restricted. This fault will not resolve on its own and requires diagnosis and repair by a qualified diesel technician. Continued operation in this condition risks further aftertreatment damage.
Recommended Action
This fault requires professional diagnosis as it indicates a history of unresolved SCR system issues rather than a single component failure. Have a technician perform a full aftertreatment system evaluation including DEF quality, dosing system, NOx sensors, and SCR catalyst condition. Simply clearing codes without repair will not resolve the inducement condition.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4360 FMI 18 mean?
 
It means the ECM has activated the SCR inducement system after detecting prolonged SCR system non-compliance, resulting in a significant engine derate condition to enforce emissions requirements.
 
 
What causes SPN 4360 FMI 18?
 
This fault is typically caused by extended operation with unresolved SCR system issues such as low DEF, poor DEF quality, or ongoing SCR efficiency faults that were not addressed within the ECM allowed timeframe.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4360 FMI 18?
 
The engine is already in active derate with this fault. Continued operation without repair will not improve the situation and risks further damage to the aftertreatment system.
 
 
Will SPN 4360 FMI 18 cause a derate?
 
Yes. SCR inducement is specifically designed to enforce a derate condition and will continue until the underlying SCR system issues are properly diagnosed and repaired.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4360 FMI 18?
 
The underlying SCR system faults must be diagnosed and repaired by a qualified technician. Clearing codes without fixing the root cause will result in the inducement condition returning. A full aftertreatment system evaluation is required.

SCR inducement is triggered after the ECM has detected ongoing SCR system issues that have not been addressed within the allowed timeframe. Common causes include:
Extended operation with low or empty DEF tank 
Prolonged SCR efficiency faults left unresolved 
Repeated DEF quality faults not corrected 
DEF dosing system failure over extended period 
Tampered or missing SCR components 
Accumulated fault counts exceeding ECM thresholds

Have a technician perform a full aftertreatment system evaluation including DEF quality, dosing system, NOx sensors, and SCR catalyst condition. What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4360 FMI 18 mean?
 
It means the ECM has activated the SCR inducement system after detecting prolonged SCR system non-compliance, resulting in a significant engine derate condition to enforce emissions requirements.
 
 
What causes SPN 4360 FMI 18?
 
This fault is typically caused by extended operation with unresolved SCR system issues such as low DEF, poor DEF quality, or ongoing SCR efficiency faults that were not addressed within the ECM allowed timeframe.

The engine is already in active derate with this fault. Continued operation without repair will not improve the situation and risks further damage to the aftertreatment system.
 
 
Will SPN 4360 FMI 18 cause a derate?
 
Yes. SCR inducement is specifically designed to enforce a derate condition and will continue until the underlying SCR system issues are properly diagnosed and repaired.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4360 FMI 18?
 
The underlying SCR system faults must be diagnosed and repaired by a qualified technician. Clearing codes without fixing the root cause will result in the inducement condition returning. A full aftertreatment system evaluation is required.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4360 FMI 1 indicates SCR intermediate or mid-bed temperature below expected where the sensor is used. Failed temperature sensor, open circuit, exhaust leak near the sensor boss, low-load duty cycle, and upstream thermal management failure are the primary causes. Unplugged sensors after aftertreatment service and open circuits from brittle harnesses are documented patterns. Replacing the SCR catalyst for a temperature sensor fault is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Failed temperature sensor — failed EGT sensor producing stuck-low reading
Open circuit — open circuit in EGT sensor harness producing stuck-low reading
Exhaust leak near boss — exhaust leak near sensor boss producing false low reading
Low-load duty cycle — low-load duty cycle preventing SCR from reaching operating temperature
Upstream thermal management failure — upstream thermal management failure preventing SCR from reaching temperature
steps: Step 1 — Multi-Temperature Correlation

Correlate the SCR intermediate temperature with SCR inlet and outlet temperatures. One stuck-low sensor is suspect. A single sensor reading significantly lower than adjacent sensors confirms a sensor or circuit fault. All sensors reading low confirms a thermal state or upstream issue.
Step 2 — Circuit Continuity Check

Check circuit continuity on the suspect sensor. Unplugged sensors after aftertreatment service are a documented pattern — always inspect the EGT connector and circuit after any recent aftertreatment service. Verify continuity through the sensor circuit. An open circuit confirms a harness or connector fault.
Step 3 — Inspect for Exhaust Leaks Near Boss

Inspect for exhaust leaks near the sensor boss. An exhaust leak near the sensor boss produces a false low reading by allowing ambient air to cool the sensor. Inspect the sensor boss and surrounding exhaust connections for leaks.
Step 4 — Evaluate Duty Cycle and Thermal Strategy

Evaluate the duty cycle and upstream thermal management strategy. A low-load duty cycle preventing the SCR from reaching operating temperature produces a legitimate low temperature reading that is not a sensor fault. Evaluate whether the duty cycle is appropriate for SCR operation.
Step 5 — Sensor and Harness Repair
Repair the sensor or harness if a fault is confirmed. Replace the sensor if failure is confirmed. Repair the harness if an open circuit is confirmed. Repair the exhaust leak if a leak is confirmed.
Step 6 — Verify After Repair
Verify SCR intermediate temperature readings are correct after repair. Confirm SPN 4360 FMI 1 does not return. Monitor for return of low temperature events over extended operation.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4360 FMI 1 on a Volvo means the SCR inlet gas temperature sensor is reading below its normal operating range. On a hot engine this almost always means sensor failure or DEF contamination at the connector, not cold exhaust. When a Volvo D13 or D11 truck logs SPN 4360 FMI 1, the aftertreatment control module is reading an SCR inlet temperature that falls below the expected range for current engine operating conditions. At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com, FMI 1 on this sensor while the engine is hot under load is almost never caused by actual cold exhaust — it is a sensor or wiring issue. The Volvo D13 uses an NTC thermistor for SCR inlet temperature measurement, with a resistance of roughly 50 to 120 kOhm at 25 degrees C. Technicians should verify this resistance value before condemning the sensor, since the high-kOhm reading can be mistaken for an open circuit. DEF vapor contamination of the connector is the second leading cause and is correctable without sensor replacement.
causes: Failed NTC thermistor (open or high-resistance internal fault)

The thermistor element degrades from prolonged exposure to high-temperature exhaust gas. An open thermistor reads OL in ohms, and the ECM interprets this as an impossibly low temperature, setting FMI 1.
DEF crystallization contaminating the sensor connector

DEF vapors from nearby dosing injectors or DEF lines migrate into the sensor connector cavity. DEF crystals create a partial conductive path between pins or a short to the connector shell, pulling the signal low.
Open signal wire in the aftertreatment wiring harness
A broken conductor in the harness run from the SCR section to the ACM causes the signal to float low. The ACM interprets the open circuit as an extremely low temperature, setting FMI 1.
Short to ground on the signal wire near the SCR canister
Heat damage to the harness insulation near the SCR canister allows the signal wire to contact the exhaust piping or chassis, creating a ground path that pulls the signal below the FMI 1 threshold.
steps: Connect a Texa Truck diagnostic tool to the Volvo 9-pin diagnostic port. Read active fault codes and confirm SPN 4360 FMI 1. Navigate to the aftertreatment live data group and observe the SCR inlet temperature reading. With the engine at full operating temperature (coolant above 85 degrees C) and under moderate load, the SCR inlet should read 200 to 450 degrees C. A reading below 100 degrees C or displaying as negative on a hot engine confirms a sensor fault.

With the engine off and cooled for at least 45 minutes, disconnect the SCR inlet temperature sensor connector. This sensor uses an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) — resistance decreases as temperature increases. At ambient temperature (approximately 25 degrees C), measure resistance between the two sensor pins: expect 50 to 120 kOhm for Volvo D13 NTC thermistors (exact value varies by part number). An open reading (OL) confirms a failed internal thermistor.

If resistance is in spec, inspect the connector pins for DEF crystallization (white powdery deposits) or corrosion. DEF vapors from nearby dosing lines can migrate into the sensor connector cavity, creating a partial short to ground that pulls the NTC signal below the FMI 1 threshold. Clean the connector with electrical contact cleaner and dry thoroughly before re-testing.

With the sensor reconnected and key on (engine off), back-probe the signal pin to sensor ground. The measured voltage should correspond to the sensor resistance at current ambient temperature. If the voltage is below 0.2 V with a known-good 5 V reference on the supply pin, the signal is being pulled to ground by the connector contamination or a wire short.

Use a NEXIQ USB-Link 2 adapter with compatible Volvo protocol software to monitor raw sensor voltage alongside the computed temperature. Replace the SCR inlet temperature sensor if resistance is out of spec or the circuit tests confirm sensor failure. Clear the fault and perform a warm-up drive to confirm the temperature rises normally.
symptoms: Amber warning lamp illuminated on the Volvo instrument cluster with an aftertreatment-related message.
SCR inlet temperature reads implausibly low (below 100 degrees C or negative values) on a hot engine under load.
DEF dosing may be suppressed because the ACM reads the temperature as below the dosing enable threshold.
Increased NOx emissions possible if DEF dosing is inhibited for an extended period.
Additional SCR NOx efficiency faults may follow if the dosing suppression persists.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4360 FMI 3 means the Mack SCR catalyst intake temperature sensor circuit is reading voltage above normal, usually an open sensor or broken wire. It is Medium severity and affects DEF dosing strategy, though the engine keeps running normally. The SCR catalyst intake temperature sensor tells the Mack ECM whether the catalyst is hot enough to effectively convert NOx using DEF, and SPN 4360 FMI 3 flags that this reading has gone open. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com stresses that while this fault doesn't cause any immediate drivability symptom, it quietly undermines the whole SCR strategy since the ECM can't confidently dose DEF without a reliable temperature input, which can snowball into more serious inducement-related codes if left unaddressed for too long.
causes: Heat-damaged sensor wiring near the SCR canister
Extended exposure to high exhaust temperatures cracks wire insulation over time, eventually breaking the conductor and opening the circuit.
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Vibration and thermal cycling loosen connector locks, and moisture intrusion corrodes the pin contacts over time.
Failed internal sensor element
The temperature sensing element inside the sensor can fail from repeated extreme heat cycling near the SCR catalyst.
Damage during a previous aftertreatment repair
Sensor bungs or wiring can be accidentally damaged during SCR component service if care isn't taken during reassembly.
steps: Connect Mack Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and confirm SPN 4360 FMI 3, then check current SCR system status and dosing activity.
Locate the SCR intake temperature sensor at the front of the SCR catalyst canister and inspect the connector for corrosion or heat-damaged wiring.
Unplug the sensor and verify reference voltage and ground are present at the harness connector.
Check sensor resistance with a multimeter against Mack spec at ambient temperature to confirm whether the sensor itself is open.
Replace the sensor or repair the harness as needed, clear codes with PTT, and confirm normal SCR dosing resumes on the next drive cycle.
symptoms: Amber warning lamp illuminated
Possible DEF dosing rate changes or dosing suspension
No immediate drivability change
Potential future SCR efficiency or inducement codes if left unresolved

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4360 FMI 16 means the SCR catalyst intake gas temperature is valid but above the moderately severe limit. Investigate DOC regen behavior, DEF dosing, and exhaust oil contamination before replacing the temperature sensor. The SCR intake gas temperature tells the Mercedes aftertreatment control module how much heat the catalyst brick is receiving before DEF is injected. When SPN 4360 FMI 16 sets, the ECM has confirmed exhaust temperatures at the SCR inlet exceed safe operating bounds. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com prioritizes upstream heat sources — DOC overtemperature, regen aborts, and oil in the exhaust — over immediate sensor replacement because the sensor is usually reporting accurately.
causes: DOC or DPF regen overtemperature propagating to SCR inlet
Very Common
An over-fueling HC doser or loaded DPF during active regen can push DOC outlet above 650°C, and that heat wave reaches the SCR intake within one exhaust pulse cycle.
Engine oil or fuel entering exhaust and oxidizing in the DOC
Turbo seal leaks and worn cylinder liners send hydrocarbons into the DOC, creating exothermic reactions that elevate all downstream gas temperatures including SCR intake.
Faulty DEF doser causing localized SCR hot spots
Moderate
A dribbling doser that injects urea into a still-cold or overheated brick can cause ammonia slip reactions and temperature spikes at the SCR inlet sensor location.
steps: Connect Jaltest or Texa and log SPN 4360 alongside DOC outlet (SPN 4766), DPF inlet (SPN 3242), and turbo outlet EGT during a 10-minute road test at steady 55-65 mph.

Mercedes OM471 normal SCR intake temperature at cruise is typically 250°C-420°C depending on load; sustained readings above 480°C at moderate load confirm a genuine overtemperature event, not sensor drift.
Review regen history in the scan tool — aborted or incomplete regens that spike DOC outlet above 600°C will propagate high heat into the SCR intake within 30-60 seconds.

Inspect the DEF doser spray pattern at the SCR inlet mixer. A stuck-open doser or crystallized nozzle can cause localized hot spots; DEF crystallization appears as white chalky deposits on the mixer screen.

If all gas temperatures are genuinely high, check for engine oil consumption past the turbo seal — oil oxidation in the DOC adds uncontrolled heat. Compare SCR intake sensor to an infrared pyrometer at the sensor boss; divergence beyond 30°C suggests sensor replacement.
symptoms: Amber or red aftertreatment warning lamp illuminated
Elevated SCR intake temperature on live data during normal cruise (often above 450°C when loaded)
Possible DEF dosing reduction or temporary urea injection cutback by the ACM
Companion codes for DOC outlet temperature or DPF regen status may be active
Reduced fuel efficiency if ECM retards timing to lower exhaust heat input

procedures_full.overview: FMI 31 is a condition-exists class that indicates the DEF pump pressure is outside the expected operating range for the platform. The DEF pump module pressurizes the DEF system for dosing. Failed pump, restricted filter or lines, frozen DEF, leaking lines, pressure sensor faults, and electrical pump control issues are all causes. Winter freeze damage and contamination plugging the pump filter are the most common fleet patterns. Pump module replacement without proving the hydraulic path and electrical supply is the primary misdiagnosis.
causes: Failed pump — internal pump failure
Restricted filter — contamination plugging pump inlet filter
Frozen DEF — winter freeze damage to pump or lines
Leaking lines — pressure loss from line damage
Pressure sensor fault — false pressure reading
Electrical pump control fault — supply or control circuit issue
steps: Single Action Gate — DEF Level and Quality Check
Verify DEF level and quality before any pump diagnosis. Low DEF level causes pump cavitation that mimics pump failure. Contaminated DEF can plug the pump filter rapidly.
Binary Decision Gate — Freeze and Restriction Inspection

Inspect DEF lines and pump module for freeze damage and restriction. In cold climates, winter freeze damage is the most common cause of DEF pump pressure faults. Inspect lines for ice blockage and pump module for freeze-crack damage.
Override Manager — Pump Command Test

Command pump operation via scan tool and observe pressure response. Compare commanded pump duty to reported pressure. No pressure buildup with valid electrical supply supports pump or hydraulic restriction failure.
Safety Interceptor — Line Leak Inspection
Inspect all DEF lines for leaks. A leaking pressure line prevents pressure buildup regardless of pump condition. Inspect fittings, connections, and the dosing injector for DEF leaks.
Resume Point — Pump Module Electrical Supply
Verify pump module supply voltage and ground under operation. Pump module connector corrosion from DEF crystals is a documented cause. Inspect connector for urea crystal buildup and corrosion.
Verification Loop — Post-Service Pressure Confirmation
After repair, command pump and verify pressure builds to OEM specification. Confirm dosing quantity returns to expected levels.
Repair Ledger Output — Pump Module Replacement
Replace pump module only after hydraulic path and electrical supply are proven. Note: some platforms require DEF system purge and prime after pump replacement.

Repair Steps
1 . Thaw frozen DEF lines and inspect for freeze-crack damage.
2 . Clean or replace pump inlet filter if restriction is found.
3 . Repair any DEF line leaks found.
4 . Repair pump module connector corrosion from DEF crystal buildup.
5 . Repair electrical supply faults if found.
6 . Replace pump module after hydraulic and electrical proof.
Verification Steps
Confirm pump builds pressure to OEM specification after repair.
Verify dosing quantity returns to expected levels.
Confirm SPN 5397 FMI 31 does not return after repair.
Monitor SCR efficiency returns to normal after repair.
Preventative Measures
✓ Inspect DEF lines and pump module for freeze damage before winter operation.
✓ Use quality DEF to prevent filter plugging.
✓ Inspect pump module connector for DEF crystal buildup at every major service.
✓ Address DEF leaks promptly to prevent crystal accumulation.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium to High Severity
Medium progressing to High if dosing fails and inducement begins. Address promptly. Hydraulic path inspection takes less time than pump module replacement and resolves many cases.
