procedures_full.overview: SPN 637 FMI 2 means the Cat camshaft/timing reference sensor is sending an erratic or intermittent signal instead of a clean pulse. It's a High severity fault that typically causes intermittent hard starting or misfire rather than an immediate shutdown. Caterpillar engines use the camshaft timing sensor alongside the crankshaft sensor to confirm exactly which cylinder is on its compression stroke, which the ECM needs to fire injectors correctly. SPN 637 FMI 2 flags a signal quality problem rather than a total loss of signal, which is why symptoms tend to be intermittent and often worse when the engine is fully warmed up. This guide from ProfessionalDieselRepair.com covers the harness and connector checks that resolve the majority of these faults before a sensor replacement is ever needed.
causes: Chafed sensor harness near the front gear housing
Engine vibration wears through wire insulation where the harness runs close to the timing gear cover, introducing signal noise.
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Moisture and heat cycling degrade the connector seal over time, creating intermittent high-resistance contact points.
Failing camshaft sensor element
Internal sensor degradation, often heat-related, causes an intermittent signal that worsens as engine temperature rises.
Timing gear wear affecting reluctor ring accuracy
Excessive gear train wear can physically alter the timing reference the sensor reads, producing a genuinely erratic mechanical signal.
steps: Connect Cat ET and pull the active and logged fault codes, checking for an accompanying crank position correlation fault.
Inspect the camshaft sensor connector for corrosion or a loose pin, and verify the sensor is fully seated against its mounting boss.
Unplug the sensor and measure resistance across its terminals with a multimeter, comparing to the Cat spec for your engine family.
Trace the sensor harness back toward the ECM, checking for chafing near the front gear housing or accessory drive where vibration is highest.
Clear codes with Cat ET, road test while monitoring live timing signal quality, and confirm the fault does not return through a full RPM range.
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 637 FMI 2: Camshaft Timing Sensor Erratic

procedures_full.overview: SPN 637 FMI 4 on a Kenworth means the camshaft timing sensor signal is below normal voltage. Start by checking for oil contamination at the connector and test sensor supply voltage before replacing the sensor. Kenworth SPN 637 FMI 4 indicates the camshaft position sensor circuit voltage has fallen below the ECM's accepted lower limit. SPN 637 covers the engine timing and cam sensor — a Hall-effect or variable-reluctance sensor that reads a tone wheel on the camshaft to provide phase information for sequential fuel injection. FMI 4 (below normal voltage or shorted low) points to a supply or signal wire grounded unintentionally, an internally shorted sensor, or a corroded connector pulling the signal toward zero. On PACCAR MX engines running the Kenworth powertrain, the ECM will attempt to continue operation using only the crankshaft sensor for timing reference, but this backup mode produces rough running and may cause a derate. Catching and fixing this fault quickly at ProfessionalDieselRepair.com-trained technicians prevents catalytic converter damage from timing-induced misfires.
causes: Signal or supply wire shorted to chassis ground
Chafing of the cam sensor harness against the engine block or timing cover grounds the signal wire, pulling the sensor voltage to near 0 V and triggering FMI 4.
Oil or coolant contamination at sensor connector
Fluid ingress into the sensor connector creates a conductive path between the signal pin and ground, causing a low-voltage reading without sensor or wiring failure.
Failed cam sensor with internal short to ground
The sensor's internal circuitry shorts its output to the ground reference, producing a near-zero signal voltage at all engine speeds.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 or a Diesel Laptops diagnostic adapter to read active fault codes. Confirm SPN 637 FMI 4 and check whether SPN 636 (crank sensor) is also present — a combined cam-and-crank fault narrows the problem to a shared ground or power supply circuit.

With the ignition ON and engine OFF, back-probe the sensor supply pin using a digital multimeter. The cam sensor supply is typically 8–12 V on PACCAR MX engines. A reading near 0 V confirms a shorted or open supply wire.

Unplug the cam sensor connector. With the ignition ON, measure voltage on the supply pin at the harness side. If voltage is restored to nominal with the sensor unplugged, the sensor itself is shorted internally and requires replacement.

Inspect the sensor mounting area on the front timing cover for oil or coolant contamination that may have wicked into the connector. Clean with electrical contact cleaner and allow to dry before reconnecting.

After completing wiring repairs or sensor replacement, use PACCAR Davie4 or the Diesel Laptops adapter to clear faults and monitor the cam sensor signal during a cold start to confirm stable RPM and timing data.
symptoms: Hard start or no-start condition, particularly when cold.
Rough idle and engine misfires at low speed.
Engine derate with reduced power and fueling.
SPN 637 FMI 4 stored as active fault in ECM memory.
Possible black or white smoke from incorrect injection timing.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 3516 FMI 2 indicates DEF concentration data unstable or implausible from the quality sensor or inferred model. Failing quality sensor, contaminated fluid layers, harness intermittents, header connector corrosion, and thermal stratification are the primary causes. Layered contamination causing changing quality readings after driving and agitation is a documented pattern. Replacing the quality sensor without fluid chemistry proof is the most documented misdiagnosis pattern.
causes: Failing quality sensor — failing quality sensor producing unstable concentration readings
Contaminated fluid layers — contaminated fluid layers producing changing quality readings
Harness intermittents — harness intermittents producing unstable sensor signal
Header connector corrosion — header connector corrosion producing intermittent sensor signal
Thermal stratification — thermal stratification producing changing concentration readings
steps: Step 1 — Sample and Refractometer Chemistry Check

Sample the DEF and check chemistry with a refractometer. Layered contamination causing changing quality readings after driving and agitation is a documented pattern. Verify the DEF concentration is within specification. A concentration outside specification confirms a fluid quality fault. Drain and refill with fresh OEM-specification DEF if quality is suspect.
Step 2 — Inspect Tank for Contamination

Inspect the DEF tank for contamination. Contaminated fluid layers produce changing quality readings. Inspect the DEF for discoloration, debris, and contamination. Drain and clean the tank if contamination is confirmed.
Step 3 — Header Connector Service

Service the tank header connector. Header connector corrosion and crystal deposits produce intermittent sensor signals. Inspect the header connector for corrosion and crystal deposits. Clean or replace the connector if corrosion or deposits are found.
Step 4 — Sensor Electrical Stability Check
Check sensor electrical stability. Verify power, ground, and signal circuit integrity at the sensor connector. A harness intermittent producing unstable sensor signal requires harness repair.
Step 5 — Replace Sensor Only If Fluid Is Proven Good
Replace the sensor only if the fluid is proven good and the circuit is confirmed stable. A sensor replaced into a contaminated fluid or circuit fault will fail the new sensor.
Step 6 — Verify After Repair
Verify DEF concentration readings are stable after repair. Confirm SPN 3516 FMI 2 does not return. Monitor for return of erratic concentration events over extended operation.

AI Diesel Tech FSM Advantage: The patented Finite State Machine forces technicians through evidence gates in order — blocking parts-cannon jumps and reducing misdiagnosis. Each gate must be satisfied before the next branch opens.
Repair Steps
1 . Drain and refill with fresh OEM-specification DEF if quality is suspect.
2 . Drain and clean tank if contamination is confirmed.
3 . Clean or replace header connector if corrosion or deposits are found.
4 . Repair harness if intermittent is confirmed.
5 . Replace quality sensor only after fluid and circuit are proven good.
Verification Steps
Confirm DEF concentration readings are stable after repair.
Verify SPN 3516 FMI 2 does not return after repair.
Monitor for return of erratic concentration events over extended operation.
Preventative Measures
✓ Use OEM-specification DEF only.
✓ Inspect DEF quality at every DEF fill.
✓ Inspect header connector for corrosion at every major service.
✓ Inspect DEF tank for contamination at every major service.
Severity & Driveability Guidance
Medium progressing to High if warnings escalate Severity
Medium progressing to High if warnings escalate. Erratic DEF concentration is fluid and sensor integrity together — chemistry first.
symptoms: DEF quality intermittent
Concentration erratic
Quality sensor fluctuating
SCR quality code comes and goes
DEF concentration unstable

Detroit Diesel SPN 4076 FMI 18 – DEF Dosing Injector Fault (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 4076 FMI 18 indicates a fault with the DEF dosing injector, which is the component responsible for spraying DEF fluid into the exhaust stream ahead of the SCR catalyst. When this injector fails or becomes restricted on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines, the SCR system cannot properly reduce NOx emissions and a derate condition will follow.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DEF or SCR warning light illuminated 
Engine derate condition 
White residue or crystallization around the injector 
Reduced engine performance 
SCR system unable to meet emissions thresholds
Cause
This code triggers when the ECM detects the DEF dosing injector is not performing within specification. Common causes include:
Clogged or crystallized dosing injector from DEF deposits 
Failed or stuck dosing injector valve 
DEF injector electrical fault or wiring issue 
Restricted DEF supply to the injector 
Contaminated DEF causing injector blockage 
Failed return line preventing injector purge cycle
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving is possible but without a functioning dosing injector the SCR system cannot reduce NOx emissions. The ECM will trigger a progressive derate condition. This fault should be addressed promptly to avoid further damage to the aftertreatment system.
Recommended Action
Have the DEF dosing injector inspected for clogging, crystallization, or electrical faults. A clogged injector can sometimes be cleaned but is often more cost effective to replace. Also inspect the DEF return line to ensure the purge cycle is functioning correctly, as a blocked return line is a common contributing factor.
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 4076 FMI 18 mean?
 
It means the DEF dosing injector is not operating correctly and the SCR system cannot properly inject DEF into the exhaust stream to reduce NOx emissions.
 
 
What causes SPN 4076 FMI 18?
 
The most common causes are a clogged or crystallized DEF dosing injector, an electrical fault at the injector, or a blocked DEF return line preventing proper purging.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 4076 FMI 18?
 
Short distances may be possible but the engine will derate without a functioning dosing injector. Address this fault as soon as possible.
 
 
Will SPN 4076 FMI 18 cause a derate?
 
Yes. The ECM will trigger a derate condition when the dosing injector cannot supply DEF to the SCR system at the required rate.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 4076 FMI 18?
 
Inspect, clean, or replace the DEF dosing injector and verify the return line is clear. Once the injector is functioning correctly and the SCR system confirms proper DEF dosing, the code should clear.

procedures_full.overview: This code indicates the SPN 4076/FMI 3 has failed high.‪
causes: This code indicates the SPN 4076/FMI 3 has failed high.‪
steps: Check for multiple codes.
If 110/3, 174/3, 175/3 and 4076/3 are present, go to step 6.
If only 4076/3 is present, go to the next step.
Disconnect the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor.
Turn the ignition On (key ON, engine OFF).
Measure the voltage between pins 1 and 2 of the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor harness connector.
If the voltage is between 2.8 and 3 volts, replace the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor. Refer to "130.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If the voltage is less than 2.8 volts, go to the next step.
Measure voltage between pin 2 of the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor and ground.

If the voltage is between 2.8 and 3 volts, repair the wire between pin 1 of the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor connector and pin 80 of the MCM 120–pin connector. Refer to "130.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If the voltage is less than 2.8 volts, repair the wire between pin 2 of the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor connector and pin 55 of the MCM 120–pin connector. Refer to "130.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Measure the voltage between pins 1 and 2 of the Engine Coolant Inlet Temperature Sensor harness connector.
If the voltage is greater than 3 volts, repair the short to power on one of the follwoing MCM pins: 77, 80, 108 or 110. Refer to "130.1.1 Verify Repairs".

If no voltage is present, repair the open between pin 55 of the MCM 120–pin connector and the Coolant Out, Coolant In, Engine Oil and Supply Fuel Temperature Sensors. Refer to "130.1.1 Verify Repairs".
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
ENGINE EXHAUST
To avoid injury from inhaling engine exhaust, always operate the engine in a well-ventilated area. Engine exhaust is toxic.‪
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.

dd_procedures.title: SPN 1127 FMI 16 – Exhaust Back Pressure High
dd_procedures.procedure_text:
Detroit Diesel SPN 1127 FMI 16 – Exhaust Back Pressure High (Meaning, Causes & Fix)
 
 
 
← Back to Detroit Diesel Fault Codes
Detroit Diesel SPN 1127 FMI 16 indicates that exhaust back pressure has exceeded the acceptable operating threshold. This code appears on DD13, DD15, and DD16 engines and signals that something is restricting exhaust flow through the aftertreatment system. Left unresolved high exhaust back pressure can reduce engine performance, damage the turbocharger, and lead to progressive derate conditions.
Symptoms
Check engine light on 
DPF or aftertreatment warning light illuminated 
Reduced engine power and performance 
Engine derate condition possible 
Black smoke from exhaust Reduced fuel economy 
Turbocharger may be affected by restricted exhaust flow
Cause
This code triggers when the exhaust back pressure sensor detects pressure above the maximum acceptable threshold. Common causes include:
Heavily soot or ash loaded 
DPF restricting exhaust flow 
Collapsed or physically damaged DPF substrate 
Clogged or restricted exhaust system components 
Failed exhaust back pressure sensor giving false readings 
Blocked exhaust pipe or muffler 
Faulty exhaust brake stuck in closed position 
High ash accumulation reducing DPF flow capacity
Can You Keep Driving?
Limited driving may be possible but high exhaust back pressure puts significant strain on the turbocharger and engine. Continued operation without addressing the restriction risks turbocharger damage and progressive engine derate. Attempt a parked regeneration and seek diagnosis promptly.
Recommended Action
Start by attempting a parked regeneration to reduce DPF soot load. If back pressure remains high after a successful regen inspect the exhaust system for physical blockages or damage. Check the exhaust brake if equipped to ensure it is not stuck closed. Have the DPF inspected for ash loading or substrate damage. If all components check out test the exhaust back pressure sensor for accuracy.
FAQ Q&As
What does Detroit Diesel SPN 1127 FMI 16 mean?
 
It means exhaust back pressure has exceeded the maximum acceptable threshold, indicating a restriction in the exhaust or aftertreatment system that is reducing engine performance.
 
 
What causes SPN 1127 FMI 16?
 
The most common causes are a heavily loaded DPF, a collapsed or damaged DPF substrate, a blocked exhaust component, or a faulty exhaust back pressure sensor.
 
 
Can I keep driving with SPN 1127 FMI 16?
 
Short distances may be possible but high back pressure puts strain on the turbocharger and engine. Address this fault promptly to avoid further damage.
 
 
Will SPN 1127 FMI 16 cause a derate?
 
Yes. If exhaust back pressure remains above acceptable levels the ECM will trigger derate conditions to protect the engine and turbocharger from damage.
 
 
How do I clear SPN 1127 FMI 16?
 
Perform a parked regeneration first. If pressure remains elevated inspect the exhaust system and DPF for blockages or damage. Once the restriction is resolved and back pressure returns to normal the code should clear.
 
 
Related codes

SPN 3713 FMI 18 
SPN 3250 FMI 16 
SPN 3480 FMI 16 
SPN 3719 FMI 0

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1127 FMI 2 means the turbo boost pressure sensor signal is erratic rather than steady. It's a medium-severity code with no formal derate, but it can cause inconsistent power delivery - check the pressure line and harness before replacing the sensor. An erratic boost signal is often more of a nuisance than a dangerous fault, but it degrades the ECM's ability to fuel accurately under load. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always inspects the small pressure sense line for a hairline crack first, since that's a far more common cause than an actually failed sensor.
causes: Cracked or loose pressure sense line
A hairline crack or loose fitting on the small line running to the sensor lets ambient pressure fluctuations mix with the actual boost signal.
Intermittent connector or wiring fault
A loose or corroded connector pin under vibration can cause the signal to drop in and out.
Failing sensor element
An internally degrading sensor can produce an erratic output even with a sound pressure line and harness.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame data on DDDL to see if the erratic signal correlates with vibration, RPM changes, or is present at idle too.
Inspect the boost pressure sensor's vacuum/pressure line for cracks, kinks, or a loose connection at either end.
Back-probe the sensor's signal, ground, and power wires with a multimeter while wiggling the harness to check for an intermittent connection.
Check the sensor's mounting for looseness or vibration that could cause an intermittent internal fault.
Test the sensor directly with a known-good vacuum/pressure source if a bench test capability is available, comparing output against the OEM chart.
Repair any wiring or line issues found, or replace the sensor if it fails a direct bench test, then clear the code and confirm stable readings across a drive cycle.
symptoms: Check engine lamp with intermittent power surges or flat spots
Inconsistent boost gauge readings if equipped with an aftermarket gauge
Possible black smoke on acceleration if fueling compensates incorrectly for erratic boost data
procedures_full.source_title: Freightliner SPN 1127 FMI 2: Turbo Boost Pressure Signal Erratic

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1127 FMI 3 on a Freightliner Cascadia means the boost pressure sensor signal is above 4.75 V — almost always a short to Vref or open sensor ground, not actual over-boost. Use DDDL to confirm and isolate the circuit fault. When a Freightliner Cascadia with a DD15 or DD13 logs SPN 1127 FMI 3, the ECM has detected a boost pressure sensor signal above the 4.75 V normal maximum, which cannot represent any real boost pressure and indicates a circuit fault. The boost pressure sensor uses a standard 3-wire Bosch absolute pressure circuit: 5 V reference (Pin A), signal output 0.5 to 4.5 V (Pin C), and sensor ground (Pin B). At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com, the most common cause of FMI 3 on this sensor is an open ground splice near the charge air cooler outlet — a corroded splice that breaks the ground return causes the signal to float toward the 5 V reference rail. DDDL with a NEXIQ USB-Link 2 provides the boost pressure live data and the fault detail needed to confirm the circuit fault before parts are ordered.
causes: Open or corroded sensor ground connection (Pin B)

A broken or high-resistance ground wire or splice causes the sensor output to float toward the 5 V reference supply, pushing the signal above 4.75 V. Common in northern-climate vehicles where road salt corrodes ground splice locations near the charge air piping.
Short from signal wire (Pin C) to the 5 V reference wire (Pin A)
Insulation damage in the harness near the charge air cooler or intake manifold allows the signal and reference wires to contact each other, forcing the ECM input above the FMI 3 threshold.
Failed boost pressure sensor with internal short to supply
The sensor's internal voltage divider circuit fails by shorting the output to the 5 V supply rail. The reading is fixed at near 5 V regardless of actual manifold pressure.
Corroded or spread connector pins bridging signal to reference
Salt and moisture corrode the 3-pin connector, sometimes creating a conductive bridge between Pin A (Vref) and Pin C (signal). Inspect connector cavity for white or green deposits.
steps: Connect DDDL (Detroit Diesel Diagnostic Link) via a NEXIQ USB-Link 2 to the Freightliner Cascadia OBD2 or 9-pin J1939 port. Read active faults and confirm SPN 1127 FMI 3. In the live data group, observe the boost pressure reading. A value above 250 kPa at idle (vehicle stationary, no boost) is the FMI 3 signature.

With the key on and engine off, locate the boost pressure sensor on the intake manifold or charge air piping (DD15/DD13: typically left-side intake manifold, 3-wire Bosch-style sensor). Back-probe Pin C (signal wire, center pin on most orientations) to Pin B (sensor ground). If the reading is above 4.75 V, the signal circuit is shorted high.

Disconnect the sensor connector. Measure Pin C at the harness side to Pin B at the harness side. If the voltage remains above 0.5 V with the sensor disconnected, the harness has a short from the signal wire to the 5 V reference circuit. Inspect the harness loom in the charge air cooler inlet area where heat and vibration cause insulation cracking.

If the voltage drops to zero when the sensor is disconnected, the sensor is internally shorted high. Measure the 5 V reference supply: Pin A to Pin B (with sensor disconnected) should read 4.95 to 5.05 V. A good reference voltage plus a signal that goes high only when the sensor is plugged in confirms the sensor has failed internally.

Replace the boost pressure sensor with an OEM or approved aftermarket Bosch part. Torque to specification (typically 15 to 20 Nm). Clear the fault with DDDL and perform a full-throttle acceleration test to confirm boost pressure reads between 150 and 250 kPa under load.
symptoms: Boost pressure live data reads above 250 kPa (36 psi) at idle when the vehicle is stationary.
Engine derate limiting power output while the fault is active, because the ECM cannot verify actual boost.
VGT or wastegate actuator may be commanded to a default position during limp mode.
Possible black smoke from over-fueling if the ECM uses an estimated boost value that is higher than actual.
DDDL displays SPN 1127 FMI 3 as active with a boost pressure circuit fault for turbocharger 1.
procedures_full.source_title: Freightliner SPN 1127 FMI 3: Boost Pressure Sensor High Voltage

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1127 FMI 14 on Caterpillar requires special instruction diagnosis for boost pressure — leak-test the intake and calibrate the sensor before replacing the turbo. Boost pressure faults on Caterpillar engines feed directly into emissions and aftertreatment strategy. FMI 14 means the standard fault definition is not enough — Cat ET walks through leak checks, sensor validation, and turbo health correlation. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com follows that sequence because most SPN 1127 cases are leaks or sensors, not failed turbos.
causes: Charge-air cooler or intake boot leak
Unmetered air leaks drop measured boost below commanded values under load.
Boost pressure sensor calibration or port blockage
Clogged sensor port or lost calibration produces readings that fail special instruction checks.
Turbocharger wastegate or VGT control fault
Mechanical boost control failure after high-mileage operation or oil starvation.
Exhaust restriction raising turbine backpressure
Plugged DPF or muffler reduces effective boost even when the turbo spins normally.
steps: Connect Cat ET via ServiceMaxx or dealer interface and read SPN 1127 special instruction workflow.
Compare boost pressure to turbo speed and engine load — low boost with high turbo speed suggests intake leak.
Pressure-test charge-air cooler and piping from turbo outlet to intake manifold.
Inspect boost pressure sensor port and harness for clogging or corrosion.
Perform Cat-specified boost sensor calibration before condemning the turbocharger.
symptoms: Check-engine or equipment warning with SPN 1127 FMI 14
Reduced power or boost derate on load
Boost reading flat or erratic on Cat ET live data
Black smoke under acceleration if underboost
Possible intake or charge-air cooler leak audible under boost
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 1127 FMI 14: Turbocharger 1 Boost Pressure Special Instructions

procedures_full.overview: Measured boost is higher than commanded (overboost), or the boost reading is high. The ECM derates to protect the engine. On a variable-geometry turbo (VGT) this is frequently a sticking vane mechanism rather than a blown turbo.
procedures_full.severity_action: Power derate likely — plan to stop soon
causes: Sticking VGT vanes (carbon/soot) holding too much boost
VGT actuator fault or calibration issue
Boost (MAP) sensor reading high or a wiring fault
Wastegate/control fault on a wastegated turbo
first_moves: Compare commanded vs actual boost — a large overshoot points to VGT/wastegate control.
Check the boost sensor and wiring before assuming a mechanical turbo fault.
Look for companion VGT actuator/position codes.
Avoid heavy load until repaired; repeated overboost can damage the engine.
common_misdiagnoses: Replacing the whole turbo when sticking VGT vanes just needed service/calibration.
Condemning the actuator when the boost sensor was reading high.
Clearing the derate without fixing the boost-control cause.
procedures_full.source_title: SPN 1127 FMI 16 — Turbo Boost Pressure — High / Overboost | Causes & Fixes | RoadService.app

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1127 FMI 16 on PACCAR MX-13 engines means turbo boost pressure is moderately above the commanded target. It's a medium-severity fault usually tied to a stuck actuator or a falsely high boost sensor reading rather than a dangerous overboost event. Overboost codes get less attention than underboost complaints because the truck usually still drives fine, but ProfessionalDieselRepair.com doesn't recommend ignoring SPN 1127 FMI 16 on a Peterbilt with a PACCAR MX-13. Sustained boost above target pushes cylinder pressures and exhaust gas temperatures higher than the calibration intended, which can shorten component life over time. The good news is the diagnostic path is straightforward - it almost always comes down to a wastegate or VGT actuator that isn't responding correctly, or a sensor reading that doesn't match reality.
causes: Wastegate or VGT actuator stuck closed or slow to respond
If the actuator can't open the wastegate or vary the turbine geometry properly, boost keeps building past the commanded setpoint.
Faulty boost pressure sensor reading falsely high
A sensor with internal drift or a partial short can report elevated pressure without any real overboost condition occurring.
Partially collapsed or restricted charge air cooler piping
An internal restriction downstream of the turbo can create a localized pressure spike that reads as overboost at the sensor location.
ECM calibration or software issue after a recent reflash
An incorrect boost target table following a software update can cause the actual and commanded values to mismatch.
steps: Pull codes with PACCAR Davie4 and confirm SPN 1127 FMI 16 is active; log actual vs commanded boost at a steady load point.
Check the wastegate or VGT actuator for a stuck-closed condition using Davie4's actuator command test - a wastegate that won't open lets boost build past the target.
Inspect the boost pressure sensor and its wiring for a partial short or corrosion that could cause a falsely high reading even with normal actual boost.
Verify the charge air cooler piping isn't collapsed or partially blocked internally, which can create pressure spikes ahead of a restriction.
Cross-check readings with a mechanical boost gauge tee'd into the intake manifold to confirm whether the high reading is real or a sensor issue.
Clear the code and road test under varying load to confirm boost tracks commanded values correctly before returning to service.
symptoms: Normal or even slightly stronger-than-usual power feel, which is why this one often goes unnoticed by drivers
Amber dash lamp without an immediate derate in most cases
Occasional turbo whistle that sounds louder than normal under acceleration
Elevated EGT readings on the scan tool relative to baseline
No noticeable smoke or drivability complaint in early stages
procedures_full.source_title: Peterbilt SPN 1127 FMI 16: Diagnosing High Turbo Boost Pressure

procedures_full.overview: SPN 1127 FMI 18 on Mack engines means turbo boost pressure is moderately below the commanded target. It's a high-severity power-loss fault most often caused by a charge air cooler leak rather than a failed turbocharger. Underboost codes like SPN 1127 FMI 18 send a lot of Mack MP7 and MP8 trucks into the shop with a real power complaint, but ProfessionalDieselRepair.com's experience says the turbo is rarely the actual problem. The charge air path between the turbo and the intake manifold is long, full of clamped connections, and lives in a hot, vibrating environment - it's the most common failure point by far. A methodical leak check before touching the turbo saves unnecessary parts expense and gets the truck back on the road faster.
causes: Charge air cooler hose or boot leak
Rubber boots and clamps in the CAC piping degrade with heat cycling and vibration, developing leaks that bleed off boost before it reaches the intake.
Restricted air intake or dirty air filter
A starved compressor inlet limits how much boost the turbo can produce regardless of turbo condition.
Sticking or binding VGT actuator/wastegate linkage
Mechanical binding prevents the turbo's variable geometry vanes or wastegate from reaching the position needed to build commanded boost.
Worn turbocharger (bearing or compressor wheel wear)
Internal turbo wear reduces maximum achievable boost, typically after high mileage or a prior lubrication issue.
Faulty boost pressure sensor
A sensor under-reporting actual pressure can trigger the code without a genuine airflow restriction, though this is less common than a physical leak.
steps: Pull codes with PACCAR Davie4 or Jaltest and confirm SPN 1127 FMI 18 is active; note actual vs. commanded boost at a steady RPM and load point for reference.
Do a full visual and physical inspection of the charge air cooler (CAC) piping - grab and shake every clamp and hose by hand looking for a boot that's slipped or a split seam.

Pressure test the entire intake tract from the turbo compressor outlet to the intake manifold with a magnehelic gauge or a shop air regulator and soap solution - even a small leak bleeds off enough boost to trip this code.
Inspect the air filter and housing for restriction on the intake side - a starved compressor inlet can't build boost even with a perfectly healthy turbo.
If no leaks are found, check the turbo's variable geometry actuator or wastegate linkage for binding, using Davie4's actuator test to command a sweep and watch for a sluggish or incomplete response.
Clear the code and road test under load while logging actual boost pressure to confirm the fix before releasing the truck.
symptoms: Noticeable loss of power, especially accelerating from a stop or climbing grades
Black smoke under hard acceleration from an over-fueled, under-boosted mixture
Amber dash lamp, sometimes with a specific 'low boost' message
Turbo whine that sounds different or quieter than normal
Increased fuel consumption as the ECM compensates for reduced airflow
procedures_full.source_title: Mack SPN 1127 FMI 18: Diagnosing Low Turbo Boost Pressure

Advanced Technical Analysis The ECM microcontroller continuously monitors signals from the exhaust temperature sensor

field_evidence.title: ISX Engine Code FMI 7 SPN 632: Troubleshooting Run Solenoid Issues
field_evidence.excerpt: The ISX engine is known to experience issues related to injector failures and run solenoid malfunctions, which can lead to engine shutdown or no-start conditions. One specific diagnostic code associated with these problems is FMI 7 SPN 632, indicating a run solenoid circuit fault. This code can stem from several underlying causes. Damage or corrosion in the wiring harness and connectors associated with the run solenoid circuit is a common contributor. Additionally, the run solenoid coil’s electrical resistance may fall outside of specification, which can cause malfunctions. Faulty fuel injectors, such as those that are leaking or clogged, can also trigger this code. Finally, issues related to the engine control module (ECM) signals to the solenoid may be involved. field_evidence.title: Freightliner Cascadia 2013 DD13 Regen Stopping with SPN 1037 FMI 15
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2013 Freightliner Cascadia equipped with the DD13 engine may experience issues where the diesel particulate filter (DPF) regeneration (regen) process stops prematurely. Frequent incomplete regenerations and DPF sensor faults are common problems reported with this model. The fault code SPN 1037 FMI 15 specifically indicates a problem with the DPF pressure sensor. This sensor fault can interrupt the regen process, preventing it from completing successfully. To address this issue, it is important to inspect the DPF differential pressure sensor and its wiring for any signs of damage or blockage. Cleaning or replacing the sensor if it is found to be faulty can help restore proper function. Additionally, checking the exhaust system for soot buildup that might restrict airflow is recommended.

field_evidence.title: 2017 Cascadia DD15: Diagnosing SPN-3510 and SPN-723 Engine Codes
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2017 Cascadia DD15 engine can experience specific issues indicated by engine fault codes SPN-3510 and SPN-723. These codes commonly appear following modifications to the Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) system, such as a DEF delete or injector repairs. Code SPN-3510 points to a sensor supply voltage problem, which often arises from faults in the wiring or the sensor itself. Meanwhile, SPN-723 relates to errors in the engine speed sensor signal. Both issues can be linked to disruptions in sensor wiring harnesses or connectors located near the Engine Control Module (ECM). It is important to check whether any programming resets have reversed the DEF delete modifications, as such reversions can trigger these fault codes. steps: [FMI 0 katalog] CAN hattında veri trafiğini izleyin; bu düğümden beklenen mesajların (PGN) gelip gelmediğini doğrulayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 1 katalog] Ağ üzerinde beklenen veri akışının kesildiğini teyit edin; düğüm adreslemesini (Address Claim) kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 2 katalog] CAN-H/CAN-L sinyal bütünlüğünü osiloskopla inceleyin; aralıklı paket kaybı ve yansıma arayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 3 katalog] Düğüm besleme gerilimini ve CAN transceiver beslemesini ölçün; aşırı gerilim koruma devresini kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 4 katalog] Düğüm besleme ve toprak bağlantısını ölçün; gerilim düşüklüğü/şasi teması arayın. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.
[FMI 5 katalog] Düğümün güç hattında açık devre, sigorta ve konektör durumunu kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

field_evidence.title: Freightliner Cascadia 2013 DD13 Regen Stopping with SPN 1037 FMI 15
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2013 Freightliner Cascadia equipped with the DD13 engine may experience issues where the diesel particulate filter (DPF) regeneration (regen) process stops prematurely. Frequent incomplete regenerations and DPF sensor faults are common problems reported with this model. The fault code SPN 1037 FMI 15 specifically indicates a problem with the DPF pressure sensor. This sensor fault can interrupt the regen process, preventing it from completing successfully. To address this issue, it is important to inspect the DPF differential pressure sensor and its wiring for any signs of damage or blockage. Cleaning or replacing the sensor if it is found to be faulty can help restore proper function. Additionally, checking the exhaust system for soot buildup that might restrict airflow is recommended.

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 1 on a Caterpillar engine means the SCR exhaust differential pressure is reading below normal range. Inspect the pressure reference tubes for DEF crystal blockage before replacing the sensor. Caterpillar SPN 4358 FMI 1 signals the SCR catalyst exhaust differential pressure sensor is reading below the normal operating floor on C13 and C15 ACERT aftertreatment systems. Unlike FMI 0 or FMI 16 (above normal, indicating a blocked catalyst), FMI 1 means the reading is implausibly low — suggesting the sensor input is being starved of the inlet pressure signal. At ProfessionalDieselRepair.com, the leading cause of this code is a blocked inlet pressure reference tube clogged with DEF crystals or soot, not a failed sensor. Clear both tubes with compressed air before any sensor is ordered. Use Texa or Jaltest to access the full SCR DP parameter set including raw voltage — Cat ET alone does not always expose the FMI 1 root cause on ACERT aftertreatment.
causes: Blocked SCR inlet pressure reference tube (DEF crystallization or soot)

The high-pressure sample port on the SCR inlet side of the sensor can become plugged with DEF crystal deposits or soot bridges, preventing the inlet pressure from reaching the sensor diaphragm and producing a near-zero DP reading.
Failed SCR DP sensor stuck at minimum output voltage
Internal sensor failure causes the differential pressure output to drop below 0.25 V even with both reference ports open to atmosphere, indicating the diaphragm or reference cell has degraded.
Cracked or disconnected pressure reference tube
A cracked reference tube equalizes the pressure on both sides of the sensor diaphragm, resulting in a near-zero differential reading that triggers FMI 1.
Open 5 V reference supply to the DP sensor
A fault in the aftertreatment module 5 V sensor supply circuit causes the output to drop below the FMI 1 threshold. Check Pin A reference voltage before condemning the sensor.
steps: Connect a Texa Truck diagnostic interface to the Caterpillar 9-pin ATA connector. Navigate to the aftertreatment system live data group and confirm SPN 4358 FMI 1 is active. Note the current DP reading in kPa. At idle, a correctly functioning sensor should read 0.5 to 2.0 kPa; at rated load, 3 to 8 kPa. A reading below 0.2 kPa at any load condition is the FMI 1 trigger.

Locate the two 6 mm diameter flexible pressure reference tubes connecting the SCR inlet and outlet to the differential pressure sensor body mounted on the aftertreatment frame. Disconnect both tubes from the sensor barbed fittings. Blow compressed air (below 30 psi) through each tube to check for blockage. DEF crystallization or soot accumulation can plug the inlet-side tube and cause an artificially low DP reading.

With both tubes disconnected and the key on (engine off), back-probe the sensor signal pin to sensor ground. With no pressure applied to either port, a working sensor should output close to the zero-pressure baseline (approximately 0.5 V, corresponding to 0 kPa differential). A reading below 0.25 V with both ports open to atmosphere indicates the sensor is failed low.

Measure the sensor 5 V reference supply: with the sensor connected and key on, Pin A (reference) to Pin C (ground) should read 4.95 to 5.05 V. An absent 5 V reference traces to the aftertreatment control module supply circuit. Use Jaltest CDG software to read the ACM sensor supply voltage parameter for cross-check.

If tubes are clear and the 5 V reference is present but the signal is below 0.25 V, replace the SCR differential pressure sensor. After replacement, clear faults with Texa and run the vehicle under load. Confirm the DP reading increases proportionally with engine load.
symptoms: Amber aftertreatment warning lamp illuminated on the Caterpillar instrument panel.
SCR catalyst DP live data reads below 0.3 kPa even under moderate engine load.
Aftertreatment system may inhibit active regeneration or DEF dosing due to unreliable DP data.
Additional SCR efficiency or NOx conversion faults may appear alongside SPN 4358 FMI 1.
DEF consumption may increase if the system attempts to compensate for an unknown catalyst state.
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 4358 FMI 1: SCR Catalyst DP Below Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 2 means the SCR differential pressure sensor is sending an inconsistent signal. It's a medium-severity code with no derate on its own - check the sense tubes for blockage before replacing the sensor. This sensor is the aftertreatment system's early-warning gauge for SCR restriction, so an erratic signal leaves the ECM without a reliable way to catch a developing catalyst problem. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always inspects both sense tubes for moisture or soot blockage first, since that's the more common cause of an intermittent signal than the sensor itself.
causes: Blocked or partially clogged sense tube
Soot or moisture accumulation in either sense tube produces an inconsistent pressure differential reading at the sensor.
Intermittent connector or wiring fault
A loose or corroded connector pin can cause the signal to drop in and out under vibration.
Failing sensor element
An internally degrading sensor can produce erratic output even with clean sense tubes and a sound harness.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame differential pressure data on Cat ET to look for erratic spikes or dropouts rather than a steady out-of-range value.
Locate the SCR differential pressure sensor and its two sense tubes routed from before and after the SCR catalyst.
Inspect both sense tubes for kinks, disconnection, or soot/moisture blockage that can cause erratic readings.
Back-probe the sensor's signal, ground, and power wires with a multimeter while wiggling the harness to check for an intermittent connection.
Clean or replace blocked sense tubes and repair any damaged wiring found during inspection.
Clear the code and monitor live differential pressure data across a drive cycle to confirm the signal is now stable.
symptoms: Amber check engine lamp, typically no derate on its own
No immediately noticeable drivability change
Possible intermittent code setting and clearing on its own
procedures_full.source_title: Caterpillar SPN 4358 FMI 2: SCR Differential Pressure Signal Erratic

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 3 on Scania means the SCR catalyst differential pressure sensor circuit voltage is above the ECM calibrated maximum. Check the 5V reference, signal wire, and sense tubes before replacing the SCR catalyst. SPN 4358 monitors exhaust pressure drop across the SCR catalyst on Scania heavy-duty platforms. FMI 3 flags a voltage-above-normal condition in the sensor circuit — an electrical fault that does not by itself confirm a restricted catalyst. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees technicians confuse FMI 3 with FMI 16 (data valid but high); the distinction matters because FMI 3 rarely requires catalyst replacement. Work the wiring and sense lines first.
causes: SCR differential pressure sensor internal short to power
Very Common
Moisture intrusion or thermal cycling can short the sensor element internally, driving signal voltage above 4.5V regardless of actual exhaust pressure.
Signal wire short to 5V reference or battery positive
Chafed harness near the aftertreatment module can short the signal conductor to supply voltage, producing a pegged-high reading at the ECM.
Blocked pressure sense line holding residual pressure
Moderate
A plugged sense tube can trap pressure and push the sensor toward maximum output, though this more often sets FMI 16; combined with marginal sensor drift it can contribute to voltage-high faults.
steps: Connect Jaltest or Texa and confirm SPN 4358 FMI 3 active. Record live differential pressure sensor voltage — Scania SCR DP sensors typically output 0.5V at 0 kPa and 4.5V at maximum calibrated range on a 5V reference circuit.

Key on, engine off: measure sensor supply at the connector. Expect 4.75V-5.25V on the 5V reference pin. Signal voltage above 4.8V at idle with disconnected sense lines confirms a short-to-power or failed sensor.

Disconnect the sensor connector and measure resistance between signal and ground at the harness side. Any reading below 500 ohms indicates a harness short; infinite resistance with sensor-side voltage above 4.5V points to internal sensor failure.

Inspect both pressure sense tubes from the SCR housing to the sensor for soot blockage or kinked lines that can trap pressure and bias the sensor — clear tubes with compressed air before condemning the sensor.

After repair, clear codes in Jaltest and monitor differential pressure at idle (typically 0.5-2.0 kPa) and under 1800 RPM loaded cruise (2.0-8.0 kPa on most DC13 applications) to confirm normal operation.
symptoms: Amber check engine or aftertreatment warning lamp illuminated
SCR differential pressure reading pegged high or erratic on scan tool live data
Possible companion SPN 4358 FMI 4 (voltage below normal) if harness is intermittently damaged
No immediate power derate on most Scania calibrations, but SCR inducement timers may start if fault persists
Freeze-frame may show implausible differential pressure values at idle (e.g., 50+ kPa when actual backpressure is near zero)
procedures_full.source_title: Scania SPN 4358 FMI 3: SCR Catalyst Exhaust Differential Pressure Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 14 on International requires special instruction diagnosis for SCR differential pressure — inspect sense lines and manometer-test before replacing the catalyst. SCR differential pressure tells the International ECM whether exhaust flow through the catalyst is normal. FMI 14 means the diagnosis is not complete until you follow the OEM procedure for line inspection, sensor cross-check, and restriction verification. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com treats plugged sense tubes as the default cause until manometer data proves otherwise.
causes: Plugged SCR differential pressure sense lines
Soot and condensation block narrow sample tubes, producing false high differential pressure readings.
Failed SCR differential pressure sensor
Sensor drift or internal diaphragm damage reports incorrect pressure after sense lines test clean.
Ash or soot loading restricting SCR substrate
Genuine catalyst restriction raises differential pressure under load when sense lines are clear.
Damaged catalyst from prior thermal event
Melted or collapsed substrate creates permanent high backpressure confirmed by direct measurement.
steps: Connect ServiceMaxx or Noregon JPRO and open SPN 4358 special instruction workflow for International aftertreatment.
Inspect SCR differential pressure sense lines at both catalyst ports for soot, kinks, or moisture plugs.
Compare scan tool differential pressure to a manual manometer tee'd into sense ports.
Run idle and loaded pressure profiles — flat high reading with clear lines suggests sensor fault; rising pressure with load suggests restriction.
Clear sense lines or replace sensor per special instructions before authorizing SCR catalyst replacement.
symptoms: Aftertreatment warning lamp with SPN 4358 FMI 14
SCR differential pressure reading stuck or implausible on ServiceMaxx
Gradual power loss if restriction is genuine
Possible companion DPF or DOC pressure codes
Inducement countdown on some calibrations if unresolved
procedures_full.source_title: International SPN 4358 FMI 14: SCR Catalyst Exhaust Differential Pressure Special Instructions

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 16 means the SCR catalyst differential pressure on a Volvo truck is reading above normal at a moderately severe level, indicating a restriction is building in the exhaust path. It is High severity and can progress toward a power derate if left unaddressed. The SCR catalyst differential pressure sensor compares exhaust pressure before and after the catalyst brick, giving the Volvo ECM a way to detect a plugging or restricted aftertreatment system before it becomes a bigger problem. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com sees this code trip a lot of unnecessary catalyst replacements because the small sense lines feeding the sensor plug up with soot far more often than the catalyst brick itself actually restricts. Working through the sense line inspection first before assuming the worst saves a substantial repair bill in most cases.
causes: Plugged or kinked pressure sense line
Soot and condensation accumulate in the narrow sense tubes over time, creating a false high-pressure reading without any actual catalyst restriction.
Ash or soot loading inside the SCR catalyst brick
Over very high mileage, ash accumulation from oil consumption or DEF quality issues can genuinely restrict flow through the catalyst substrate.
Damaged or corroded sensor
The differential pressure sensor itself can fail and produce an inaccurately high reading independent of actual exhaust conditions.
Physical damage to the catalyst substrate from a previous overheat event
A prior severe overheat or thermal event can melt or collapse catalyst substrate cells, causing a genuine and permanent restriction.
steps: Connect Volvo Premium Tech Tool (PTT) and confirm SPN 4358 FMI 16, then check live differential pressure readings against Volvo's normal operating range at idle and under load.
Inspect the pressure sense lines running to and from the SCR catalyst for soot blockage, kinks, or disconnected fittings at either end.
Clear any blocked sense tubes with a stiff wire or compressed air, since a plugged sense line reads as high pressure even when the actual catalyst is clean.
If sense lines are clear and pressure remains elevated, inspect the SCR catalyst brick for physical restriction using a borescope or by checking backpressure directly with a manometer.
Address any confirmed catalyst restriction or ash loading issue, clear codes with PTT, and monitor differential pressure trend on subsequent drive cycles.
symptoms: Amber warning lamp illuminated
Gradual loss of power, especially noticeable under heavy load or uphill
Increased exhaust backpressure symptoms like harder-than-normal breathing at high RPM
Possible accompanying DPF differential pressure codes
procedures_full.source_title: Volvo SPN 4358 FMI 16: SCR Catalyst Backpressure High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 16 means the pressure drop across the SCR catalyst is above normal on your PACCAR MX engine. It's a medium-severity early warning with no derate - check the sense tubes for blockage before assuming a genuine catalyst restriction. This code is one of the aftertreatment system's earlier warning stages, giving you time to investigate before an actual derate-triggering backpressure fault develops. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com checks the sense tubes first since a partial blockage there is far more common than genuine catalyst restriction.
causes: Partially blocked sense tube
Soot or moisture accumulation in either sense tube produces an elevated differential pressure reading without a proportional actual restriction.
Developing soot or ash restriction in the SCR catalyst
Extended service intervals or DEF quality issues can gradually restrict flow through the catalyst substrate over time.
Failing differential pressure sensor
A drifting sensor can report elevated pressure independent of the actual condition, though this is uncommon compared to a sense tube issue.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame differential pressure data on PACCAR Davie4 and compare against the OEM specification.
Check overall exhaust backpressure and DPF soot load percentage on the same scan to see if a broader restriction is developing upstream.
Inspect both sense tubes for the SCR differential pressure sensor for soot or moisture blockage.
Verify no physical damage or crushing has occurred to the SCR catalyst housing that could create a genuine restriction.
Clean or replace blocked sense tubes as needed, and repair any damaged wiring found during inspection.
Clear the code and monitor differential pressure over the following drive cycles to confirm the trend stabilizes.
symptoms: Amber check engine lamp, typically no derate at this stage
No major drivability complaint yet
Possible slight increase in exhaust backpressure readings
procedures_full.source_title: PACCAR SPN 4358 FMI 16: SCR Differential Pressure Above Normal

procedures_full.overview: SPN 4358 FMI 18 on Mercedes-Benz heavy-duty engines means the pressure differential across the SCR catalyst is moderately below expected. It's a medium-severity fault most often caused by a sense tube or sensor issue rather than genuine catalyst damage. Differential pressure across the SCR catalyst gives the ECM an indirect way to monitor the catalyst's physical condition, and SPN 4358 FMI 18 means that reading has come in lower than expected. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com approaches this fault the same way as most aftertreatment pressure codes - check the sense tubes and sensor connections first, since a disconnected or cracked line produces this exact symptom far more often than actual physical damage to the catalyst.
causes: Disconnected or cracked differential pressure sense tube
A compromised sense line on either side of the catalyst directly skews the pressure differential reading without any actual change in catalyst condition.
Corroded sensor connector or wiring
Electrical issues at the sensor can produce an inaccurate low reading independent of the true pressure differential.
Physical damage or partial collapse of the catalyst substrate
Structural damage to the catalyst can reduce its normal flow resistance, though this is a less common cause than a sensing issue.
steps: Pull the fault with Mercedes-Benz Xentry and confirm SPN 4358 FMI 18 is active; review the reported differential pressure value against the expected range for current exhaust flow conditions.

Inspect the differential pressure sensor's sense tubes on both sides of the catalyst for disconnection, cracking, or blockage - a disconnected line on the higher-pressure side will read artificially low.
Check the sensor's electrical connector and wiring for corrosion or damage that could produce an inaccurate reading independent of the actual pressure differential.
If the sense lines and wiring check out, inspect the SCR catalyst substrate for physical damage such as cracking or partial collapse that could reduce its normal flow resistance.
Cross-reference with SCR conversion efficiency data - if efficiency is normal despite this reading, the fault is more likely sensor-related than a genuine catalyst problem.
Clear the code and confirm the reading stabilizes within the normal range during a drive cycle before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Amber Check Engine lamp with no immediate power loss
No obvious drivability symptom in most cases
Possible correlation with reduced SCR efficiency if the underlying cause affects catalyst performance
Fault often discovered during routine diagnostic scans rather than from a driver complaint

procedures_full.overview: This fault typically results from high load operation in high ambients. No action is necessary (this is a “silent” fault, the fan will be turned on).‪
causes: This fault typically results from high load operation in high ambients. No action is necessary (this is a “silent” fault, the fan will be turned on).‪
steps: Note: This fault is a concern only if the fan on times are excessive but coolant temperatures are in the normal operating range.
Temperature Warning Check
Check for multiple codes:
If SPN 110/FMI 0 is also present, repair the cooling system first. Refer to "129.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If only SPN 4228/FMI 15 is present, go to step 2.
Visually inspect the turbo for signs of exhaust leak in the area of the actuator.
If exhaust leaks are present, repair as necessary. Refer to "129.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If no exhaust leaks are present, go to step 3.
Remove and inspect turbo and actuator cooler lines and fittings.
If coolant lines or fittings are kinked or plugged, repair/replace the damaged component. Refer to "129.1.1.1 Verify Repairs".
If coolant lines are not damaged and problem still persists, contact the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
Verify repairs as follows:‪
Turn ignition OFF.
Reconnect any electrical connections that were disconnected to perform the diagnosis.
Clear codes with DDDL 7.0 or latest version.
Start and bring engine up to operating temperature (over 140°F/60°C).

Verify operation is satisfactory and no warning lamps illuminate. If warning lamps illuminate, troubleshoot the codes. If assistance is required, call the Detroit Diesel Customer Support Center at 313–592–5800.
procedures_full.source_title: Series 60 DDEC VI Troubleshooting - Section 129.1 SPN 4228/FMI 15 - Detroit Diesel Engine Troubleshooting

field_evidence.title: 2013 Kenworth T660 Cummins ISX15 SPN862 Engine Light Issue
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2013 Kenworth T660 equipped with the Cummins ISX15 engine can experience an SPN862 engine light warning. This code points to a fault with the turbocharger boost pressure sensor. Common problems associated with this vehicle include clutch wear and excessive engine oil consumption, especially after heavy use or repairs. These issues may contribute to the engine sensor fault and trigger the SPN862 code. The sensor fault can stem from several factors. Clogged air filters reduce airflow and affect boost pressure readings, while faulty sensors themselves are a direct cause. Following a clutch replacement, vacuum leaks or damaged hoses may disrupt sensor signals. Additionally, damage to the turbocharger actuator or related wiring can impact sensor function. dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 29 - Remote Throttle Enable
dd_procedures.overview: This fault indicates an electrical failure of the relay that allows the remote throttle to operate. The relay and wiring are installed by the OEM. When troubleshooting an Inactive code See "Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode" for more information on troubleshooting Inactive codes.
causes: Remote Throttle relay Harness
steps: A. Verify Remote Throttle Enable is functioning per OEM requirements. Follow OEM troubleshooting guidelines to ensure the Remote Throttle Enable Relay has not failed. If relay is functional, Go to Step B . If relay is not functional (faulted), test complete. Go to Step V

B. Check for active or Inactive fault codes, noting FMI Key on. Retrieve active fault codes and FMIs with ServiceRanger using the 9-way diagnostic connector. What FMIs are present? Note: The Remote Throttle Enable relay must be wired according to Eaton Gen 3 requirements (shown on previous page) for tests to work properly. If wired differently, consult OEM for correct wiring schematic. If FMI 4 is present, Go to Step C If FMI 5 is present, Go to Step D

C. Test the Remote Throttle Relay circuit for shorts to ground. Key off. Disconnect battery cable. Disconnect the Vehicle Harness 38-way connector. Measure the resistance between Vehicle Harness 38-way connector Pin 24 and ground. If the resistance between 24 and ground is OL. (If fault code is Active) replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Heavy-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Go to Step V If resistance is out of range, repair the Vehicle Harness. Go to Step V

D. Verify continuity of the Remote throttle relay circuit. Key off. Disconnect battery cable. Disconnect the Vehicle Harness 38-way connector. Disconnect the Vehicle Harness from the Throttle Enable Relay. Measure resistance between Vehicle Harness 38-way connector way 24 and way 86 of the Throttle Enable relay connector. If resistance is 0 to 0.3 ohms, (if fault code is Active) replace the: Medium-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Heavy-Duty Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) Go to Step V If resistance is out of range, repair the Vehicle Harness and Go to Step V

V. Verify repair. Key off. Reconnect all connectors. Key on. Clear codes, see "Fault Code Retrieval/Clearing" Drive the vehicle and attempt to reset the code. Check for fault codes, see "Fault Code Retrieval/Clearing" If no codes, test complete. If Fault Code 29 appears Go to Step A to find error in testing. If fault code other than 29 appears, See "Fault Code Isolation Procedure Index"

dd_procedures.title: Fault Code 29: Remote Throttle Enable
dd_procedures.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with a relay circuit that allows the throttle of the engine to be located in a remote location. The relay and associated wiring are installed by the OEM. Fault Code 29 sets when the Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) detects an open or a shorted condition in the wiring between the TECU and the relay.
causes: Check for Active or Inactive fault codes. Record the transmission fault codes, FMIs, occurrences, and timestamps from the Service Activity Report created during the Diagnostic Procedure. If Fault Code 29 is Active, Go to Step C If Fault Code 29 is Inactive and there are other Active fault codes, troubleshoot all Active fault codes first. If Fault Code 29 is Inactive, Go to Step B
steps: A. Check for Active or Inactive fault codes. Record the transmission fault codes, FMIs, occurrences, and timestamps from the Service Activity Report created during the Diagnostic Procedure. If Fault Code 29 is Active, Go to Step C If Fault Code 29 is Inactive and there are other Active fault codes, troubleshoot all Active fault codes first. If Fault Code 29 is Inactive, Go to Step B

B. Use Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode to locate intermittent failures. Set parking brake and chock wheels. Place transmission in PD Mode. See more about Product Diagnostic (PD) Mode . Note: Transmission does not enter PD Mode when Active fault codes exist. Wiggle Vehicle Harness wiring and connections between TECU and Remote Throttle Relay. Note: Wiring from the Remote Throttle Relay to TECU is OEM proprietary. Refer to OEM guidelines for proper repair or replacement procedures and proper wiring schematics and pin out locations. Exit PD Mode by powering down. Notice Allow 2-3 minutes for the TECU to perform a complete power-down sequence before proceeding. If any fault became Active while wiggling wires in the system, refer to OEM guidelines for repair or replacement of wiring between TECU and Remote Throttle Relay. Go to Step V If no fault codes became Active, Go to Step C

C. Inspect relay wiring and socket condition. Key off. Remove Remote Throttle Relay from socket. Inspect Remote Throttle Relay Socket and wiring for damage or bent, spread, corroded or loose terminals. If no issues are found, Go to Step D If any issues are present, refer to OEM guidelines for repair or replacement of wiring of Remote Throttle Enable Relay circuit. Go to Step V

D. Verify power supply to relay. Key on with engine off. Measure voltage between Remote Throttle Relay socket Pin 86 (power) and Pin 85 (ground). Record reading(s) in table. Compare reading(s) in table. If readings are out of range, Go to Step E If readings are in range, refer to OEM guidelines for replacement of the Remote Throttle Relay. Go to Step V Pins Range Reading(s) 86 to 85 Within 1.5 V of Battery Voltage

E. Verify continuity of Remote Throttle Relay Circuit wiring between TECU and the relay. Key off. Disconnect 38-Way Vehicle Harness Connector from TECU. Disconnect Remote Throttle Relay from socket. If readings are in range, replace Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) . procedures_full.overview: The UltraShift PLUS transmission is equipped with a relay circuit that allows the throttle of the engine to be located in a remote location. The relay and associated wiring are installed by the OEM. Fault Code 29 sets when the Transmission Electronic Control Unit (TECU) detects an open or a shorted condition in the wiring between the TECU and the relay.
procedures_full.detection: The TECU monitors the remote throttle enable circuit for opens or shorts. If either condition is present for 1 second or greater, the fault is set Active.
procedures_full.conditions_set_active: FMI 4 – Voltage Below Normal or Shorted Low: TECU detects a short to ground in the circuit. FMI 5 – Current Below Normal or Open Circuit: TECU detects an open circuit or excessive resistance in the circuit.
procedures_full.conditions_set_inactive: All FMIs: Short or open condition is not detected by the TECU for 2 seconds.
procedures_full.fallback: Remote throttle will not function. Conditions to Set Fault Code Inactive All FMIs: Short or open condition is not detected by the TECU for 2 seconds.

field_evidence.title: 2008 C-15 Engine Code SPN 172 FMI 3 Diagnosis and Fix
field_evidence.excerpt: The 2008 C-15 engine may display the error code SPN 172 FMI 3, which points to an issue with the air intake temperature sensor circuit. This problem can stem from sensor faults or related engine performance concerns commonly experienced with C-15 engines. Although replacing the air intake temperature sensor and its plug is a common initial step, the fault may persist. In such cases, it is important to examine the wiring harness for any damage or poor connections that could disrupt the sensor circuit. Additional checks include inspecting the sensor connector for signs of corrosion or bent pins that might interfere with proper operation. SPN_172.description_en: Diagnostic fault check for charge air cooler downstream temperature sensor after low-pressure intercooler
causes: FMI 0: Data valid but above normal operational range.
FMI 1: Data valid but below normal operational range.
FMI 2: Data erratic, intermittent or incorrect.
FMI 3: Voltage above normal, or shorted to high source.

steps: [FMI 0 katalog] Sensör besleme hattını ve fiziksel aşırı basınç/sıcaklık durumunu mekanik test portundan doğrulayın.
[FMI 1 katalog] Sensör besleme hattını ve fiziksel düşük basınç/seviye durumunu kontrol edin. Sorun sürerse ağ ve düğüm tanılaması için yetkili servise başvurun.

[FMI 3 katalog] Sensör soketini ayırın; voltaj şasiye göre düşmüyorsa kablo demeti akü besleme hattına ezilmiştir.
[FMI 4 katalog] Sinyal pini ile şasi arasındaki direnci ölçün (<1.0 Ω ise tesisatta şasi teması vardır).

procedures_full.overview: SPN 172 FMI 3 means the air inlet temperature sensor circuit is reading above normal voltage, consistent with an open circuit or short to power. It's a medium-severity code with no derate, but it affects cold-start fueling accuracy. This is a low-drama electrical fault, but leaving it unresolved means the ECM is guessing at air temperature for cold-start fueling. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always checks the harness near the turbo heat shield first, since that's the most frequent failure point for this circuit.
causes: Chafed signal wire near the turbo or frame rail
Heat and vibration wear through wire insulation over time, letting the signal wire short against a grounded or powered surface.
Internally failed sensor
A cracked thermistor can present as an open circuit, mimicking the same high-voltage fault signature.
Corroded connector pin
A corroded or loose pin can intermittently open the circuit, producing the same signature at the ECM.
steps: Pull the fault and freeze-frame air inlet temperature on Jaltest to confirm the value is pinned at an unrealistic high reading.
Locate the air inlet temperature sensor near the turbo inlet or air filter housing and unplug the connector.
Back-probe signal and ground with a multimeter, key on engine off - a reading near 5V with the sensor disconnected confirms a harness-side fault.
Trace the signal wire for chafing against the frame or turbo heat shield along its full routing.
Test sensor resistance at the connector against the OEM temperature/resistance chart to rule out an internally open sensor.
Repair the wiring or replace the sensor as needed, then clear the code and confirm a plausible reading returns.
symptoms: Check engine lamp illuminated, no derate
Harder cold starts or extended cranking in cold weather
No noticeable symptom in warm weather operation
procedures_full.source_title: International SPN 172 FMI 3: Air Inlet Temperature Circuit Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 172 FMI 3 means the air inlet temperature sensor signal is reading a voltage above the normal range, consistent with an open circuit or short to a high voltage source. It's a medium-severity electrical fault with no derate, but it affects cold-start fueling accuracy. This is a low-drama code compared to most heavy-duty fault codes, but ignoring it means the ECM is fueling cold starts based on a default assumed temperature instead of real data. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com always checks the harness routing near the turbo heat shield first, since that's the single most common failure point for this sensor circuit.
causes: Chafed or pinched signal wire near the turbo or frame rail
Heat and vibration wear through wire insulation over time, allowing the signal wire to short against a grounded or powered surface.
Failed sensor with an internally open thermistor
A cracked or corroded sensor element can present as an open circuit, which the ECM interprets identically to a high-voltage fault.
Corroded or backed-out connector pin
A loose or corroded pin can intermittently open the circuit, producing the same high-voltage signature at the ECM.
steps: Pull the fault code and freeze-frame air inlet temperature on Cummins INSITE - a value pinned at an extreme high reading confirms the circuit fault.
Locate the air inlet temperature sensor, typically mounted near the turbo inlet or air filter housing, and unplug the connector.
Back-probe the sensor's signal and ground pins with a multimeter set to DC volts, key on engine off - a reading near 5V confirms an open or high-side short.
Check the signal wire for chafing against the frame, engine mounts, or turbo heat shielding along its full length back to the ECM.
Test sensor resistance directly at the connector against the OEM temp/resistance chart; an open sensor will read infinite resistance regardless of temperature.
Repair or replace the chafed harness section, or replace the sensor if it tests open, then clear the code and verify a plausible reading returns.
symptoms: Check engine lamp illuminated, no derate
Harder cold starts or extended cranking in cold weather
Slightly rougher idle quality when temperatures are near freezing
No noticeable symptom in warm weather operation
procedures_full.source_title: Cummins SPN 172 FMI 3: Air Inlet Temperature Circuit Voltage High

procedures_full.overview: SPN 172 FMI 4 on PACCAR MX-13 engines means the intake air temperature sensor circuit is reading below normal, consistent with a short to ground. It's a medium-severity fault that affects fueling and boost compensation strategy until it's fixed. The engine air inlet (intake) temperature sensor feeds the ECM's fueling and boost strategy, so when SPN 172 FMI 4 shows the circuit shorted low, the ECM ends up compensating with conservative defaults rather than accurate data. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com typically finds this comes down to connector corrosion or a chafed wire more often than a genuinely failed sensor - the sensor sits in the intake tract where road grime and moisture accumulate at the connector over time.
causes: Corroded or moisture-damaged sensor connector
The connector's exposed location in the intake tract makes it prone to moisture intrusion, which can create a low-resistance short path.
Chafed wiring shorting the signal to ground
Harness rubbing against intake piping or a bracket can wear through insulation and short the signal circuit directly to ground.
Failed sensor element
Internal sensor failure can produce a zero-resistance or shorted reading independent of external wiring condition.
steps: Pull the code with PACCAR Davie4 and confirm SPN 172 FMI 4 is active; note the reported intake air temperature value, which is likely pegged at an unrealistic extreme (very cold reading).
Locate the air inlet temperature sensor, typically in the intake tract near the turbo inlet or intercooler piping, and inspect the connector for corrosion or looseness.
Disconnect the sensor and measure resistance across its terminals, comparing against the resistance-vs-temperature spec - a reading of zero ohms or an open circuit confirms sensor or wiring failure.
With the sensor disconnected, check the signal wire for a short to ground back at the harness using a multimeter - continuity to ground with the ECM disconnected confirms a chafed wire.
Repair the wiring if a short is found, or replace the sensor if it fails the resistance test, then clear the code.
Verify the reported intake air temperature now matches ambient conditions reasonably closely before returning the truck to service.
symptoms: Slightly reduced performance as the ECM defaults to a conservative fueling map
Amber Check Engine lamp
Occasional rough cold starts if the sensor is defaulting to an unrealistic value
No dramatic drivability change in most cases - it's primarily a compensation/derate-avoidance strategy issue
procedures_full.source_title: Kenworth SPN 172 FMI 4: Diagnosing a Low Intake Air Temperature Reading

procedures_full.overview: SPN 172 FMI 16 means the intake air temperature sensor reports above the ECM normal range on Kenworth PACCAR MX engines. The ECM may derate boost and torque to protect the turbo, and sustained high readings under load can trigger shutdown. Compare live data to ambient before replacing the sensor. When SPN 172 FMI 16 sets on a Kenworth, the ECM believes combustion air entering the turbo is hotter than its calibrated limit. That reading feeds fueling, fan, and boost protection tables, so an inaccurate high value can cut power even when the engine is not actually overheating. ProfessionalDieselRepair.com recommends verifying live data against ambient temperature and inspecting charge-air plumbing before assuming the sensor has failed.
causes: Failed or heat-soaked intake air temperature sensor
NTC sensor drift or internal failure can report temperatures 50°F or more above ambient, especially after heat soak near the turbo housing.
Restricted airflow or collapsed intercooler boot
Low airflow past a restricted filter or collapsed silicone boot raises measured charge-air temperature under boost, producing a genuine high reading at the sensor location.
Chafed harness causing biased signal voltage
A high-resistance connection or partial short can pull the signal voltage low, which the ECM interprets as an abnormally hot intake air temperature.
steps: Connect PACCAR Davie4 and confirm SPN 172 FMI 16 is active; record the reported intake air temperature and compare to ambient air temperature (SPN 171) — a spread greater than 30°F at key-off indicates a sensor or heat-soak issue.
Inspect the intake air temperature sensor in the charge-air piping near the turbo inlet; verify the connector is fully seated and pins are clean with no green corrosion.
With the key on and sensor connected, measure signal voltage at the sensor — typical NTC sensors read 1.5-2.5V at 70°F ambient; values below 0.5V indicate the ECM sees an unrealistically hot reading.
Check for collapsed or oil-soaked intercooler boots and restricted airflow upstream of the sensor; charge-air leaks can raise measured temperature under boost.
If wiring and plumbing check out, disconnect the sensor and measure resistance — at 77°F (25°C) most PACCAR sensors spec 2,000-3,000 ohms; replace only if out of range.
Clear the code after repair and road-test under load; confirm intake air temperature tracks within 15°F of ambient at cruise.
symptoms: Amber Check Engine lamp with possible progressive torque derate under load
Reported intake air temperature reading 40-80°F above ambient on PACCAR Davie4
Reduced boost pressure and sluggish acceleration when pulling grades
Cooling fan may run at high speed even when coolant temperature is normal
Fault may appear intermittently in hot weather or after extended idle
